en: Externally, he relinquished his physical form and cast aside all conventional boundaries; those who adhere strictly to ritual propriety could not distinguish him from others.

Yet, while following his heart’s inclinations, he never transgressed the moral compass, ultimately achieving harmony with the natural state. Thus, the efficacy of cultivating one's nature—by disregarding the external to regulate the internal—is clearly seen herein.
Even when lust, desire, anger, and hatred are all termed "the Way," this is merely the Great Hero (the Buddha) employing provisional speech as a metaphor. It is intended to...
This was intended for the instruction of those of superior wisdom; yet the foolish do not discern this and proceed entirely according to their own whims.

Those charged with teaching were concerned about this, and thus established clear regulations (*qinggui*) to provide detailed safeguards. For several hundred years, these have been observed without fail. However, as the age grows increasingly degenerate, [the laxity increases].
Yet worldly customs became increasingly extravagant; rare, bizarre, beautiful, and splendid objects filled the realm.

Master Xianze first compiled [the *Baoyu jing*], expanding upon what was incomplete by consulting the elderly and verifying it against ancient manuscripts, producing ten volumes of the *Beiyong* (Supplementary Use) to rescue the world from its extreme degeneration.
His diligent and arduous resolve is fully evident in this work. I have previously heard that Master Xianze was strict in observing the Vinaya.
He took this as his meditation, adhering strictly to his teacher’s doctrines and refusing to follow others. Pure, austere, and dignified, he never ceased lecturing on the Way;
the obstinate and the frivolous respected him from afar. His death was particularly extraordinary. I lament that the teachings of our Confucian school have fallen into such decline and corruption;
had someone like Xianshi been there to rectify them, success would have been achieved. I have prefaces for his writings so as to record my [regret].
The common people have not yet been able to achieve this.
June, the second year of Taiding. By the Layman Qingrong, Yuan Yue.
Rites constitute the great constant of the world, serving as the refined expression of human sentiments. Their evolution, modification, reduction, and increase follow the demands of the times.
Therefore, the human sentiments of all times, ancient and modern, have obtained the fundamental principles and systems to guide the Way;
thus, the great ordinances of Heaven and Earth remain intact. Furthermore, our Sage took the *Prātimokṣa* as his life-force, and from this, the Baizhang *Qinggui* emerged.
This is indeed the great ordinance of the monastic community’s ritual law. However, from the Tang dynasty until the present, it has been nearly five...

A century has passed; customs have changed repeatedly, and human sentiments have differed. How, then, could the discourse on reforming, following, diminishing, or augmenting [the tradition] be avoided?
Recently, the two patriarchs Dàchuān and Xiàowēng propagated the Way in the North and South Mountains, and their daily regulations flourished in their own time.
In the Wuyin year of the Zhìyuán era, while staying with Shílín Wéngshàng at Nánpíng, I was still able to witness their lingering influence.
Furthermore, Ye Lye and the West Hall Master Youyunming retrieved a manuscript from their collections. With diligent inquiry and research, they compiled it into a volume;
thus began the production of this book. Some begin it with the "Monk Receiving Precepts," while others begin it with the "Abbot Entering the Monastery.
In the year Renwu, I followed my late teacher Jue’an at Chengtian Temple, where I questioned him morning and evening; it was through this that I was able to offer [this preface].
The birth of the Holy Tathāgata stands as the crown before the two realms of heaven and earth. The remaining sections have been categorized and compiled into ten fascicles;
yet, I had not yet dared to transmit them to students. In the summer of the Bingxu year, while staying at Xuedou, the West Hall Master Qiānfēng Wǎn discussed their details with me.
In the spring of the Dinghai year, the Venerable Xīxīzé corrected their errors. Having thus gained a thorough understanding through both sight and hearing, [I now present this work].

Nevertheless, I still felt ashamed that I had not yet put this into practice myself. In the summer of the Renchen year, while presiding over the assembly at Shuangjing, there arose a dispute regarding the seniority of seating during the small-scale serving of soup (*xiǎozuǒtāng*).
Such matters are often neglected and not observed in various monasteries. I, however, considered it necessary to establish the order: the West Hall Preceptor (*xītáng*) takes precedence once;

the Head Seat (*shǒuzuò*) twice; the Administrative Director (*dū sì*) thrice; the Rear Hall Preceptor (*hòutáng*) four times; followed by the Librarian (*zàngzhǔ*), the Rector (*wéiná*), the Guest Master (*zhīkè*), and the Attendant (*shìzhě*).

According to his office, he was assigned to the position at Yunfeng, where he requested that his paternal uncle, Boli, take charge of its implementation. Once the matter was concluded, none dared to raise a clamor.

In the year of Yuzhen Yiwei (1295), he served as a member of the staff at Tianning Monastery in Yongjia; in the year of Dade Gengzi (1300), he was appointed to Yongfu in Fanyang; and in the year of Yisi (1305), he presided over Donglin on Mount Lu.
In all these instances, he carried out his duties without deviation, hoping thereby to provide a standard for human relations. However, as for observing...

Are not the ancient codes of pure discipline (*qinggui*) nearly too elaborate? Indeed, the use of a simple grass mat and a drum of pounded earth cannot be employed during an autumn of harmonious music accompanied by wind and percussion instruments;
nor can the drinking from a muddy vessel and a cup be practiced on a day when sacrificial vessels and ritual figures are arrayed in rows.

To call this work the *Chanyuan Beiyong Qinggui* (Pure Rules for General Use in Zen Monasteries) is precisely what is meant by "having prepared them, yet not employing them. Whether they understand me or condemn me, let it be up to [posterity].

For the Ascending the Seat and Chanting of Sutras on the Imperial Birthday.

When the date for the inauguration ceremony arrives, no leave shall be granted to the monastic community. The Hall Administration prepares the yellow proclamation, the list of scriptures for the hall services, and the roster for the rotation of monks.
Five days prior to the ceremony, after the morning gruel has been served, the Rector (Vina) prepares a tray, cloths, an incense burner, candles, incense, and small slips of paper.

He proceeds to the Secretary’s Office, offers incense, and prostrates. The attendant who records the vacancies returns the incense and, together with the others, prostrates and addresses the assembly, saying:

(Heavenly ○ Festival. Petition for the composition of the following text. It has been composed. First, present it to the Abbot. He shall personally deliver it to the Hall Office (*dōji*). Upon returning, perform prostrations.

For the *rinso* (petitionary document), the *weina* shall use yellow paper; affix the seal at the [blank] space, ensuring it is strictly formal and orderly. The night before, prepare a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, candles, and an incense case.
The *weina*, assuming a dignified demeanor, accompanied by attendants carrying manpower, shall carry the tray. Go to the Abbot’s quarters to affix the seal on the petition, then proceed.
The attendant reports to the Abbot. Upon exiting, he offers incense and announces: "Tomorrow, the [specific] festival will be inaugurated; we request the Master to sign the formal petition.

Having presented the petition and received the signature, he withdraws. The ritual attendant then reports to the Abbot’s quarters. Early the next morning, the sutras are chanted, and banners for chanting in various locations are hung.
The incense-bearer reports to the Abbot’s quarters. On the morning of the main day, the assembly enters the hall for the communal meal; the mallet is struck once, then struck again.

The lower section says: (Address the assembly: "After the morning gruel has been finished, upon hearing the sound of the bell, each of you shall assume your dignified demeanor and proceed to the Great Buddha Hall to inaugurate the observance of the Imperial Birthday. This is respectfully announced. Then, strike the mallet once more. Proceed to the abbot’s quarters to pay respects.
Facing north, circumambulate the hall once, moving from the lower section of the outer hall to the upper section. Return to the center of the inner hall to pay respects and exit.
When the incense offering on the main day is concluded, the attendant informs the abbot that the gruel service is finished and that he is to ascend the hall for the guest reception.

The "Hall Signboard" (shangtang pai) is hung above the entrance. In the Great Hall, incense, candles, hot water, tea, *niao* and *bo* gongs, and hand-incense burners are arranged. The Hall Master (*tangsi*) reports to the Abbot’s quarters.

The Guest Master (*ketou*) first informs the Abbot, who then instructs the Attendant (*shizhe*) to strike the drum. The Hall Master pre-emptively strikes the board in front of the various quarters three times to assemble the assembly for the formal sitting in the hall.

Those from the private quarters (*danyao*), the Monks’ Hall (*mengtang*), and all other quarters, as well as those from the outer halls, sit in their respective places. The Abbot emerges from his quarters.

The Abbot sits in the hall. The attendant stands in the eastern row to inquire after his well-being; the ritual assistant (xingzhe) stands in the western row. The drum is struck. The attendant descends from the Dharma Hall and stands at the upper corner.
The head officers descend to the floor and inquire after the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni). Leading the assembly, they exit the hall and ascend to the Dharma Hall.

They stand in a single file before the seat to inquire after his well-being, then return to stand in the western row. The assembly follows behind in a geese-formation. The hall attendants strike the wooden board.

Three prostrations. The head of the assembly leads the group to line up before the storehouse hall or the local deity hall (Jindìtáng). They wait there until they have paid their respects to the administrative officers (zhīshì).
Once the ranks have assembled in the Dharma Hall and the western division has returned to its place, they likewise line up single-file before the seats and pay their respects.

The Abbot (Dùsì) leads the procession back to the left; once they stand fixed in the morning salutation posture, the various attendants (xíngzhě) arrive at the upper section of the Dharma Hall, where they line up on the left to welcome the Abbot.
The attendant enters to invite the abbot. When the abbot’s sedan chair arrives before the assembly, the ritual assistants line up behind the *zhishi* (administrative officer).

The assembly removes the sleeves from their heads and performs a formal greeting (*wensun*). The abbot returns the greeting with a bow (*huinan*) and ascends the seat. The attendant follows behind the senior monk, holding a covered incense box filled with incense.
The drum is struck to signal the presentation of incense. After the Abbot has finished offering the incense, the Attendant receives it and inserts it into the burner with his left hand;

with his right hand, he takes a stick of incense from the reserve and covers the burner. The Abbot steps onto the footstool to perform a *wensun* (greeting), then folds his robes and sits cross-legged.

The Attendant descends from the seat, leads the lowest-ranking monk past the front of the seat, and they line up in a single file to perform a *wensun*. The Attendant leading the incense ceremony then leads them forward.
The assembly returns to their positions. Next, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) leads the group; they stand in a single file before the seat and perform a collective inquiry (wenshen).
They then return to their ranks. Next, the East Hall group steps out of the ranks; the attendant (xingzhe) follows with an inquiry, and they return to their positions.

If there are members from both the East and West Halls, those from the West Hall step out from below the seat to perform an inquiry (crossing the hands to step out, then joining the palms to return to position). The Attendant (shizhe) ascends the seat, opens and closes the canopy, and offers one incense stick on the left hand, then covers and closes the canopy.

Turning around, he takes up his sitting mat and pays his respects to the Abbot; this is called "requesting the Dharma. He stands to one side with hands clasped in reverence, listening attentively as questions and answers are exchanged and the core principles are summarized.
It is not permitted to offer thanks to officials or nobles, much less discuss other matters. At the conclusion of the session, he announces: "The assembly shall each assume their dignified demeanor."
Proceed to the Great Buddha Jewel Hall to inaugurate the ○○ Festival. Descend from the seat. Strike the great bell. When the assembly reaches the hall, serve tea and soup.

Once the attendants have finished their duties, strike the incense-burning cymbals. The Rector turns toward the incense burner and bows to the Abbot as he offers incense; the attendant then presents the incense case.
Next, the monks of the East Hall and West Hall come forward from their ranks; the two orders emerge facing one another. There is no mutual inquiry regarding the incense.
If there is a senior monk (shouzuo) standing in the hall, such as a Great Dharma (dafang) West Hall monk, he shall first step out from the ranks in front of the West Hall.

Those of the East Order offer incense with the right hand and turn left to return to their positions; those of the West Order offer incense with the left hand and turn right to return to their positions. Once the procession has concluded, the entire assembly...
Perform three prostrations together. This prostration is for the purpose of informing the heavens and offering prayers for longevity.
It is improper for the abbot not to remove his ritual implements and instead kneel directly at the incense burner. The Rector (Vina) announces the Buddha and proclaims the memorial text (*shu*).

Upon reaching the phrase "Rightly bowing," the abbot burns incense again, performs prostrations, and kneels at the burner. The Guest Master (Zhike) kneels to present the hand-incense burner, and the Attendant (Shizhe) kneels.

The incense box is presented. Once the proclamation of the memorial (shūsū) is finished, the Guest Master (chikaku) kneels to receive the incense burner, and the Abbot (jūji) withdraws his implements.

Alternatively, if the Abbot has received an official invitation from a prefecture or county, the Head Official (chōzu) and the Administrative Officers (chiji) kneel at their respective positions to receive the burner. The Guest Attendant (katō) of the Treasury Office (kosu) kneels to present the hand-incense burner, which is then received while kneeling.

The Tea Attendant (chadō) of the Treasury Office kneels to present the incense box. The Ritual Master (nōza) recites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* for the dedication of merit (ekō). The ceremony is thus inaugurated.

The Hall Attendant (Tángsī xíngzhě) shall, on the day prior, prepare the *suǎnbó* (monastic roster) for the upcoming turn. He shall invite the Abbot (*zhùzhí*), the Head Officers (*tóushǒu*), and the assembly of monks to sign their names in both large and small characters.
A formal list of assignments shall be prepared, with the titles of the scriptures to be recited arranged in order above; this shall be posted and displayed within the hall.

On the appointed day, the Abbot and the assembly shall ascend to the hall to recite the scriptures, each maintaining strict solemnity. The great bell shall be struck as they enter the hall, and each person shall offer three incense sticks.
Prostrate. Return to your position and read the scriptures. The Rector (Weina) shall proceed to the hall and offer one incense stick, performing three full prostrations with the robes spread out.

The Guest Master (Zhike) shall personally serve the hot water and tea. The Kitchen Office (Kusi) shall solemnly prepare incense, candles, refreshments, and tea; the Hall Office (Tangsi) attendants shall provide these offerings to ensure no ritual is omitted.
The Rector shall oversee these matters at the appropriate time. At evening, the great bell shall be struck, and the assembly shall descend from the hall. This is the daily routine.

The monastic staff, according to the regulations of the Precept Wheel, shall include the Hall Attendant, the Treasury Assistant, and the Temple Guards. They must constantly maintain vigilance against the arrival of officials.

When incense is offered and the bell is struck, they shall assemble the community to chant sutras. During the imperial birthday celebrations, the Abbot and the officers of the Treasury shall escort the sacred procession.

On the eighth day, when encountering the Buddha Hall, the recitation begins; the corridor patrol sounds the wooden board, and the assembly gathers, standing in formation like a flight of geese facing one another. The Abbot presides.

Carry it there. Strike the large wooden board; immediately strike the great bell. Burn incense and return to one’s place. The Rector (Vina) steps out of the ranks to lead the recitation, as seen in the ritual procedures below.
Upon completion of the recitation, strike the bell in front of the Sangha Hall three times, and the assembly disperses. Note that tea is not served beforehand.

Whenever a sacred festival is celebrated, the Guest Office shall issue a temporary pass for those who have arrived briefly to serve as identification. The Abbot leads the assembly to view the scriptures.
The administrators shall prepare offerings and distribute alms, and offer prayers for the longevity of one person;
they must strive for sincerity, as this is a way to repay the kindness of the land and water. The ritual procedures for the concluding distribution are identical to those previously mentioned.

The Hall Administrator (Tangsi) prepares the formal document (shu), listing the relevant scriptural passages in full. By custom, materials for the printing blocks are set aside in preparation for handover.

Whenever the Abbot goes on official business, upon his return—regardless of whether it is near or far—the bell is struck to assemble the community. They welcome him at the gate, proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to pay their respects, and then the assembly disperses.
The abbot shall not further tour the quarters to offer formal greetings.

Ascending the seat for the dedication of merit (the meaning of the preceding "same-banner" [confraternity] section is as follows): On this auspicious day of the commencement of the ceremony, I, the subject-monk serving as abbot, ascend this seat to proclaim the vehicle of our school.

The vast merits thus accumulated are solely for the purpose of praying for the ten-thousand-year peace and security of the Emperor’s life. Buddha-Verse of Homage: The jade-like radiance surges forth; the golden hue blazes brilliantly. Endowed with the marks of a Great Man, he is titled the Perfectly All-Knowing One. Beholding and gazing upon him, blessings fill the realms as numerous as grains of sand.

Furthermore, [the Great Perfection Awakened One, whose traces were left in the Western Continent of India, whose mind encompasses the great void, and whose measure extends throughout the sands of the world-system],

dedicates [the aforementioned recitations and vast causes to pray for the ten-thousand-year peace and security of the Imperial Majesty’s longevity, and for the Vajra Amitāyus Buddha, the Benevolent Kings Bodhisattvas, and so forth].

Recitation in the Buddha Hall: (May the imperial wind forever fan, may the sovereign way flourish afar, may the Buddha-sun increase its brilliance, and may the Wheel of Dharma constantly turn. For these aforementioned causes and conditions, [I take refuge in] the Pure Dharmakāya Vairocana Buddha.)

Route: (Temporarily visiting a monk. This is I, the Elder [Name]. On the [number] day of this month, we respectfully celebrated the [Heavenly] ○ Festival. We have already completed the distribution of offerings at our own temple. We rely on this as a certificate of verification.)
Year, Month, and Day. The Guest Master of [Name of Temple], [Name] hereby issues this.
The above statement:
(Opening) We humbly observe that when the red sun rises, the four seas rely upon the blessing of its illumination; in the depths of the white clouds, ever...
This year, I extend my sincere wishes for your longevity; by virtue of your inconceivable meritorious achievements, may your lifespan increase manifold beyond all calculation.

Your Majesty, the Emperor: We humbly pray that the deep waters shall yield pearls and the jeweled mountains shall offer jade, so that both the barbarians and the Chinese may turn toward benevolence, chariots share the same ruts, and scripts share the same characters, achieving a unified empire across all mountains and rivers.
As for this humble monk [Name], his innermost feelings are beyond restraint as he gazes upon Heaven and looks toward the Sage;
he is moved by the utmost urgency and trepidation. This memorial is respectfully submitted.
(Scattered Verse: Heaven opens the gates of Changhe; at this auspicious moment, blessings flow as rainbows wind and lightning flashes. People offer their finest responses;

at this juncture, all gaze upon the sun and look toward the clouds. Having thus completed the Flower Treasury [Sutra] over the course of three decades, we now solemnize the "Ten Thousand Years" mountain-cry.

We respectfully pray that the mandate of the calendar shall rest with Your Majesty, that civilization and supreme governance prevail, and that among the nine and five blessings—wealth and longevity—there be none lacking.
To force a rest. Eight thousand years constitute a spring and an autumn.

From this day forward, at dawn and on the first day of each month, when the Abbot is about to ascend the seat for the morning service and the attendant is to burn incense in the evening, the attendant shall go to the Abbot’s quarters to seek instructions for the formal discourse (*shàngtáng*). On the following morning, during the time of mutual inquiry, [the attendant] shall raise [the matter].
The guest master attendant is ordered to post the notice and inform the various quarters that for the early morning gruel, the bell for descending from the hall shall not be struck.
The guest master of the Abbot’s quarters prepares the Dharma seat; the tea master holds a candle and arranges the incense. The hall office attendant informs the Head Seat (Shouzuo).

Three strikes of the wooden board are sounded before the assembly quarters (to notify the community to enter the hall). The Head Seat and the various head officers stand before the Sangha Hall, waiting for the drum to strike its first beat before entering the hall. The Head Seat enters last; once the drum rolls, the Head Seat leads the assembly to [the Abbot’s quarters].

In the Dharma Hall, the two classes of officials inquire after the Dharma seat, each lining up in their respective rows to the east and west. The Abbot ascends the seat; having offered incense, he steps out of the ranks. The rites for the Imperial Birthday are performed identically.

In ancient times, when students had doubts they could not resolve, they would step out from the assembly to seek instruction. The Master’s response was valued for its ability to untangle attachments and loosen fetters.

The practice of "seeking a story" (solving riddles) today has already lost this ancient spirit; the Great Master Dahui deeply censured it. When the Abbot raises the teaching to offer his sincere prayers, [the assembly should respond].
Regarding the lifespan of a single person, there are visiting guests; these shall be briefly set forth to inspire scholars.

As for the causes and conditions of both the minute and the great—such as the five morning assemblies, entering the hall, the abbot’s tea meetings and formal discussions, and the evening assembly for training novices—each has its appointed time.
In the Dharma Hall when expounding the vehicle of our school, one must not engage in talk concerning worldly truths, nor indulge in weariness.
The Assembly Listens. On the first and fifteenth days of the month, the scripture is chanted in the Xuanzang Hall to offer prayers for the Emperor.

As for the chanting of scriptures in the Xuanzang Hall to offer prayers for the Emperor on the first and fifteenth days, it is intended that the imperial way may flourish far and wide and that the Wheel of Dharma may turn perpetually.
After the congee meal is finished, the attendant reports to the hall. The bell is struck to assemble the assembly; the drum is beaten to recite the Tripitaka. The attendant strikes the gong.

The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) announces: (Recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*). The Abbot leads the assembly in circumambulating the Tripitaka three times to symbolize the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma.
Once they have stood still, the *vinaya-dhara* intones the *Mahākaruṇā-mantra*.

Dedication: Within the Great Perfectly Radiant Sphere lies the Flower Treasury Ocean. Its merit transcends the workings of nature; its Way is beyond names and words. The three luminaries roll like lightning, yet the true mark remains tranquil; the six directions thunder like a storm, yet it is profoundly still and silent. This is the inconceivable Dharma.

Beyond the power of words to fully extol. At such-and-such a temple in such-and-such a province, the presiding monk and subject [name], on this auspicious day of the first moon, respectfully convenes the monastic assembly of this mountain.

Together they circumambulate the Scripture Hall and perform the Way, chanting the sacred name of the Mahābuddhamātṛ and reciting secret mantras. The vast merit thus accumulated is solely for the purpose of praying for the longevity and peace of the present Emperor, and for the Vajra-Amitāyus Buddha, the Benevolent Kings Bodhisattvas, and so forth.

Furthermore: (The Wheel of Dharma was turned thrice throughout the great chiliocosm; that wheel is inherently and eternally pure. That devas and humans have attained the Way serves as its witness; from this, the Three Jewels have appeared in the world.)
Yellow: On All Occasions of Imperial Prayer.

Whenever performing rites for cultivation or offering prayers, one must be reverently pure through ritual bathing and fasting. The offerings must be arranged according to the Dharma; flowers and fruits must be fresh, and the incense and candles must be of superior quality.

The temple halls must be swept and sprinkled with water at all times. The monastic community must maintain solemn and dignified deportment. When officials offer incense, they must act with added reverence.

The abbot and the administrative officers shall personally attend to the rites of welcoming and seeing off, remaining free from other entanglements. The quarters of the senior monks must be constantly and earnestly kept clean and pure;

one must ensure that these efforts yield their intended results so that merit may be properly attributed. Regarding prayers for the mountain gate (the monastery), the administrative office shall first consult the abbot, present the intent in advance to the *vinaya-dhara* (rector), and have the hall attendant report to the various quarters to post the notice. The assembly shall gather twice daily to chant sutras, with the proceedings beginning and concluding with solemnity.

When making offerings, during summer retreat prayers, or at the *Śūraṅgama* assembly, one must not take these as mere opportunities for convenience. On the day of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one announces the completion of the service.
Every morning, after the gruel meal, one descends from the hall to the shrine hall to chant scriptures and turn the wheel of the Dharma. The dedication follows the local Vinaya;

in some places, when the five periods of attendance (*pañca-saṃkrama*) involve ascending the hall, one does not chant scriptures—this is contrary to the Dharma. If one descends from the hall on the first or fifteenth of the month, one must invariably offer prayers for the Emperor.

When chanting the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī, one must first form the *dhāraṇī-mudrā* (the heart-seal of the mantra). Only then should one gradually and slowly raise the voice to recite the dhāraṇī. Set a specific period for its efficacy, and each person should hope to maintain single-minded sincerity.
[The Buddha’s Birthday of] the Tathāgata.
As the anniversary of the Buddha’s birth approaches, the attendants of the Hall Office lead the assembly to deliver a number of ritual implements to the treasury to prepare offerings;

this is the ancient custom. When the Abbot is presiding over the ceremony, the Rector orders the Secretary to draft the following notice, which is identical to that used for the Holy Festival (the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa).
The Storehouse Office instructs the attendants in advance to solemnly arrange the Vimalaprabhā Garden, wherein they install a bronze statue of the Prince.
Boil fragrant water and place two small ladles inside the basin. Arrange them as offerings before the Great Buddha.

When the day’s morning gruel is finished, the Abbot ascends the seat, offers incense, recites the essential themes (*tígāng*), performs the dedication of merit, and concludes the session. Descending from the seat, he says: "The assembly, each assuming their proper dignified demeanor, shall proceed to the Great Buddha Hall to bathe the Buddha and chant the sutras.
The assembly proceeds together to the hall; the Abbot offers incense, performs three prostrations, does not withdraw his ritual implements, and steps forward to present the hot water.

The meal is served. When the attendants have finished distributing it, the assembly returns to their positions and performs three prostrations. They offer incense and distribute alms-food. Tea is served; they perform three prostrations and withdraw the ritual implements.

The gong is struck. The Rector bows toward the incense. The Abbot offers incense, and the attendant holds the censer. The two classes of officials do not exchange incense or inquire after one another.
Once they have left the ranks, the entire assembly together performs three prostrations. The detailed procedure for the rites of the Imperial Birthday is the same as this. If, however, the Abbot...

Hold the incense burner for others. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) kneels at his designated position before the brazier. The Attendant for the Holy Monk (Shengseng), the Hall Administrator (Tangsi), and the Storehouse Keeper (Kuzi) kneel to present the hand-incense burner and the incense casket;
the Abbot’s Attendant may also do so (out of respect for the Dharma). This is the consensus of the ancient masters, yet it is observed only during the anniversaries of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

On these occasions, the Head Seat acts on behalf of the Abbot for the sake of transmitting the Dharma; on the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday (Shengjie), the Administrative Officers (Zhishi) act on his behalf for the sake of the Mountain Gate (the monastery). Dahui and Xiaoweng both practiced this. The Rector (Weina) announces the Buddha, and once the proclamation of the memorial text is finished, he recites the Bathing the Buddha Verses. After circumambulating, they bathe the Buddha. Copper coins must be prepared for this rite. As the bathing of the Buddha nears completion, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is recited.

At the assembly, the incantation was recited. Upon its conclusion, the dedication was made as follows: "The merit of the sutra recitation above is dedicated to the true suchness of ultimate reality (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*). May it adorn the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit, repay the four debts of gratitude, provide sustenance for all within the three realms of existence, and [extend to] the ten directions and the three periods of time, etc."

Ascending the Seat for Dedication of Merit: (At [Name] Temple in [Name] Prefecture, on the eighth day of the fourth lunar month, on the auspicious occasion of the birthday of our Master, the Great Monk Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the assembly of bhikṣus, led by those who have contributed wealth to the monastery, have prepared incense and offerings to extend their veneration.

I, Bhikṣu [Name], a remote descendant of the Bequeathed Teachings, now ascend this seat to proclaim the Dharma of the School. May the extraordinary merit thus accumulated be offered upward to repay the compassionate protection of the Buddha.)

A Verse Addressed to the Buddha: When the single moon dwells in the sky, its reflection is contained within all waters; when a single Buddha appears in the world, he sits upon each individual flower. The white tuft of hair extends forth and illuminates the three realms; the nectar is sprinkled and moistens the four modes of birth.

Verses for Bathing the Buddha: I now bathe all the Tathāgatas, The assembly of merit adorned with pure wisdom. May the sentient beings of the five turbidities be freed from defilement, And together realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
To the right, he speaks from the Tuṣita Heaven palace without rising from his seat, yet constantly preaches this Dharma.
Within the Lumbinī Garden, riding upon the wheel of great vows, he manifests birth. Surveying above, below, and the four quarters, he proclaims himself the Sole Honored One within the three realms.
As the fragrant influence of the Semblance Teaching flows forth, it coincides with the anniversary of his birth; as auspicious signs surge from the dragon-pool, they emulate those of that year.

For this ritual ablution, we humbly pray that our Great Preceptor, the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Tathāgata, shall employ the ocean of his most profound wisdom to turn back the surging tide of decadence.

May the radiance of this prosperous age extend the boundless longevity of the Sovereign, and may all sentient beings, as numerous as motes of dust, together realize the pure Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. This is respectfully drafted.

Regarding the dedication of the commentary on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: on the very day [of the Buddha’s] entering *nirvāṇa* and attaining enlightenment, he prepared the commentary in advance and led the assembly in dedicating their resources as offerings.

[The monks] leave their seats and perform prostrations; the ritual for the Buddha’s Birthday is the same. However, for the *Nirvāṇa* (Mahāparinirvāṇa) ceremony, one should first descend from the hall during the morning gruel.
In the Scripture Hall (*Zangdian*), incense is offered and sutras are chanted to offer prayers for the Emperor.

For the Buddha’s Birthday, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the Attainment of Enlightenment, the monastery provides offerings. There are no monetary gifts (*kṣiṇa*). (Note: Only for the Buddha’s Birthday, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the Attainment of Enlightenment, the abbot takes the incense from his breast pocket and personally inserts it into the burner.)

Verses Offered to the Buddha: The body of the pure Dharma-realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing; yet, through the power of great compassion and vows, it manifests coming and going. Before the Mountain of Perfect Enlightenment, he beheld the morning star and awakened to the Way; within the great trichiliocosm, he drives the sun of wisdom to radiate its brilliance. Dedication:

May the merit from reciting the sutras above be dedicated to the true suchness of ultimate reality (bhūtakoṭi), adorning the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit. May the four debts of gratitude be universally repaid, and may all beings in the three realms of existence be equally sustained.
All sentient beings within the Dharma-realm shall equally realize the Perfect Wisdom. All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth). The above words:
His thousand, billion-fold bodies pervade the realms of dust without ceasing; for seventy-nine years, he conformed to the world through impermanence.
As I contemplate his compassionate countenance like the full moon, I shed tears against the backdrop of mid-spring. Alas for this "Plucking of the Flower"!
The subtle purport of this has gradually become like overgrown weeds, making it difficult to remedy. To offer my humble service, I sincerely extend this tribute in remembrance of the distant past.
May our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Great Monk, graciously grant his blessings: may the sky of awakening be vast and open, so boundlessly sublime that it defies all names;
may the radiance of the sun of wisdom flow forth, so brilliantly white that it can never be surpassed. May all beings throughout the entire *dharmadhātu* be brought into accord with [this truth].
The wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*. (Attaining the Way) Snow covers the thousand mountains; spring returns to the cold valleys across the great earth. The stars shine brightly at midnight;
the clouds of the heavens disperse from the vast sky. He manifested the cause of six years of ascetic practice and realized the fruit of cultivation throughout kalpas. [I,] (Name), [bow].
I, who have humbly received the dharma in this final age and am unworthily the successor to the ancestral legacy, feel deep regret at the thought of subsisting on a meal of hemp and wheat;
yet, as for reverently offering the simple provisions of pondweed and duckweed, I can truly never forget them. My original teacher, the Great Monk Śākyamuni Tathāgata—
I humbly pray that the remaining radiance may shine upon us, awakening our ignorance and delusion.
May the sovereign’s blessings, longevity, and peace endure forever throughout the great trichiliocosm, and may all sentient beings together realize the wisdom and virtuous marks of the Tathāgata.

As the anniversary of the passing of the Patriarch Master Hongdao approaches, the Hall Administration issues a preliminary order to prepare the memorial text and sign the document; the ritual is identical to that for the Buddha’s birthday, as both honor the Buddhas and Patriarchs.

Ritual propriety requires a unified body of practice; yet at present, matters remain simplified and lack detailed manuals. This does not accord with the intent of honoring the ancestors and revering the Way.

The abbot must apply himself with single-minded sincerity, while the administrative officers of the mountain gate prepare everything in full: the *vinaya-dhara* (Vina), the attendant (*shizhe*), and the supervisor (*tidian*) shall oversee the arrangements. The head of the assembly (*candou*) shall dispatch attendants to set out the ritual implements and scrolls in the Dharma Hall.

The duty officer (*shouzhi*) shall organize the seating and prepare the ceremonial seat for the presiding master, hanging the portrait of the deceased. The sacrificial banquet shall be solemnly laid out, complete with incense burners, vases, and incense.
The seating arrangements follow the prescribed ritual for each instance. In the upper section, meditation chairs, fly-whisks, and clothing racks are set out to hang the dharma robes.
In the lower section, only chairs, a scripture table, incense burners, vases, incense, candles, and scrolls are provided; it is improper to set out beds or couches.

The Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the attendants notify the Abbot’s quarters and all the monastic offices. That evening, they recite scriptures and announce the midday meal for the following day. Each person shall maintain a dignified demeanor.

[The ritual for] the Memorial Service (Ji). Chant the sutras. Before the assembly gathers, ring the bell in front of the Sangha Hall; once the assembly has assembled, beat the drum. Offer the special hot water (táng).

The Abbot offers incense and performs three prostrations, without withdrawing his sitting cloth (jù). He steps forward to offer the hot water. Once the attendant has finished distributing it, [the Abbot] returns to his position and performs three prostrations.

He steps forward again to invite [the assembly] to drink the hot water, bows with hands raised in greeting, and performs three prostrations. He withdraws his sitting cloth. The attendant rings the hand-bell (shǒuqìng), and the Rector (Weina) emerges.

Recite the mantras as prescribed in the ritual manual. Upon completion, strike the bell in front of the Sangha Hall three times; the assembly disperses. When the evening bell tolls, gather the assembly to chant sutras.
The Abbot offers incense, and the Rector (Vina) recites the Śūraṅgama Dhāraṇī and performs the dedication of merit.

Next, the Head of the Retreat leads the assembly to the front of the hall to announce the session, prostrate, and chant sutras. Those from the various quarters line up to acknowledge their presence with a "shenyue" (bow), prostrate, and chant sutras. Next...

Early in the morning, after the gruel has been served, the Abbot conducts the service as usual: offering incense and hot water. The Rector recites the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and performs the dedication of merit.
At half-past noon, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community. In the upper and lower sections of the Dharma Hall, the monks stand facing the Patriarchs in rows.

The Abbot offers incense and performs three prostrations without removing his sitting cloth (*kaṣāya*). Hot water is served and food is presented. Once the attendant has finished distributing it, the monks return to their positions and perform three prostrations. Then they advance.

First, burn incense. Distribute the offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) and perform three prostrations. Retire the ritual implements and strike the drum. For the special tea ceremony held for this occasion, burn incense, bow to the tea, and perform three prostrations.
Strike the drum three times. Once the Abbot has completed the ritual of offering incense (*xiāng fóshì*), the attendant strikes the *xingxiāng* gong.

The Rector turns to face the incense burner and bows to the Abbot as he offers incense; the Attendant holds the censer. Next, the two classes of officials—the East Hall and West Hall—step out from their ranks.
Once they have finished, there is no separate offering of incense; the entire assembly performs three prostrations together. The Rector announces the truth and proclaims the memorial.

Kneel before the incense burner. Once the ritual petition (*shu*) is completed, recite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and perform the dedication of merit (*huixiang*). As for the offerings set out at the mountain gate, there is no monetary gift (*qin*).
If there are those who perform three prostrations with prepared dishes, one fears that such excessive ritual might become mere flattery.

Recitation Ritual [Reflecting that] one’s compassionate vows are profound and weighty, and the Way is so vast as to be difficult to name; yet, having humbly received the nourishment from its lingering waves, I have brought some luster to my descendants.

I now look up and rely upon the Great Assembly to recite for the Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Buddha, whose ten titles are fully realized. I offer the merit of the above recitation to the First Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, to repay his compassionate protection. [For all beings of the ten directions and three periods of time... (and so forth).

Dedication of Merit at the First Watch of the Night The Body of the Pure Dharma Realm is fundamentally without appearing or disappearing; yet, through the power of great compassionate vows, it manifests coming and going. We look up with hope that Your True Benevolence will graciously deign to inspect us from on high.

On the fifth day of this month, coinciding with the anniversary of the Great Master Bodhidharma’s entry into Nirvana, the assembly of bhikṣus, led by Changcai, has entered the permanent property to prepare incense and offerings, extending worship in advance.

They have chanted the Divine Mantra of the Great Buddha-Top of Myriad Practices Śūraṅgama. May the extraordinary merit thus accumulated be offered upward to repay the shade of Your compassion. We humbly pray: may all sentient beings find reliance upon it, so they may propagate the family tradition of Shaoshi (the Small Room); and may their wondrous wisdom be inexhaustible, so they may perfect the faculties and vessels for the Mahāyāna. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time...
All Buddhas... (and so forth). Dedication of Merit (*pariṇāmanā*):

"The merit from reciting the sutras above, I respectfully dedicate for the sake of the First Patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, to adorn the unsurpassed *bodhi* of the Buddha-fruit. Throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).

Inscription. In the Western Land of India, there were no teachers of heterodox views; [Bodhidharma] utterly shattered the delusions of the six schools. In the Eastern Land of China, there were those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna;
he first opened the springtime of the five patriarchs. Now, encountering this occasion of the burial of his sandals, I venture to offer this simple tribute of water plants and herbs.
Great Master Bodhidharma, I humbly pray that you will further strengthen your original vow and ensure that the single transmission does not decline, so that the four and seven [patriarchs]...
The Way of the Two and Three [Teachings] becomes ever more radiant; it shall flourish eternally for billions of tens of millions of years.
Regarding the anniversary of the Patriarch Baizhang:
formerly, Chan Master Baiyun Dan established the Patriarchs’ Hall. The preface to its organizational regulations states: "Our Way flourishes here in this land. The Bodhi..."
It was he who established the纲 (guiding principles) of the Dharma and initiated the regulations for Chan monasteries; this is the legacy of Baizhang the Great Wise One.
This is truly what is universally known throughout the world. Yet, alas, within the ancestral halls of the world, each lineage takes as its patriarch merely the founder of that particular mountain.
How can they fail to reflect upon the true source and ancestor—the one who transmitted and upheld the essential teachings? Alas!
Five hundred years after the teachings were called forth, Bodhidharma finally arrived. How could the worthies of the various schools of the past not have known that nature is itself the Sage?
Why did they ultimately bind themselves with the mire of "nature" and "the Sage"?

Thus, it was required that even after the Shaolin era, in a mere snap of the fingers, one should be liberated—without relying on words, silence, existence, or non-existence—and find release, casting off all that is awaited.
Thus, one naturally returns to one's own fundamental source. Furthermore, those of antiquity who dwelt among crags and caves took the Dharma alone as their excellence and flavor;
they did not at all consider the arrogance and exclusivity that arose among them later. It was Master Dazhi of Jingde who foresaw this and expanded it with the regulations of the Chan forest.
By relying on these, the tradition of Shaolin has remained a pervasive fragrance throughout the world to this day.

I desire that within the ancestral halls of the world, Bodhidharma, the Great Wise One, be placed in his proper position, while those who successively transmitted the founding of the mountain are doubled in number.
This is to honor those who come by venerating their origin and to return to the greatness [of the source]. Is this not so? How great indeed is Chan Master Baiyun!
He has brought forth the legacy of the ancestors; his hidden virtues and profound radiance are as clear as the sun and moon, enabling all students throughout the world—

One should know what is to be revered and honored. Nowadays, in the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*) of various regions, when encountering the anniversary of a Great Master’s passing (*dàzhì jì*), they are unable to establish the proper rites.

As those who preside over the Dharma, you ought to reflect upon the intention of Báiyún: on the seventeenth day of the first lunar month, which is the formal anniversary of the忌 (jì), the *vina* shall prepare the liturgical text (*shù*) in advance and circulate it for signatures;

the Dharma Hall shall be adorned with offerings; during the preceding night, the scriptures shall be chanted, food offerings presented, incense offered in a ritual service (*fóshì*), and the assembly shall perform prostrations and kneel before the incense burner.
The ritual for reciting sutras and the distribution of offerings on the anniversary of the Master’s passing is identical to that for the anniversary of Bodhidharma’s passing;

the procedure is as stated above. His great wisdom was profoundly clear, like the ten suns shining upon the world; his true mechanism of truth reached across a hundred generations, universally reaching those in the six realms of existence.
Gathering and transforming all living beings, the monastic groves have been renewed; the Way has not yet perished.
Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang—humbly we pray that you remain majestic, establishing your standards with successive layers of excellence, appearing before us and yet vanishing behind;

that your influence resounds like morning bells and evening drums, bringing peace to the aged and solace to the young; that you shall propagate your ancestral teachings and continue the footsteps of your forebears. This is respectfully inscribed.

On the anniversary of the founding patriarch’s memorial day, one should follow established tradition; never forgetting one's ancestors, one should strive to carry this out. If a donor establishes a temple, they should invite the founding patriarch, and it is customary to observe the memorial rites for him.
However, if there are those who have performed meritorious deeds for the mountain gate, one need not be restricted by these rules; yet, one must certainly act in accordance with the Dharma.

In the center of the hall, the seats are laid out and the assembly gathers. They chant the sutras, exit their rows, and perform prostrations with the same ritual as the memorial service for Bodhidharma.

The dedication of merit follows: "The precious, luminous ocean of emptiness stirs the waves of the whirlpool of birth and death; the gate of great tranquil concentration merges the appearances of past and present, coming and going. We look up in hope that your true compassion will look down and grant clear illumination. On the [day] of this month..."

I humbly submit that on the occasion of the passing of the founding patriarch, Venerable [Name], the permanent residents have prepared offerings of food and drink to extend their veneration. The assembly of bhikṣus has chanted the Great Buddha-Top Myriad Practices Śūraṅgama Divine Mantra and invoked the holy name.

By virtue of the extraordinary merit thus accumulated, we respectfully dedicate it to the True Compassion [of the deceased]. We pray with humble submission: May the *tāmarasa* flower bloom once more, reopening the springtime of the Garden of Enlightenment; may the Sun of Wisdom shine forever long, eternally illuminating the night of the dark alleys.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time... (and so forth).

On the anniversaries of the passing of the various patriarchs, their spiritual practice is held in the highest esteem and they have governed the mountain gate. On the day preceding the memorial, the Dharma Hall must be prepared according to established precedent and may not deviate from this rule.

If it concerns the listed patriarchs as usual, after the morning gruel, the sutras shall be chanted; at that time, the name tablets and seats should be requested, the Dharma seat shall be spread out for offerings, and the ritual should be performed according to the regulations.
The two classes of officials (the *zhuchi* and his attendants) perform prostrations; the attendant bows at the end of the line. He requests incense and makes inquiries.

Alternatively, if the entire assembly performs prostrations, there is a practice where he proceeds directly to the Patriarchs’ Hall. As for the serving of food, it is customary to recite a scripture for one position [of the patriarchs]; however, this is highly improper.

Dedication of Merit (I humbly look up to Your True Compassion; may You deign to grant Your clear inspection. On the [day] of this month, the mountain gate has encountered the anniversary of the passing of the late Abbot, the [number]th generation of this mountain, Venerable [Name].

We have prepared incense and offerings to extend our veneration, and we chant the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī. By the extraordinary merit thus accumulated, we respectfully pray that Your True Compassion may be elevated to higher ranks. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time... etc.)
Master Ying’s Successor’s Memorial Service:

The former masters merely used vigorous exhortation to proclaim the essential vehicle (zongcheng), to reveal their own realization, and to instruct those yet to come, so that there might be known the transmission of the Dharma.
This is to repay their virtue. Regarding the three turns of the word at Ba Ling, they established a memorial service that did not fall into vulgar custom.

In later generations, the Way has not reached the level of antiquity; yet one’s efforts are focused on extensively arranging sacrificial tables and preparing lavish offerings—is this not cause for shame?

Recently, Da Chuan performed the memorial service for Zen Master Zhe Weng, and Hengchuan established the memorial service for Zen Master Tianmu; the Abbot set up the seat and provided a single portion of food.

[The ritual is] divided as follows: burn one stick of incense and perform nine prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths; the recitation of sutras is not permitted. The two great elders have deep intentions regarding this.

Nevertheless, in honoring the teacher and revering the Way, the rites must not be deficient. On the anniversary of the death (the *jichén*), one must prepare offerings within the robe-closet (*yigé*).

Money and goods should be calculated in advance and returned to the monastic community (*chángzhù*) to arrange the memorial service and offerings. Seats were arranged in the communal hall for a public discourse for the assembly. Only Master Mahāmati’s transmission of the essence and his transmission of the teaching were not constrained by time nor restricted by place.
38. Going for Recitation: Following the sequence of the summer retreat (varṣā) based on the precepts, draw the diagram. On the appointed day, sweep and sprinkle water before the Sangha Hall.

In the afternoon, the attendant of the Hall Office (dōji gyōja) notifies the Abbot’s quarters and the various lodgings; the recitation plaque is hung, and the bell-ringer is assigned his duties. Before the evening assembly, inspect the Sacred Monk (honzon).

In front [of the hall] and in all the pavilions, incense and candles are fully prepared. First, the *weina*, attendants, the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), the treasury office (*kusī*), the head seat (*shouzuo*), and the heads of the various private quarters are covered.
Three strikes of the *zhao-tang* board are sounded; next, the board is struck while patrolling the corridors; then, ascending again, the board is struck for the abbot’s quarters.
When the assembly has gathered, they take their positions according to the diagram. The temporary attendant stands with his shoulder lowered. The abbot arrives.
The Abbot burns incense. The large wooden board is struck three times, followed by the striking of the great bell. The two classes of officials assemble in advance outside the Sangha Hall.
Only when the large wooden board sounds do they return to their assigned seats. Next, the Abbot enters the hall. The offering master strikes the bell in front of the hall seven times.
The Abbot burns incense before the Sacred Monk (Śāstṛ). The attendant holds up the incense censer, while the guest-inviting attendant immediately proceeds to the front of the western section.

The abbot circulates to inquire after everyone’s well-being. He issues the invitation: (The Abbot of the Main Hall invites [the assembly]. After the recitation is finished, they proceed to the Quarters Hall for the offering of hot water. He invites those of the East Section to join him and take their places standing according to the designated positions in the formation.
Before the Abbot exits the hall, he stands facing outward. The incense-bearer attendant follows him out and returns to his position.

The Rector (Vina) first leaves his seat and goes to the entrance, standing facing the Abbot with palms joined; having finished his recitation, he returns to his place in the assembly. The Abbot then enters the hall.
Next, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) enters, followed by the West Hall (Xitang) monk, who stands at the head of the Holy Monk (Shengseng) shelf.

Next, the Head Officers (Tou-shou) enter one after another, followed by the third group of three, who perform a greeting before the Holy Monk. They turn around and greet the Abbot (Zhuchi), facing north, and then circumambulate the hall while performing greetings.

They stand with palms joined according to their assigned positions in the diagram. Finally, the newly arrived guests and the junior attendants (Mo-shizhe) enter following them. Upon reaching [the designated spot]—

The visiting attendant stands at the entrance facing the shrine of the Venerable Monk. Having briefly stood before the shrine, the administrative officers (zhishi) enter the hall and perform a circuit of salutations before exiting.
The visiting attendant follows them out. A hall attendant goes before the Head Seat (shouzuo) to announce that the formal visit has concluded.
Turning from behind the shrine, they exit through the front gate. The offering master strikes the bell three times; the Abbot emerges, followed by the two ranks of officials. The hall [is cleared].

First, there is the *xiè-tāng* (thanksgiving bath). Next, on the eighth day of the month, there is the *fù-tāng* (bath for the deceased). In the dormitory hall, the wooden board is struck; the attendants burn incense and perform the rites according to the usual protocol.
When the bath is finished, the *yàoshí* (medicinal food) is served. According to ancient regulations, the *tāng* is provided on all three eighths (the first, middle, and last eights of the month);
however, on the upper and middle eights, the *yàoshí* is omitted (one does not sit for the assembly, though one sits in the hall in the evening as usual).

Recitation Ritual (Upper Eight, Middle Eight): May the imperial wind forever spread; may the sovereign way flourish far and wide; may the Buddha-sun increase its brilliance; may the Wheel of Dharma turn eternally.
May the local deities of the monasteries protect the Dharma and protect people; may the donors of the ten directions increase in merit and wisdom.
With these aforementioned intentions, [recite] "Vairocana Buddha of the Pure Dharma Body" ten times. (When the sacred name is finished, perform the dedication.)
(8b) I inform the great assembly: Since the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, entered parinirvāṇa until the first year of the Zhì period, two thousand two hundred and seventy years have already passed.
This day has already gone by, and my life likewise diminishes accordingly, like a fish in shallow water. What joy can there be in this?
You, members of the assembly, should exert yourselves with diligent vigor, as if your hair were on fire; you must contemplate only the [impermanence of] non-existence.
Always be careful and never be negligent. May the local deities of the monastery protect the Dharma and its practitioners; may the donors from the ten directions increase in merit and wisdom.
With these aforementioned aspirations in mind, [I take refuge in] the Pure Ten Epithets.

During the four seasonal festivals of autumn, the commencement of the retreat (*jie-zhi*), the conclusion of the retreat, the winter solstice, and the New Year’s Eve, offerings are solemnly arranged in the Land Deity Hall (*tǔdì-táng*).

The Head of the Storehouse (*kù-sī*) and the Guest Master (*kè-tóu*) inform the Rector (*wéi-nà*), while the Attendant of the Hall Office (*táng-sī xíng-zhě*) informs the Abbot (*fāng-wǎng*). Plaque boards for communal recitation are hung in the two classes of quarters and all the monastic lodgings, and the assembly is notified. The ritual is performed as follows:
This is the same as [the procedure for] the eighth day of the third month. When the assembly has gathered, they stand facing one another in a formation like wild geese.

The abbot enters the main hall, offers incense, and performs three prostrations. The large wooden board is struck three times, and the great bell is tolled. When the abbot arrives, the entire assembly joins their palms and bows their heads to welcome him.

The attendant stands with hands crossed, following behind. They enter the Hall of the Local Deity (Tudi) to burn incense; upon exiting, they stand outside. The Rector (Vinaya Master) bows from outside the front of the incense burner.
The abbot offers incense; the attendant holds the censer. Next, the two classes of officials emerge in pairs. There is an exchange of incense and inquiries.

Once they have exited the ranks, the *weina* faces inward and recites the dedication of merit. A single strike of the meal drum signals for the assembly to return to the hall for the hot water offering.
The ritual for the summer retreat (Jie-xia) is the same as that for the tea ceremony.

The Liturgy for Recitation (Jie-xia): We reflect that as the warm breeze fans the fields and the God of Fire presides over the quarter, this is the time when the Dharma King observes the *pāda-bandhana* (the foot-binding retreat), and the day upon which the sons of Śākya protect all living beings.
We respectfully assemble the great multitude and solemnly proceed to the sacred shrine to recite and maintain [the sacred texts].
The vast and majestic name of ten thousand virtues is dedicated to the True Sovereigns of this hall. We pray that you grant protection so that we may successfully achieve peaceful dwelling.
We now rely upon the Great Assembly to recite the Ten Holy Names of the Buddha Vairocana of the Pure Dharma Body. (Recite the Ten Holy Names.)

The Dedication (Huixiang) states: We now dedicate the merit of the foregoing recitations to the local deities of this mountain (the various ranks), as well as to the true sovereigns of this entire hall.

We pray that their divine radiance may provide harmonious support, manifesting illustrious deeds for the benefit of all; and that the Buddhist garden may flourish most exalted, forever bestowing impartial blessings.
Once again, we ask the assembly to recite: "To all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).

(Dismissing the Summer Retreat) I humbly observe that the golden wind fans the wilds and the White Emperor presides over the quarter. This is the occasion when the Buddha, the King of Awakening, concludes the retreat;
it is the day when the Dharma-year reaches its full cycle. For ninety days there have been no difficulties, and the entire assembly has remained at peace.

We recite the great name of the One Possessing Ten Thousand Virtues to reverently respond to the true lords of this hall. We rely upon the Great Assembly to recite: "The Pure Dharma Body... (and so forth).

[At the Winter Solstice] I humbly reflect that as we approach the end of the year and the season of the "Cloud-Recording" [Winter Solstice] arrives, it is the moment when the first yang energy returns and the beginning of the emergence of the myriad species.

We respectfully assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the sacred shrine to recite and uphold the vast and majestic names of the Ten Thousand Virtues, dedicating the merit to the True Sovereigns of this hall. We rely reverently upon the assembly to recite [as follows].

On this New Year’s Eve, we reflect that as the Great Transformer works in secret, the annual calendar has completed its cycle. All rejoice in the stability of the four seasons and prepare to inaugurate the auspiciousness of the three yang months.
We respectfully assemble the great assembly and solemnly proceed to the spirit shrine to recite the vast names of the myriad virtues, dedicating the merit to the true lords of this hall.
We rely reverently upon the assembly to contemplate the Pure Dharma Body (*viśuddha-dharmakāya*)... [and so forth].

**Requesting Instruction** To request instruction based on one’s sincere devotion: first go to the attendant’s office (shìsī) and report in detail. The attendant shall consult with the abbot (zhùzhí). [The petitioner says:
"I, Upadhyāya [Name], wish to visit the Abbot’s quarters this evening to request instruction. If the request is granted, wait at the attendant’s office after the striking of the *ding* bell.
The attendant follows the abbot to his seat, instructing him to light a candle and prepare incense. The guest is led in to offer greetings;

he offers a single stick of incense, performs nine prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan jiubai*), and then withdraws his implements to step forward for a greeting, saying: "I, [Name], recognize that the matter of birth and death is great and impermanence is swift. I humbly beseech the Venerable Master’s compassion to provide me with skillful instruction.

He stands upright with a solemn posture, slightly to one side, and lowers his hand to listen attentively to the Dharma teachings. When the abbot asks about his background, he answers truthfully from beginning to end.

Step forward to offer greetings. Upon exiting the furnace room, insert a single stick of incense and perform three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths; this is called "thanking for the causal conditions.
If one is exempted from this, a mere touching-prostration suffices. Next, proceed to the attendant’s office to express thanks.

Winter: On the day the *bǐngfú* (the master of ceremonies) arrives in the afternoon, the attendant orders the guest prefect to carry the master’s staff, plaque, and whisk; the servants carry the tray and cloth, as well as the incense burner and candles.

They inform the head administrator (*shàngshǒu zhīshì*), and the *rènwéi ná* (chanting master) accompanies them to the quarters of the head officers (*tóushǒu*). There, they light incense and perform one prostration with touching the forehead (*chùlǐ*) to announce their arrival.

Please say: "Venerable Abbot, you have commanded us to go to the quarters to extend an invitation that this evening we shall uphold the whisk for the assembly. Having made each request in this manner, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) receives the invitation together with them.
Next, the head official instructs an attendant to take the name plaque, fly-whisk, and master’s staff. They then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer their formal leave.
Once the Abbot has finished his exhortation and sent them forth, the Head Seat turns around and takes the Dharma seat and the Dharma drum.
The person holding the whisk (the *bǐfú rén*) shall immediately instruct the tea-head attendant to serve tea to the Holy Monk (*shèngsēng*), the Attendant (*shìzhě*), and the Zen guests (*chánkè*).
He shall then burn one incense stick, saying: "Tonight there is the holding of the whisk; we trouble the Attendant to burn incense, and the Zen guests to engage in dialogue.

The Abbot shall then instruct the Guest-Master (*kètóu*) to invite the Head Monks (*tóushǒu*) for medicinal refreshments (*yàoshí*), which they shall attend before the midday meal. The Hall-Office attendants shall arrange the Dharma seat (*fǎzuò*) in front of the hall and spread the cushions.

At the *guasī* (screened window) chair, the seat for the Abbot is established. At twilight, the ritual assistant covers the person holding the whisk (*bǐfú rén*), followed by covering the Chief Administrator (*fāngzhàng*).

A single roll of the drum is sounded, and the assembly gathers. The procedure for the informal sermon (*xiǎocān*) and the prostrations is the same as usual. The Abbot stands fixedly before his position.

The Chief Steward (*dūsu*), the Ritual Master (*wéinà*), and the Attendant (*shìzě*) together approach the person holding the whisk, perform a formal greeting (*wènxùn*), and return to their positions. The person holding the whisk then proceeds to the Abbot.

First, inquire after the well-being of those before him. Next, proceed from the head of the administrative staff (*karmadāna*) to inquire after their well-being, moving along until the end of the row.

Then, turn back to the head of his own class to inquire after his well-being, moving through salutations until the end of the row. Raising his hands, he inquires after the well-being of the entire assembly in unison. He then ascends the seat.

Once seated, the attendant who holds the whisk (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*) steps out of the ranks, followed by the two classes of officials stepping out, then the East and West Halls, and finally the Abbot steps out. The Abbot should rise to receive the prostrations. The whisk-holder says: "Attendant, please invite the Head Monk (*sthavira*)."

Sitting cross-legged, the attendant goes before the Abbot to inquire after his well-being. [The Abbot] ascends the seat, burns one stick of incense, and, holding up his sitting cloth, inquires after his well-being once more.

Standing to one side, the person who holds the whisk requests a discourse. Once the question and answer are concluded, he presents the outline of the talk and offers thanks to the Abbot and the entire mountain assembly (the congregation).

The public case for the Abbot’s informal sermon (xiaochan gongan) is presented. Having finished the verses of praise and commentary (nian song), he descends from the seat. The Abbot comes forward to inquire after his well-being, and he returns to his original position.
The next person performs the same prostrations as before, ascends the seat, and concludes the formal dharma-discourse (bingfu). The guest master (ketou) calls for tea and fruit.

Upon descending from the seat, he immediately carries incense and proceeds together with the others to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to offer thanks. He takes his place for the tea and fruit. On the following day, the Abbot invites him for tea; the administrative head (dusi) [performs the same].
A vegetarian feast is prepared, along with an invitation for tea and mid-morning refreshments; on another day, a formal reception is arranged. The abbot ascends the hall to express his gratitude.

Nowadays, in various quarters, the heat of the summer retreat and the cold of New Year’s Eve are avoided, and these rites are abandoned. Consequently, those in later generations have nothing upon which to model themselves.
Alternatively, one may request that the West Hall Abbot of the Great Dharma Assembly be appointed.

On the third night, during the abbot’s *xiaocan* (small sermon), one should earnestly and persuasively invite him to expound upon the *suixi* (following the breath) and to present *gong'an* (public cases) with verses and commentaries. To thus successively stimulate and exalt this Way—how could this be a trivial matter?
The Supplementary Manual for Zen Forests, Volume Two;
The Supplementary Manual for Zen Forests, Volume Three;
Compiled at the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi* Assembly.

The Hall Attendant prepares incense and candles according to the ritual protocol. He personally petitions the Secretary to compose the formal documents (*shu*), following the same procedure as for the Opening Ceremony.

The ritual diagrams and registers are prepared in advance. On the fifteenth day before the ceremony, the assembly convenes; those brothers who provide musical accompaniment serve as the *Lengyan* leaders.

The *Venerable of the Ritual Office* (*weina*) leads them to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to pay respects, and they subsequently proceed to the Kitchen Administration (*kusu*) to pay their respects. They are all invited to partake of refreshments (*dianxin*), with the *Venerable of the Ritual Office* acting as their host.

When the appointed time arrives, the attendants of the Hall Office post a notice to inform the various quarters, strike the board while patrolling the corridors, and ring the bell before the Sangha Hall to assemble the community.

They stand according to their designated positions in the diagram; the incense is offered and the assembly steps forward from their ranks. The attendant holds the incense case. Next, the West Hall Preceptors stand in formation, followed by the two classes of officers offering incense.

Incense is not borrowed for this occasion. The entire assembly performs three full prostrations with the robes fully spread out. To realize enlightenment within a fixed period is an extraordinary matter indeed.
At present, it is improper not to prostrate because of the incense and candles. The *Vīnā* (Chant Leader) announces the *shū* (petition) to the Buddha.

Upon reaching the phrase "Rightly Vowing," the Abbot kneels before the incense burner, passes the burner, and presents the offering bowl; the ritual is identical to that for the Buddha’s Birthday. When the *shū* is finished—(The *Lengyan-tou* [Leader of the Śūraṅgama Assembly] chants "Śūraṅgama Assembly Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" three times.

After the assembly has chanted together, they rise. At that time, the World-Honored One says: [Recite the mantra]. Once the recitation is complete, the *Vīnā* performs the dedication, saying: "By the merit of the sutra recitation above, we dedicate it to the True Suchness and Ultimate Reality, to adorn the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha-fruit, and to the Four Graces."
"Equal retribution. The three realms of existence are equally sustained," and so forth. "All [beings] of the ten directions and three periods of time," and so forth.

Aside from the birthday celebrations held in the Zangdian (Sutra Hall) on the first and fifteenth days of the month, during the *Śūraṅgama* Assembly, the birthday celebration likewise takes place; however, this is specifically for the dedication of merit performed by the *Vina* (Choir Master).
The daily verse for universal dedication is written and posted on both sides so that beginners may easily see it. At the conclusion of the ritual, the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* must first be chanted;

the rector (*vina*) then proclaims the memorial text (*shu*). The rites of worship are the same as those performed at the opening of the retreat. According to the ancient method, after the evening meal has been dismissed, the monks chant at the head of the mountain gate.
Master Zhenxie, while residing at Mount Jing, remarked that because the assembly was not single-minded in their devotion, this practice should instead take place after the morning gruel.
Every day, the attendant of the Hall Office reports to the Rector, the Head Seat, the administrative officers, and the Abbot.

He then patrols the corridors and strikes the wooden board three times, followed by the striking of the bell before the Sangha Hall. The assembly gathers in the Great Hall and stands according to their assigned positions in the seating chart to chant.

The Verse of Universal Dedication was composed by the Venerable Master Zhenxie himself. One can truly know that when a venerable elder of such name and conduct makes a single pronouncement, it becomes the universal standard throughout the four seas.

Verse of Petition to the Buddha: "O Wondrously Profound, All-Holding, Immovable Honored One, Suraṅgama King, rare in this world! May you dissolve my inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas, So that I may attain the Dharma-body without passing through the aeons of saṃsāra. I look up with hope for your vast compassion."

Humbly looking upward for your illuminating discernment: [Name], Abbot of [Name] Temple in [Name] Prefecture. On the fifteenth day of this month, coinciding with the commencement of the retreat of our Great Master Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Great Monk, we have prepared in advance on the thirteenth day to reverently establish an auspicious assembly of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* at the Great Buddha Treasure Hall.

We have arranged incense, flowers, lamps, and candles to extend our offerings. The assembly of bhikṣus shall chant the Divine Mantra of the Supreme *Śūraṅgama* of the Great Buddha-Crown and extol the holy name.
Having offered the merit thus accumulated to the divine seat—herein, as it is said: "Rightly, we humbly consider... (etc.).
Universal Dedication. The above verses were recited by the assembly of bhikṣus present here, chanting the Secret Mantra of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra.

This merit is dedicated to the assembly of Dharma-protecting beings—the dragons, devas, local deities, monasteries, and all the holy ones—so that those in the three miserable realms and the eight difficulties may all be freed from suffering, and that the four debts of gratitude and all beings within the three worlds may fully receive its grace.
May the realm be peaceful and secure, may weapons and warfare be extinguished, and may the winds and rains be harmonious and timely.
The people are healthy and joyful; the entire assembly redoubles their cultivation, hoping for further advancement. To leap suddenly to the ten stages will be without difficulty;
the mountain gate remains tranquil, free from all misfortune. Lay patrons take refuge, increasing their merit and wisdom. All Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time...
All Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas. The Great Prajñāpāramitā.
(Invocation) Herein we humbly gaze upon the mark of the invisible crown, from which jewel-light surges forth, proclaiming the emanated Buddhas.
At the city of Śrāvastī, the supreme banner was erected, dissolving the illusory delusions of Māraṇḍa. May the secret canon be eternally adorned.

Having vowed to uphold this extensively, we enter upon the long-term summer retreat, commencing from this very day. With one voice we shall proclaim it far and wide, so that the forests and ponds shall all resound with the Dharma.
May all beings universally receive its benefit, and may every wriggling creature and sentient being alike be graced with its bounty.
We reverently pray:
May the Sage Emperor eternally maintain his sagacious calculations, surpassing the lifespan of the Great Chun tree by sixteen thousand years.

May the House of Anāthapiṇḍada truly assist the flourishing court, with auspiciousness radiating in grand and magnificent splendor. May the assembly of the ocean-like multitude realize the intent of the single transmission, and may the Jeta Grove gather the portents of eternal stability.
