This humble petitioner [Name], unable to contain his most earnest and anxious sentiments, respectfully submits this memorial. (Date)
The vast and pure breath ascends into the void at the Bodhimanda. The ninety-day retreat is completed; the fragrant breeze disperses at dawn as the *Śūraṅgama* is realized.
With the myriad practices perfected, together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, we uphold this mantra-heart. Thus, the entire assembly of bhikṣus has attained the full power of the Way.
We respectfully offer this extraordinary benefit to look up and repay the gracious repose of our Original Teacher, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, the Great Harmony.

Furthermore, I humbly observe that you have widely fanned the true wind, utterly sweeping away the demonic strongholds; you have poured down the rain of Dharma, nourishing and causing the withered and parched to flourish and grow. How joyful!
Ultimate transformation is achieved through non-action; the transmission of the orthodox lineage shall endure forever (and so forth).
The *Lengyan* Assembly is illustrated for the supplementary period;
the various quarters observe the summer retreat.

In the fourth lunar month, the head of the quarters (Liaoyuan) arranges the following: the diagram for the scripture cabinets (jinggui), the diagram for tea and soup services, the ordination seniority plaques (jilabai), the plaque indicating the order of entry into the quarters, and the plaque for shaving the hair.
These are arranged according to ordination seniority. The scripture cabinets are divided into four sections. If there are many people, those with junior ordination share a cabinet;
however, it is contrary to the Dharma for an elder to occupy two cabinets himself while forcing those with junior ordination to share one. During the summer retreat...
The "Diagram of the Tea Service Vessel and Cups" (Juxing chashang pingzhan tu) is displayed. Those among the brothers who share a karmic connection may write their names upon it as they please;

this is to establish a bond with the assembly. After the Hall Office has brought forth the diagram and register, and following the morning gruel, the assembly bows in greeting. At that time, the diagram is displayed in the corridor.
(Various hanging plaques follow the standard protocols observed in all quarters).

On the afternoon of the twelfth day of the fourth month, the hall attendants (dangsi haengja) informed the Abbot’s quarters, the two ranks of officials, and all the monastic lodgings that the remaining quarters would hang their plaques for the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* recitation.

Announce to the assembly. Recite the sutras. The head of the quarters shall sweep and sprinkle the interior and exterior of the quarters. Prepare a formal petition in advance to invite the honored assembly of the entire quarters for a special tea service.
Set out the name plaque; the small-seat tea name plaque is to be offered before Guanyin. Incense and candles are prepared for both the upper and lower sections. Pre-boil the tea.

First, invite the assembly for the small-seat tea, specifically serving the tea from the pitcher and cups to the Head of the Quarters, the Assistant Head of the Quarters, and the fellow practitioners (brothers).
The Abbot personally invites the Head of the Quarters (Liaozhang) to serve as his attendant. They bow to take their seats, bow for incense, and bow for tea.

The Head of the Quarters personally escorts the Abbot to the quarters to offer tea, distributing it to all the various quarters. (After the tea service and the small seating session are concluded, the large board is struck in front of the quarters. The Head of the Quarters and the assembly take their seats.

He has already invited the Rector (Weina) and the Attendant (Shizhe) to serve as attendants. They bow to take their seats. The Head of the Quarters faces the Head of the Quarters’ seat, and they distribute the light [of the tea] between them.

[The Master] attends. Regarding the seating arrangement for the assembly: the Head of the Quarters (Liaozhu) and the Assistant Head (Fuliao) arrange the seats and perform the rites. They bow to the seats, bow to the incense, and bow to the hot water.

When the three rounds are completed, the Head of the Quarters proceeds before the brazier to offer thanks for the hot water. Then, the board in front of the quarters is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats. The two classes of officers enter the quarters;

the Head Seat (Shouzuo) and the Chief Administrator (Dusi) burn incense, then return to their respective positions in the ranks. The Head of the Quarters (Liaoyuan) stands outside the door on the right.

He waits to escort the abbot into his quarters. Once they have entered the *liao* (monastic cell) and finished offering incense, he recites the *Śūraṅgama-mantra* and performs the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). He then sees the abbot out the door.
On the twelfth day of the seventh month, the ritual for dispersing the assembly is performed as before.

Formal Memorial (Submitted by the monk on duty in the quarters: [Name]. Hereby, [Name] respectfully requests that this evening, while at the quarters, a single pot of medicinal broth be prepared specifically for the venerable assembly of the entire monastery, as a modest mark of the ritual for the commencement of the retreat.

We humbly entreat the compassion of the assembly to deign to descend in person. Respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. Submitted by the monk on duty in the quarters: [Name]).
(Ke Lou) Formally requests the venerable assembly of Chan masters of this monastery and the bhikṣus maintaining the quarters: I, [Name], respectfully seal and dedicate this merit.
The Sovereign of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, Wondrously Profound, All-Upholding, and Immovable, is a rarity in this world; may it extinguish my billions...
To overturn the deluded perceptions of kalpas and, without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, to attain the Dharmakāya:

At a certain monastery in a certain province, within the Sandalwood Grove, I, the bhikṣu [Name], keeper of the quarters, on the fifteenth day of this month, reverently encounter my original teacher, the Great Upādhyāya Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
On this occasion of the commencement of the retreat, we have prepared these offerings in advance to extend our worship.

We assemble the community of bhikṣus to chant the Great Buddha-Top Myriad Practices Śūraṅgama Divine Mantra and to proclaim the sacred name. (The extraordinary merit thus accumulated is first dedicated to:
May the present Emperor enjoy ten thousand years of peace and security. Next, we extend our dedication toward the True Suchness and the Ultimate Reality, adorning the Unsurpassed.
To the Buddha-fruit Bodhi; to the protective deities who offer prayers; to the great empowered sovereigns; to the myriad spirits of the three realms;

to the holy assemblies of the ten directions; to the presiding stellar officials of one’s natal destiny; to the monastic community and the celestial phenomena of their birth; to the mountains, rivers, and streams; to the local administrative seats and the precincts of the region;
to the ancestral shrines near and far; to the watching and protecting deities; and to the local tutelary deity of this mountain (listing the positions within the temple)—first, the vow:
The imperial wind fans forever; the sovereign way flourishes afar. The Buddha-sun increases its brilliance, and the Wheel of Dharma turns constantly.

Next, we pray that the mountain gates remain tranquil and both the internal and external realms be at peace. May all matters concerning fire and theft, whether public or private, be auspicious and celebratory.

May the present monastic community practice in orderly succession, advancing on the Path without demonic interference. May Prajñā-wisdom manifest before them, and may their Bodhicitta never regress. [May they repay] the four debts of gratitude.
Universal Vow: May all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, supported equally by the three realms of existence, together realize the Perfect Wisdom.

All those newly enrolled from the ten directions and the three periods of time—after entering the quarters for tea—shall pay the departmental fees according to custom and await the head of the quarters to arrange the date on which tea will be served. Upon enrollment, [the new member] shall...
Announce to the assembly: (On the left, it says: "After the meal, so-and-so shall take the seat of honor to serve tea. One must prepare fine incense and assume a dignified demeanor.
Wait for those who are to serve tea on the same day; first, hang up the alms bowl and exit the hall. Pre-arrange the assembly in front of the monks' quarters, standing in rows in the lower section.

Upon hearing the striking of the hall bell, the tea server immediately strikes the large board in front of the quarters to welcome the assembly with a bow and lead them back to the quarters, where each person takes their place according to the original seating chart.
The positions are established. Following the entry into the hall, they stand in single file. They inquire after one another and bow to the assembly as they take their seats.
They inquire once more. Each advances before the incense burner; two by two, they burn incense. If there are many people, four from the center of the row step back, doing so with deliberate slowness.
Once again, they stand in single file and inquire after one another. They advance to the four head-positions to inquire, then withdraw. Finally, they stand in single file and inquire once more.
This is called the "Bowing Incense" (Yi-xiang). Strike the small board inside the quarters twice. Serve tea to everyone. The tea pitcher must enter through the central hall.

After performing a greeting, proceed to the head of the four boards; after performing another greeting, withdraw. Stand facing the assembly with a single-file greeting. Strike the small board once. Collect the cups.

When the assembly has descended from their seats and is standing still, the Head of the Quarters (Liao-yuan) goes before the brazier and, on behalf of the assembly, expresses thanks for the tea to the person serving it.

The assembly expresses their thanks. The assembly takes their seats and simultaneously bows in greeting. Having finished expressing their thanks, the Head of the Quarter (Liaoyuan) returns to his position.

Once again, each group divides into four sections at the head of the rows and bows in greeting. This is to express gratitude for the assembly’s presence and to demonstrate the principle of mutual respect.

Generally, when tea is served in the Sangha Hall, it is specifically prepared for this occasion and consists of three rounds. The assembly once again bows in a single file. The large board is struck three times; the assembly—

They pay their respects by bowing and disperse. The head of the quarters (Liaoyuan) orders the tea attendant (Chadou) to invite [the assembly] for tea. When everyone has finished drinking the tea, those who have been exempted from the duty do so; this would be a breach of propriety.
Annually, during the summer, tea is served according to one's seniority in the monastic precepts (Jielao).

After the tea service in the quarters is concluded, every day tea is served according to the full list of names arranged by seniority (*jì*). The ritual procedures are identical to those previously described.

In the great monastic communities (*cónglín*), the *cǎodān* (temporary residence list) is hung up; on the first day of the third month, the *cǎodān* is removed and the hanging of names ceases. The Hall Administration (*tángsī*) arranges and writes the list according to seniority.
Regarding the number of monks: the attendant of the Hall Office shall first present the list to the Head Seat, and subsequently to the Abbot and the two classes of officials.
A table, brushes, and inkstone shall be prepared and set out before the Sangha Hall or before the communal quarters for three days. Should there be any errors, please correct them yourselves;

should matters involve significant implications, report them in detail to the Rector (Vina). The Rector shall conduct a fair inspection with skillful means; private vendettas or acts intended to cause disturbance are strictly prohibited.
[This] destroys the Dharma of the forest community.
[The seating order for the assembly is as follows: (The pure assembly’s years of seniority; the precepts of King Vimalacitra; the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya; the Abbot; the precepts of the Yuan year;
the Senior Monk So-and-so—all are arranged and written according to the sequence of their ordination).
(The above is provided in full as previously stated. Fearing there may be errors, we hope you will correct them yourself. We humbly await your favor.
[All members] (Today, [Date]. Prepared by the Hall Superintendent, [Name]).

Lu has completed the draft of the seating chart for the retreat. Based on the precepts, he has transcribed the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and performed recitations. He has arranged the order of the hall, the seating positions, and the bowl positions. He has also drawn up the plaques indicating the seniority of the precepts (*śīla-varga*).

Regarding the bowl positions alone, they are divided into sixteen sections; once the ranking of names and status has been determined and the seating has been finalized, [the preparations] are made in advance.
Prepare the draft. Consult with the Head Seat (Shouzuo). Present it to the Abbot for review and obtain his signature. This will ensure that no disputes arise at the last moment.
As for the original copies of the various charts, have the attendants of the Hall Office present each one to the Abbot.

The Head Seat and the two classes of officers shall present the bowl-seating chart to their private quarters and the Monks’ Hall (Mengtang) for the senior monks. On the day of the Buddha-Bathing Ceremony, present them all together in the Buddha Hall.
First, inform the assembly of the seating arrangement for the *pātra* (alms bowl). Furthermore, one must first prepare the seating chart for the *pātra*.
On the morning of that day, before the early congee has been served, post notices at the front and rear doors of the Sangha Hall and illuminate them with candles.

Diagram of Descending from the Hall. Arranged before the hall (Format for the note: After the gruel meal, the bedding and alms bowls are arranged in their respective positions. I humbly request that all members take note. Noted by [Name] of the Hall Administration).

Yang: The ordination rank tablets for the Hall Administration (Tangsi), the Attendant Administration (Shisishi), and the various quarters (Zhongliao) shall be prepared in advance according to the seniority of ordination. On the afternoon of the fourteenth day, the tablets of the Hall Administration shall be arranged in the upper section in front of the Sangha Hall;

those of the Attendant shall be arranged in the lower section of the Dharma Hall; and those of the various quarters shall be arranged within their respective quarters. Each [tablet] shall be placed accordingly.
The *zhuofu* (table), incense, and candles are set out for offerings. The assembly each burns incense and performs prostrations (after which they each withdraw their offerings).

At the abbot’s quarters, the "Small Seat Soup" (*xiaozuo tang*) is traditionally served during the four seasonal festivals; nowadays, it is only offered once at the commencement of the summer retreat. Lest the brethren rely on their strength to vie for high or low positions, [the following protocol is observed].
Consequently, [the practice] was discontinued; it has long been unheard of in the monastic communities (*saṃghārāma*), which is truly lamentable.

The abbot should ascend the hall for a formal discourse (*upadeśa*) prior to the summer retreat, offering detailed exhortations so that they may respect one another and dwell together in the six harmonies. According to the established ritual, there are three seats. The first seat is divided into two positions:

the head seat (*shouzuo*) of the East Hall and the head seat of the West Hall, who serve as the primary companions. The second seat consists of four positions: the two classes of senior monks (*qizhong*).

1. The former Head (Jù tóushǒu) comes forth. 2. The Administrative Officers (Zhīshì) come forth. 3. The elders of the West Hall (Xībān) come forth. 4. The elders of the East Hall (Dōngbān) come forth. 5.
The West Hall Attendant (Xītáng guāngbàn) takes the third seat; he generally comes forth six times. 6.

Those who have served in administrative duties at this mountain (Běnshān bànshì) or in various other places (Zhūfāng bànshì), including the Head Seat (Shǒuzuò) acting as an attendant, take their seats according to the rank of their respective offices. Those with identical offices follow in succession. The Service Office (Shìsī) prepares the arrangements in advance.

A rough sketch is presented to the Abbot for deliberation and determination; should there be slight discrepancies, all must exercise forbearance. On the appointed day, according to the names [on the list], the name-boards are inscribed.
In the afternoon, tables and cloths are prepared, and one, two, or three seats are arranged in a row in the lower section of the dormitory hall.

The head of the Eastern and Western Halls and the Head of the Administrative Office (Dusi) each go to their respective quarters to invite the guests by prostrating themselves; if an invitation is declined, this must be reported.

[The bell] tolls: "The Abbot requests that tonight, in the Hall for Resting, a special offering of hot water be made [for him]. The remaining head officers, the various quarters, the abbot’s quarters, the guest master, and the attendants announce:

"The Abbot of the Abbot’s Quarters requests, prior to the evening assembly, that a special offering of hot water be made in the Hall for Resting. Once the seats have been arranged and hung in the Hall for Resting, the candles are lit and the incense is prepared.
The guest-head attendant covers the chamberlain, followed by the covering of the Abbot’s quarters. The drum is struck, and the guests for the initial session assemble.

The chamberlain welcomes the Abbot with a bow, receives his greetings regarding the weather, and leads them to their positions where they stand still. The chamberlain specifically bows before the person of honor, then circumambulates to bow to those seated and inquire after their well-being.
Once everyone is seated, he returns to the center and burns a single stick of incense. He proceeds before the person of honor, bows for the incense, inquires after their well-being, and returns.

Stand in the center. Strike the wooden board twice. Serve hot water. Return to the front of the person for whom the special service is intended; bow to the hot water and inquire after their well-being. Return to the center and burn the *guāngbàn* incense.
Strike the wooden board once. Withdraw the bowls. Strike the drum three times. Retire from the seat. Second Seat: Guests assemble. Welcome them as they enter and stand in their positions.
The two attendants look up and down at one another. Circulate and inquire after their well-being. Bow to them as they sit and burn the incense. One.
[The incense] wick. [The participants] circumambulate by position, bowing for the incense and the hot water. Burn the *guāngbàn* incense. Withdraw the bowls. Strike the drum three times.
Retire from the seats (arrange the ritual implements and express thanks for the hot water; if this is waived, perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloths. This is the same for every seat).

Third Seat: When the guests have assembled, they are received and the ritual greetings are performed as before. Since this seat is largely occupied by the heads of the various sections, one must inquire after them in their proper order;
only then will the refined etiquette be maintained.

On the fourteenth day of the fourth month, the Monastery Administration (Kusi) and the Guest Master (Kektou) attendants prepare the notice for the special soup offering for the Sangha Hall, along with the ceremonial cloths, the incense burner, and candles. Following the midday meal, they proceed to the hall.
The head administrator goes to the abbot’s quarters to request hot water. Approaching the abbot, he offers incense, spreads his formal sitting cloth (*kaji*), and says:

"Tonight, in the Cloud Hall, we shall specially serve hot water for the Head Seat and the assembly. We humbly beseech the Venerable Master to graciously deign to attend us. He performs two prostrations with the sitting cloth spread and three prostrations touching the ground. The abbot returns one prostration.

If the abbot declines the prostrations, the administrator performs three prostrations touching the ground while announcing the request, then withdraws. Immediately, he leads the guest attendant (*kakutō*) to the Head Seat.

In the quarters, the attendants place the tray upon the table. The Abbot steps forward and offers incense; the Head Seat returns the incense. The administrative officers (zhishi) assume the posture for unfolding their sitting cloths;

if they are exempted from this, they perform a prostration with touching of foreheads (*chubai*). He reports: "This evening, we shall serve hot soup specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly in the Cloud Hall. We humbly pray that you will, out of compassion, deign to grace us with your presence.

Having presented the notice to the Head Seat, once he has accepted it, he orders the Guest Master to hand it to the Provisions Master, who shall post it on the lower section of the front wall of the Sangha Hall.

The guest master replied accordingly: "The administrative office (kusi) has finished the invitation for the medicinal soup; please take your seats for the meal. Next, the head officers, the retired elders, the *mōngtáng*, and the various department heads [were invited].

In front of the various quarters and the Sangha Hall, a "Soup-Serving Sign" (dian-tang-pai) is hung for each; having invited everyone individually, a "Mirror-Board" (zhao-pai) is arranged in front of the Sangha Hall.
Seats are set up facing one another for the Head Seat (shouzuo) and the Abbot (zhuchi), with the name-boards of the assembly placed above and below them.

The attendant in charge of offerings (gongtou) is ordered to arrange a special table and chair behind the lattice screen (guasi), along with mats, bowls, plates, vegetable cups, spoons, and chopsticks. A novice (xingzhe) is assigned to attend to the person who is being specially honored.
After the recitation in the Land Hall (Tandiang) is completed, the drum for the meal is struck once in front of the storehouse hall.

The assembly returns to their bowl-positions. The group of head monks (shousuo) returns to the front board; the administrators (zhishi) follow them in and bow. The Head Seat (shouzuo) leaves his position and bows. Next, the head monks take their seats in order of seniority.
They escort the Head Seat to his special seat, where they exchange formal greetings. He exits to the right behind the shrine (kan), and the Abbot is welcomed as he enters.
In the Hall, the *gongtou* (officer in charge of offerings) slowly strikes the front hall bell seven times. The administrative officers enter their positions and perform a bow (*wensun*).

Turning around, they specifically bow before the person at the head of the row, then exit to the right. Following the head seat’s bench, they perform a series of bows as they complete one circuit. They then exit the outer hall.

First, descend from the upper section to the lower section. Return to the hall and stand in the center to perform a greeting (*monshin*). When the assembly is seated, step forward to burn incense. Next, proceed through the upper and lower sections and the outer hall.
Once you have returned to the hall and closed the door, go immediately before the person for whom the service is specifically intended to perform a greeting.

Exit to the right and perform a greeting before the Abbot. Circumambulate the hall performing greetings once, including the outer hall, then return to the center to perform a greeting. Stand to one side. The bell is struck.
Two strikes on the hall bell. First, the special bath for the individual is served; then the bath for the assembly is served. The pitcher is brought out. Returning to the center, one bows in inquiry.
Going before the person for whom the special bath is intended, one bows in inquiry. Exiting to the right, one performs three full prostrations with the robes spread wide before the Holy Monk.

Circumambulating the hall once, one exits the outer hall and leads the entire assembly inside. The Abbot goes forward first to perform the rites. For the first spreading of the robes, he says: "On this day, the coarse bath is specially prepared for the Venerable Master."

[The petitioner] bows deeply. [He states: "Your humble servant is overcome with the utmost gratitude. The second exchange says: "On this day of the early summer month, at this auspicious time, we respectfully wish that the Venerable Master’s health and daily life may enjoy ten thousand blessings. Immediately, [the petitioner] performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*sōrei*).

The Abbot returns one bow. [The petitioner] returns to his position. The entire group of administrators (*chiji*) turns right from behind the Sacred Monk (*shōsō*), proceeds directly to the upper hand in front of the hall, and stands in their respective order.
The Head Seat (*shuso*) follows by turning right and exiting; they perform a single prostration with unopened sitting cloths facing each other.

Prostrate. Thank the hot water. Return and enter from behind the kitchen, turning to the left, and take your place. The administrative official (zhishi) returns to the center, burns one stick of incense, and withdraws.
The attendant of the Hall Office (tangsi) calls out: "I request the assembly to lower their bowls. The attendant advances with the special table for the abbot.

Once the assembly has unfolded their bowls, the medicinal food (yao-shi) is served. When the meal is finished, the drum is struck three times; they leave their seats. [The drum] is not struck [for departure].
The bell for descending from the hall is struck. The attendants line up outside the board area and wait for the abbot to emerge from the hall; they then bow in greeting and exit together with him.

When the assembly disperses, the remaining protocols are identical to this rite. However, on the winter solstice, after the serving of hot water, fruit is distributed before the medicinal food (yao-shi) is served.
Notice: The Administrative Office (Kusi) respectfully announces that this evening, in the Cloud Hall (Yuntang), one serving of medicinal soup will be served.

This is specially prepared for the Head Seat and the assembly to briefly commemorate the formal observance of the commencement of the retreat. We humbly entreat the compassion of the assembly to deign to descend and grace us with your presence.
On this day of this month, The Bhikṣu [Name] of the Administrative Office respectfully informs you.
Write seven lines of calligraphy; the characters should be the size of small coins. Use either plain paper or fine stationery as you prefer.

On the morning of the fifteenth day of the fourth month, when the retreat begins and the ritual is performed, the attendants (*shizhe*), those who have previously served, junior disciples (*xiaoshi*), and practitioners (*xingzhe*) shall all insert [the slips].

Incense Offering and Prostrations: If one sees the notice posted before the Sangha Hall stating that the incense offering has begun, everyone need not go early to the Abbot’s quarters for formal greetings.

When the Abbot arrives at the various halls for the incense offering, the Attendant of the Abbot’s Quarters shall hang the "Plaque for Entering the Hall" in the Sangha Hall, the Community Lodgings, the Meditation Hall, and the four quarters, and notify the assembly. He shall also inform the Head Monks and the Elders residing in single quarters.

[The Master] said: "When the meal is finished and the Abbot ascends the hall for the formal conclusion of the session, the Abbot shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual proceedings once, so that everyone may understand.

Then he says, 'Descend from the seat. First, one performs the ritual greetings with the Dongtang; next, the ritual greetings with the Xitang, performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*).

When these greetings are concluded, one performs the ritual greetings with the administrative officers (*zhishi*), performing two unfoldings and three prostrations. Next, [one greets] the Chief Seat (*shouzuo*)."

The assembly performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloths and three full prostrations (*sanbai*) as a matter of courtesy. Once the courtesy has been concluded, the *zhishi* (officer in charge) first returns to the *kusisi* (storehouse office).
The *shouzuo* (head seat) leads the assembly to the *kusisi* to perform courtesy; they perform three prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*chuli*).

When the courtesy is finished, the *shouzuo* returns to the upper section of the hall in front of the *sengtang* (monks' hall), while the *houtang shouzuo* (head seat of the rear hall) leads the assembly to the lower section in front of the *sengtang* to perform courtesy with the *shouzuo*, performing three prostrations with opened sitting cloths.
Perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). Once the human affairs are concluded, stand in position according to the diagram for recitation.

The Head Seat (*shouzuo*) leads the assembly into the hall and circumambulates it, then stands in their respective positions. The Head Seat expresses gratitude to the assembly by performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground.

Next, the administrative officers (*zhishi*) enter the hall, burn one incense stick, perform three full prostrations (*dazhan*), and circumambulate the hall once. The administrative officers express gratitude to the assembly by performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground.

Prostrations. Exit the hall. The Abbot enters the hall, burns one stick of incense, performs three full prostrations with the robes spread out, circumambulates the hall once, and returns to his position.

He exchanges greetings with the assembly, performing three prostrations with the head touching the ground. Thereafter, the assembly collectively performs a formal salutation. They wait in order for the Abbot to visit the various quarters and descend from the seat.
The attendant in charge of guests (kètóu xíngzhě) then advances with the incense table, burner, and candles, arranging them in a single row in front. First...

The duties of the East Hall Master; next, the duties of the West Hall Master; next, the class of administrative officers (*zhishi*) proceed forward and insert incense. The first formal address is recited:

"At this time of the summer retreat, having obtained the opportunity to rely upon [the Master’s] robes and staff, we earnestly depend upon the Dharma-power of the Venerable Abbot for support, that no difficulties may arise. The second address is recited: "On this day of early summer, at the proper season, we respectfully wish that the Abbot of the Hall enjoys ten thousand blessings in his health and daily life.

Immediately, they perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*). The Abbot replies with one prostration, saying: "In being permitted to dwell together in this retreat, I also hope..."

Supported by the power of the Dharma, may there be no difficulties or obstacles. One group of administrative officers (zhishi) returns to the Treasury Office (kusisi). Those who yield precedence and perform prostrations do so for the sake of receiving the Head Seat (shouzuo) and the assembly.
Led by the Head Seat, the assembly steps forward to offer incense, performs two full prostrations with hands extended (liangzhan) and three prostrations (sanbai).

Next, the members of the Meditation Hall (mantang) and the four dormitories (siliao) offer incense, perform two full prostrations with hands extended and three prostrations; the wording of their address is identical to that of the administrative officers. At each extension of the prostration, the Abbot (zhuchi) returns the bow.
Next, the former residents, fellow villagers, dharma relatives, and lay associates offer incense and perform prostrations.

Once this is completed, the attendants at the guest office of the abbot’s quarters bring forward a screened chair. The abbot then sits cross-legged. A group of attendants steps forward, offers incense, and performs nine prostrations.
Next, the junior attendant in charge of affairs offers incense and performs nine prostrations (performing only three prostrations today is improper, as it interferes with the assembly).
Next, the head attendant (*canchou*) and the line of attendants offer incense and perform three prostrations.

If it is during winter or a festival, the senior attendants before the quarters, the sedan-chair attendants for the Abbot, those on duty in the hall, and the *gongguoren* (those who have passed through) must all announce their presence and pay respects. The Head Seat leads the assembly to...

Regarding the administrative affairs of the storehouse: the *chiji* (administrative official) and the gatekeeper receive [the guest] and lead him inside. They perform a bow before the incense burner in the storehouse hall.

Facing the [image], they perform three prostrations with hands touching the ground. The words of the petition are: "The sacred regulations have now arrived, and we are fortunate to dwell together in this retreat.

We rely solely upon the power of the Way for support, so that no difficulties may arise; our humble feelings of gratitude are beyond measure. The *chiji* replies: "These are indeed the sacred regulations. We are deeply honored to dwell together here."
Relying on the spiritual power and support of the Head Seat and the assembly, may there be no demonic obstacles. [The attendant] escorts the assembly out.
Next, the Head Seat of the Rear Hall leads the assembly and stands fixed at the lower section in front of the Sangha Hall. The Head Seat of the Front Hall moves to the upper section.

The attendant of the Hall Administration (Tangsi Xingzhe) calls out: "The assembly pays their respects to the Head Seat. [The Head Seat] performs three prostrations with touching of foreheads (dui-chu li). He steps forward and says: "As the year begins anew, we have been able to dwell together in this summer retreat. We earnestly rely upon..."

"May the power of the Dharma sustain us, and may there be no demonic interference. The reply was: "We have obtained the opportunity to dwell together in retreat; fearing that our three karmas may not be virtuous, we venture to hope for your magnanimity so that we may together establish this Dharma community.

When the formal affairs were concluded, the Head Seat led the assembly and stood in formation according to the diagram for recitation. They proceeded in order through the hall and returned to their positions to stand. (The attendant circulates through half the hall, and the ritual assistant calls out: He said:

(The Head Seat bows in thanks to the assembly) and performs three prostrations with the whole body (*pūtóng chùlǐ*). Next, the group of administrators (*zhīshì*) enters the hall, burns one incense stick, and performs three full prostrations (*dàzhǎn sānbài*).

They circumambulate the hall once and stand in a row before the incense burner. They call out, and (the administrators bow in thanks to the assembly), performing three prostrations with the whole body.
The administrators exit the hall, followed by the group of attendants (*shìzhě*) who exit after them. Next, the Abbot enters the hall to make offerings.

The bell at the head of the hall is struck seven times. The Abbot burns incense and performs three prostrations with opened sitting cloth (*sanbai*). He circumambulates the hall once and returns to his place.
The junior disciples merely join their palms, bow their heads, and exit through the rear door. This is to avoid disorder. He then calls out: "The Hall Head Monk and the assembly exchange greetings.

Everyone performs three prostrations with touched heads (*santurei*). Again he calls out: "The assembly shall all together perform a salutation. Everyone together performs three prostrations with touched heads.

The attendant returns to the center to inquire after the master’s well-being. He bows to the assembly and seats them. He proceeds to the central incense burner to burn incense in both the upper and lower sections, as well as in the outer hall.

Having returned the incense sticks to their original places, he withdraws slightly, stands in the center to inquire after the master’s well-being, and then performs inquiries after the well-being of those in the upper and lower sections and the outer hall.
Return to the center and stand. Ring the bell twice; the tea pitcher is brought out. Once again, circulate and inquire after everyone's well-being as before, then stand in the center.
Ring the bell once; collect the bowls. Ring it three more times and descend from the hall. Wait in succession for the inspection of the quarters.

The attendants set up chairs and tables in the central bay of the Dharma Hall. Ring the Abbot’s board three times; the Resident Master emerges and proceeds along the eastern corridor, circling until he reaches the west.
When the time arrives, go before the quarters and enter solemnly to offer incense. The abbot receives the incense; escort him out, and upon his command, collect the incense that was offered.

Immediately move the incense table to the front of the door, and follow behind as you proceed on the inspection tour. Attendants and junior disciples shall not receive the incense within the quarters.
At the front of the Kūsi (Storehouse) and the Mōngtáng (Dining Hall), the various quarters for those with seniority stand outside the door on the lower side. They receive the abbot as he enters.

Incense is offered. The assembly escorts the abbot out and lines up outside the gate. They wait for the person who patrols the quarters (*xunliao ren*) to follow behind them as they proceed to the Dharma Hall.
Once there, the abbot stands fixed by the incense burner. Then, the third person leads the way, bowing in greeting as they pass.

Each party stands before their respective quarters until the entire circuit is completed without omission. During the summer retreat, it is intensely hot; during the winter months, it is bitterly cold.
Exemption from formal bows is contrary to the Dharma.
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month, during the rain, the Abbot specially prepares tea for the Head Seat and the assembly.
After the morning gruel, the Guest Master Attendant writes the tea invitation; the Guest-Master’s attendant prepares the trays.
Carrying the incense box, burner, and candles, he proceeds to the Head Seat’s quarters (*shouzuo liao*). He offers incense and performs a prostration with contact (*chubai*) to invite him.

The Head Seat responds by accepting the incense and responding to the prostration. The Attendant (*shizhe*) reports: "The Abbot (*tangtou heshang*), having finished his midday meal this morning, will serve tea in the Cloud Hall (*yuntang*) specifically for you; we humbly hope that you will condescend to attend out of compassion. He then presents the formal notice (*bang*).

Once the Head Seat has accepted it, he escorts the Attendant out and instructs the Guest Master (*ketou*) to deliver it to the Offering Master (*gongtou*), who shall post it above the entrance of the Sangha Hall.
Next, the head of the quarters (shoushou) and the various attendants of the various halls, including the guest master (ketou), post the notice and issue the invitation.
Only the administrative staff (zhishi) announce: "We request your presence. The guest attendant (qingke shizhe) is instructed in advance to strike the long board slowly.

When the time arrives, they enter the hall, burn one stick of incense, perform three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (dazhan sanbai), and circumambulate the hall once. Upon reaching the outer hall, they proceed first from the lower section to the upper section.
Return to the hall. After making a formal inquiry (wenson) in the center, withdraw. Pre-announce the preparation of hot water and have the cups, tea sets, and utensils brought out.

When the meal is finished, the incense-burning attendant instructs the guest master of the abbot’s quarters to set up special name-boards (*chōhapa*) in front of the Sangha Hall. Seats are arranged opposite the Abbot for the Head Seat;

the senior administrative officers sit on either side of the Abbot, with the Rector (*vinaya-dhara*) in the next position, followed by the junior administrative officers. Special seating is provided for the [specific guests].
To arrange the seating positions for the assembly: place two large signs for the "Great Assembly" (dàzhòng pái) at the upper and lower ends.

Once the layout is established, inspect the incense tables and candle stands, and assign attendants to serve the cups for the special guests. Next, inform the Guest Master (kètóu), then inform the Chief Attendant (shìzě), and finally inform the Abbot (fāngzhàng).

Sound the drum to assemble the community. They shall stand according to their bowl-seating positions (bówèi), while the Attendant waits outside the hall for the Head Monks (tóushǒu) to arrive as a group.

Return to the previous station. Next, the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) enters the hall and bows to invite [the guest]. He bows while leaving his position, then bows at the shoulder-position. He then escorts the Head Seat back to the special seat (te wei).
Exiting from behind the shrine (kaṅ), he proceeds to the front of the hall and reports that the Abbot (Vihārasvāmin) is entering the hall.

The hall bell is struck seven times. The Abbot returns to his position. The Attendant goes before the person for whom the service is intended and performs a formal greeting (praṇāma). He then turns from behind the shrine.
At the head of the seating platform, one performs a circumambulatory greeting once. In the outer hall, one proceeds from bottom to top in intervals, then returns to the center to perform a greeting.

Once the assembly has taken their seats, Master Yuanzhao’s community strictly observed this rite (formerly called "sending back to one's place"; it was only after the abbot had entered the hall that it was called "taking one's seat").

Master Yuepo, while residing at Tiantong, practiced this rite with diligence. (In the present day, people hinder the assembly by standing for too long and do not go specifically to offer greetings before others; [this] rite may yet be revived.)

"How could this be omitted? The attendant first burns incense in the upper and lower sections of the central brazier and outside the outer hall. Having finished, he returns to the center to perform a greeting (*wensun*).

He proceeds directly to the head seat (*shouzuo*) to perform a greeting, then exits to the right. Following the edge of the wooden floorboards, he performs a circumambulatory greeting once around until he reaches the outer hall.
Return to the center to inquire after [the abbot’s] health. Stand to the side of the upper hand. The attendant strikes the bell twice. First, serve tea specifically for the person being honored.

Once the tea has been served to the entire assembly and the pitcher has been removed, go before the person being honored to inquire after their health. Exit to the right and proceed before the incense burner to perform three full prostrations with the robes spread out.
Circumambulate the hall once, inquire after [the abbot’s] health at the center, and stand to the side. First, collect the cups for the Head Seat and the Abbot; when the Head Seat arrives...

Before the Abbot, perform the ritual prostrations. For the first unfolding of the robe, say: "On this occasion, we have been specially graced by the Venerable Master’s preparation of tea; our humble hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude. For the second unfolding, exchange greetings.

Perform three prostrations with full obeisance. At each unfolding of the mat, respond with one bow. The Head Seat turns behind the shrine and exits to the right; the Abbot escorts him briefly before returning to his position.
Holding the cup, he accompanies the assembly and burns a single stick of "light-accompanying" incense. The bell is struck once, and the cups of the great assembly are collected.
The drum is struck three times, and the session concludes. The Head Seat first waits for the Abbot in the Dharma Hall to offer thanks for the tea, and then proceeds.

[The attendant] escorts [the guest] to the Abbot’s quarters. The formal notice reads: “Venerable Abbot, this day after the midday meal, we shall serve one round of tea in the Cloud Hall (*yuntáng*). This is specially prepared for the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the assembly, to briefly commemorate the commencement of the retreat (*jiézhì*).

We also respectfully invite all the administrative officers (*zhīshì*) to join us and grace us with their presence. For those of advanced age, it is said: ‘The ceremony of offering congratulations. [Written in seven lines: This day of this month, Attendant [Name], Inviting Guest Attendant [Name]. Respectfully submitted.

On the sixteenth day, after the morning gruel has been consumed, the Ku-si (Storehouse Office) prepares tea for the assembly with the Lu-ku-si (Director of the Storehouse) presiding as head seat. The Ku-si’s guest attendant prepares the tea notice, using a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, candles, and incense.

The administrative official proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and request tea, saying: "This morning, following the conclusion of the midday meal, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for the Head Seat and the assembly.

We humbly entreat the Venerable Master to graciously deign to attend. Next, he proceeds to the Head Seat’s quarters to request tea. Notices are posted at all the various quarters to announce the invitation. He then awaits the sounding of the long board.

Circulate through the hall to invite tea. Arrange the tablets according to rank. (The procedure for the Abbot on the fourteenth day is the same as for the soup ceremony; however, after bowing for the tea, the administrative officers and the sacred monks perform three full prostrations before the Abbot, circumambulate the hall once, and exit.

They lead the entire assembly before the Abbot, where they perform two-fold prostrations and three bows. They exit from behind the shrine to the right and outside the hall. The Head Seat performs a face-to-face bow to express thanks for the tea. The administrative officers enter the hall to inquire after the Abbot’s well-being and collect the bowls. There is no incense for the light-accompaniment. The format of the notice is the same as the soup notice, with the sole modification being the substitution of the character for "tea" [for "soup"].)

**The Abbreviated Procedure for the Head Seat’s Special Tea Service for the Assembly of the Rear Hall** On the seventeenth day, after the morning gruel has been consumed, the Head Seat (Shouzuo) carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) to extend an invitation, saying: "Today, following the midday meal, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall (Yuntang), specifically for the assembly of the Rear Hall.

We humbly hope that the Venerable Master (Heshang), out of compassion, will deign to honor us with his presence. He performs two bows to exchange greetings and then prostrates three times. If the prostrations are waived, he performs three "touching bows" (chuli).
Next, prepare a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, candles, and an incense box. Carrying these to the Rear Hall (Hou-tang), light incense and perform prostrations to invite [the Abbot].
The Abbot returns the incense; having thus received his instructions, pass the formal petition (zhuang) and escort it out to be entrusted to the Tea Head (Cha-tou).

Order the Service Head (Gong-tou) to post the notice on the lower section of the front wall of the Sangha Hall, with the seal affixed to the front of the petition. Subsequently, order the attendants of the Hall Office (Tang-si) to post the notices at all the various quarters to invite them for tea.

The procedure for hanging up the plaque is the same as the tea ceremony for the Abbot. At the time of the midday meal, the announcement is made to remove the shoulder-pole. During the hall service, the food is chanted over.

One waits for the long board (gong) to sound, then burns incense and performs three full prostrations with the sitting cloth spread out. Tea is requested by circulating through the hall. When the meal is concluded, the drum is struck to assemble the community.

Once the rites are finished and tea has been served to all, the Head Seat approaches the Abbot to perform a prostration. The first part of the prostration formula says: "At this moment, though the tea is coarse, we have especially received the compassion of the Venerable Master..."

[The recipient] bows respectfully. [The donor] expresses their deepest gratitude for the kindness shown. They perform two prostrations with the cloth spread and three prostrations with the cloth folded (chuli). Each time the abbot spreads the cloth, he returns the bow, out of respect for the assembly. When the abbot returns to his position, he is the first to exit; this is not the proper rule.
The head seat exits from behind the shrine to the right and proceeds to the front of the hall. The chief attendants of the Rear Hall follow him out.

They perform one prostration with the cloth folded facing each other to express thanks for the tea, and then depart. [The person who received the invitation goes to the Head Seat’s quarters to offer thanks. The former hall members return to the main hall.]
Inquiries after the health [of the assembly]. Collection of the large cups for the multitude. No incense for accompanying light. Format:

[Name of Bhikṣu of the Front Hall]. [Right] [Name] respectfully informs: Following the conclusion of the midday meal this day, we shall proceed to the Cloud Hall to serve one round of tea for the entire assembly of the Rear Hall, as a modest mark of the formalities of the commencement of the retreat.

I further request all the administrators: I humbly hope that, out of your collective compassion, you will deign to descend in person. Respectfully submitted. On the [day] of the [month] of the [year], this memorial is presented by the former hall-monk, [Name]. Written in nine lines.
[Seal] Respectfully addressed to the Chief Seat of the Rear Hall and the Assembly. Sealed by the Bhikṣu [Name] of the Front Hall.

On the first and fifteenth days of the month, following the tea service during the hall inspection and the conclusion of the formal sitting, the Chief Seat leads the assembly to stand in their designated positions before the Sangha Hall according to the *nian-song tu* (recitation diagram). The Chief Seat performs a *vaṃdana* (bowing).

Entering the Hall: The West Hall Master returns directly to stand at the head of the Holy Monk (the central altar). Next, the heads of the assembly and the general congregation enter in procession behind them.
The visiting attendant enters in turn and stands facing the entrance. According to ancient custom, the junior disciples exit through the rear door.
Once the Abbot has entered the hall, the bell is struck seven times; he burns incense, circumambulates the hall once, and returns to his seat. The junior disciples then re-enter the hall.
Nowadays, many disciples from various quarters come and go, making the hall seem noisy and chaotic. The master should instruct them to keep their heads bowed and hands joined in *añjali*;

even when observing the hall during rounds, it remains orderly and solemn. Next, the group of administrators performs a greeting to the Sacred Monk (*Sengsheng*), turns to face the Abbot for a greeting, and completes one circuit of the hall.
Those who have arrived temporarily follow them out of the hall; the Attendant receives them as they exit and burns incense.

The attendant asks after the health [of the abbot]. He bows to the assembly and sits. He steps forward to the central incense burner and burns incense in the upper, middle, and lower sections, as well as in the outer hall.
Again, he performs the inquiry of health as before and stands in the center. The bell is struck to serve tea. Again, he performs the inquiry of health as before and bows for the tea.

The cups are collected. The bell is struck three times. They withdraw from their seats. If the tea is not served by circulating through the hall, they sit down to drink tea after the morning gruel has ended. This is done twice daily when the abbot is away.

Regarding tea: it is the administrative officers (*zhishi*) who burn incense; if the abbot (*zhuchi*) does not attend the hall and the attendant (*shizhe*) does not burn incense, this is contrary to the Dharma.

Regarding the two rounds of tea during the lectures in the *conglin* tradition’s ancient rules: at the commencement of the retreat (*jie zhi*), two rounds of tea are served at the Great Seat (*dazuo*) within the Sangha Hall (*sengtang*). The drum is struck to assemble the assembly, after which the formal rites are performed.
This is the same as the special procedure. Upon reaching the point of the bow for tea, one proceeds before the Head Seat (Shouzuo) to inquire after his well-being.
One does not prostrate before the Sacred Monk (Shengseng). Having made a single circuit around the hall, both inside and out, one collects the Head Seat’s cup.

The assembly places their cups on their mats and sits with hands crossed. The attendant burns incense again. The ritual is performed as before. When the tea pitcher is brought out again, one goes before the Head Seat and bows for tea. Only then—

Turning before the Holy Sangha, perform three full prostrations with the robes spread wide. Circumambulate the hall once. Next, collect the cup of the Head Seat and proceed before the Abbot to perform the rites;
the words spoken are the same as those used for a special memorial service. Turn to the right behind the shrine and exit. The Abbot briefly sees them off and returns to his position.
The attendant holds up the cups. The attendant burns incense again. The assembly performs prostrations as before in the upper and lower sections and outside the hall, then withdraws.
The bell is struck to collect the cups; the drum is struck three times, and the assembly leaves their seats.

At the Abbot’s quarters, after the tea service for the Hall has concluded on the first and fifteenth days of the month, during seasonal festivals, and at the end of the year, the Attendant, together with the Guest Master, proceeds to the Hall to serve tea.

The Guest Master first notifies the Head of the Assembly, hangs the notice board, and informs the community. He prepares the hot water and brings out the cups, then invites the Head Cook to join as a companion. The Abbot prepares [the necessary items] in advance.

The tea is served. The attendant goes to the administrative office (*kūsō*). The head cook (*tensō*) receives him inside. The head of the assembly (*santō*) and the hall master (*dōju*) lead the group to welcome him at the gate.

The attendant takes the seat of honor, acting on behalf of the abbot. The head cook takes the seat to his right. The attendant steps out from the central incense burner and burns a single stick of incense;

then he returns to his position and gestures with his hand for the assembly to be seated. When the serving of tea is finished, the head cook escorts them out through the gate, with the head of the assembly and the hall master leading the way.
Upon being sent, he immediately goes to the Abbot’s quarters to offer thanks for the tea.

When the Kitchen Administration (Kusi) serves the tea in the Hall of Practice (Xingtang), and the Abbot has finished serving the tea in the Hall of Practice, the administrative officials (Zhishi) go to the Hall of Practice to serve tea. The administrative officials occupy the position of the presiding master. The Ritual Master (Dian) [occupies the seat of honor].

The attendant of the seat (zuòguāngbàn) performs the same prostrations as at the abbot’s quarters (fāngzhàng). Upon exiting the gate, he shouts: “The head of the assembly and the congregation shall proceed to the administrative office (kùsī) to offer thanks for the tea. The announcement is made:
“The administrators have conveyed their words that the offering of thanks for the tea is waived.”

The Head Official (Dushou) serves the tea in the Hall of Practice (Xingtang), and after serving the "River and Lake" tea in the Sangha Hall, he instructs the attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi) to notify the Head of the Retreat (Cantou). The attendant hangs the notice board to inform the assembly, prepares the hot water, and brings out the cups.

He then invites the Kitchen Steward (Dianzuo) to join as a companion; the Head Official takes the seat on the right, and the ritual procedures are identical to those previously described. Finally, there is a call to express gratitude for the tea.
Again, the *He Mian*.
Volume Three of the *Chanlin Beiyong* (Practical Applications for the Chan Forest).
Volume Four of the *Chanlin Beiyong*.
Water: The Special Envoy requests the Abbot to reside.

Once the selection for the abbot’s succession has been determined by public drawing and the formal decree has been issued to the temple, the administrative office (Kusō) shall convene the two classes of officials and the senior elders for tea.

They shall determine the auspicious date and first draft the written invitation for the production of the mountain gate proclamation (*sanmon-so*) and the tea and soup notice (*chō-tō-hō*). If the position of Record Keeper (*shiki-shi*) is vacant, one shall be selected based on talent and virtue.
The people prepare the banner using silk cloth; its dimensions must be according to the Dharma. The administrative office (kusi) sends paper to the various quarters for writing.

A capable attendant or an elder monk proficient in calligraphy is appointed. Next, a person is invited to serve as the special envoy—either a senior administrator (*shushu*), a venerable elder (*chijū*), the Rear Hall secretary, or the Librarian (*zōshu*).
Once the selection has been finalized, if a venerable elder or a head official serves as the special envoy, the *chiji*...

They shall go together with one official to take charge of the finances and deliberate on affairs. A detailed inventory must be prepared of all temple lands, properties, and utensils under their jurisdiction, as well as the ceremonial protocol for the reception;
everything must be fully prepared. The special envoy and his entourage shall be hosted and entertained until the day of departure.

When visiting the various administrative offices (*ryōjin*), one is accompanied by attendants who offer their salutations (*neigi*). The assembly sees them off at the gate. At the mountain gate (*sanmon*), tea and soup are served;
the senior administrators (*chiji*) go to greet the junior administrators, and the head officers (*tōsu*) go to greet the senior administrators.

Having performed the ritual bow and sat down, one burns incense. After bowing for the incense, one returns to one's position. Tea is served. Rising again, one burns incense and bows for the incense. Soup is served.

Once the bowls have been cleared away, one boards the palanquin and departs. At the mountain gate, a seat is prepared inside the hanging screen; the two classes of officials and the senior monks are invited to accompany the special envoy.
Upon arriving at the temple, they first see the guest prefect and proceed together to the administrative office (kusi), where they are escorted to their quarters.

Prepare the formal letter of introduction (*menzō*). Upon seeing that the head official (*shushu*) occupies a private quarters (*tanryō*) and there is no formal letter, go to the Attendant’s Office (*jisshi*) and report your background in detail.

The Attendant shall direct the Guest Master (*kakutō*) to arrange tables and cloths in the dormitory hall (*shindō*) and to place the written petitions (*sho*) and notices (*chō*) there. The Attendant then enters the Abbot’s Quarters (*hōjō*) to present the formal letter of introduction.
The abbot comes forth. The special envoy inquires after his well-being and requests him to sit cross-legged. The abbot stands facing the temple hall.

The special envoy offers incense in large quantities, spreads his ritual implements, and performs three prostrations. Stepping forward, he says: "I, [Name], a messenger from the Monastery Gate, have humbly entreated your venerable presence to grace us with your august countenance; my humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. He performs another three prostrations. The formal words are:

"On this day of the early summer month, as the season is solemn, we respectfully wish that the newly appointed Abbot, Great Monk, may enjoy many blessings in your daily life. He performs another three prostrations, withdraws his implements, and the abbot remains standing.

Each person shall respond with a single bow. The words are: "I have received this summons by chance, which brings me into disrepute within our school's tradition; yet, that you have taken the trouble to travel so far from afar moves me beyond measure. The special envoy then presents the memorial and the letter.
Once the Abbot has accepted [the offerings], the Attendant bows to invite him to be seated. After tea is finished, he is escorted to the Guest Seat. The attendants of the Hall Office strike the bell;

the Head Seat leads the assembly to the Abbot’s Quarters to offer congratulations. The Kitchen Office presents incense, and the Head Seat and the Administrative Officers each insert a single stick of incense. For the first prostration, the formal statement reads:

"We are most fortunate within the Dharma Gate and rejoice at this honorable promotion. We celebrate this merit for the monastic community; we, your humble servants, are moved by a sense of profound gratitude. For the second prostration, the statement reads:

(On this day, the first month of summer, at the proper time. We respectfully wish that the Great Master in the Hall at [Name] Place may enjoy good health and abundant blessings. Perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). The Abbot returns each prostration with one bow. The guest says:

(Reflecting upon my own incompetence and errors, I have mistakenly received this selection. Your profound courtesy and concern are beyond measure; I am deeply moved. When the assembly has dispersed, the Guest Master leads the special envoy on a tour of the quarters.
Upon completion, they present the temple’s *Xuzhi* (Regulations), ceremonial implements, and miscellaneous articles. If the Abbot does not grant the request, [the envoy departs].
Having been entreated three times, he consented, and the ritual was performed as before. That evening, a special meal of soup and medicinal confections was prepared;
the night soup and fruits were all served with the two classes of senior monks invited to grace the occasion. The administrative office (kūsi) made the necessary arrangements.

When the chief officers of the West Hall, the abbot’s special envoys, arrive at the temple, they first see the guest prefect and proceed together to the attendants’ office. They are then ushered to have an audience with the abbot, where they insert incense and perform prostrations.

They look upon one another and perform the same rites as when drinking tea; then they escort [the candidate] to his guest quarters. Next, having completed the formal greetings at all the various administrative offices (*liao*), they report to the attendant (*shizhe*).
Together they go to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to present their petition: "At our monastery, we now invite such-and-such a person to serve as abbot.

Having finished the report, the attendant and the others go together to the quarters of the person invited. Upon meeting, they insert incense and perform the rites as before. If he does not accept, they immediately go to the Abbot’s quarters to inform him.

[The abbot] strikes the gong. Together they extend their formal invitation. Once the invitation has been accepted, the Abbot invites the newly appointed official and the senior members of the two ranks for tea.
The newly appointed official escorts the guests to their seats and receives congratulations in succession. He then conducts the formal greetings throughout the monastic quarters.
That evening, the Abbot invites the special envoy of the newly appointed official for a special serving of hot water, medicinal congee, and fruit; the two ranks serve as companions.
Emerging [from the hall], he accepts the invitation of the assembly to ascend the seat.

Having accepted the invitation, on the following day he is invited to ascend the seat; the ritual is the same as that for the first and fifteenth days of the month. This is the public regulation established by the Great Masters of the Dharma; such has been the ancient custom.

Upon ascending the seat, he provides detailed guidance and reminders for those below to stir the minds of the students, who then offer their thanks. The special envoys follow the prescribed order for making their offerings.
Regarding the settlement of accounts, the handover of items, the serving of tea and refreshments, and the selection of the date for departure:
the West Hall Head (Xitang Touzhu) accepts the invitation and ascends the seat;

the special envoy and the assembly finalize the arrangements. Tea and refreshments are served the following day. The envoy proceeds before the newly appointed abbot, offers incense, and formally requests him to accept the position. The Abbot then leads the way to the Dharma seat.

The liturgical text says: (Having prostrated, invite the Abbot: "Tomorrow, please act as the presiding master for the newly appointed Abbot. On that day, the ritual documents are arranged to the right of the Dharma seat. To the left of the seat, the position of the incumbent Abbot is established.

When the Abbot ascends the seat, the procedure is the same as on other days. He offers thanks to the newly appointed Abbot, exhorts him to accept the invitation, and proclaims the Dharma so that it may endure for a long time.
After descending from the seat, the special envoy, together with the attendant and the guest prefect, jointly inquire after his well-being and formally invite the newly appointed Abbot.
He immediately went out before the abbot to inquire after his well-being. Whether or not he cited a koan was not restricted. When Yan-shi accepted an invitation, Song-yuan led the assembly;
when Song-yuan accepted an invitation, Xiao-an led the assembly—neither cited a koan. When Jian-tang accepted an invitation, Shi-qiao led the assembly;
when Chun-an accepted an invitation, Xi-an led the assembly—both cited a koan. Whether or not one cites a koan depends on the person. This applies if the head monk is...

The入室 disciple (入室弟子) approaches the abbot to inquire after his well-being. The dharma robe is conferred, accompanied by a formal discourse (*dharmapada*). When the new person dons the robe, there is likewise a discourse.
Having finished adjusting the robe, they don the dharma robe once more. The abbot sits cross-legged; [the disciple] performs three full prostrations with the robes spread out, reciting these words:

(To settle this matter once and for all, I look up with shame before the sages of old. Since your invitation has been so insistent, it is difficult to evade your command. Your humble servant can do nothing but feel the utmost trepidation. Again, three prostrations. The address says: (On this day, [Name] respectfully addresses the occasion.)

"Respectfully considering the Hall Master, our Founding Teacher, the Great Monk: we pray that you enjoy good health and abundant blessings. (Another three prostrations; fold the sitting mat, step forward to inquire after his well-being.

The Abbot says: "The needle in the bag has already been revealed; the rain of flowers falls with difficulty. Fortunately, it is you, sir; we humbly wish you joy and celebration. Next, he presents the memorial scrolls and notices, each having its own specific wording. If [the recipient] is not a Dharma heir, [the wording is adjusted accordingly].

Alternatively, the West Hall [Abbot] immediately steps forward from before his seat to exchange greetings with the presiding Abbot, then proceeds directly to his own seat. He picks up his robe and the ceremonial documents (shu-tie);
for each of these, there are specific verses. The special envoy first reports this to the Rector (Vina), requesting that the documents be proclaimed.

Once the proclamation is finished, he ascends the seat to deliver a formal address, engage in question-and-answer, present the core outline (ti-gang), offer thanks, and conclude the session. Descending from the seat, he approaches the presiding Abbot, performs two full prostrations with both hands extended (liang-zhan) and three prostrations (san-li), and then requests to be excused.

[The Guest] says: "I have presumptuously accepted this request, which brings disgrace upon our ancestral tradition. I look up to you for your guidance in bringing this to completion; my humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. The Abbot replies:

"We rejoice at the invitation from the realms of humans and devas, and are honored by the radiance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost joy. In succession, the Guest Master and the Attendant lead the tour of the quarters to offer thanks.

The Dharma Heir descends from his seat and performs two prostrations with hands opened (liang-zhan) and three prostrations, saying: "My words are vulgar and crude, bringing shame to your venerable hearing. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. He then performs another three prostrations and exchanges greetings.
[The ceremony] is concluded. The inspection of the quarters (*xúnláo*) and the expressions of gratitude for the gifts are the same as before.

Regarding the serving of tea and snacks (*jiāndiǎn*), the incumbent abbot and the special envoy should first consult with one another to determine the appropriate scale of the vegetarian meal and the monetary offerings (*zhāikěn*), ensuring that the gravity of the gift accords with propriety. As for the two classes of senior monks and the local elders...

The person responsible for the legal affairs of the monastic community prepares the supplementary offerings and the costs for the vegetarian feast. A special messenger personally delivers these to the Treasury Office to be set aside for the meal.

On the appointed day, the messenger goes to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense and extend an invitation. The first formal presentation of the petition states: "On this day at the hour of the horse (noon), we have specially prepared [this feast] in the Cloud Hall;

we humbly pray that you will compassionately deign to attend. Your subordinate feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. The second presentation consists of inquiries after one's health, followed by three prostrations with the full body touching the ground (*chuli*). The Abbot returns the bow. Both parties then...

The Head of the Administrative Office (Bansuanliao) and the Guest Master (Ketou), together with the special messenger and attendants, shall go to each of the quarters one by one to formally request [the assembly].

They shall post the notice boards to announce the invitation to the four quarters and arrange the seating for the presiding chair in the Sangha Hall. At the head of the guest master’s seat, they shall arrange the seats for the special messengers.

When it is time for the meal, the special messengers shall wait before the Sangha Hall for the Abbot to enter; they shall escort him in and out and assist him in taking his place, after which they shall bow and withdraw.

Inquire after the health [of the abbot] from within. Bow to the assembly seated [in the hall]. In the central burner, between the upper and lower sections, and outside the hall, once the incense has been burned, go before the abbot to inquire after his health.
Having inquired after his health at the upper and lower sections and outside the hall, inquire after his health in the center. When the meal distribution is complete, burn one stick of incense.
After the distribution of alms is finished, he exits the hall and returns to his seat for the meal. Once the meal is concluded, the water for rinsing the mouth is served, and the drum is struck.

The special messenger enters the hall, burns incense at the central burner, and performs prostrations in both the upper and lower sections outside the hall. Having completed these rites in the outer hall of both sections, he proceeds to the abbot’s presence to exchange greetings.

After performing the same sequence of greetings in the outer hall of both the upper and lower sections, tea is served throughout. When the greetings are completed as before, the abbot’s cup is collected, and the special messenger performs the formal ritual. First, he unfolds his sitting cloth and says:

[On this day, there is rice and water for the meal. We humbly receive the Venerable Master’s gracious visit; our hearts are filled with the utmost gratitude. Second, exchange greetings of cold and warmth, perform three prostrations with the *chulu* (touching the ground), and escort the Abbot out.
Return to the hall once more, burn one stick of incense, perform three full prostrations (*dazhan*), and circumambulate the hall once, including the area outside.

Return to the center to inquire after his well-being, collect the bowls, and strike the drum three times. Retire from the seat. The special envoy proceeds to the administrative office (*kusō*) to thank them for preparing the meal. Next...
Please invite the Abbot. For the evening meal, the night soup, and the fruit offering, one should always invite the two classes of senior monks to serve as honored companions.

The Jian, Jian-dian, West Hall Head, Head Officers, newly appointed officials, and special envoys shall go before the newly appointed official to finalize the offerings for the Abbot’s quarters, the protocol for the introductory seat and the expression of gratitude, and the offerings for the hall and supplementary offerings.

The person who proclaims the formal invitation (xuānshūtiè) shall accompany the offering of alms (*pīqìn*). On the appointed day, after the morning gruel has been finished, the special messenger goes to the Abbot’s quarters (*fāngzhàng*) and makes this request:

"This noon hour, we have prepared water and rice in the Cloud Hall specifically for the newly appointed Abbot. We humbly hope that you will look upon us with compassion and deign to descend and honor us. The Abbot replies, "I respectfully comply with your command. The messenger then proceeds to the newly appointed Abbot and makes the same request according to the aforementioned protocol.

The Abbot’s guest master (*kètóu*), together with the special messenger and his attendants (*xíngzhě*), then issues invitations to all the monastic quarters (*zhūliáo*) for the midday meal. At that time, they inform the newly appointed Abbot.
The appointee proceeds to the hall. Waiting before the hall, he enters the hall together with the abbot and performs a bow of inquiry (*wènxùn*). He follows them in;

first, he bows to the abbot and returns to his position, then he bows to the new appointee and returns to the position adjacent to the abbot’s. He burns incense and performs the rites exactly as before.

When the food is served and the monetary offerings (*kǔn*) are distributed, and the tea ceremony is concluded, the bowls of the new appointee are collected first. The special messenger then goes forward and performs a bow. The first unfolding of the mat says: "On this day, water and rice [are offered]."

"I have received the Master’s compassionate honor with the utmost gravity. My humble feelings are filled with boundless gratitude. (Second display of the robe. A prostration with the forehead touching the ground; the abbot returns the bow.

The new appointee is escorted out through the rear gate. The special envoy enters; the abbot proceeds forward to perform a bow. For the first display, he says: "On this day, I have humbly received the Master’s honor.

My humble feelings are filled with boundless gratitude. (Second display. A prostration with the forehead touching the ground; the abbot returns the bow. The abbot is escorted out through the front gate. [The envoy] returns to the hall to light incense.

Incense is offered; prostrations are performed; one circumambulates the hall once and exchanges greetings throughout the outer hall. The bowls are collected, the drum is struck three times, and the assembly withdraws from their seats.
For the evening soup, fruits, and medicinal food, the attendants follow the same procedure as before.
Title: *Shanmen Guandai Xinming Dangdai Zhuanshi Zhongzhishi Huiyi* (The Assembly for the Reception of the Newly Appointed Special Envoy by the Monastery Gate).

Reception and Offering of Alms: The food offerings are according to the ritual protocol. On the day following [the appointment], the Head Administrator goes before the newly appointed official, offers incense, and prostrates to invite him.
Next, he proceeds to the Guest Quarters to inform and invite the Special Envoy, instructing the Guest Master of the Treasury Office (*Kusi*) to prepare accordingly.

Please request the two classes of officials and the venerable elders to serve as honored companions. The wording for the ritual and the performance of the rites shall be identical to those previously specified. Nail and hang the portraits in the main hall;
arrange the seating for the abbot’s position, with the special envoy and the presiding abbot on the left and right, and the elders facing them.
The attendants shall receive the administrative officers at their lower rank, while the servants are received from afar with noodles and rice, and they shall be provided with monetary rewards.

When the Chief Administrator (Jū) and the Head of the West Hall (Sittō) receive the command to provide hospitality, they shall likewise set up their seats in the sleeping hall. The Abbot occupies the central seat; the newly appointed official faces him; the special envoy and the newly appointed official take seats to either side;
and the two classes of senior monks occupy seats to the left and right as attendants. The formal words and the performance of the rites are identical to those previously described.
