[The Abbot] declines the invitation; the assembly ascends the hall for tea and soup.
On the day of departure, the current incumbent rises from his seat and ascends the hall to offer thanks to the two ranks of officials, the elders, and the great assembly.

The assembly descends from their seats. The drum is struck three times. [The Abbot] stands facing the Dharma seat and performs three prostrations with the full body (chuli) together with the entire assembly. The tower bell and other instruments are sounded according to the ritual.

The ritual vessels are sent out. The assembly of monks escorts them to the gate. The two ranks of officials escort from the near side to the far side. The attendants stand in a line outside, waiting. They escort [the vessels] to the head of the mountain gate.
Prior to this, a shrine position has been prepared and hung; [the official] sits facing inward. The West Hall Master and the senior elders divide up to serve as companions.

The Head Seat occupies the central position, with the two ranks of officials seated on either side facing him. The Head Seat performs the rites: he bows to invite [the official] to sit, and then bows again.

[The attendant] burns incense, returns to his station, serves tea, and collects the bowls. He rises again to burn incense, bows to the incense, and serves hot water. When the water service is finished, he boards the sedan chair.
The two classes of officials and the senior elders prepare a sedan chair to escort him a long distance; the abbot should exert effort to decline this honor.

The special envoy and his entourage first visit the various quarters to take their leave. The bell on the tower is struck; they must wait until the abbot’s sedan chair has moved out of sight before they may stop.

When the bead-counter (zhū) sees that the head seat (zhǔzuò) is taking leave of the assembly, he must dispatch a special messenger to the abbot’s quarters (fāngwáng) to request the use of the Dharma-seat for the formal address to the assembly. No seat is to be prepared for the head seat.

Upon descending from the seat, the head seat first takes leave of the abbot by performing three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (chùlǐ). Next, he stands facing the abbot and performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths in common with the entire assembly. This concludes the formal leave-taking.

The assembly shall set up their seats at the entrance of the mountain gate for a special tea service. The two classes of officials and the elders shall serve as honored companions, while the senior administrators perform the rites.

The bell on the tower is struck, and they are escorted out the door. If the West Hall Dharma Master or the Head Official takes leave of the assembly, they first accompany the special messenger to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), where they insert incense and perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*) to offer their formal leave. Only after this do they proceed to visit the various administrative offices (*xunliao*).

Taking leave. At the entrance of the mountain gate, tea and soup are served. The two classes of attendants accompany him and perform the rites. The great bell is struck to see him off; all these follow the same protocol as before.
This is called the ancient method for entering the monastery.

Carrying his bundle and wearing his rain-hat, he approaches. If he encounters those coming out to welcome him, he removes his hat and bows in greeting. If he happens to meet officials or nobles, he sets down his bundle and merely bows.
Upon reaching the head of the mountain gate, he takes off his bundle and hat, burns incense, and if there is a formal discourse, he listens.

Arriving before the Sangha Hall, he places his bundle on the rear rack, washes his feet, and returns to the front of the hall. He takes his robes, puts them on, and enters the hall; if there are attendants accompanying him, they enter together.

Before the Honored Sangha, perform three prostrations with the robes fully spread out. Circumambulate the hall once; the attendant monks exit first, and the Rector (Vina) escorts [the new monk] back to his bowl-position, where he performs three prostrations with the head touching the ground.

Once the formal enrollment is complete, proceed to the Buddha Hall for the "words" and prostrations; next, perform the same at the Land Deity Hall and the Patriarchs’ Hall. The administrative officers invite him into the Abbot’s quarters to take up residence.
Following this, the opening of the hall and the offering of longevity prayers are performed. Recently, this has been practiced following the tradition of Dachuan.
When the Abbot went to Jingci, and after Master Xiaoweng entered Yuyang, no one heard of him.

At night, when the new Dharma-abbot arrived at the monastery, one must observe whether his lodging was near or far. If it was near, the assembly would go out to welcome him; if it was far, then both...
The senior members of the two classes of officials shall simply attend. The special envoy shall pre-arrange the petitions for exemption from labor for the assembly.

Once the senior members of the two classes have finished their incense-offering rites, they shall accompany the guest with tea and fruit. On the day of entry into the monastery, the administrative office (Kūsi) shall prepare everything in due order.

The attendants of the Hall Office (Tángsī) shall post the notice boards the night before; at the appointed time, the great bell and other ritual instruments shall be struck, and the assembly shall welcome the guest at the gate. The guest shall proceed.

[The new appointee] stands outside the ranks. When the new appointment reaches the gate, he burns incense and offers his formal address. Upon reaching the Buddha Hall, he performs the ritual of burning incense and delivers a formal discourse.

He performs three full prostrations with wide-spread sitting cloths (*daizhan*). The bell is struck to signal the end of the service, and he returns to the Sangha Hall to register for his quarters. Once the assembly has entered the hall, the new appointee enters the hall, burns incense, and performs three full prostrations with wide-spread sitting cloths.
Those accompanying him likewise perform three full prostrations. The *Venerable Leader* (*vinaya-dhara*) leads him on a circuit around the hall once; the attendants go first.

Exit. Escort [the guest] back to his bowl-position (*bowl-wei*) and provide him with formal registration (*guatapa*). Perform three prostrations with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli sanbai*). (When the Abbot of Shaolin resided at Jingci or Lingyin, it was required that both classes of officials escort him back to his bowl-position.

Next, offer incense in the Hall of the Local Deity (*tudi tang*) and the Patriarchs’ Hall (*zutang*), for which there are respective ritual instructions (*fayu*). Enter the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) and take possession of the room. The attendant burns a single stick of incense;

after the formal inquiry (*wenxun*), the Abbot delivers a turning word (*chuishu*). The Chief Steward (*zhishi*) first prepares a formal petition and sets out a table and offering cloth (*zhuofu*). The attendant performs an inquiry. The acolyte (*xingzhe*)...

Present the temple record seal. The newly appointed official examines the seal while it is still sealed; he hands it to the administrative officer (jishi) to open. Once the inscription has been inspected, the official seals his signature on the document (first signing his name, then recording the date).

He then hands it over to the attendant (shizhe) who is in charge of robes and bowls to receive. The entire assembly of administrative officers stands in front; the head administrative officer [leads].

Inserting Incense. First unfolding [the mat], he says: "Now that the Venerable Master has graced this Dharma assembly with his presence, my humble heart is filled with the utmost gratitude. He replies: "Having humbly occupied this renowned monastery, my heart is filled with shame and trepidation.

Second unfolding, the exchange of greetings; prostrating three times by touching the ground. Each of the various mountain monasteries inserts incense and offers congratulations (though they shall be excused from offering incense). The Head Seat leads the assembly.

Incense is offered and congratulations are presented. The elders each offer incense; the local people, those who speak of the past, and the Dharma relatives follow by offering their congratulations thereafter.

The guest master bows to invite the various mountain abbots and the two classes of elders to take their seats, where hot water is served. Next, the official guests and the various mountain abbots are invited to ascend the seat for the morning refreshment (*dianxin*).
If the predecessor has been transferred elsewhere and has not yet arrived, or if he has retired to serve as the Eastern Hall Abbot, [the ceremony] takes place before his quarters.
The ceremony of handing over the abbotship is performed. After receiving congratulations, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck.

The newly appointed abbot personally escorts the predecessor back to his quarters (performing one bow with hands touching the ground and offering incense as a formal courtesy). Next, the Head Seat leads the assembly in paying their respects; all the attendants and servants must also pay their respects.

Form for Submitting the Temple Records (The temple storehouse monk [Name]. One temple seal. Right: Respectfully submitted to the newly appointed Abbot, Great Monk. Awaiting your compassionate instructions.
[Year] [Month] [Day], submitted by the temple storehouse monk [Name]).
[The Abbot] requests the meal.

Having completed the formalities in his quarters, the administrative officers prepare a written invitation, arrange a tray with cloths, an incense burner, and candles, and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and extend the invitation for the meal.

First Opening of the Robe: "At the hour of noon, we have prepared rice and water in the Cloud Hall. We humbly await your arrival. We beseech your venerable compassion to deign to honor us with your presence. Your humble servants are moved by a sense of profound gratitude. Second Opening of the Robe.

Regarding cold and warm [seasons]: perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground; the abbot returns one prostration. Present the formal petition (zhuang), which the guest master of the Abbot’s Quarters (fangzhang) shall receive.
The guest master of the Administrative Office (kusī) shall prepare the seating for the abbot in the Sangha Hall. The protocol for the reception and hospitality is the same as above.

Formal Notice (From the Temple’s Storehouse Officer, Bhikṣu [Name]: The undersigned respectfully informs you that this coming day at the hour of the Horse (noon), we shall prepare a simple meal of water and rice in the Cloud Hall to welcome you. We humbly entreat your venerable compassion to deign to honor us with your presence.
Respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] of the [year]. A memorial from the monks of the temple’s treasury office, [Name] and others.
(Sealed with the respectful request for the new appointment of the Abbot, Great Zen Master, before the Honorable Seat; respectfully sealed by [Name] and others of full rank).

**Fruit: Opening the Hall to Pray for the Emperor** In ancient times, at the various monasteries within the imperial capital, the court would dispatch an official to deliver an edict, earnestly inviting the abbot to open the hall (*kaishō*) at a specific temple.

The government provided funds and provisions to establish a vegetarian feast (*sai*). In recent times, a seat is prepared beneath the dais; when the time arrives, the attendant (*shijō*) assigns the guest quarters.
First, the Dharma seat is prepared. The administrative office is notified and the notice board is posted. After the formal ascent to the hall is completed, the various quarters are inspected.

A written list of the names and ranks of the officials and the various mountain abbots is prepared and presented in advance to the Abbot for his review. The special messenger is given instructions. To the left of the seat, a table and cloth are set out, and the ceremonial invitations are arranged in order.
The person appointed to read the proclamation shall first be sent to review the official documents. According to custom, the *weina* (rector) shall read the *shanmen su* (monastery petition);

the *shouzuo* (chief seat) shall read the remaining petitions; and the next-ranking head officials shall read the rest. The administrative office (*kusō*) shall prepare incense and send it to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*).

They shall pre-arrange for the various mountain masters to strike the gavel and set out the seating positions for the officials facing the seat before the abbot. Incense shall be lit and candles prepared. Then, the attendant shall be notified, followed by the notification of the [abbot].

At the abbot’s quarters, the drum is struck to assemble the community; the ritual is identical to that of the morning and evening services. The attendants enter with the special envoy to invite the abbot.

The ritual assistants ring the gong (*ghaṇṭā*), while flower banners and lamps are carried before them as they lead him to his position in the Dharma Hall, as during the time of receiving the invitation.

Before the robe is presented, he should cite a *gong'an* (koan) and don the Dharma robes. Next, the special envoy offers incense and performs the prostrations. For the first unfolding [of the mat], he says: "On this day, we humbly receive..."

The Abbot occupies the Dharma seat; your humble servant is overcome with the utmost gratitude. (2) Exchanging pleasantries, [the guest] performs three prostrations with full-length bows (*chuli*). The Abbot replies with one bow each. First, the official document (*gongwen*) is presented;
if it contains a verse, it is handed to the Rector (*weina*) to proclaim. An attendant carries the memorial (*shu*).

Next, the documents from the various mountains and the monastic community are presented and recited one by one. The stories (*hua*) are cited and read aloud. If it is a memorial from an incumbent official requesting the opening of the hall (*kaitang*), [the procedure follows accordingly].

The officials must first personally present their memorial. Next is the memorial from the mountain gate. When the abbot points to the seat, he delivers his remarks; then he ascends the seat, picks up the incense, and offers it for the Emperor.

Next, he picks up the incense for the local magistrates and officials. If there is a great donor who has established the temple or donated land, incense should be offered for them as well (the attendant presents each incense one by one).
Only the incense for the Dharma heir is drawn from within the robe; once offered, the abbot himself inserts it into the burner. According to...

[The Master] takes his seat. The attendant burns incense and descends from the platform. The two classes of officials come forward to perform the ritual of inquiry (wèn-xùn). Once this is completed, the attendant ascends the platform, burns incense, and performs the ritual of inquiry;

the protocol is the same as for the morning and evening services. To the right of the seat, the mallet is struck, and it is said: "In this Dharma assembly of dragons and elephants, one should contemplate the primary truth (paramārtha).

[The Master] delivers a formal statement (chuí-yǔ), provides answers to questions, presents the essential outline (tí-gāng), and offers words of gratitude. Regarding the officials and the various mountain monasteries, he says: "For the opening of the hall and the blessing of the Emperor’s longevity, I dare not praise his virtue. For the special envoys and the two classes of officials who are elders...

The Elder briefly mentions the transgressions of the assembly; the expression of thanks was given during the *xiao-can* (small lecture). As the session concludes, he strikes the gavel and says: "Contemplate the Dharma-King’s Dharma; such is the Dharma-King’s Dharma.

He descends from the seat and walks forward a few steps. The administrative officers escort him to the guest seat, while the guest-master attendant and the ritual attendants immediately advance with incense burners and candles, arranged in a single file before him.
First, they present the offerings for the special envoy. The ritual attendant of the Hall Office then calls out:

(On the Affairs of the Various Mountains) Next are the affairs of the West Hall (the incumbent should be exempted from the incense offering). The group of administrative officers performs two prostrations with palms joined and three bows.

Next, the head seat, the retired elders, those of seniority in the meditation hall, and the various quarters each offer incense and, together with the assembly, perform two prostrations with palms joined and three bows.

Next, the stewards, the storehouse keeper, the hermitages, and the stupas, as well as Dharma relatives and countrymen who have arrived temporarily, first perform the rites together with the assembly; if they are exempted from the formal bows, they perform three prostrations with palms joined.

The General Formula says: (Having humbly received the Honored Monk’s gracious acceptance of the Dharma seat, your humble servant is overcome with the utmost gratitude. The Reply says: (I have presumptuously occupied this famous monastery; I am overcome with shame and trepidation. [The guest] proceeds to the chair behind the *guasizi* screen and takes his seat.

The attendant inserts incense and performs nine prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan jiubai*). The junior disciples insert incense and perform nine prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths. In both cases, there are no spoken words.
Next, the practitioners from the various mountains, the practitioners of the Abbot’s quarters, and the six divisions of personal attendants [perform the same]. Next...

The head of the assembly leads the group in offering incense and performing three prostrations. The sedan-chair attendants remain in the hall. The village headmen and the heads of the various quarters present offerings to the retired masters.

The chief of the quarters leads the way for the prostrations. The abbot then proceeds to the guest seat to express his gratitude to the officials and the monastics from other mountains, thereby fulfilling all the rites of propriety.

The Master of the Hall inspects the various quarters. Incense, seats, censers, candles, and incense-burners are arranged within each room; all maintain their proper decorum and wait in sequence for the inspection.
The Chief Guest Official first announces the arrival to the Abbot. Upon the Abbot’s arrival, the Head of the Quarter first steps forward at the entrance.

He stands; [the guest] is welcomed inside and invited to sit cross-legged. Incense is inserted, and the abbot responds to the incense. After briefly exchanging pleasantries regarding the weather, he expresses his thanks and is escorted out.

Upon hearing the call to "collect the incense," the assembly from the Meditation Hall and the four quarters of the monastery all line up outside the gate with their hands lowered. They enter together and exit together.

It is said that for the residents of the various quarters, it is contrary to the Dharma for the head of the quarter alone to escort them in and out. Once the rounds of the quarters are completed in succession, they return to the Abbot’s Quarters.
The Abbot. To attend to visiting officials and monks from various mountains:

If the Abbot wishes to avoid formalities, he may issue a pre-emptive notice exempting them from tea and soup services. The administrative office (Kusi) shall prepare the invitation documents and set out the trays and cloths.

Carrying incense and candles, go to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense, perform two prostrations with the hands extended and three full prostrations; if these are waived, perform a touching bow (*chubai*). Then make the request, saying: "After the midday meal, we shall proceed to the Cloud Hall (*yuntang*) for tea. This is a special occasion;

we humbly pray that you will look upon us with compassion and deign to descend. Having made the request, present the formal document and instruct the guest master (*ketou*) to invite the two classes of officials and the senior elders to serve as companions.

The nameplates are hung and the quarters are notified. The abbot’s seat is prepared in the Sangha Hall. When the long board gong sounds at the time of the meal, he burns incense and performs prostrations.
He then inspects the hall and requests tea. After the meal concludes, the drum is struck to assemble the assembly. The head administrative official bows to the abbot and leads him into the hall.
Return to your seats and bow as they take their places. Burn one stick of incense; the abbot bows before the incense, stands to exchange greetings, and remains standing.

When the serving of tea is finished, the incense burner is brought out. Go before the abbot, bow for the tea, and withdraw. Exit from behind the altar to the right, burn another stick of incense, perform three prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*kṣepa*), and leave the hall.

Lead the entire assembly to the abbot’s presence to perform the ritual of gratitude for the tea, using the appropriate words of thanks. Escort them out, then return to the hall to burn incense once more.

The incense offering, the mutual inquiries between the upper and lower sections, the withdrawal from the seats after collecting the cups, and all other details are identical to the special tea ceremony held for the commencement of the summer retreat (*pravāraṇā*).
On the day of the official announcement, the new appointee shall first present it at his temporary quarters; on the day of entering the monastery, it shall be hung before the Sangha Hall.

For the tea and soup offerings between the upper and lower sections, one need only offer incense and submit a formal request. Once the soup offering has concluded, he shall return to his seat to partake of the medicinal food (*bhaiṣajya*).

Formal Memorial (The bhikṣu [Name], Storehouse Officer of this monastery. Right: This [Name] respectfully submits that following the conclusion of the midday meal this morning, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall to extend the rite of congratulation. We humbly hope for Your Reverence’s compassion and pray that you will deign to honor us with your presence.

Respectfully submitted. [Memorial for Tea Service]. Only the character "táng" (tea) is changed; all other details are the same. On the [Day] of the [Month] of the [Year]. Submitted by the bhikṣu [Name], Storehouse Officer of this monastery.)
(Sealable) (Formally bowing and respectfully requesting before the honorable seat of the newly appointed Abbot Dàhéshàng: This bhikṣu [Name], Treasurer of this monastery, respectfully seals it.)
After the *nài* (jujube) small session and the serving of soup, the attendant informs the Abbot. The guest master is then ordered to notify the quarters to post the notice board.

This is prepared for the special emissaries, the two classes of officials, the senior monks, the four quarters, the granary, the storehouse, the hermitage, the pagoda, those temporarily visiting the hall of practice, the attendants of the new entry, the ritual attendants, and the Zen guests who have come along.

If there are guests who have stayed overnight outside the mountain precincts, they should be listed one by one and presented in advance to the newly appointed abbot; these names are then withdrawn until the time for expressing thanks arrives.

At that point, the attendant holds a candle while the server presents the list, and the guest formally expresses their gratitude. For officials and abbots from other mountains who have stayed overnight, seats must be prepared for them.

The assembly descends from their seats. The Chief Seat (Fangzhang) and the Guest Master (Ketu) issue the formal invitation, saying: "Venerable Abbot; we invite the venerable masters of all mountains, the two classes of officials, the West Hall masters, the great elders, the monks of the Enlightenment Hall, the attendants, and the visiting Zen guests."

Immediately upon retiring to the sleeping hall, the officiant serves hot water to the visiting officials. They return to their seats, and after the assembly has dispersed, the tea and fruit are served.
The special envoy and his attendants are then invited to join the party.
Vegetables. When a donor ascends the seat to establish a temple and donate land, the Great Donor and the administrative officers must inform the Abbot the night before.

The following morning, the Attendant instructs the Guest Master to hang the signboard and notify the various quarters. The Treasury Office dispatches personnel to solemnly prepare the ancestral hall and provide offerings. After the morning gruel, specifically...

Having ascended the hall and descended from the seat, the assembly is gathered to proceed to the ancestral shrine. The administrative officers arrive first to burn incense, serve tea and hot water, and present offerings.
When the Abbot arrives, he burns a stick of incense and returns to his place. The Rector intones the sutra and performs the dedication of merit; this follows the local Vinaya regulations.

First, the administrative staff shall present a formal petition to the Abbot regarding the reception of the special envoy. The envoy shall be given a generous *kṣānti* (offering); those who proclaim the memorial and the official documents shall also receive offerings; and those who prepare the vestments and bowls for the hall shall likewise receive appropriate offerings, with the scale of each gift being proportionate to the service rendered.
On the appointed day, the sleeping quarters shall be prepared by nailing up the banners and arranging the seating positions, and the two classes of officials and the senior monks shall be invited.

In the "Accompanying Light" (Guāngbàn) section, a special seat is established specifically for the Special Envoy (zhuǎnshǐ). The guest-inviting attendant (qǐngkè shìzhě) personally invites the Special Envoy, while the rest of the participants are invited by the Abbot’s guest-master (fāngzhàng kètóu).
The ritual protocol is identical to that of the previous "Special Invitation" (tèwéi).

The *kaie* (junior monk) requests the two classes of officials (*ryōban*) to wait until the reception of the special envoy is complete. In the afternoon, they all proceed to the abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*), where they submit their formal report and withdraw. (The head seat [shuso] reports the assembly for the western order;

the chief administrator [tōji] reports the assembly for the eastern order. The abbot treats them with great courtesy, escorting them out with meticulous care. The attendant instructs the guest master to prepare trays and cloths.
Regarding the incense burner, candles, and hot water vessels: the abbot and the attendant shall go to each of the quarters one by one to offer hot water and encourage the guests to remain.

The guest master first notifies the quarters; [the abbot] exits through the right side of the gate and welcomes [the guests] into the hall. He takes his seat at the host’s position, and the attendant burns incense, serves the hot water, and collects the bowls.
Once the abbot has finished offering detailed exhortations, he escorts them out of the gate. This procedure is the same for all the various quarters and the administrative offices.

If one’s term of office has expired and one must wait for a long time, one should likewise visit the various quarters; the provision of hot water and earnest efforts to retain the visitor are the full extent of the host’s etiquette.
Once the abbot has finished his visits, the guest should again submit a formal petition of leave and withdraw in due order.
Regarding the protocol for visiting:
prior to entering the monastery, one must first submit a *mensō* (formal letter of introduction) to pay respects to the local magistrates and their subordinates.

Next, one visits the patrons (*dānapati*), resident officials, nobles, and other mountain monasteries; for these as well, a *mensō* is required. All matters that ought to be visited should be handled by the administrative officers (*chiji*) one by one.

Having submitted this report, the Abbot shall exit his quarters and instruct an attendant to convey his message: "The Head Seat, the Rector, and all the chief officers and administrators should proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to await his departure.
The administrative office (Kusi) shall calculate the estimated time of the Abbot’s return and order the Hall Office to post a notice to inform the assembly.

Once he has entered the mountain, the hall bell shall be struck before the hall to assemble the community for a formal welcome at the gate. When the Abbot descends from his sedan chair, they shall inquire after his well-being, saying: [End of Text]

(Do not trouble the assembly. Immediately proceed to the Buddha Hall and the Local Deity Hall to burn incense. The Head Seat leads the assembly to the Abbot’s Quarters; once received there, the assembly withdraws.
The Guest Master bows and invites the two classes of officials and the senior monks to offer hot tea; after brief conversation, they retire. The Abbot’s attendant inserts incense and prostrates.
Next, the Head of the Retreat leads the assembly in prostration. The Abbot must visit the various quarters to acknowledge these greetings. City...

Guo Jinbian enters and exits at dawn and dusk without a fixed time; there is no necessity for formal protocol. Whenever a public official returns from a distant journey, the Head Seat leads the assembly to welcome him.

The Abbot transmits a message to exempt him from visiting the Abbot’s quarters. He may either return secretly to his seat in the *bō* hall, circumambulate the hall once, and then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters;
or he may return directly to the Abbot’s quarters. In both cases, the two classes of officials (the *qijiu*) must all go to the Abbot’s quarters to inquire after his well-being.

Once, while Wuzu Huikai was residing at Mount Jing, he frequently traveled out to solicit offerings for the monastery. Every time it was mealtime, he would return directly to his bowl station to eat with the assembly.
Once he had hung up his bowl, the guest master from the abbot’s quarters would shout, "The Abbot is making his rounds for greetings! Upon hearing this, the assembly would descend from their seats.
The abbot would burn a single incense stick and make one circuit around the hall, then exit the hall and shout, "The Head of the Hall sends his greetings; there is no need for further formality."

When visiting the elders of the two classes of officials, one should likewise go to the abbot’s quarters to pay respects. One should light incense, offer tea, engage in courteous conversation, and then depart.
[The new abbot] shall take over the communal utensils and personal effects.
The Abbot invites the two classes of senior elders for tea and discusses the affairs of the monastery in detail.

Next, they proceed to the Treasury Office (Kosi) where, with eyes wide open, they together inspect the imperial calligraphies, precious vessels, mortars, foundations, and various articles; these are first presented to the Abbot, and subsequently presented to the Head Monks and Senior Elders.
Each item shall be verified and settled; the accounts of wealth and grain shall be calculated, and the ledgers made clear, showing exactly how much is currently held.

These shall be presented to the Abbot for reference against the *Xuzhi* (Regulations). The tenant households of all manors shall exchange their contracts, and the Abbot shall prepare a public notice to be posted at all manors for general information.
In many places, during the transition of monastic leadership, the administrative officers engage in corruption and extort money and goods from the residents; the subsequent harm is no small matter.
One must not fail to exercise careful scrutiny. Today, the Treasury Office prepares refreshments for the occasion.
*Chanlin Beiyong*, Scroll Four;
*Chanlin Beiyong*, Scroll Five:
Salty [Tea], Boiled [Tea], Serving the Abbot.

If the Dharma heir arrives at the temple for the tea service, he shall be accompanied by the administrative officer (xingzhi) to the storehouse (kusī) to consult on the preparation of food, calculate the funds and goods required, and arrange for their delivery.

The previous evening, they first go to the attendant’s office (shìsī) to report and request permission to announce the matter to the Abbot. They then proceed with full ceremonial decorum to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang).

They insert incense and perform prostrations to invite him; if the Abbot waives formal bows, they perform abbreviated prostrations (chubai). The invitation states: "On the coming day, we shall gather in the Cloud Hall (yuntáng) to prepare this humble meal..."

Offerings. We humbly pray that you will look upon us with compassion and deign to descend [to our assembly]. Your humble servants are moved by the utmost gratitude. The attendant is instructed to direct the guest master to invite the two classes of officials from the single quarters and the four quarters.
Notices are posted to announce the invitation. On the appointed day, the abbot’s bowl seat, table, and cloth are prepared.

The positions for those serving the tea and snacks are assigned. When the fire-board sounds, the assembly proceeds to the hall. The tea and snack servers follow the abbot into the hall and bow as he takes his seat. In the center...
Burn one stick of incense and perform a greeting before the Abbot. After the bier has been turned, the Abbot extends his hand;

the person in charge of the tea service and the hall attendant bow. The Abbot calls out: "Please, the assembly, set down your bowls. When the meal is finished, the person in charge of the tea service burns incense, distributes alms, and performs a greeting.
The Abbot bows and returns to his seat, then instructs someone to distribute the alms. Once the meal is concluded, the kitchen staff opens the meal box, and the bowls are wrapped in their cloths.

The abbot withdraws from his high seat. The person serving tea burns one incense stick and bows in greeting before the abbot. He exits behind the shrine, returns to bow before the incense burner, and strikes the bell as the tea is served throughout.
He proceeds to the abbot’s presence to offer the tea invitation, then exits behind the shrine again and advances to the abbot’s front for a formal prostration.

He states: "On this day, we have offered meager gifts and needlessly troubled you; we are deeply honored by your gracious acceptance. We, your humble servants, are overcome with gratitude. He performs two prostrations with palms joined at the forehead (hanwen), followed by a full prostration (chuli).

Three prostrations; the respondent returns one prostration. [The guest] exits the hall and is escorted out. The person serving tea and refreshments returns to the hall, burns a single stick of incense, and performs inquiries (wensun) between the upper and lower sections to thank those who accompanied him.
He then performs inquiries in the center. The bell is struck to collect the bowls. Next, he proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters to thank him for his gracious visit.
The Abbot follows him to the Guest Hall to offer thanks. If the tea and refreshments are provided by various mountain monasteries, the meal is prepared accordingly.
The co-residents and the abbot proceed to the hall together. They bow to the abbot as he takes his seat; at this point, formal prostrations are waived.

They bow to the person serving tea and snacks and return to their places. Once seated, they rise to burn a single incense stick. They go before the abbot to perform a greeting and distribute alms (kṣānti). Alms are distributed to the assembly, followed by the burning of a "light-accompanying" incense stick.
Returning to their seats, the food is served. The ritual for tea is not explained here. When the tea ceremony concludes, they proceed together to the abbot’s quarters (upādhyāya-vihāra).
The abbot must first go to the guest quarters to express his gratitude.
On the day of the *ranyian* (tea service) for the two classes of officials in the dormitory hall,

the head seat (*shouzuo*), the administrative officers (*zhishi*), and the senior elders (*qijiu*) shall proceed to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense and formally request the abbot to preside over the ceremony.
Next, invite the attendant junior monk (*shishi*). The abbot shall occupy the temple seat, while the two classes of senior monks sit as usual;

the junior monk sits within their midst. When the time arrives, the head seat (*shouzuo*) invites the abbot to emerge. He bows to the seated assembly and performs the formal rites. If he is exempt from these rites, he exits from the right side of the incense burner.

Having burned one stick of incense, he steps forward to inquire after [the master’s] well-being and then distributes the monetary offering (*dakṣiṇā*). The head seat (*śouzuō*) and the three preceding persons inquire after his well-being and return to their positions.
When the meal is finished, the head seat rises, burns incense, and—exempting himself from formal bows—takes his seat to offer tea.
In the *Dàn* (plain) style, the seating positions for the tea service in the mountain dormitories are arranged as usual.

After the tea server has entered the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense and invite the Abbot, he then instructs the Guest Master (*kètóu*) to invite the two classes of officials, the elders, the *méngtáng* attendants, the stewards, the junior disciples, and the companions. When the time arrives, they are invited out.

In the dormitory hall, one briefly exchanges greetings regarding the weather before the incense burner; the abbot is exempt from formal prostrations, and thus there is no bowing when taking one's seat.

Once everyone has entered their positions, a single stick of incense is burned and a monetary offering (*dakṣiṇā*) is presented. The abbot rises and bows to the person serving the tea and refreshments. After the meal is finished, the tea offering is completed.

Before the incense burner, he expresses gratitude for the honor bestowed upon him. The abbot escorts the two classes of officials [the *shangzuo* and *zhuchi*] for several paces, after which he proceeds to the quarters to express his thanks.

If it is a Dharma relative or junior disciple who has handled the administrative affairs, they prepare tea and snacks. On the following day, he goes to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) to pay respects and extend an invitation.

Furthermore, the two classes of officials, the elders, those serving in the *mengtang*, Dharma relatives, fellow countrymen, and junior disciples shall have their seats arranged in the dormitory hall; others shall occupy the remaining seats.

Next, follow the usual procedure. The junior attendant sits inside and performs the ritual of inviting the guest to sit and serving tea; these are all identical to the rituals for preparing and serving tea in the Sangha Hall.
If a senior dharma-kinsman prepares and serves the tea, all other rituals are waived, and one merely burns incense and offers a monetary gift (*dakṣiṇā*).

When a venerable elder visits a monastery, once it is known that he has arrived at the temple, the *weina* (rector) is notified in advance to post the signboard to receive him. Upon his arrival, first present the formal letter of introduction.

When he reaches the *fangzhang* (abbot’s quarters), the great bell is struck and the assembly greets him at the gate. If he declines the formal reception, he enters the temple incognito; only then is the formal notification made.

The Hall Protocol: In the main hall, incense is lit and candles are held. If the visiting dignitaries are senior members of the Dharma family (*dharmabandhu*), the bell at the front of the Sangha Hall is struck to signal their arrival, and they proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) for formal greetings.
They offer incense, though the Abbot may waive this requirement. Before the assembly arrives, the Abbot invites them to be seated;

the attendant (*shizhe*) performs prostrations, burns incense, and serves tea. Once the assembly has arrived, the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) and the administrative officers (*zhishi*) complete their greetings by offering incense; only then does the attendant [resume his duties].
Incense is inserted and prostrations are performed. The guest master (kakutō) bows and invites the two classes of senior monks (kobun) to accompany the guests for tea.

When the tea is finished, the attendant monks (gyōgyōsha) carry incense and perform prostrations. Next, the attendants of the hall (chikishitsu), the palanquin carriers (kyōsō), and the monks of the abbot’s quarters (bōzō) perform their prostrations.

The head of the assembly (san’tō) leads the group in prostration. Once the attendants of the hall and the palanquin carriers have finished their prostrations, the attendant (shijū) burns incense, offers hot water (tō), and escorts the guests out.
The host takes his place on the right and escorts the guest inside. Incense is offered; the guest declines further greetings, briefly exchanges pleasantries regarding the weather, and departs.

Both parties offer incense as a formal greeting. The attendants see them off separately and escort them to their quarters. The guest master orders a palanquin to be prepared. The abbot leads the procession to tour the various administrative offices (*liao*), with the attendant following behind.
The guest master has previously notified all the offices. Once the tour is complete, the abbot returns to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*) together with the guest.

Narrative: It is like a countryman recounting old acquaintances. Once the formalities have concluded, the attendant in charge of guests prepares a written invitation to request a special serving of medicinal soup (*tang*).

He proceeds to the guest quarters, offers incense, and performs a prostration to extend the invitation. If the guest declines the full prostration, he performs a *chuli* (a light bow with hands touching). [The attendant says:

"The Abbot invites the Venerable Master to partake in a special serving of medicinal soup this evening in the Hall of Rest. We humbly pray for your compassionate presence. Having presented the document, the Guest Head reports: "We invite the Venerable Master; after the soup is finished, please take your seat for the medicinal food (*yaoshi*). Then they proceed to the Hall of Rest.

Nail the hall pins and hang the ceremonial placards. Set up special seats for the accompanying guests (*guānbàn*). Urge the guests to perform the rites. After the soup and medicinal food are served, escort them out; all these follow the same protocol as the aforementioned special rites.

The guest master goes to the guests' quarters and invites them, saying: "The Abbot requests the Venerable Master for this evening’s soup and fruit. He then invites the two classes of officers to serve as accompanying guests.
The attendant reports back that they will attend the morning assembly to express their thanks. On the following morning, the attendant invites them for soup. The attendant...

Incense is burned. The practitioner (the abbot) inquires after [the guests’] well-being; the attendants respond with a bow. He requests [them for] gruel and tea. The attendant reports that they are ready to enter the hall.
At the half-day meal and the light refreshment, the Head Seat and the various heads of the assembly go to the Abbot’s quarters to formally request [him to preach].
The Abbot first proceeds to the Guest Seat, burns incense, and states his intention. The Head Seat prepares a formal document, and the two classes of officials and the entire assembly join him.

Proceed to the Guest Seat. Insert incense and bow, making the request: (Bow and request the Abbot to provide instruction for the assembly. Next, request the Chief Administrator: (Bow and request the Abbot to lead the way to the seat.

The Hall Superintendent orders an attendant to notify the quarters to post the notice and prepare the Dharma Seat. Two seats are arranged beneath the platform; when the time arrives, the drum is struck again.
The Abbot descends with the assembly and stands before their positions. The Abbot first leads the way to the seat and then descends from it. Both...

The two ranks proceed to the senior monk (zunsu) to exchange greetings. The senior monk proceeds before the abbot (zhuchi) to exchange greetings, then returns to the center to exchange general greetings.

He ascends the seat. The two ranks step forward from their positions. The attendant (shizhe) ascends the seat to exchange greetings. Having finished the formal instruction, he descends from the seat, exchanges greetings before the abbot, and then exchanges general greetings to thank the assembly.
The abbot immediately proceeds to the guest seat (keli), where he offers incense and bows in thanks. The two ranks [proceed as before].
The assembly follows [the guest] to offer incense and pay their respects. The attendant in charge of invitations prepares a formal document to request that the guest be specially hosted;

the mountain gate (the monastery) prepares the food and provides the primary *dakṣiṇā* (offering), while the robe-casket chamber provides the supplementary *dakṣiṇā*. The attendant in charge of burning incense performs the rites. The procedure for the tea ceremony is the same.

If the guests are fellow monks of the two ranks, nephews, or grand-disciples, they should not be overly diligent in their courtesies during ordinary occasions, lest they invite the ridicule of those who understand the proper way.

Statement on the Serving of Soup (The resident monk of this temple, [Name]. On this evening, I, [Name], have ventured to serve soup in the dormitory hall specifically for you. I humbly beseech your venerable compassion to graciously deign to attend.
Respectfully submitted. [Year] [Month] [Day]. Submitted by the resident monk of this temple, [Name]).

Formal Statement for Hosting (The bhikṣu so-and-so, abbot of this temple. On the right: I, so-and-so, venture to prepare a simple meal of water and rice at the dormitory hall on the coming day. I humbly beseech your venerable compassion to deign to honor us with your presence.
Respectfully submitted. (Year, Month, Day; same as above).

A Memorial from the Head Monks (The head monk of this temple, [Name]. Right: We, [Name] and others, venture to request on the coming day that you exalt the fundamental tenets and provide instruction for future students. We humbly hope that your venerable compassion will graciously grant us your consent.
Respectfully submitted. [Year], [Month], [Day]. Memorial from the head monks of this temple, [Name] and others).
(Sealable) (Formal Request: To the Great Zen Master Abbot of [Place], respectfully sealed by the bhikṣus [Name] et al. of this monastery).

When visiting various mountains in secret, if one learns that the abbot has hung up his name-tablet, one should receive him, meet with him, and perform the customary rites of courtesy as previously described. When visiting neighboring monasteries, seal the letter as before.

Upon arriving, one should first perform the ritual of washing the feet. Those who wish to simplify matters may proceed directly to the abbot’s quarters to avoid mobilizing the assembly for a formal reception;
this is the ancient custom.
If a venerable member of the Dharma family visits, one should take their seat according to monastic rank, offer incense, and prostrate, after which they return to their place as a Dharma relative.

Rituals: Next is the ritual for the mutual greeting of abbots from various mountains. When seated within the abbot’s quarters, one should yield the position of honor to the visiting master and go out to receive him.

If the visitor is a venerable elder (zunsu), he should personally perform the ritual of offering hot water; however, the host should firmly decline this, and instead have an attendant perform the ritual on his behalf.
If a successor to the Dharma, an administrator of Dharma affairs, or a Dharma nephew visits, one should personally go to the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*).
The abbot shall then order the bell before the Sangha Hall to be struck to assemble the community. First, invite the abbot to take his seat; perform the rites of a Dharma relative.

Next, perform the rites for the various mountains (*zhushan*). The protocol for welcoming and escorting is the same as before. However, for a special reception with medicinal broth (*tang*), no formal invitation letter is required. The guest-inviting attendant (*qingke shizhe*) shall light incense...
When a guest arrives to offer incense, one must also observe the seniority of their years of ordination and adapt accordingly to the circumstances.

When an official visits the mountain gate, a notice board shall be hung to inform the assembly; they shall be scouted for and welcomed. As he approaches the gate, the bell on the tower shall be struck, and the assembly shall receive him into the Great Hall.
The Abbot offers incense. After the Chief Seat has offered tea and soup, the guest is escorted back to the guest quarters. Once the refreshments have been served, he is accompanied on a tour.
The administrative office (Kusi) prepares hot water and fruit to attend to him. During their conversation, they discuss many words concerning transcendence from the mundane world.

If there are urgent matters regarding the mountain gate, they should be mentioned with skillful means, and one should visit separately to make a formal request. If he is to stay overnight, one must go up [to the abbot].
The Abbot offers thanks. If the donor departs immediately, the bell in front of the hall is struck to assemble the community to see them out the door.

When a donor invites the Abbot to ascend the seat for a meal, the guest prefect receives them at the gate, leads them to the Abbot’s quarters, presents tea and soup, and escorts them to their place of rest. If it is an official...

Venerable Great Donor: You should ring the bell to assemble the community and receive them; then, invite the administrative officers (*zhishi*) to deliberate together and proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters (*fangzhang*).
There, light incense and formally request the Abbot to ascend the seat. On the appointed day, prepare the Dharma Seat (*fazuò*). (In front of the seat) arrange a place for the donor.

Hang up the "Ascending the Hall" plaque (*shàngtángpái*) and notify the assembly. Strike the drum to gather the community. The Guest Master (*zhike*) shall accompany the donor to the Abbot’s Quarters to invite the Abbot; you must prepare [the necessary items].
With lanterns, banners, hand-bells, and cymbals, [the master] is welcomed before the seat to inspire deep reverence in those present.

The donor performs prostrations before the seat; the guest prefect bows and leads them to their place to listen to the Dharma. (To merely accept the bow and remain seated would be to treat the Dharma with contempt. Upon descending from the seat, he bows in thanks to the abbot.

If there is a meal for the monks, this must be discussed and settled with the administrative officers regarding the ingredients and expenses. The rector shall accurately record the number of monks and their conduct, while the offerings of alms follow accordingly.

Distribute the funds equally. Do not suppress them or cause them to withdraw their intention to give, for it would benefit neither them nor us. Within the Sangha hall, designate a seat for the donor adjacent to that of the Abbot.
Once the meal is concluded, the Abbot and the administrative officers (zhishi) shall go together to the guest quarters to express their gratitude.

If the donor has sent money to provide a meal for the monks, the Abbot must entrust the matter to the administrative officers to ensure the funds are used entirely to prepare offerings and distribute alms; they must not be diverted to other uses.
One should reflect that cause and effect are distinct and clear; how could one not feel anxiety and dread?

Formerly, while Master Zhi of Yungai Monastery in Hunan was sitting in his quarters at night, he saw a monk wearing an iron collar around his neck and with fierce flames enveloping his body. Leaning against the door threshold, the monk said to Zhi:
When Shouyong was previously residing on this mountain, he used the funds donated by patrons for the monks' feast to relocate the Sangha Hall;
consequently, he suffered this retribution. He requested the Master’s compassion to restore the offerings for [Name] so that he might be spared from this transgression.
The Master granted his request, and subsequently, Shouyong indeed attained liberation. The remains of the Patriarch Yangqi are enshrined in a stupa on this very mountain.

Compiled by the Bhikṣu Yi-xian, Abbot of Taiping Xinglong Chan Temple at Mount Lu’s East Forest (Donglin).

The Dragon requests the appointment of the Head Seat (Shouzuo) of the Great Dharma West Hall, a man of renowned virtue who serves as a teacher and model for humans and devas; his words and deeds are in perfect accord, and the entire assembly places its heart in him.

Only then may you formally propose [him] for invitation. This matter is of great gravity; it must be presented with full detail and sincerity. If permission is granted, the assembly shall gather in the hall.
As there are many people here, we require a worthy individual to join us in establishing the banner of the Dharma and opening the great forge, so as to satisfy the hopes of the multitude.

Fortunately, there is a certain person among us in the mountains whose insight is lofty and clear, upon whom the life of wisdom depends. [The Master] descends from his seat. [The two classes of officials.]

The assembly collectively extends this invitation for you to open the chamber for the sake of the multitude. We humbly entreat your compassion and pray that you will graciously grant your consent. [The assembly] descends from their seats.
The Abbot’s quarters prepares an incense table, and the Abbot inserts the incense while joining the assembly in the formal request. The words are as follows: (The assembly inclines their hearts.)

"I have long desired your instruction. I humbly beseech you with compassion to grant me your special permission. He replied, "Since I have received your earnest request, I dare not firmly decline. Having requested this, they all performed a single prostration with full-body contact (sōtō chūrei). The request was thus concluded.
The guest-head attendant presents the two plaques for the "Universal Announcement" (*pūsè*) and "Entering the Room" (*rùshì*). He first places them in a wrapping cloth (*bānfù*).

Once they have been accepted, the hall-administrator attendant collects the plaques. Thereupon, he burns incense before the Abbot’s quarters and performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chùlǐ*) to express his thanks; the Abbot declines the formal bow.

The words of thanks say: "I, [Name], have fortunately found refuge here, seeking only to conceal my own inadequacies. Having been so honored with this invitation, I dare not disobey. The reply says: "Since the elephant-vehicle has arrived, the Wheel of Dharma shall turn constantly. It is not fitting to trouble you; I hope you will value the Way of the Dharma and provide instruction for the sake of the assembly.

The words of a monk of equal standing who rises to receive a visitor say: "I was merely planning to attend your teachings; why would I presume to act as a host? Your honorable command has descended upon me, and my humble heart is filled with shame. The reply says: "The Buddha-Dharma rests upon a heavy responsibility;

I look up to you and beg you to show your compassion. The words of a kinsman of the Dharma coming for study say: "Having received your instructions, I am ordered to receive the inquiries of my brothers. Although I possess no profound realization, I dare not firmly decline. My humble feelings are beyond measure."

Feeling ashamed and apprehensive, he replied, "Since there is still light remaining, I hope you will accept my gratitude for the Buddha-Dharma. Having finished his thanks, the attendant of the Hall Office struck the bell before the Sangha Hall;

the assembly then escorted him together back to his quarters. The Abbot performed a single prostration with full prostration (chuli) in his presence and saw him out. Thereafter, he exchanged greetings with the assembly.
Furthermore, if a man of learning and virtue accepts this invitation and is seated upon the throne to preach, he shall immediately withdraw from the hall, return to his quarters, and close the door.

The abbot descends from the seat and leads the assembly to knock at the door. Upon opening the door, they receive him; the abbot enters, offers incense, and together with the assembly, performs a single prostration with full-body bows (*chuli*).
He then presents the plaque for the general discourse (*pushe*) and entry into the room. Next, having completed the formal greetings with the assembly, the Rector (*weina*) approaches...

In the quarters, one should consult and request a single attendant. It is contrary to the Dharma for there to be an attendant who burns incense for the Holy Monk during the *zhīhuó* (solemn assembly).
In the past, when Master Pò’ān was at Jìngshān, he served as the *lìsēng* (monk-stander) while Wǔzhǔn served as his attendant;

that his lineage flourished in later generations had its origins therein. When hanging up the plaque for the general discourse (*pǔshuō*), the arrangements in the *zhàotáng* (hall of illumination) include a Zen chair, a fly-whisk, an incense burner, and candles.

The *mingzhai* drum is struck once; the assembly gathers and stands in formation. The standing monks return to their positions. The *weina* steps out of the ranks to inquire after the well-being [of the abbot], burns a single piece of incense, and the assembly together performs one prostration with touching the ground (*chuli*).

At this point, they should be excused from further prostrations. They sit cross-legged. When the general discourse (*pushe*) is concluded, the *weina* and the assembly together perform one prostration with touching the ground to express their gratitude.
The standing monks then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*), where they insert incense and unfold their ritual implements. The Abbot should...

[The guest] is exempted [from prostrations]. They perform one bow upon touching [the host’s feet], which is the response to the previous bow. The visiting Dharma-kinsman (saṃgha-member) offering thanks should perform two *zhǎn* and three prostrations, saying these words:

“Having received your command, I have forced my countenance to accept it. Your compassion embraces all things; I am overcome with shame and trepidation. Next, the attendant of the Hall Office leads [the guest] to the Kitchen Office (*kūsī*).

Regarding the formal greetings at the various quarters, the Abbot prepares a simple meal and invites [the guest] for a special medicinal soup and a vegetarian feast. In the evening, there is a serving of soup and fruit for the two classes of officials.

The attendant for the newly appointed monk stands by; the attendant serving the Abbot sits at the same seat. Early the next morning, the Abbot invites the Sangha to a special tea ceremony in the Sangha Hall.
The guest-attendant prepares the tea notice and goes to the quarters to offer incense and extend the invitation, which is identical to the procedure for the special tea for a new Head Seat.
The newly appointed monk shall attend the special tea for his subordinate assistant, which is identical to the special tea for a new Rear Hall official. On another day, the Abbot [invites them to]...

They were treated with great hospitality, and both groups of attendants served as companions. This office was difficult to accept for two reasons; it was one that all must regard as a heavy responsibility.
In the past, when Meng’an of Mount Jing invited Pò’ān, and Sōngyuǎn of Línghyìn invited Yǎnshì, they exhorted and inspired one another so that the Dharma might endure for a long time.
Within the room of Pò’ān, he raised a koan regarding Old Monk Bǎo, who had no place to open his mouth, and immediately passed away while sitting.
The posthumous bequest of his skull relic was presented to the Head Seat; he may indeed be called a man who has settled his affairs.
Yet, one must not fail to realize that Pō’ān’s karmic path was perfectly fluid and difficult to grasp; he was someone whom all people revered.
The Master requests that the Virtuous Head Seat (Śraddhācārya) be invited to serve as the attendant;
this must first be announced in advance. If he expresses his consent, the Abbot shall first invite him for tea, with the two classes of officials serving as companions.

Thereupon, the drum shall be struck to ascend the seat; no placard need be hung to notify the assembly. The Abbot, with sincere devotion, shall entrust him with the affairs of the monastery, keeping the Dharma in mind.
With sincere earnestness, the assembly descends from their seats and performs a single prostration with full-body contact (chuli) to request [the abbot’s departure].

The bell is struck to escort him back to his bowl-position, and as he returns to his quarters, there is likewise a single prostration with full-body contact. Subsequently, the two classes of officials and the general assembly offer congratulations, providing tea and soup as a formal reception.
The ritual is the same as before. Advancing and retreating are not intermingled; there is no handover between the two classes [of officials].

Regarding the fire [ceremony], the two classes advance and retreat either at the conclusion of the retreat period (*kaji*) or on New Year’s Eve; this is the constant custom for each location. The head officers and personnel should [be appointed] during the summer months.

Thoroughly examine those who have completed their studies and assign them to positions according to their abilities. Matters concerning the affairs of the various departments, as well as the annual accounting of the temple storehouses, must all be handled with meticulous care.

When the term of office is about to end, one should report one’s intention to retire in advance to the Abbot. Once the personnel selection is finalized and it is intended that the appointments will take effect the following day, the attendant should privately inform the two classes of officials.
At the tolling of the evening bell, the first group of administrative officers shall proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer incense. Universally...

They perform a single prostration with full prostration (tongchu) and withdraw. Among them, if some remain for a second time, the abbot lights a lamp and escorts them back to the administrative office (kusō).
The attendant burns incense and serves hot water. At the striking of the five-watch bell, a group of head officials (doushou) enters the Abbot’s Quarters (shangfang) to offer incense.
Having prostrated and touched the ground, he withdraws. If the candidate is to be retained for a second time, on the evening of the day prior, the Abbot visits the quarters;

the attendant burns incense and serves hot water, urging him to stay. He is then requested to select a head official from among the eminent and senior members of the assembly, consulting them to ensure that the choice is made with ten-thousandfold certainty.

Regarding the administrative officers (*zhishi*), the Abbot must consult those of public-mindedness and long-standing seniority, as well as the senior administrative officers, ensuring his countenance remains harmonious throughout.
Meeting. Once this is concluded, the various offices shall be assigned by entrusting them to those close to you—your heart and belly—who are harmonious and capable.

Each position must be predetermined before the formal appointment and invitation proceeds. I have observed that among all the positions in the Eastern Wing, none is more heavily burdened than this one.

Lately, however, abbots have often yielded to private favoritism, making no distinction between the worthy and the unworthy; they invite anyone back to the administrative office (*kusō*), and there is nothing they will not do to exploit and diminish the regular provisions.

[The Abbot] resides [here], yet he treats his own abundance with disdain toward the public interest. Matters concerning the maintenance and construction of the mountain gate (the monastery) are of grave importance, yet he shows not the slightest concern;
this is truly lamentable. Observing this, one should assemble the great assembly to deliberate in public accord with a unified mind.

Those whose reputation accords with their reality shall be invited by the community, with the dragon spirits invoked as witnesses. All offices, whether high or low, shall be shared equally through the drawing of lots, so that private interests may be eliminated. [End of] Monastery Rules.

The monastic groves must not fall into neglect. As for the incumbent abbot, he should carefully examine the candidates. The abbot shall personally visit the quarters of the former Hall Head Seat (Skt.

*śrāmaṇera-ācārya*), where the attendant (*karmadāna*) shall burn incense and serve tea; he should extend the utmost courtesy in his formal invitation, for this individual serves as the model for the entire monastery.

Following this, the other head officers (*śīrṣa-dhara*) should also be provided with due consideration. On the appointed day, regarding their advancement or dismissal, the attendant shall discreetly inform the abbot and prepare a list of those invited to witness the ceremony.

The attendant shall provide the names of the guests and instruct the guest-head acolyte to serve tea. While waiting for the monks' hall meal, he shall invite them again. He shall assign acolytes to guard the invitation and serve tea.
When the guests arrive at the dormitory hall, he shall invite the West Hall Master and the senior elders to accompany them. He shall then invite a group of former administrators.
Once the meal distribution is complete, they shall enter through the rear gate. The head official shall strike the wooden mallet once and announce: (Addressing the assembly: We, [Name] and others...)

Having received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, we were ordered to return to the administrative office (*kūsī*). Now that one year has passed, our mental and physical strength are exhausted; we respectfully request leave to return to the hall. (This is the formal announcement. Strike the mallet once more.

From the left side behind the shrine (*gàn*), the attendants exit and proceed before the Abbot. They perform two prostrations with the sitting cloth unfolded and three prostrations with the sitting cloth folded. For the first unfolding, they say: "Yesterday, we were honored by your selection; we deeply regret our lack of talent. We are overcome with a sense of shame and trepidation.

For the second unfolding, they exchange greetings. They perform three prostrations with the sitting cloth folded, then withdraw. From the right side behind the shrine, they exit and proceed before the Sacred Monk (*shèngsēng*). Great...
Perform three prostrations. Turn around and inquire after the abbot’s well-being. Circumambulate the hall once while facing north, perform an inquiry in the center, and then withdraw.

After the morning gruel, do not recite sutras. Each person shall attend the invitation to the dormitory hall. Once the abbot has received them and the tea offering is complete, each person rises personally to burn a single incense stick.

Return to their positions and arrange themselves according to the order of the invitation. The attendant [name] bows and addresses the assembly: "The two preceding classes have requested to retire; it is not permissible to leave these positions vacant."

I respectfully request [Name] to serve as the head of [position]. (The attendant presents the list; the abbot finishes the formal request. Proceeding before the incense burner, the attendant bows and invites the new) head. Each one proceeds before the incense burner to accept the invitation.
If they do not yet consent to the request, the assembly of elders shall exert themselves to encourage them.

Once the abbot has first performed a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*), the head performs a corresponding single prostration in response. Having finished the formal request for the entire class of administrators (*zhishi*) and the class of heads, they step forward.

The ceremony proceeds as follows. First, the initial unfolding [of the mat] is performed, saying: "We, [Name et al.], feel deeply ashamed that we are unworthy vessels; yet, having been undeservedly selected for inclusion, our hearts are overcome with humiliation and trepidation.

Second, the formal greetings are exchanged. Three prostrations are performed (chuli), and the abbot returns each prostration. The abbot returns to his seat, and the assembly takes their places to drink the medicinal broth (*tang*).

The new members of the eastern and western ranks sit facing the abbot, while the senior monks are seated in alternating rows above and below. The attendant burns incense and serves the broth; in some traditions, there is a formal bow before sitting down.
To bow before the incense and the hot water is contrary to the Dharma; this [offering of] hot water occurs later that evening. The lecture is held specifically as a formal rite.

The attendant (kōtō) strikes the bell before the Sangha Hall. The assembly enters the hall and stands. A group of new administrators (shinjisho) stand in a row facing the wooden board in the West Hall.

The Abbot escorts those from the front hall to their respective bowl-positions and performs a single prostration with touching the ground (saitokurai). Next, the head officers (zuishu) follow and perform the same prostration.
Perform one bow according to the ritual. Next, escort [the assembly] to the rear hall and return to the bowl-position. Perform one prostration with touching (chu-lì) facing the altar.
If the front hall is absent, ascend the hall on a separate day and speak of it. Only after the rear board has been turned to the front board do they insert their mats and chant for food.
The Abbot returns to his position and stands firm. Once the Rector and Guest Master have withdrawn, the Attendant goes before the Abbot, bows, and stands to one side. The Abbot...

Hand over the mallet to the attendant. Face the assembly and inquire after their welfare. Moving behind the shrine and around the side of the mallet, strike it once and say: "The former administrator has requested to retire. This office must not be left vacant.
Having just received the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, I have appointed [Name] to serve as [Position]. This is respectfully announced. Strike the mallet once more.

The guest master then bows and invites the newly appointed official to come forward in a single file to the presence of the Abbot. They perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chul-ri*) and receive their appointment.
The attendant announces: (Having requested the administrative officers [zhishi] to attend). Again, the mallet is struck once. The assembly of administrative officers performs their prostrations:

the first unfolding of the mat and the second unfolding of the mat (the words of greeting are the same as those for the Head Seat). They perform three prostrations with full prostration (*chuli*) in unison. The Abbot returns one prostration.

The administrative officers turn behind the shrine and exit to the right, standing in a row in front of the Holy Monk (*shengseng*). They perform three prostrations with full unfolding of the mat. The attendant leads them before the Abbot and asks.
Inquire. Facing north, circumambulate the hall once, then return to the center to inquire. Step back two or three paces sideways and stand at the head of the West Hall platform.

The attendant of the Hall Administration (Tangsi Xingzhe) calls out: "The new administrator greets the assembly. [The assembly] performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (*chuli*). Again he calls out: "The assembly pays its respects and congratulates the new administrator.

[The assembly] performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths. Again he calls out: "The new administrator expresses his thanks to the assembly. [The assembly] performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths.

Three prostrations. [The abbot] shouts: (The assembly escorts the new chief administrator back to the administrative office). The head of offerings strikes the bell in front of the Sangha Hall to escort the new chief administrator.
The former head of the front hall (*qiantáng*) and the *weina* (recluse master), as well as the former general administrator (*dūsuì*) of the front hall, then cease striking the bell.

A group of administrative officers stands to the right outside the door of the storehouse (*kūsī*). The incumbent enters, performs a single prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*duòlǐ yībài*), escorts the incumbent out, and then exchanges duties with the former occupants.

He bows with unopened sitting cloth once to the former occupant on the left; the new occupant turns to the left and bows with unopened sitting cloth once. Each party then exchanges greetings regarding their health and welfare.

[The new Head Seat] offers congratulations. When the Head Seat leads the assembly to arrive, [the incumbent] receives them at the entrance, exchanges inquiries of well-being, and offers congratulations.

He then escorts them out, shouting: "The assembly escorts the new Head Seat back to his quarters. Next, he receives the Abbot entering; they perform a single prostration with touching of foreheads (*pratigha-vaṃdana*).

He escorts him out. Next comes the handover of duties; the two, acting as guest and host, perform a single prostration with touching of foreheads. He escorts him out. Next, the Head Officers lead the assembly to offer congratulations, shouting: "Head Seat and Assembly..."

(Sending off the new *vinaya-dhara* to his quarters: The Abbot escorts him in. [The new official] performs one prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*tuchil*). He is escorted out. The handover is celebrated as before. Again, he calls out:

(Please invite the Head Seat and the assembly to escort the former Head Seat and the Chief Administrator back to their private quarters. Again, he calls out: (Please invite the two classes of officials, the elders, and the Rear Hall Secretary, Librarian, and Guest Master to escort them to their respective quarters.

Having announced and escorted each one accordingly, he calls out: (Escort the former head officers and administrators back to the Monks’ Hall and the Quarters for Former Benefactors. The Abbot escorts them in. [The officials] perform one general prostration with unopened sitting cloth. They are escorted out.

He carries [the items] out. Standing in the position of the presiding master, he receives the attendants and offers congratulations; he escorts them out. He receives the two classes of the assembly and offers congratulations; he escorts them out. Standing in the position on the right, he performs the ritual of exchanging greetings with the *sachal* master. This is done for both the new and the senior classes.

He shall immediately proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to pay respects and invite the new and former *duwei* (head administrators) and the *shouzuo* (head seat). Each shall offer incense; these matters shall be prepared and sent by the Storehouse Office (*kusu*). (The new and former members of the two orders shall together tour the quarters.

For the midday meal and light refreshments, as well as the informal rice meal at the time of the main meal, they shall all attend at the Abbot’s quarters. The *xitang* (western hall monks) and *qijiu* (venerable elders) shall accompany them. Those holding duties in the storehouse or administrative offices shall not be included in the replacement roster.

Having first conducted a thorough examination, he shall then promptly invite replacements for the following positions: the *lioyuan* (head of the quarters), the *yanshou tangzhu* (master of the long-life hall), the *jingtou* (purifier), the *lutou* (incense-burner), the *tantou* (charcoal-burner), and the *shuitou* (water-bearer).)

The various officials of the subordinate ranks shall wait until the two classes of monks have finished their invitations. On another day, they shall visit the Hall Administration Office (Tangsi) to announce their retirement. Those with the Way-mind shall be selected to take turns in succession.
The Abbot shall offer greetings, and the Kitchen Administration (Kusi) shall attend to the personnel matters; they shall be provided with refreshments according to custom.

The Emperor hung up his alms bowl and invited Dahuì Jiāntáng to serve as the *zhīshì* (administrator). His virtue and character were held in the highest esteem. Whenever he was to be requested to serve as an administrator, no prior consultation was held.

After the morning gruel was finished, the attendant of the Hall Office (*tángsī xíngzhě*) called out: "I request the assembly to stand slightly back. The *wéiná* (chant leader) burned a single incense stick before the Sacred Monk (*shèngsēng*) and made one circuit around the hall.
Approach the Abbot to inquire after his well-being. Stand to the right, facing him. Once the greetings have been exchanged face-to-face, turn behind the shrine and move toward the side of the mallet.

Strike the mallet once and announce: "In accordance with the compassionate instructions of the Abbot, [Name] is appointed to the position of [Title]. Having completed the announcements for each person one by one, the Guest Master bows to the invitees and leads them before the Abbot to receive their appointments;
the ritual is identical to that described previously. Next, the assembly invites the head officers, the elders, and the senior monks.
Tea. Exhortation. Once the invitation is concluded, gifts are presented; these procedures are all the same as before.

When the attendants have advanced and retreated and the heads of the community have withdrawn, a group of attendants, assuming their proper decorum, shall present a formal petition. The Abbot should beforehand select the appropriate person to serve as the inviter.

When the two ranks [of officials] have finished, the attendants approach the abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to offer incense and perform three prostrations with fully opened sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*).
