Having reported their departure, the abbot issues an order to the Hall Office (*tangsi*). The office immediately dispatches an attendant to invite the newly appointed official to the Hall Office for tea.

Upon arrival, the official is ushered in with a bow. After offering incense and serving tea, he rises again to burn another stick of incense. Returning to his position, he stands and makes the following announcement: "Just now, having received..."

The Abbot, by his compassionate decree, commands that this senior monk (upāsaka) be appointed to such-and-such an office. Having made these formal requests one by one, the person receiving the appointment steps forward and performs a full prostration with the hands touching the ground.

He then shifts his position to offer hot water (*kāṣāya*). The Rector (*vinaya-dhara*) performs the rites, including the gestures of invitation to sit, the incense, and the hot water. He then invites the Head of the Quarters (*karmadāna*) to accompany him as a guest.

Once the offering of hot water is concluded, they proceed together to the Abbot’s quarters (*upādhyāya-śālā*). Upon arrival, the assembly of attendants stands in formation; the attendant in charge of burning incense [leads the way].

Insert the incense. After performing three prostrations with the full prostration (dazhan), the Rector (Weina) escorts the attendant back to his quarters. [The attendant] performs one prostration by touching the ground (chuli) and escorts the Rector out.
The protocol for the exchange with the former incumbent is the same as that for the head officials (tou-shou). The Venerable’s attendants (fangzhang xingzhe) insert incense and perform prostrations.
The sedan-chair bearers go directly to the hall to pay their respects. If the guest is a man of renowned virtue, the abbot shall waive formal greetings upon first meeting him;

he shall personally escort him to his quarters and perform one prostration with touching of foreheads (*sōraku-irei*). This concludes the protocol for the *naikan* (attendant) and the *rinji* (guest).

The attendants of the Hall Office then lead the new and former *shisho* (attendants) on a tour of the quarters. On a separate day, after the *naikan* has entered the quarters, the *naikan* and the *dōshin* (one who possesses the Way-mind) shall immediately hold a harmonious assembly.
The brothers take their respective offices. The *vina* leads them up to pay obeisance to the Abbot; those exempted from this perform a greeting and withdraw.

They are provided with tea and soup according to custom, and treated with refreshments. On that same day, the Hall Office issues a notice to invite the former attendants for tea and escorts them back to the communal quarters.

The head *vinaya-dhara* performs one prostration with full contact (*sāṃghāṭī-vaṃdana*) facing [the master], and another prostration with full contact facing him as he turns away. He then escorts the *vinaya-dhara* out the door.
Next, he exchanges greetings with the head of the quarters (*liao-yuan*).
The Official: The Abbot specially invites the guests for the hot water ceremony for the new and old two classes of attendants.

The Attendant-in-Charge (Kisō) is instructed to prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles. He proceeds before the Head Seat (Shuso) of the New and Old Front Halls to offer incense. The Head Seat returns the incense;

[the attendant] performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (churitsu) and returns the bow. He then reports: "The Abbot requests that we attend to the special service in the Sempin Hall prior to retiring."
Offering Hot Water: Next, before the former and current *dusi* (abbots), incense is lit; there is no bowing. The wording is the same as before.

Next, the two classes of officials, both former and current, along with the venerable companions, are invited by the *katō* (guest master) to the *shindō* (sleeping hall) for the formal seating arrangement. The *itō* (head of ranks), *sittō* (head of the west hall), and *shuso* (first seat) serve as the companions.

One representative from each class of new head officials (*shuto-shu*) comes forth, two representatives from the new administrative officers (*shichiji*), and three representatives from the old head officials (*koto-shu*). The old...

The administrative officers (zhishi) exit four times; the senior monks of the western class exit five times; the senior monks of the eastern class exit six times. The assembly generally divides up to share their seats.

The incense-burning attendants (shaoxiang shizhe) pre-arrange the name tablets (zhao-pai). When the time arrives, the drum is struck and the guests assemble. The two attendants perform the ritual prostrations. The protocol for the small-seat soup (xiaozuo tang) is the same.
In the evening, there is soup and fruit; early the next morning, tea is requested in the Sangha Hall. New and old monks follow their respective [seating] positions.

He is invited [to the ceremony]. As there is no accompanying light (attendant), the procedure follows the usual custom. The administrative office (Kusi) invites him for tea; as he is unable to attend, he declines.

After the tea at the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang), they go together to the administrative office to express their thanks. At the midday meal, there is a snack. On the following day, the administrative office provides a snack.

The administrative office presents the outgoing [official] with a bowl of congee and rice, along with five-flavor soup, bowls, plates, and various utensils and implements, which the Guest Master (Kektou) distributes according to precedent.
Sending Off. On the third day, they are sent back to their bowl positions. The diagram of the positions is the same as the third seat for the minor seats; the six people exit the positions together.
The Hall Master specially prepares hot water and tea for the new and former attendants.
After the meal of coarse rice is finished, the *vinaya-dhara* orders the attendants of the Hall Office to go before the new and old *śrāmaṇeras* and submit individual requests;

they also invite the *seng-seng* (the sacred monk) and his attendant. Before the morning assembly, they proceed to the quarters to offer hot water. In the evening, the Hall Office prepares the seats and arranges the name tablets (*zhao-pai*).

They invite the head of the quarters (*liang-yuan*) and his companions, and after the guest is summoned by the striking of the board in front of the quarters, he is ushered in, bows to take his seat, and performs the formal rites together with the storehouse keeper.

The procedure for the *sītānglì* (offering of tea) is the same. When it is performed specifically for the Abbot (*fangzhàng*) at the head of the hall, it takes precedence and prevents the attendant (*xingshizhe*) from performing his own rites.

After the Abbot has finished the special tea service in the Sangha Hall, the Hall Administration (*táng-sī*) conducts the tea ceremony. On the following day, the new and former attendants go to the Hall Administration to offer their thanks.

The Imperial Treasury Office (Ku-si), having specially prepared the medicinal decoctions, rice, and vegetables for both the new and old classes of officials, ordered the guest master (Ke-t’ou) to prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, and candles. The presiding administrator (Shang-shou Chih-shih) proceeded to the quarters of the new head seat (Shou-cho) to offer incense.

The head seat returned the incense, saying: "Tonight, following the tea service at the Abbot’s quarters (Fang-chang), we have been specially invited by the Treasury Office to partake of this tea offering. We humbly pray that you will deign to honor us with your presence. The guest master then invites him [to the treasury].

[When the meal is finished, they take their seats for the medicinal food. Next, invite the new and old officials of all ranks, the elders, and the *guangban* (attendants). The *kusu* (storehouse office) shall nail up the hanging boards and arrange the seating positions according to the tablets.
The *xitang* (West Hall) serves as *guangban*; if none is available, the elders or the *shouzuo* (Head Seat) shall do so. The positions are divided into six sections:

one section for the new head officials, two sections for the old head officials, three sections for the administrative officers (*zhishi*), and four sections for the stewards and storekeepers; these shall be received in order.

They take their seats in order of rank. The new chief administrator (shinjishu) does not join the seating below the head position; the new *vinaya-master* (*vinaya*) stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the senior administrators.
The elders of the western and eastern groups stand in fixed positions according to their respective signs, at five or six paces from the front.

The head administrator (*dutō*) steps forward from the first row and bows in a straight line, then proceeds directly through the center to bow to the assembly. Once the assembly is seated, he steps forward once more.

Burn two sticks of incense. From the first stick, emerge from one side and perform a greeting facing [the assembly]. Circulate until you reach the end of the row, then again perform a greeting facing [them].
Repeat this greeting as before when emerging from the second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth sides. Having completed the circuit, return to the center and perform a greeting.
Burn one stick of "light-companion" incense, take your seat at your position, and perform the morning bows with the assembly. Serve the hot water; once the serving is finished, rise.

The *shen* (body) [officiant], one senior from each of the new and old classes of monks, goes forth before the incense burner to offer thanks for the medicinal broth. Each withdraws their robe and takes their seat for the medicinal meal (*yaoshi*).
This marks the beginning of the procedure for sending the alms bowl to its designated place.

Three days after the retirement of the two *bans*, before the opening of the *sōjō* (small retreat), the hall attendants (*dōshi gyōja*) and laborers light lamps and invite the former head seat (*shuso*) and the former chief administrator (*dutera*).
They proceed to the *weinā*'s quarters to offer hot water (*tō*). Upon entering, they burn incense and present the water. The attendant states the purpose:

"As your pure office has now concluded, it is the duty of this mountain gate to extend the formal invitation for you to occupy a seat in the assembly. The *weinā* has already designated the head position of the seating row; he first escorts the former head seat inside.
At the bowl position, [the monk] performs a prostration with touching (sōtsu-rei). Next, the head administrator (jissatsu) receives the bowl and escorts him to the bowl position.

[The monk] performs a prostration with touching and bows in greeting. The rector (wina) exits through the front gate. The head seat (shuso) and the head administrator hang the bowl and proceed to the hall.

If it is a renowned West Hall (saitō) monk who has arrived at the temple to register as a resident, the abbot invites him for soup; they then go together to the hall to escort him back to his bowl position. If there is an East Hall (tōtō), [the same applies].

After the funeral rites, the *shen* (separation) board and *bō* (alms bowl) positions for the Rear Hall (*houtáng*) are assigned. Monks from various regions who have been registered as *dūtsì* (administrators) in the Front Hall (*qiántáng*) yield one position to the native monastery (*běnshān*).

The remaining positions are arranged in order for the Rear Hall Secretary (*shūjì*), the Chief Administrator (*jiānsì*), and the Librarian (*zàngzhǔ*), with the latter serving as the secondary bowl-position holder (*fù bōwèi*).

These assignments follow the seniority of the mountain gate (*shānmén*). For instance, when Master Dàchuān resided at Jìngcí Monastery, he followed this precedent by arranging the two venerable patriarchs, Dōngsǒu and Shílín, in their respective positions.
On the day of the arrival, at the head of the upper board [of the assembly] sits the *shoushuo* (head monk), and at the head of the lower board sits the *dutsi* (abbot).
A special seat is prepared for the abbot to ascend and offer a formal address to entertain both the new and old officials of the two classes.

After the abbot has descended from the seat to express his gratitude to the new and old officials of the two classes, the assembly steps forward to offer their thanks. The *zhuzhu* (resident master) then ascends the seat.

The administrative office (kusi) shall first notify the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to prepare food offerings. The attendant for guests (qingke shizhe) shall instruct the guest-head acolyte (ketou xingzhe) to prepare trays, cloths, incense burners, candles, and incense cases.
They shall then proceed to the quarters of the new and former head seats (shouzuo) and the chief administrative officer (dusi) to offer incense and make the following request:

(For the Abbot of the Main Hall: at the hour of noon, he is invited to the Dormitory Hall for a formal reception. He shall return the incense. Next, the two classes of officials—both new and incumbent—and the elder dignitaries who accompany them, shall all be invited by the Guest Master (*kettō*).

In the Dormitory Hall, seats shall be arranged and designated tablets hung; these are supervised by the attendant in charge of incense (*shōkō jishu*). Before the meal, the guests must be urged to assemble.
The Abbot receives them with a bow of inquiry (*monshun*), followed by the reception of the accompanying dignitaries, each respectively.
Take your seats. Stand according to the order indicated by the tablets. The two attendants perform their bows. Circulate and bow as you take your places to burn incense;
you must step forward to offer the incense. After bowing for the incense, serve the hot water; step forward again to bow for the hot water. Bring forth the tables.

The group of attendants stands before the Abbot and performs a *wensun* (inquiry). Enter your positions and serve the rice. The attendant in charge of burning incense leaves his position to offer one stick of incense. Serve the monetary offering (*dakṣiṇā*) once more.

The procedure follows the standard protocol. Upon finishing the meal, the drum is struck and the tea ceremony is performed. The attendant burns incense, and the two attendants step forward to bow for the incense and the tea;
this is identical to the ritual for the special serving of hot water (*tokui-tō*). However, there is no single round of bowing for the seating. When the tea is finished:
He expresses his thanks before the incense burner. The Abbot escorts him out, followed by the attendants.

Text: After the Abbot has finished the tea service for the Mountain Gate following his visit, and after the Abbot has concluded his midday meal, he visits the various quarters to serve tea; this is intended as a gesture of kindness and warmth.
If one inspects the monastic quarters and finds inconveniences or a deficiency in utensils and supplies, the administrative office (kusi) shall be tasked with procuring them.

The laborers assigned to the Hall of the Preceding Elder (qiantangliao) and the Guest Office (zhikeliao), as well as the tea masters, are traditionally exempt from communal labor (pucheng). The laborers of the Rector’s Office (weinaliao) are exempt from communal labor during the summer retreat.
Regarding the communal labor of laborers in other quarters, if it does not interfere with public duties, it must be carefully reviewed and permitted; this is often due to minor matters.

Do not be negligent, lest you cause harm to the harmonious atmosphere. When visiting monks arrive, do not restrict them by fixed times; once the midday meal has passed, one must strike the bell to serve them food and receive them with hospitality.
The officials in charge of the storehouse and kitchen must not treat them with contempt or harshness. Tea, soup, and the five flavors should be distributed appropriately and equitably.

Regarding items such as paper, pens, and fruit, as well as robes, alms bowls, and attendants, they should be provided for and looked after at the proper time. Since the duties of the abbot are manifold, those who stand by his side should be virtuous and worthy.
"Very well. [The guest] writes his name. The Abbot personally serves tea for the new Head Seat;
after the Abbot has attended to him with hospitality, on the following morning, the Incense-Burning Attendant informs the Abbot, and the Guest-Master prepares a tray, cloth, and incense burner.

Light incense and candles. The attendant in charge of guests writes the tea notice (*chábǎng*). He proceeds to the Chief Seat’s quarters (*shǒuzuò liáo*) and offers incense (the Chief Seat returns the incense).

He performs one prostration with full prostration (*chùlì yībài*) (the Chief Seat returns the prostration). He makes his formal request, saying: "The Abbot has retired from the midday meal; we shall serve special tea in the Cloud Hall (*yúntáng*) specifically for you. We humbly hope that you will deign to honor us with your presence. The guest master reports this to the various quarters and posts the notice.

He invites the administrative officials (*zhīshì*) to accompany [the Abbot]. In the Sangha Hall, a seat for the Abbot is set facing him, with seats for the accompanying officials arranged on either side. The *weina*...
The *nā* (monk official) stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the *dusi* (abbot’s attendant). Next, the *chishi* (administrative officer) and the *tokui* (special guest) take their respective seats.

Four *hantō* (senior monks) do not set up incense stands. Attendant monks are assigned to serve the cups directly for the *tokui*. Awaiting the sounding of the long board, the guest-inviting *shisō* (attendant) performs three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloth (*taizen*) before the Sacred Monk (*shōsō*).
He then circumambulates the interior and exterior of the hall once to invite the tea. When the midday meal has concluded, the guest-master strikes the drum.
The assembly gathers. The incense-bearer performs the ritual prostrations. The entire western class returns to the front row. The attendant bows to the front hall and returns to his special position.

He then bows to those in the lower shoulder-seats and escorts them to their places. Once they have entered their positions, he exits to the right of the shrine and reports to the Abbot to return to the hall.
The offering master strikes the bell seven times. The attendant burns one stick of incense and proceeds directly to the person for whom the service is specially intended.
First, inquire after his health. Exit to the right and stand in the center. Ring the bell twice. First, serve tea specifically for the person being honored; next, distribute tea to the assembly.

When the distribution is finished, go before the Head Seat (Śraddhādeśaka) and bow for tea. Exit to the right and stand in the center. First, collect the cups used by the Head Seat and the Abbot (Upādhyāya).

The Head Seat (Shouzuo) proceeds directly to the front of the Abbot and performs a prostration. For the first unfolding of the incense burner, he says: "On this day, we have been specially honored by your hospitality; your courtesy is excessive, and I am overcome with shame and trepidation. For the second unfolding, he exchanges greetings.

He performs three prostrations with the forehead touching the ground (*chuli*), and each receives one bow in return. The Head Seat exits to the right of the shrine niche and out through the front gate. The Abbot escorts him for a short distance. Upon returning to his position, he takes up the cup.
The Attendant burns a single stick of "light-accompanying" incense. The bell is struck once, and the ritual concludes.
One cup. The drums are struck three times. Retire from the seat.

Proclamation Form: "Venerable Abbot: This day, following the midday meal, we shall serve one round of tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for the newly appointed Head Seat (Shouzuo), as a modest expression of our congratulations.
We also request the attendance of all the administrative officers (Zhishi). On this day of this month, The Attendant [Name] The Guest Master [Name] respectfully informs you."
The new Head Seat specifically prepares tea for the assembly of the Rear Hall (if there is no Rear Hall, it is for the next-ranking Head Official).

After the tea service at the Abbot’s quarters is concluded, early the following morning, the Head Seat prepares a formal petition, sets out a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, and candles, and proceeds to the Rear Hall quarters.

He burns one stick of incense (and returns the incense to the burner), makes his request, saying: "This day, after the midday meal, we shall serve tea in the Cloud Hall specifically for you; we humbly hope you will deign to honor us with your presence. Having presented the petition, once it has been accepted, he escorts him out.

Instruct the tea-head (chádóu) to hand over the offerings to the offering-head (gòngtóu). Affix the seal on the front of the formal document (zhuàng) at the lower section of the front of the Sangha Hall.

Order the Hall Office (táng-sī) to notify the quarters and post the notice board; arrange the seats and spread out the name-boards (zhào-pái). When the long board gong sounds, the Sangha is invited for tea.

The drum is struck to assemble the assembly for the performance of rites. One proceeds in person to the Abbot’s quarters (fāngwǎng) to request tea; the protocol is identical to that of the previously mentioned special tea service.

Formal Memorial (The bhikṣu so-and-so of the Eastern Hall, and the attendant so-and-so, on this day after the midday meal, shall proceed to the Cloud Hall to serve one round of tea specifically for the Head Seat of the Western Hall, as a formal ceremony of congratulation.)
I again request that all the administrators deign to visit me in person. On this day of this month, [the monk] so-and-so of the Former Hall submits this petition.
(Sealable) (Formal Request to the Rear Hall Head Seat and the Assembly. Respectfully sealed by the Fore-Hall Bhikṣu [Name]).

The "Tea for the Handover of Duties" (*fù jiāodài chá*) is a grand ceremony of the monastic groves (*cónglín*). Nowadays, tea ceremonies have been dispensed with at various monasteries; instead, they specifically provide one portion of refreshments (*diǎnxīn*), which is contrary to the Dharma.
When the head monk has finished the tea service for the Sangha hall, he shall perform the ritual for handing over his duties.

Dignified in demeanor and carrying incense in his sleeve, he proceeds in person before the successor, offers incense, and performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*chuli*). He then makes this request: "The meal having been concluded, I humbly beg the Venerable One to condescend to visit my quarters for tea.

Following this, he instructs the tea server to invite the two classes of officials and the senior elders to serve as companions. Within the quarters, the seating is arranged with a special seat set in the center, while the others take their places to the left and right.
The attendants accompany the person of high rank; the administrators take their seats at the head of the hall, while the others sit in order according to their positions.

The hall attendant and the novice report to the head of the assembly to dispatch novices to the standing positions to serve tea. Upon the conclusion of the meal, the board in front of the quarters is struck; this is followed by a bow specifically for the person of high rank.

Next, receive the light-accompanying person (*kōbannin*). They enter their position at the lower corner of the *guasī* (lattice screen). They burn incense and bow to the incense. Again, they inquire after one’s health and burn incense for the light-accompanying person.

They enter their position and sit down for tea. When the tea ceremony is finished, the person taking over the duties goes before the incense burner, returns the incense previously requested, performs a prostration with touching the ground (*chūrei*), bows in thanks, and withdraws.
They see them out. Next, the light-accompanying person is escorted out. On the following day, the midday meal is served in the hall.

The *sìxíng* (officer in charge of conduct) requests the person taking over to partake of refreshments (*diǎnxīn*). One senior elder (*qíjiù*) shall serve as an honored companion. Alternatively, it may be said:

"If it concerns the Front Hall (*qiántáng*), one may request a senior elder to serve as an honored companion; if it concerns the transfer of the entire office of the Storehouse (*kùsī*), each shall request their respective counterpart.

If no such person is available, let it be. This shall be conducted for a single day only. Request the West Hall Elder (*xītáng*) and the senior elders to attend, with the head officers of the West Wing (*xībān*) serving as honored companions. [Regarding] the Storehouse...
In the hall, nails are driven into the wall for hanging. Inside the front [of the hall], a special seat is established; to the left and right are the seats for the attendants (*guāngbàn*).

The head officials (*tóushǒu*) take their seats in the guest positions, while those of equal rank follow the order of the assembly. The Head Seat (*shǒuzuò*) attends to assist the administrative officers (*zhīshì*). The ritual is the same as before. This applies to the Guest Master (*zhīkè*) of the western wing.

The eastern assembly halts at the *vinaya-dhara* (Weina). The attendants (*shizhe*) hand over their duties. Only the head of the quarters (*liaoyuan*) is invited to serve as the companion. The seating order and ritual etiquette are the same as before.
[This concerns] the tea ceremony for entering or leaving the quarters.

For those entering the *Mengtáng* (Hall of Favors) or the *Wèi* (Ranking Hall), they inform the *Liáozhǔ* (Head of the Quarter). A plaque for serving tea is hung, and only the members of their own quarter are invited.

Incense, tea, and candles are prepared; everyone bows together and sits. Rising, they burn incense; once the incense bow is completed, they enter their seats and the tea is served. After the cups are collected, they rise before the incense burner to express their thanks.

For those entering the *Zhòngliáo* (General Quarters), the ritual for serving tea is the same as the tea service for those leaving the quarters, with the sole exception that [the plaque] must not be hung.
[The Abbot] takes his seat.

Once those who have come from the *mengtang* (hall for receiving guests) have finished their cups of tea following the exchange of formalities, he instructs the tea attendant to notify the *liaochang* (head of the quarters). The *liaochang* then hangs the "Tea Service" plaque (*diancha pai*).

On a small slip of paper attached to the left side of the plaque, it says: "(Name) respectfully invites the honored assembly of the entire monastery; please proceed to the quarters after the midday meal. The *liaochang* assigns personnel to prepare the hot water and serve it.

A cup [of tea]. Serve the tea, candles, and fine incense. When the meal has ended, strike the small wooden board in the quarters. Stand to the right and bow to the assembly as they enter the quarters. Before the incense burner, perform a formal greeting (*wensun*).

The Head of the Quarters bows and invites the person serving the tea to enter. They take their respective seats; once settled, the server immediately rises, burns one stick of incense, and performs a greeting to the Head of the Quarters.
He bows again for them to be seated. Once the tea has been served, he rises, expresses his gratitude before the incense burner, and escorts the guest out the door.

The person receiving office in the communal quarters (zhòngliáo) prepares the tea. He instructs the tea-head (chátóu) to notify the head of the quarters (liáoyuán) in advance to post the notice board, boil the water, set out the cups, and provide the tea candles.
Once the midday meal has concluded, he first goes to stand to the right outside the door of the communal quarters. He bows to the assembly as they enter their positions;

once they are settled, he bows again and invites them to sit. He then bows once more, steps forward to burn incense in both the upper and lower sections of the hall, and proceeds to do so again in the upper and lower sections as well as along both sides.
Inquire after his health, then inquire again from the center of the hall. The head of the quarters (liaoyuan) leads him in by bowing.

They sit facing each other at their respective seats. Strike the small board twice; tea is served. Again, strike the small board once; the cups are collected. The head of the quarters goes before the incense burner to offer thanks and escorts him out.

The lower robe. When the tea from the Head’s quarters and the tea from the various halls has been served, prepare the tea notice and have the tea attendant post it on the lower section of the wall in front of the communal hall. Prepare the formal deportment and proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to request tea.
Hang the notice at the four halls; notify all the other halls of the invitation. Notify the *gongtou* (supply officer) to prepare the hot water and bring out the cups. [The] storehouse...

The Director of Rites prepares the tea and candles. Four boards are installed in the Sangha Hall, along with incense stands and water basins. When entering or exiting the four boards of the hall or the outer hall, one burns incense, performs a formal greeting (*wensun*), and serves tea;
the procedure for tea on the first and fifteenth days of the month is the same.

Notice: [Name of Hall/Quarters] is cramped and narrow, and we do not dare to invite you there to sit. This day, after the midday meal, we shall serve one round of tea in the Cloud Hall (Yuntang). We humbly hope that all the compassionate ones will deign to descend in person.
(On this day of this month, the bhikṣu [Name], holding the office of [Title], respectfully invites you.)

(Chan Master Handling Temple Affairs; Chan Master Recalling the Past of the Local Community; Chan Master Renowned for His Travels; Chan Masters of the Combined Quarters; respectfully inscribed by Jiuxing; plain paper, no specific restrictions).
The Retiring of the Head and Deputy Head of the Quarters (*Liaozhu*):

When the term of office for the Head of the Quarters (*Liaozhu*) has reached ten days, at the sounding of the *wugeng* bell, he shall proceed to the Hall Office (*Tangsi*) to announce his retirement, saying:

"I, [Name], having recently received your honorable command to serve as Head of the Quarters, have now completed my term of ten days and hereby request leave to return to the hall. He shall then perform one prostration with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). The *Vina* (Reverend of Affairs) shall escort him out the door and instruct the Hall Office to carry out the formalities.
[The Abbot] requests the Assistant Head (Fuliào). After the morning gruel is finished, [the Abbot] proceeds to the Hall Office (Tangsi) to offer tea.

When the Assistant Head arrives, he receives him; once seated, they burn incense and drink tea according to the usual custom. The Rector (Weina) rises again, burns one stick of incense, and says: "The term of the former Head of the Quarters has expired. This duty must not be left vacant;

we trouble you to serve as Head of the Quarters. We humbly beg for your consent. He then performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (chuli) and escorts him back to the communal quarters. The attendant of the Hall Office sounds [the bell].
Three short strikes on the small board within the quarters. The Rector (Vina) enters through the upper gate; [the new resident] performs a prostration with touching of foreheads.

They turn to face each other and perform another prostration with touching of foreheads. The Head of the Quarters (Liaozhu) escorts the Rector out the door. Next, he exchanges positions with the former resident.

Perform a prostration with palms joined as before. The *liàoyuán* (head of the quarters) shall receive him in succession, burning incense and serving tea. The attendants of the Hall Office (*tángsī*) shall invite the new head of the quarters.
After the midday meal, the Hall Office shall offer tea. When Master Xiàowēng resided at Línghyìn, the new and former heads of the quarters held a tea ceremony for the handover of duties;
this practice continues to be observed to this day.
Regarding the position of Assistant Head (Fulião): it is first held by one who has completed the final precepts. It is requested by the Head of the Hall (Liáoyuán) as usual.

After burning incense and drinking tea, he rises again and burns another stick of incense, making this formal announcement: "The term of the former Assistant Head has expired; it is not possible to leave the post vacant. I humbly request that you be appointed to the office of Assistant Head; I pray for your gracious consent.
Once the thanks for the tea have been offered, he immediately escorts him back to the Assistant Head’s quarters. After performing the ritual bowing (wènxùn), he sees him out the door.

Regarding the duties of the *wangliao* (superintendent of quarters): one must immediately arrange the neighboring precepts-holders, submit their names on a placard, and mutually ensure their completion of practice.
One should anticipate all minor and major affairs within the quarters so that, when the time comes, everything may be ready for the brothers who are pressed by urgent external circumstances;
these matters must be reported in advance to the *liaoyuan* (head of the quarters), so that those whose term is ending may be moved up, and the next in line shall assume the responsibility.
Regarding the positions of various supervisors and collectors:

these are the very lifeblood of the community, and their value lies in the careful selection of personnel. One should therefore invite impartial elders, both senior and junior, [to conduct this selection].
This humble disciple and fellow countryman cannot bear [to hear such things]. If one employs the wrong person, they will fail to recognize cause and effect;

they will conceal the property of the monastery and exploit the tenant farmers to an extreme degree, leaving nothing undone. Not only will the annual budget fall short, but it will also bring disgrace upon the mountain gate.
When Huìtáng saw that Huánglóng had a look of displeasure, he questioned him directly, and Huánglóng replied: "I have not yet found a person to oversee the collection of revenues."
Huītáng recommended the Vice-Abbot Jiàngǎn. Yùlóng said, "Gǎn is impetuous; I fear he might plot with petty men. Huītáng then asked, "How about the attendant Huà?
He is honest and prudent. Yùlóng replied, "Although Huà is honest and prudent, he is not equal to Zhuāngzhǔ Xiù, who possesses great capacity and is loyal."
Lingyuan asked Haitang, "Huanglong requested a supervisor for the granaries; why was he so overcautious?

Haitang replied, "Those who possess a state or a family have never failed to base their governance on this. It is not only Huanglong who acts thus; the former sages offered many warnings regarding it. How profound these words are!
When the various fields reach maturity, one must carefully harmonize and manage them with integrity and long-standing experience."

When the seating order for the minor *jìjiù* (senior elders) or the *shīfāng* (ten directions) brothers has been finalized, on the appointed day, tea is served to the two classes of senior elders (*dà jìjiù*).

After they have been individually invited into the *qiǎntáng* (sleeping hall) and the incense-water (*xiàn tāng*) offering is completed, they are escorted back to their guest seats. The two classes of elders lead the assembly in offering congratulations and proceed sequentially through the various quarters.
This includes the *cǎofàn* (grass meal), the special soup service, the special soup service from the storehouse, the *yàoshí* (medicinal food), and the formal procedures for entering and exiting.

The etiquette for the two classes of officials was the same; however, at the various estates of Cheontong, the ancient customs have not fallen into decline. The stewards, fearing the consequences of failing to meet expectations, never dared to pocket any income for themselves.

Every year, they would convene twice to offer increased hospitality and earnest invitations specifically for Master Ryōnen. Upon arriving at the lower estate, the notice would be hung at the main gate, where the ritual of tea and soup was performed.
The tower bell was struck to assemble the community, and the Master was escorted to his sedan chair from the gate; these traditions remain as a legacy to this day.
The *Fengzai* (Wind-in-Residence) shall transfer the head official’s quarters.

The administrative office (*kusō*) shall maintain a single general ledger for the transfer of utensils among all the various quarters, recording the items transferred and sealing them with the treasury seal.
The administrative officers (zhishi) shall verify all items and present them to the Abbot. Each of the various quarters shall maintain two small ledgers that correspond exactly with one another.

Whenever a head official (toushou) undergoes a rotation, the Chief of the Storehouse (kusi) shall, together with the Upper and Lower Storehouses or the Guest Master (ketou), cross-check the inventory numbers and hand over the miscellaneous articles.

Any item moved, used, or damaged must be returned in its original state; if it is lost, the respective quarter must provide compensation by replacing the missing or worn-out items. Upon encountering...

When a monk passes away, his effects are brought into the administrative treasury (kūsī). They must be inventoried before the eyes of the public officials, and the inventory number must be recorded in the register;

if necessary, the number should be adjusted to ensure nothing is lost or omitted. I frequently observe that when items are moved or distributed at various locations, there are often deficiencies in the inventory of utensils.
Lists are prepared and requisitions are made, yet the treasury fails to hand them over, and the abbot does not oversee the matter. This is not the way to employ worthy men.
Furthermore, those who serve as head administrators must examine the physical state of the buildings. Once residing in the monastic quarters, they must also maintain and repair them.

When it is time for succession, every single item must be inventoried and accounted for. If one leaves behind personal belongings with added labels, or preserves items such as the "five flavors" (condiments), this will be of benefit to future occupants.
This is the very foundation of the monastery and a model for those who follow; if one were to sweep everything clean and empty, [the tradition would perish].
To invite derision from those with discernment—how could one not feel shame? The Abbot’s quarters, the administrative office, and the Sangha hall each have their own registers.
Regarding the handover of items belonging to the Sangha hall, the rector (venerable) must oversee this; it requires the collective attention of all. I have recorded this for that reason.
Essential Provisions for Chan Monasteries, Volume Six;
Essential Provisions for Chan Monasteries, Volume Seven;
National Model for Baizhang.
Now, when two cassias hang their shade and a single flower manifests as an auspicious omen, from that time forth the establishment of monastic groves has essentially been for the sake of the Saṃgha.
It is for this reason that there are elders (*sthavira*) to instruct and reveal the Dharma to the Saṃgha; there are head seats (*śrāmaṇera*) to serve as models for the Saṃgha;
there are administrators (*karmadāna*) to bear the burdens of the Saṃgha; there are disciplinarians (*karmadāna*) to harmonize the Saṃgha; and there are those who provide offerings to the Saṃgha.
There is the *diànzuo* (steward), who performs labor for the community of monks; the *zhísuì* (yearly supervisor), who manages the receipts and disbursements for the community of monks;
the *kùtóu* (storekeeper), who oversees the brushes and ink for the community of monks; the *shūzhuàng* (scribe), who preserves the sacred teachings for the community of monks;
the *zàngzhǔ* (repository master), who welcomes and attends to donors for the community of monks; and the *zhīkè* (guest prefect), who issues invitations for the community of monks. Thus, there is...

Because there were attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) to guard the robes and bowls for the community of monks, there was the *liáozhǔ* (cell master). Because there were those to provide medicinal decoctions and attend to the needs of the community of monks, there was the *tángzhǔ* (hall master).

Because there were those to wash for the community of monks, there was the *yùzhǔ* (bath master) and the *shuǐtóu* (water head). Because there were those to protect the community of monks from the cold...

Therefore, there are the charcoal-heads and stove-heads who beg for the sake of the community of monks; there are the street-wardens and fundraising masters who perform manual labor for the sake of the community of monks;
there are the garden-heads, mill-heads, and estate managers who provide cleansing services for the sake of the community of monks; there are the sanitation officers who serve the community of monks;

and there are the lay attendants (*śrāmaṇera*) who provide personal service for the sake of the community of monks. Thus, the conditions for practicing the Way are fully provided, supporting the physical needs of the body.

All requisites are spontaneously complete; in all matters there is no anxiety. With a single mind one pursues the Way, becoming honored and noble within the world while enjoying leisure beyond the mundane.
Pure and non-active, the assembly of monks acts as the support. Recalling the strength of many people, how could one not recognize this kindness and repay it?
By attending at dawn and requesting instruction at dusk, never wasting a moment of time, one repays the elders. Thus, there is order between the honorable and the humble.

Maintaining a composed and dignified demeanor is how one repays the Chief Seat (Śayanāsana). To outwardly comply with the laws and regulations while inwardly observing the rules and restraints is how one repays the Steward (Karmadāna).
To dwell together in the sixfold harmony, blending like water and milk, is how one repays the Rector (Karmadāna).

To partake of this food for the sake of accomplishing the path to enlightenment is how one repays the Cook (Mahānasa). To reside peacefully in the monastic quarters and cherish and protect the communal property...
One manages the property to repay the steward (*zhisui*). One does not violate even a hair’s breadth of the monastery’s permanent assets (*changzhu*) to repay the storekeeper (*kutou*).
One does not take up a brush, acting as if putting out a fire on one's head to repay the scribe (*shuzhuang*).

At the bright window and quiet desk, one illuminates the mind with the ancient teachings to repay the librarian (*zangzhu*). One conceals one's brilliance and hides one's traces, refusing to engage in social pursuits, to repay [the community].

The guest prefect (*zhikè*) must always abide by established regulations and arrive first when making requests; this is how he repays the attendant (*shìzhě*). Carrying only a single flask and a single bowl, he dwells among the community as immovable as a mountain;

this is how he repays the head of the quarters (*liáozhǔ*). He endures the suffering of mental illness and accepts medicinal gruel and medicine as appropriate; this is how he repays the hall master (*tángzhǔ*).
He moves with lightness and slowness, remaining silent and composed, never neglecting the cause of water; this is how he repays the bath master (*yùzhǔ*) and the water steward (*shuǐtóu*).
To maintain silence and fold one's hands, withdrawing oneself and yielding to others, is how one repays the charcoal-heads and stove-heads.
To reflect upon whether one’s own virtue and conduct are complete or deficient in providing offerings is how one repays the street-wardens and solicitors.

To calculate the amount of labor performed and measure the distance from which [the food] has come is how one repays the garden-masters, millers, and estate managers. To draw water and manage affairs with a sense of shame and remorse is...
This is to repay those who maintain the purity of the head [of the community]. It is broad and easy to follow; it is simple and easy to practice. This is how one repays those who purify the person.
Therefore, beneath the monastic groves (*saṃghārāma*), the work of the Way is ever renewed. Those of the highest capacity achieve completion in a single lifetime;
those of middling capacity nurture the holy embryo (*āryagarbha*). Even for those who have not yet awakened to the source of the mind, their time is never spent in vain. These are true monks.
O Venerable One, you are a field of merit for the world and serve as a bridge and raft for the final age, destined to fully realize the ultimate fruit of the two kinds of adornment.
If the monastic groves are not well-ordered and the Wheel of Dharma does not turn, it is not for an Elder to lead the assembly in such a manner.

If the three karmas are not disciplined and the four modes of conduct are not solemn, it is not for the Head Seat to lead the assembly in such a manner. If the capacity to accommodate others is not broad and the love...

If the hearts of the assembly are not sincere, it is not the duty of the *jianyuan* (superintendent) to protect them. If practitioners find no peace and those who ruin the community are not removed, it is not the duty of the *weina* (rectifier) to gladden the assembly.
If the six flavors are not refined and the three virtues are not provided, it is not the duty of the *dianzuo* (steward) to serve the assembly.
If the quarters are not repaired and the utensils are not complete, it is not the duty of the *zhisui* (yearly manager)...
To store up permanent assets while embezzling from the Sangha is not how a storekeeper should provide for the community.
To have poorly drafted documents with corrupted characters is not how official records should serve to adorn the community.

To have disordered desks and chairs where clamor and distraction never cease is not how a library director should attend to the community. To hate the poor and love the wealthy, to value the laity and slight the monks—this is not...
If the guest prefect (zhikè) does not assist the assembly, it is because his etiquette is not reverent and the order between the honorable and the humble has been lost.

If the attendant (shìzhě) does not issue commands to the assembly, it is because he is not diligent in cleaning and not careful in guarding [the quarters]. If the head of the quarters (liáozhǔ) does not reside among the assembly, it is because he is unacquainted with serving others and disturbs the sick.
If the hall master (tángzhǔ) does not show compassion for the assembly, it is because the hot water and drinks are insufficient, and the cold... [is not relieved].

If the heating is improperly managed, it is not the duty of the bath master or the water-head to wash the assembly. If preparations are insufficient, it is not the responsibility of the stove-head or charcoal-head to attend to the assembly.
If one is unfair regarding wealth or fails to exert full effort, it is not the role of the street-warden or the fundraising master to provide for the assembly.
If there are profits left behind on the land or if individuals do not achieve complete merit, it is not the function of the garden master [to fulfill these duties].

The head of the bathhouse (*śauca-pāla*) serves the community on behalf of the assembly. One who is indolent and fails to eliminate all distracting conditions does not serve the community as a head of the bathhouse.
One who cannot be restrained by prohibitions nor made to comply with commands does not serve the community as a lay attendant (*karmadāna*).
If the monks of the assembly treat their teachers with contempt and the Dharma with disdain, following their own whims and circumstances, they do not repay the elders.
To sit and lie down in a disordered manner, and to act with inconsistent conduct, is not the way to repay the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera).
To hold the royal law in contempt and disregard the monastic community (saṅgha) is not the way to repay the Steward (Karmadāna).

For superiors and subordinates to be disharmonious and for strife to become entrenched is not the way to repay the Rector (Karmadāna). To covet fine delicacies and disparage coarse food is not the way to repay the Cook (Mahānasa).
To dwell and enjoy [the monastery's resources] without considering future generations is not the way to repay the *zhisui* (yearly steward).
To greedily crave offerings and gains while showing no compassion for the permanent property (*changzhu*) is not the way to repay the *kutou* (storekeeper).

To attend to brushes and inkstones and devote oneself to literary pursuits is not the way to repay the *shuzhuang* (secretary). To treat the golden scriptures with contempt and seek out secular texts is not the way to repay the *zangzhu* (library master).

To follow after worldly men and form alliances with the noble is not the way to repay one's *zhike* (guest master). To forget invitations and remain seated for long among the assembly of monks is not the way to repay one's *shizhe* (attendant).
To hinder others for one's own sake and to store things carelessly, leading to regret over theft, is not the way to repay one's *liaozhu* (hall master).
To harbor much anger and little joy, and to fail to comply with the conditions of illness, is not the way to repay one's *tangzhu* (hall director).
To let the buckets and ladles make noise or to use water without moderation is not the way to repay the bath master or the water steward.
To have one’s own body feel warm and comfortable while causing hindrance to others is not the way to repay the stove master or the charcoal steward.

To fail to contemplate spiritual practice while peacefully accepting offerings is not the way to repay the street-wardens or the fundraising masters. To eat one's fill all day long without applying the mind to anything is likewise improper.
To spit and sneeze upon the walls and leave the latrine in a state of disarray is not the way to repay the master of the garden (yuántóu mótóu zhǔzhù).
To be preoccupied solely with outward decorum while lacking virtuous instruction from the past is not the way to repay the head of purification (jìngtóu).

Indeed, even after a thousand circumambulations like a whirlwind, one may still fall short; one should simply know how to set aside shortcomings and follow what is excellent, working together to bring about the realization [of the Way].
(Chì shuì fǎn) Regarding the service of the Tiger [Year]: it is our hope that within the lion’s den, all shall become lions, and beneath the sandalwood forest, there shall be nothing but sandalwood.
May we, in the final five hundred years, once again behold the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Thus, the flourishing or decline of the Dharma-gate depends upon the monastic community.
The Sangha is a field of merit and should be revered; when the Sangha is honored, the Dharma is honored; when the Sangha is slighted...
Thus, the Dharma is held in light esteem. Since internal protection is already strict, external protection must likewise be diligent.

Whether the master of the gruel and rice serves for a single term, or the administrators of the monastery happen to hold office for a time, they should always serve their fellow practitioners with respect and must not arrogantly exalt themselves.
If one is conceited and self-important, treating private matters as public business, how can one maintain this for long when all things are impermanent? I.
Returning from the morning alms-round, how can one face the multitude? Cause and effect leave no room for error; it is difficult to evade them. As a monk, you are a son of the Buddha;

your right to receive offerings is no different [from others]. Whether in heaven or among men, you are revered by all. Your morning and evening meals ought to be refined and abundant; the four requisites of life must not be lacking.
For two thousand years, the shadow of the World-Honored One’s legacy has covered us, his descendants. [Behold] the white tuft between his brows...
A single portion of its merit is inexhaustible in enjoyment; one need only know how to serve the assembly and need not worry about poverty.

Since the Sangha comprises neither ordinary nor holy beings and universally encompasses the ten directions, and as it is called "the monastery of all quarters" (*caitya*), everyone has a share therein. How can one falsely give rise to discrimination and treat visiting monks with contempt or aversion?
In the guest quarters, they may stay temporarily for three mornings; there, one should provide service with full courtesy. Before the Sangha Hall, they may briefly seek [shelter].
During the fast, offer sustenance with an impartial mind. Even lay guests should still be looked after; how much more so should members of the Sangha not fail to welcome one another?

If one is free from a limited heart, there will naturally be inexhaustible merit. When the monastic community is harmonious and those above and below are of one mind, they will cover each other’s shortcomings.
Do not let the family’s internal flaws be heard by outsiders. Although this may cause no harm to the matter at hand, it must be brought to an end.
In the end, this diminishes the veneration of others. It is like worms within a lion’s body devouring the lion’s own flesh;

it cannot be destroyed by celestial Māras or non-Buddhist paths. If one wishes for the wind of the Way not to fall, for the sun of the Buddha to remain ever bright, and to augment the brilliance of the ancestral realm, [one must act accordingly].
May this sacred writing serve as a mirror for the sage-transformations of our Imperial Dynasty.
Therein resides the Abbot,

who upholds the transmission of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, prolongs the life of wisdom, serves as a model for the three realms, and opens the way for humans and devas, clarifying the matter that transcends the ordinary.
He turned the Great Dharma Wheel and occupied the position of the abbot of the Golden Grain Tathāgata. He attained the name of the Venerable Elder Subhūti.

Entering the inner chamber and ascending the hall, he delivered universal discourses after the incense was offered. Regarding both mundane and supramundane matters, he taught the Dharma according to the Dharma; his practice and his teaching reached their full realization, such that his reputation and his reality were in accord.
Citing the ancients to illuminate the present, his lineage of masters had a firm basis. At times, he raised the essential point directly and abruptly, confronting [his disciples] head-on.

He connects with those of superior faculties, or provides transformative teachings according to their capacities; he exhorts and encourages those of middling and inferior faculties, establishing excellent conditions. He employs the scales of authority to grant or withhold as required.
Even during the intervals between practicing the Way and preaching the Dharma, he audits the ledgers of money and grain, providing for the assembly and undertaking repairs as circumstances dictate.

Although these are called mundane secondary matters, they have been deemed difficult to coordinate throughout past and present. If one can achieve such comprehensive benefit, this is truly what is meant by...

A person of complete talent who does not fall short of this will exert their utmost strength and employ their strategic wisdom; they will cultivate and construct with total dedication, provide for the assembly and bring peace to the Sangha, and appoint worthy individuals to various offices so that no duties are neglected.
These are called the three grades of abbots, which is by no means a trivial matter. They shall perform incense-burning rituals and offer prayers.
The essential point lies in single-minded sincerity. Whether presiding over the assembly or dwelling in seclusion, one must never be negligent or casual.

Since the establishment of monastic communities prioritizes the elderly and the infirm, you must especially maintain a mind of compassionate care for them. When high-minded practitioners arrive from afar, treat them with the utmost courtesy in welcoming and seeing them off, leading by personal example.

There is no task that cannot be accomplished. For instance, Miyun donned his robes and slept at night to act on behalf of his former master in maintaining the precepts, thereby reviving the family’s reputation;
Dizang pointed to a stone to explain the mind, attaining great wisdom through a karmic resonance with his disciples.
These are all ancient precedents and the heavy responsibilities of the Buddha-dharma.

Yuan: Formerly, he served as the head of the assembly in the front hall. As the eyes of humanity and the pupils of the Buddhas, he sat on the teaching seat to expound the Dharma, opening the way for future generations.

Whether partaking of congee or rice, or attending tea services, he looked back and looked ahead to instruct his brothers. He enacted codes of conduct and followed established precedents, acting with perfect decorum and propriety. He led the community in seated meditation.

Everything has its regulations. Whether the morning and evening meals are refined or coarse, they are assigned to the administrative officers. The funeral rites for deceased monks are inspected and overseen.

If one arrives slightly late for the assembly, a message is sent to have them lower their shoulder-bag; only when the meal is announced does one approach to receive it. When seeking instruction, one requests detailed and comprehensive elucidation.
How could this lineage, spanning a hundred generations, be considered a trivial matter? It is like Yunmen’s relation to Lingshu, or Dahui’s relation to Yuanwu.
How could one whose name and station are such as these be entrusted with a light task?

Though his rank was that of a Rear Hall attendant (Houtang), he assisted in promoting the monastic tradition; his conduct was dignified and upright, and his character was exemplary for those junior to him. He managed the affairs of the monastic community.

The brothers are admonished and reprimanded. The *shu* (assignment) takes place in the front hall; if the front hall is unavailable, the assignment is instead conducted at the bowl-positions in the rear hall.

On a separate day, one ascends the hall, speaks [the formal address], and then turns back to the front board. The single mat (*dān*) is inserted, the food is announced, and the board is struck for seated meditation.

When the third strike of the board before the communal quarters ceases, one returns to the hall. After burning a single stick of incense, one immediately ascends to their assigned seat and practices seated meditation. Having thus withdrawn from the front...
The Hall. Other matters are of one principle.

In the Tang dynasty, the position of *Dujiansi* (Chief Administrator) was a heavy responsibility for the mountain gate; the priority lay in obtaining the right person. At Baizhang, the *Jianyuan* (Superintendent) managed both public and private affairs; today, this role is that of the *Dusi*.

Furthermore, in a great monastery there are many offices. The scribe is specifically tasked with bearing this responsibility; it is vital that his calligraphy be fresh and elegant, so as to adorn the imperial altars.

He must be diligent day and night in the incense offerings and lamps, and conduct annual accounting according to the ledgers. He attends to the formal leave-taking of officials and offers thanks to the donors.

He manages income and expenditure to ensure the provisions for the assembly are prepared, maintaining a constant supply of morning and evening meals. With a superior mind, he should treat all things and must never be negligent.

It is easy. If one commits an offense while practicing benevolence (*ren*), one should measure the transgression and adjust one's conduct; thus the guilt shall not be heavily penalized. I sincerely appeal for your clemency.
Regarding the duties of the treasury and storehouse, select and appoint those with public-mindedness. Honor the worthy and tolerate the masses, so that a harmonious atmosphere may prevail.

When the community lacks necessities, exert your strength and devise plans. In matters of construction and repair, apply your whole heart to ensure excellence. As for colleagues of talent and virtue, promote their conduct and character. Do not involve yourself in private affairs.
Admonition: Should matters of great consequence ever implicate the mountain gate (the monastery), inform the abbot in secret without letting the pure assembly know.

Handle the situation through skillful means; thus, you will never fail in even one instance. Attend the two daily assemblies without delay. Regarding other affairs, speak only of those that concern your colleagues.
Distinguish clearly between public and private interests, down to the smallest detail. Protect the permanent property in every way, as Yangqi did for Ciming and Shichuang did for [Foyan] Qingshui.

Hongzhi. On another day, he encountered the conditions for his realization and attained the essence of the school. He was a model for humans and devas; his magnificent brilliance was truly immeasurable. Regarding Secretary Ri:

his reputation is refined and elegant, and his calligraphy is dignified and solemn. In composing writings, he must accord with ancient regulations; in crafting his speech, he should serve as a new mirror for posterity.

It stirred the hearts of those who heard and saw it, its brilliance illuminating the forests and springs. If one were to speak of the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, could it truly reside in such things?
When Master Nanyuan of Huanglong met Chan Master Yunfeng Yue, he was directed toward Ciming; only then did he resolve the great matter and plan his journey to the West River.
While serving as a secretary under Master Huazang Dun’an, he was sent in his stead to attend the court of Prince Zhang Xunwu. Upon ascending the seat at the palace gate, he asked:

"If a secretary understands Chan, he already has instruction within his own home. He then immediately returned to the monastery, burned all the texts he had accumulated, and went straight to Tiantong.
There he silently cultivated this Way for ten years, never leaving the monks' hall, until finally completing his practice.

A great matter. Later he resided at Xuedou, where his Dharma path flourished greatly upon reaching Tiantong. That he bore heavy responsibility and reached far is known by all in the monastic communities.
Recorded by the layman Zhangzhu.

One should master the *jinwen* (bronze script) inscriptions. Strictly arrange the tables and desks, and always keep ready hot water, incense, tea, and candles. Extend a formal welcome to the brothers as they come to read the scriptures.
Upon first entering the scripture hall, one must first inform the Hall Master (*tángzhǔ*) and go together to the Library Office (*zàngsī*) for an inspection;

once escorted back to one’s assigned seat, one performs a single prostration with full-body contact (*duòchù lǐ*). This was the ancient method. Nowadays, people gather like a dense crowd, and the libraries are arranged from east to west; the primary concern is merely to seek fame.
Regarding the duties you hold: you must simply have a thorough mastery of the *zong* (the fundamental school) and a comprehensive understanding of the sacred teachings.

You should carefully examine the scriptures for discrepancies, fill in missing characters and strokes, and apply yourself with all your heart to the tasks of baking, dusting, patching, and pasting to bring them to perfection; this, too, shall serve as a repayment for the Buddha’s kindness.
He is named Bao Wugu. Regarding the position of *vinaya*:

in Sanskrit it is *vinaya*, and in the Tang language it means "one who gladdens the assembly. He administers every regulation of the monastic community (*saṃghārāma*) according to established protocol and is ranked among the eastern class of officials.
Holding an office of pure dignity, one must be diligent and respectful in seeing off and welcoming guests. When a sick monk recovers, ensure his care is appropriate;

if his brothers are careless, provide detailed protection and support. Upon his entry into the hall, inspect his ordination certificate (*duce*), and post it on the upper curtain to record his presence.

When closing the furnace or fanning the coals, one must calculate the cold and the heat. Regarding the robes and belongings of a deceased monk, one must ensure they are distributed with public fairness and clarity.

When chanting or reciting sutras, the delivery must be detailed, slow, and rhythmic. When striking the mallet at the two daily sessions, the hall bell rings; one leaves their station and enters the hall, offering a single stick of incense with the left hand.
Stepping back two and a half paces, one bows in greeting with palms joined and enters. Standing by the side of the mallet, one first observes the daily return [of the assembly].
Facing the deities, the bell is struck once. The assembly spreads out their alms bowls. The mallet is struck again once;
with palms joined, they silently dedicate the merit to the deities of that day. With a soft and slow tone, the sound leads [the merit] to the realm of the Pure Dharma Body.

The left hand makes a covering gesture, pressing the base of the mallet sideways, while the right hand strikes the mallet, no higher than five inches. Only when the sound has ceased does one lower the mallet; this must be done swiftly.

Gently close the door. The Head Seat (Shouzuo) chants the meal invocation; when reaching the word "existence" (you), he turns toward the shrine (kan), steps back to stand at the edge of the platform, and once the food has been distributed throughout, he moves forward and strikes the mallet once.
With palms joined, he reaches inside the threshold, turns to face the Holy Monk (Shengseng), bows with palms joined, and returns to his bowl position.
If a patron is providing a meal for the monks, after the universal distribution and the striking of the mallet, he proceeds from behind the shrine and turns to the left side.

The Head Seat (Chao Shouzuo) first performs the inquiry of well-being (*wenshen*). He then turns and strikes the mallet once to request the offering of funds. If it is for the *Śūraṅgama* Assembly, he requests incense and candles;

if there are other circumstances, such as matters concerning the register of ordination seniority (*jiezha*) or the register of leave (*jiabobo*), these should be sent to the Guest Office (*Guosiguan*).

Furthermore, he requests leave and asks for the mallet to be struck for the dedication of merit (*huixiang*). All matters, both minor and major, are listed in the various regulations. Regarding all affairs related to the Sangha Hall, including the water-head and charcoal-head positions...

The head server must attend to every detail, always keeping the welfare of the assembly in mind. As for the case in Master Xinghua’s hall, where Kebin was fined and expelled from the monastery after being struck with a staff—this remains a standard for a hundred generations.
[The guest] commits an offense.

The guest master shall inform the officials, the noble patrons, the venerable elders, and the attendants from the various mountain monasteries; they shall go out in advance to welcome him at the gate. Next, he shall notify the Abbot’s quarters and the administrative office (*kūsi*).

The guest master shall then escort him for an audience and receive him with the appropriate rites, adapting the gravity of the reception to the circumstances as required. Once he has been settled in his quarters, [the formalities conclude].

Regarding matters of personnel and social relations: when visiting mountains or perusing texts, one must not engage in frivolous talk of vulgar affairs. When receiving incoming brothers (monks), they must be attended to with tea and soup according to the prescribed ritual.
When a patron enters the mountain monastery, they must be received and guided in advance. The same procedure applies to the *vinaya-dhara* (Rector) when he goes out on business for the community;
or if he has personal affairs, he must inform the attendant (*śayanāsana-grāhaka*), as the matter is treated identically. [The same applies to] the *dan-kuo* (guest quarters).

The quarters must always keep a supply of lamp oil, firewood, and charcoal. Before the Sangha Hall, one should inspect the provisions for guests and ensure that the rice gruel and meals are prepared with order.

Upon encountering the death of a monk, one should join the attendant in closing the curtains; if the death occurs while a guest is on a temporary visit, one shall preside over the funeral rites. This was practiced by Xuedou at Dayang.
Under the assembly of Chan Master Yue of Shishuang, all [senior monks] held this office, leaving a legacy for a hundred generations.

Zhou Zhiyu bathed whenever a bathing session was opened; before the midday meal, he would hang up the notice board. During cold months, he bathed once every five days; during the heat of summer, he washed daily to remove sweat.
After the congee has been served, the fire is lit. The bathhouse is prepared: hand towels are hung, face basins and slippers are set out, and foot cloths are laid down.
The head of the assembly dispatches an attendant to enter the bath directly. In the late afternoon, the bath master covers the heads of the Head Seat, the Abbot’s quarters, and the Rector.

The drum is struck three times for the "Bathing of the Holy Ones. Hot water is placed in all the buckets; they are then passed in succession along the corridors while the wooden clapper is struck three times. Finally, the drum is struck again to open the bath.
1. Announce to the entire assembly of monks. 2. Announce to the heads of the community. 3. Announce to those in charge of affairs and practitioners. 4. Mobilize the laborers and supervisors;

strike the drum at the bathing sequence and post the notice at the entrance. The Abbot strikes the drum twice, before and after [the bathing]. Inside the room, there is a small sign with white characters:
"1. Hot Water; 2. Water; 3. Full. Strike the small board; exit the bath. Check for the presence of patrons who have provided the bathing facilities, and recite the sutra for their merit.

Toward this end, when the wondrous touch is clearly manifested, one attains the station of a Buddha’s son. If the preceding thought is that of an ordinary person and the succeeding thought is that of a sage, then one's efforts have not been in vain.

(In ancient times, it was the custom for the abbot to enter the bath at the third watch; the use of a screen was to shield those walking by. When Chan Master Zangshi was residing at Nengren Monastery in Wenzhou, he entered the bath at the second watch because of official business.
After bathing, he requested to be reproved by the head officers.)

In the Fayu (Fazhi) Hall, ensure that the altar is adorned and pure, and that the oil for the lamps is always full. The sacred images must be dusted at the appropriate times, and offerings should be prepared according to the circumstances.

Funds provided by donors for incense, money, and oil must not be diverted or used interchangeably; they must be strictly required to be applied toward diligent service, such as the offering of incense and lamps. Should one encounter...

When the wind rises, the hearth fire must be extinguished and the ends of the banners tied down; do not approach the lapis lazuli [statues]. On the first and fifteenth days of the month and during festival periods, it is permissible to open the temple gates so that officials and commoners may come and go, gazing upon [the icons] at their own leisure.
In the Buddha halls of great monasteries, when the sutras have been recited following the commemorations of the Enlightenment or the Parinirvāṇa, one should prepare hot water;
however, do not collect lamp oil money in excessive amounts, as this will cause people to feel weary and lead them to incur evil karmic results.
Furthermore,

the attendant Shang holds the office of incense-bearer. He serves as a close attendant at all times, receiving instructions morning and evening, with the aim of bringing the Way of the Dharma to its ultimate perfection and promoting the worthy.
One must be able to harmonize with public opinion and consult with others to ensure comprehensive coverage.

In all matters of courtesy and protocol, such as welcoming and seeing off venerable elders and abbots of various mountains, one should inquire extensively of those who possess prior knowledge so as not to become an object of ridicule. From the superior to the subordinates, the conduct within the abbot’s quarters should be like that of a son serving his father.

At other times, one must not sit preemptively in the abbot’s quarters. Whenever conduct or duties are neglected, one should admonish them from time to time. The affairs of the abbot are manifold; this is the matter at hand.

When the *guānbào* (the attendant who escorts the deceased) has departed, the *weina* (chant master) and *zhikè* (guest master) return; the striking of the mallet for the dedication of merit (*huíxiàng*) is identical to the previous procedure.

For a deceased monk, the *lúnbǎzhàng* (the monk on duty holding the account book) remains present while the abbot temporarily refrains from attending the hall. The assembly stands in formation as usual to chant the sutras; after a long absence, the abbot returns to the congregation.

When visiting other monasteries, one takes a position behind the two ranks of officials. During formal greetings, one inserts incense and performs prostrations. When government officials arrive, one stands with hands clasped in reverence to listen to their responses.
Correct. If there is any point regarding the abbot’s response that might be overlooked, you should speak on his behalf at that time.

Any formal discourses (*shangtang*), ritual services (*foshi*), or inquiries for instruction (*qingyi*) should be recorded and presented immediately. As Ānanda served Gautama and Xianglin served Yunmen, the Buddhas and Patriarchs place great trust in this;
how could it be treated with negligence?
The office of the Secretary (Shishō) stands out for its exceptional talent and resources, serving as an ornament to the patriarchal lineage.

This official handles the exchange of formal correspondence with other monastic institutions, composes ritual documents and public notices for the mountain gate, and drafts preliminary versions of decrees issued by the Abbot (Hōjū) for formal presentation. In the absence of a Secretary, these literary duties are performed by the same body of officials.
This refers to assisting the abbot. Since one does not participate in the dedication of merit or the striking of the mallet, the deceased monk should not be made to keep the accounts.

Nevertheless, while following the local vinaya, one must investigate the essential vehicle (zongcheng) and aspire to transcend birth and death; do not concern yourself with brushes and inkstones, lest you spend a lifetime in vain.
This is like Shitian’s service to Po’an, who did not prize calligraphy, for the life of wisdom is what truly matters.

The duty of the Guest Master (qingke zhizhe) is to distinguish the eminent and select the outstanding, thereby assisting and supporting the monastic community (*conglin*). When officials, nobles, or venerable elders (*zunsu*) visit from various mountains, one must extend a formal and hospitable welcome.

Tea and soup should be served according to the season, and special provisions must be prepared for their reception. First, a formal invitation slip (*qingzhuang*) must be prepared, upon which the Guest Master’s own name is written.

If the incense-burning attendant is absent, the person acting in his stead shall perform the duties of returning the merit (*huixiang*), striking the gavel (*dachu*), and holding the register (*bazhang*) in unison. Upon the arrival of the high-ranking guest...
Gate. Or, if the abbot is unaware [of the visitor's arrival], one should first welcome him, inquire after his well-being in the morning and evening, and thus perfect the path of practice;
from this point, one sets out on the journey that will lead to becoming a leader of the monastic community in the future.

The duties concerning robes and alms bowls are to be entrusted to those who are mature and experienced, having spent their lives within the monastic community (saṃghārāma). It is not a minor matter for juniors from various quarters to assume these responsibilities;

such actions would gravely damage their virtue and lead to failure in their affairs. One should instead advance worthy and virtuous individuals, offer loyal counsel regarding faults, and attend to others in accordance with the circumstances.
One must not let the proper time pass. Regarding all matters of etiquette within the Abbot’s quarters, one should investigate and supervise with a focused mind.

Should there be vacancies among the administrative officers (*doutou*) or in the various monastic residences, each must be attended to and cared for at the appropriate time. When appointing or dismissing members of the two orders (*liangxu*), it is essential to consult in advance;

the priority lies in securing the right person so as to accord with public consensus. For instance, when Master Fozhao served as the abbot of Yuyang twice, Yuan’an always attended him on his left and right. Zhejiang...

After the Elder retired as the Guest Master (zhikě), he concealed his former attainments for seventeen years. Yuan Yi took notice of him. When Master Mimuan resided at Huazang, Songyuan Yue served as the keeper of the treasury keys.

Due to a chronic spleen ailment, he was unable to attend the assembly for the performance of monastic duties. Mimuan rebuked him. Later, when Yue went to Lingyin, he was not permitted to accompany the Master on his travels;
yet he served as an attendant, managing the robe and bowl cabinet, moving to the left and turning to the right around him. These two great...
In their old age, they shall inherit their families' estates. Those who serve as *zhuchi* (abbot) must not fail to exercise due scrutiny.

As for the attendants of the Sacred Monk (*shengseng*), what is valued is their aspiration for the Way (*daoxin*). They provide offerings at the two meal times, strike the hall gong, and attend to the placement of the bowls and seats morning and evening.
At midnight, they trim the lamps. Together with the *weina* (chanting master), they collect funds for deceased monks. When the *zhuchi* passes away, it is... [the responsibility].
