The curtain is drawn. The head monk does not enter the hall, but strikes the gavel from within. The *gongtou* (offering master) makes the offerings, and the *cantou* (assembly leader) strikes the gavel for the departure from the hall.

The attendant of this mountain is named Monk Tuigeng. From this point, he ascends through the various offices up to the position of the front board (*qianban*), and only thereafter does he emerge into public office.
This is the model for establishing one's character according to the predecessors.
Tang was appointed to the position of Vice Director of the Bureau of Provisions.
Though the office was small, the responsibility was grave, for it was upon this that the lifeblood of the multitude depended. Thus, the rice and flour had to be meticulously refined and pure.
Congee and rice should be prepared with care for quality and abundance. Soy sauce, yellow beans, and fermented soybeans must be prepared in a timely manner.

Salt, vinegar, ginger, and oil should be provided in full measure for the assembly. If there is a deficiency, the head monk must plan ahead; one must always be cautious of those who withhold portions, showing no favoritism toward private interests and never scheming for personal gain.

One should exercise empathy and protect these resources as if guarding one's own eyes. The virtuous predecessors established these divisions of labor and assigned these duties fundamentally for the sake of the community.

Now, being ignorant of the profound source, I have further subjected it to harsh pruning. Coarse rice and thin gruel, stinking vinegar and bland pickled vegetables—this is not only due to the ignorance of those who bear responsibility, but truly lies in the faults of the abbot.
Regarding the office of the Chief Cook (*diànzuò*): if there is no one with a sincere heart to provide offerings, it is inappropriate to comply with requests made through back-channel influence.

One should consult with the Head Seat of the Front Hall (*qiántáng shǒuzuò*) and select a candidate by consensus from among the community; in this way, one will never fail in even a single instance. One should cultivate vegetables extensively and diligently clear away weeds and filth.

Various crops should be planted according to the four seasons. One must know that the gardener should be supervised with diligence, as an old gardener is required for the task. The gardener should be...

The kindness of private benefactors exceeds that of the changing seasons. To harmonize the soups and vegetables, the five flavors must be complete; yet the oil, sauces, peppers, and seasonings held in the monastery’s permanent store are limited.

One must therefore draw from one's own purse to assist in preparing the offerings for the hall. When a single person resolves their mind, the various devas provide the offerings—this is frequently seen wherever it occurs.
Under the pretext of holding official positions and maps of the land, they occupy half the garden grounds and plant hemp and ramie to serve as their means of livelihood as "gardeners."
Washing. This has been handed down through successive generations until it became a habitual vice. It is not permitted to discard any items deemed base within the kitchen.

Those appointed to service must be diligent practitioners who are mature and experienced. When a great vegetarian feast (*dazhai*) is prepared, one must consult with the head administrator during the meal;

neither over-provision nor wasteful reduction is permissible. If a practitioner is undisciplined, they should be admonished up to two times. Should they still refuse to accept instruction, they shall be reprimanded.
Punish them. Distribute benefits and rations equally. When the rice and gruel are served in the upper buckets, burn incense and prostrate toward the Sangha Hall.
Always hold all people upon the crown of your head; you will thereby obtain blessings and merit for yourself—do not deceive yourselves.

The duties of the *zhisui* (year-round steward) involve daily affairs that must not deviate from their proper timing. He protects the mountain forests to preserve the geomantic flow of wind and water;

he oversees the herding and cultivation of fire-fields to maintain the permanent property (*changzhu*). He sweeps the corridors and courtyards, dredges the ditches and channels, and procures firewood and fuel.

He patrols against fire and theft, marking leaks with ash, and waiting for dry weather to repair them. For all major construction projects, there are specific officials assigned to each task; he must be diligent in these matters.
Strive forward to fulfill your duties. The ancients said, "If one does not work for a day, one shall not eat for a day. Reflect on this.
The duty of the estate manager (*zhuangzhu*) is to supervise agricultural affairs; you must not let the seasons pass by. Inspect the fields and cultivate the tenant farmers.
Punish those who are obstinate and violent. Provide generous relief to those who are poor or afflicted by illness. Assign corvée labor to single adults only at appropriate times.

In the event of droughts, floods, or calamities, perform recitations and prayers for protection; do not permit licentious sacrifices that recklessly harm living beings. Regarding the serious offenses of tenant farmers: [punish them accordingly].

I have submitted this to the Mountain Gate (the monastery). As you pass through here for a brief visit, may you provide us with warm hospitality regarding our food and lodging; do not be intent on parsimony or exploitation.

Exert yourself in planning and management so that the tenant farmers may feel a sense of gratitude and the permanent endowment of the monastery may enjoy surplus benefits—only then will it be truly excellent.
Regarding the duties of the *liàoyuán* (cell master): they follow the *vinaya* in every circumstance.

During the flourishing period of the monastic forests on the Left Bank of the Yangtze, when Dahui hung up his plaque for the general discourse (*pǔshuō*), those who stood in the ranks below the western order should know their own origins therein.

Every day after the morning congee, the tea attendant strikes the large board in front of the cell three times; the assembly returns to the cell to exchange greetings, at which point the cell master and vice-master separate from one another.

The positions to the left and right facing the *liáo* (dormitory). The *fu-liáo* (deputy dormitory master) comes forward to burn one stick of incense and returns to his position. The *chá-tóu* (tea attendant) stands in the center and calls out: "Bùshěn" (Not well?).

After the assembly has performed their *huánmén* (greeting), each returns to their own quarters to perform a *wènxùn* (inquiry). On the first and fifteenth days of the month, the *liáo-yuán* (dormitory head) personally burns the incense.
He orders the hanging of the *diǎntāng-pái* (tablet for serving hot soup), burns the soup, and brings forth the cups. The large board in front of the *liáo* is struck; the assembly proceeds as usual.

Entering the quarters. The *shōchō* (head of the quarters) distributes the handkerchiefs; the residents of the quarters rise. They burn incense in the central brazier, moving between the upper and lower sections. After the mutual greetings are completed, they return to their seats.

When the serving of hot water (*tō*) is finished, they rise before the brazier to express thanks for the tea. Daily, one must supervise the preparation of tea and hot water, as well as the charcoal fires during the winter months.

In the summer, he prepared hot water; he boiled decoctions to soak robes, washed clothes, and rinsed feet. He attended to the collection and maintenance of all utensils and implements, including scriptures and playthings, treating the community as if it were himself.
What task was there he did not accomplish? Every matter was conducted with precision and propriety, and the demeanor of every person was worthy of admiration.
This is what is meant by a sandalwood grove surrounded by sandalwood trees.

The duties of the Head of the Quarters (Liaozhu) are as follows: he shall create conditions for the community by ensuring mutual respect among them; the Rector (Weina) shall invite him to take charge, and he shall escort the new arrivals back to their quarters.

He shall inspect the scriptures and study materials, which may be borrowed by fellow practitioners during the summer retreat; these must be recorded by name on a list and returned at the end of the summer.

When the brothers enter the hall, the *liàoyuán* (hall head) shall receive and welcome them. During public periods of sitting meditation (*zàn*) or scripture reading (*kàn jīng*), he shall guard the scripture chest.

At night, he shall patrol the scripture tables together with the other residents; if a lock is lost, he shall leave a record of it and secure it. At dawn, he shall report this to the hall administration.

On festival days or the end of the year, he shall lead the recitation of scriptures for the dedication of merit (*huíxiàng*). When his term of office for one decade ends, he shall retire and inform the Hall Administration (*tángsī*). As for the departure of the *liàoyuán*, the remaining matters are as follows.
The same applies to the position of Assistant Official (Fuliáo). Their duties are numerous and burdensome. All items and utensils within the office must be handed over clearly and individually.

For one’s ten-day term of duty, one shall oversee all affairs; however, from before the morning gruel until after the evening assembly, entry into the tower is not permitted. Should there be urgent matters requiring attention, one must...
Report the date and sign your name in the register for the Chief Administrator (Biaozhu). Strike the board and announce it from the upper gallery;

this will help avoid future trouble. Constantly attend to the hot water pitcher. At night, check the lamps and candles for thieves. Sweep the floors, wipe the desks, change the water, and replenish the incense.
Do not allow outsiders to stay overnight. Carefully store any items received for sale. The clothing rack, ironing board, and the laundry bucket are for the common use of all.
These items should each be returned to their original places. By skillfully employing one's mind in this way, one shall obtain supreme and wondrous merit.

Regarding the office of the *wangliao* (warden of the quarters), my predecessors have held it in high regard. Upon assuming the office and arriving at the quarters, one should already be familiar with all matters within the ward, both great and small.

The assistant official (fùliáo) brings out the cups and prepares the tea. Together they clear away the items used during the evening session, such as the medicinal decoctions, and serve the vinegar and salt; these are matters pertaining to the establishment of karmic connections.
The Hall Master of Longevity (Yǎnshòu-táng zhǔ) provides for the sick monks, always keeping ginger, dates, oil, candles, and the five flavors ready, attending to them according to the season.

When a patient groans in pain, one should give rise to compassionate thoughts. When the illness has slightly subsided and they feel at ease, do not indulge them with excessive nourishment or allow them to eat to their heart's content without restraint.

Nor should they occupy the room and bed for too long. Illness is a wholesome medicine for sentient beings; one should reform one's faults and renew oneself daily. At times when the solitary lamp shines alone—
This is precisely when one must exert effort.

It is the duty of the neighborhood steward (*kaivartika*) to solicit donors to provide support for the monastery’s permanent endowment (*sthavira-saṃgha*). One must follow the donor's intention without altering it by even a hair’s breadth.

If the requests are too frequent, one must not press them repeatedly; this would cause the initial donor to feel weary and contemptuous. When the World-Honored One went on almsround, he did not bypass [a house].

Seventh: The Seven Families. Just as Ānanda passed through the streets and encountered a poor woman who offered him a tattered felt blanket; he conceived the thought that such an encounter was difficult to find, which was indeed appropriate.

Regarding the duty of the water-head (the monk in charge of water): every morning he boils hot water so that everyone may wash their faces and their hand-towels remain clean; in the winter months, he dries them over a fire.
Always keep lamps, candles, and tooth-cleansing medicine ready. Before departing, relight the lamps and arrange the face basin.

Wait until the washing of the face is finished, then return the basin to its original place and lift the hand towel to prevent it from becoming soiled. Leave one or two basins and an old towel for those who follow.
Pre-arrange firewood and fuel, keeping virtuous causes in mind.
Regarding the duties of the charcoal master: during the hot months, one must manufacture charcoal lumps and accumulate white charcoal.

Whether by soliciting donations from patrons or drawing from the storehouse, one must beforehand apply the mind to ensure sufficient preparation for use. After the furnace is opened, once the morning gruel is finished and before the midday meal, while the incense sticks have not yet been lit, the furnace is prepared;
thereafter, it is replenished as needed after the noon meal, never deviating from the established routine. It is appropriate to maintain this practice with the Way in mind.

Regarding the duties of the miller: the assembly of pure monks remains silent; the wheat is washed until it is neither too dry nor too wet. The sieves in the kitchen are fine and dense, and the flour is sorted by grade.
The rice is pounded until pure white, and the husks and chaff are sifted out. It is sold at the proper time, or returned to the storehouse.
He distributed benefits equally among all, prioritizing public integrity and fairness. Beyond attending to the affairs of the community, he cultivated his spiritual practice;
like Dongshan, his wondrous functions were unrestrained in every direction—he was a lotus blooming amidst fire.
The duties of the garden master involve diligent and pioneering labor: irrigating the plots, planting and distributing vegetable seedlings, and caring for the gardeners.
Morning and evening, never be indolent. Gather the seeds and plant them; when the season arrives, follow the timing. Plow with fire and till with the axe—take the ancients as your model.
Suddenly casting down the mattock and returning home—would this not be most joyful?
Regarding the duties of the Head of the Tree-Grove (Shùtóu): one must protect and cherish the pine-lined paths of the mountain gate and the bamboo and trees that provide shade for the monastery.

One should maintain the buildings and facilities, constantly and diligently inspecting them; planting and repairing should be done in a timely manner. The law of cause and effect is manifest—merit is never bestowed in vain. If there are few people and the pines wither, it will not be too late to come again.

Regarding the duties of the bath attendant (*snānaka*): these indeed arise from their causes. Every morning, he sweeps the floor; prepares incense at the proper time; trims the lamps and lights the candles; changes the counting sticks (*śalākā*) and cleans the latrines;
removes the buckets and washes the sandals; ensures the hand towels are clean; provides ample hot water; and frequently replenishes the bath powder (*snānacūrṇa*).
The ashes and dust are constantly accumulating; at times they lie in disarray, requiring clearing and sweeping.

One should diligently gather firewood and wash the tally-sticks, showing compassion for the laborers' efforts, ensuring that the perimeter remains bright and clean so that one’s spiritual practice may reach completion. During his time at Lingyin, Xuedou, as well as in the assemblies of Muguan, Miaoxi, and Baofeng, all were devoted to these tasks.
Seated: A Verse on the Rules and Standards of Baizhang.
According to the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang, since the inception of the Chan school at Shaoshi Mountain until its arrival at Caoxi, practitioners had mostly resided in Vinaya monasteries.
Although they occupied separate quarters, their methods of preaching the Dharma and maintaining the community did not accord with formal standards. Therefore, he constantly...
He took this to heart and said: "The Way of our ancestors was intended to be widely disseminated for transformation, hoping that it would never perish in the future.
How could it possibly be made to follow along with the various *āgama* teachings (the Sanskrit term *āgama* is now called *āgama*; these are the Hīnayāna teachings)? Or if someone asks:
'Why do you not rely upon the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Ābharaṇa-sūtra*, or the Mahāyāna precepts? The Master replied: 'I..."
This is what we take as our fundamental principle: it is neither restricted to the Mahāyāna nor the Hīnayāna, nor is it distinct from them.

One should strike a balance between the broad and the concise, ensuring that the established rules and models are appropriate to the circumstances. Thereupon, he conceived a new idea and separately established a meditation hall. The verse says:
In the past, while residing at Yulsa Temple, he opened the gate of Chan in a separate courtyard. It was only after the Great Wisdom Chan Master that the majesty of the ancestral Way was truly known.
How great is the Great Wisdom Chan Master’s establishment of the Dharma! He honored the abbot to flourish virtue and conduct, and arranged the ranks of the assembly in proper order.

To manifest talent and ability and to provide a framework for the monastic community, one must illuminate the path across all eras; thus, every person of noble standing should observe these principles, causing the ancestral way to shine ever more brightly.
Should anyone contravene the Dharma or disrupt the moral order, the culture of our tradition will perish. Therefore, I have established regulations to distinguish between the wise and the ignorant.
Behold the worthy and strive to equal them; may we together ensure the stability of our community.
Should any articles of clothing or other items be lost within the hall or the quarters, one must record the color, quantity, time, and location of the loss, and report it to the administrators.
They shall then verify whether the account is true or false. If the circumstances are deemed serious, they shall notify the Hall Office to convene an assembly.
The assembly searches the halls and the quarters. Those who have committed offenses are brought forth publicly; those who are deceitful are exposed before the multitude. A verse says:
"In the midst of the assembly, as if searching for something lost, The types and quantities of items must be clearly distinguished. If the objects are heavy, they must be thoroughly inspected;
If the circumstances are minor, the matter may be judged accordingly."

Within the community of the noble ones (āryasaṃgha), there may be those who commit theft, indulge in wine or women, engage in quarrels that defile the assembly, or cause clamor and disorder through lack of discipline;
all such individuals shall be assembled and expelled from the monastery. If they do not comply, the matter shall be reported to the authorities. As the verse says:
Those who steal property or engage in strife, those defiled by alcohol or lust who corrupt the ranks of the Sangha—expel them swiftly from the assembly of the pure;
to harbor them is to ruin the community.

Furthermore, should there be those who falsely assume names or disguise their forms to mingle with the pure assembly, or who cause other disturbances and clamor, the Hall Master (Tangsi) shall [deal with them].
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) shall investigate the matter, remove [the offender] from their assigned seat, and expel them from the monastery, so as to ensure the peace and purity of the assembly.
A verse says:
Disbelieving the Buddha of True Nature, You come as a false bhikṣu; Immediately, you are removed from your seat.
"Depart! Do not look back.
Should you commit this offense again, you will bring disgrace upon your peers and the monastery itself.
You must then assemble the community to strike you with a staff, burn your ritual implements, and expel you through a side gate—this is to demonstrate your humiliation. A verse says:
If one commits a grave offense or burns their robes and alms bowl, one must assemble the multitude; with a cane of mountain rattan, they are shown shame and expelled through a side gate.

Within the hall, if the pure assembly is insufficient to provide a leader who can manage the monastery, they shall simply follow the assembly for meals and participate in the morning and evening sessions.
Please depart. You should each examine yourselves and maintain your proper station, accumulating virtue and exalting the Way to bring glory to this monastic assembly.
You must not interfere in the affairs of the monastery from outside, nor arbitrarily change regulations to create disturbances, nor spread rumors of right and wrong to disturb the pure community.
Do not allow a lack of tranquility; those who violate this shall be dealt with according to the monastery’s regulations. As the verse says:
A guest beneath the three rafters / May personally bring his own life to rest. / Fortunately there are monastics to manage affairs;
/ Why must one force oneself to emerge?
Examining these regulations, there are four kinds of benefits: (1) One does not defile the pure assembly and gives rise to a mind of respectful faith; thus, the three karmas...
This is unwholesome and one with whom it is not permissible to dwell. According to the Vinaya, he should be dealt with by means of the Brahma-maṇḍala rite; he must be expelled from the monastery.

Once the pure assembly is at peace, reverence and faith will arise. (2) Without destroying his monastic appearance—so as to comply with the Buddha’s regulations—he should be punished according to the circumstances.

(3) One may retain the Dharma robes, for later one will surely regret it. (4) One does not disturb the public offices, because it reduces litigation and disputes. One does not leak [secrets] to external protectors, for the sake of the fundamental principles.
When those from the four quarters dwell together, who can distinguish the ordinary from the sage? Moreover, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, there were still the factions of the Six Groups;
how much more so now in this age of the Semblance Dharma—how could they be entirely absent? Previously I saw a certain group who, upon seeing a single monk...

There are those who, upon encountering a transgression, immediately join in derision and mockery. Yet they fail to realize that to slight the assembly and treat the Dharma with contempt causes immense harm.

Now, if the Chan school is free from such obstacles, it would be appropriate to follow the regulations of Baizhang’s monastic community, distinguishing matters according to their specific circumstances.
Although establishing rules to prevent misconduct is not itself the mark of a true sage, it is better to have rules and no violations than to have violations and no rules.
No instruction. I defer to the Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang regarding the immense benefit of protecting the Dharma.
This concludes Volume Seven of the *Chanlin Beiyong* (Practical Manual for the Chan Forest). [Volume Eight follows].
Morning Ritual for Observing and Violating Precepts:

The Buddhas of the three periods of time and the ancestral masters of successive generations have strictly purified the *vinaya* and expanded the Way of the Patriarchs—the Three Studies of precept, concentration, and wisdom.
Precepts are the fundamental root; from concentration arises wisdom. One vows to sever all evil and vows to cultivate all goodness.
One vows to deliver all sentient beings and maintains the three pure minds to perfect the precepts. Regarding the Hinayana *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, one uses its prohibitions like medicine;
at the outset, it explains what is permitted and what is forbidden. Regarding the Mahayana *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, one would rather die than transgress.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* sternly rebuke and strictly prohibit violations. The *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Uphold the pure precepts with diligence, as if protecting a bright pearl."

Question: When traveling abroad to seek instruction and pursue the Way by visiting various monasteries, one’s primary task is to prepare the necessary requisites. Former masters wore bamboo hats, while others carried bundles on their shoulders.

The three robes and alms bowl shall be complete and without deficiency. The master’s staff, the razor for the precepts, and all other items required for personal use, as well as those needed for cold and heat, shall be kept in order wherever one stays.
All belongings must be stored and maintained with strict adherence to the rules. With body at ease and mind joyful, one shall advance upon the Path and cultivate dhyāna.

Do not befriend those who are not virtuous; do not take as your master those who are not sages. Strive to repay the four debts of gratitude and do not fail yourself. You must exert yourselves with earnest diligence;
these bequeathed instructions are clear and manifest.
The Master and the guests look upon one another;

they look upon the name and the excellence [of the monastery], and then look upon the abbot’s quarters. This should take place after the morning gruel and before the formal inquiry (san). Having arrived in advance at the office of the attendant (shisō), the attendant leads them in. They take their seats and tea is offered.

After briefly recounting their journey and origins, they rise before the incense burner to express thanks for the tea and address the Master, saying: "We, so-and-so and others, have come specifically to pay our respects."
"Venerable Master, I have troubled you by having High Attendant Tong-fu inquire on my behalf. [The attendant] says: "Please sit for a moment; I shall inquire in detail regarding your origins.

If it is one who has previously acquainted himself with the Abbot, or a relative of the Dharma, or a fellow countryman coming to attend to affairs, he says: "Please sit comfortably for a short while, and allow me to report your arrival. He then reports to the Abbot.

If the visitor is an official guest, or if the Abbot is pressed by urgent business and must delay slightly, the reception must nevertheless be arranged immediately. The attendant is then ordered to prepare incense, hold a candle, and set out tea, reporting the arrival of the newcomer to the Abbot.

The guest is escorted out to the dormitory hall. An attendant leads him forward with a bow. The abbot receives him and leads him before the incense burner. The newly arrived monk says, "Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged.

[The abbot] declines. The guest then inserts incense and spreads his ritual implements; [the abbot] again declines. He then performs three prostrations with unopened sitting cloths (chuli) and takes his seat. The attendant burns incense and serves tea. They engage in conversation.

Rising, he goes before the burner to express thanks for the tea, then is escorted to the guest seat. He returns the incense and performs a return bow. This constitutes the complete protocol for the guest.

Regarding the etiquette for the Abbot: one must perform two prostrations with both hands extended followed by three full prostrations, thereby demonstrating mutual respect and providing a model for future students.

Upon arriving at the attendant’s office, one offers thanks, saying: “I have troubled you with my presence; I hereby express my gratitude. The attendant replies: “The ceremony was duly performed; why do you trouble yourself to show such honor? One then returns to one’s quarters. The guest master (kètóu) shall request a half-meal and refreshments.

Before the noon meal, a special soup (*tāng*) is served; after the soup, the medicinal diet (*yàoshí*) is provided. On the following day, after the morning gruel is finished, he is invited to offer incense.
Tea. On another day, a formal reception (*kankan-tai*) shall be arranged. According to ancient custom, the ritual of receiving incense during a formal reception must not be omitted.

Lately, however, when brothers who have been attending to affairs travel abroad for sightseeing and lodge wherever they may be, the abbot should likewise go to visit them in person to express his gratitude.
This is the culmination of the ritual of hospitality.

Regarding the procedure for hanging up one's belongings and entering the hall (*guàdā guītáng*), at the beginning of Baizhang’s establishment of the rules, one first goes to the Guest Office (*kèsī*) for an interview, and subsequently proceeds to the Hall Office (*tángsī*) to register one's quarters. This constitutes the primary unit of the rite.

Once the protocol for the formal visit has been established, one proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) for the customary greetings (*renshi*). This is not the same as the situation when the monastic community was at its peak;

in those times, upon first arriving at the guest quarters (*danguo*), there would be a notice from the Guest Office stating: "Please come early tomorrow morning for tea and a formal reception. Thus, one would be invited to receive tea and have an audience the following morning.
There is no formal announcement. Upon arriving at the Guest Office (Ke-si), the assembly selects a senior monk well-versed in monastic customs (*cong-lin*) to serve as the leader (*can-tou*).

Leading the group with full ceremonial decorum, they stand to the right of the gate and say: "We have come for a temporary visit. The Guest Master then admits them inside, saying: "On this day, I respectfully wish that the Venerable Abbot, the Senior Chan Master, may enjoy good health and abundant blessings in your daily life.

Having long admired your reputation for the Way, I am now honored to meet you in person. My humble feelings are filled with the utmost gratitude. He replies: "The mountain gate is fortunate to receive your visit from so far away. They bow and take their seats, then burn incense.
They partake of tea. After briefly inquiring into their origins, they rise to thank them for the tea and return to the *danguo* (guest quarters).

The *zhiké* (guest master) subsequently goes to return the courtesy. The *cántóu* (head of the assembly) receives them and performs a general bow. The *zhiké* says: "I respectfully wish all you venerable Zen masters a long life and much merit.

I have just received your great honor and come specifically to express my gratitude; your humble servant is moved by the utmost appreciation. He replies: "The ritual requires that I first pay my respects to you; why do you trouble yourself to show me such honor? The *cántóu* personally escorts him out the door. Next, he proceeds to the *shì* (attendant).

The attendant (sishi) shall receive them. After the preceding rites have been performed, he shall announce: "We, [Name] and others, have come specifically to pay our respects to the Venerable Master. We venture to trouble the attendant to report this to him. The attendant shall inquire into the reason for their visit.
If they are local residents, dharma-relatives, or there to conduct business, he shall clarify the matter and say: "Please return to your lodgings first; allow me to report this to the Master.

He shall then immediately go to the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) to report: "[Name] has come specifically to pay his respects to the Venerable Master. If permission is granted, he shall report back: "An audience has been granted. If not yet granted, he shall report: "An audience has not yet been granted. When the morning bell tolls, the attendant...

Holding a lamp, they proceed to the abbot’s quarters to offer greetings. Upon arrival, they are received for an audience. After the morning gruel is finished, the sleeping hall is opened to them. The head of the assembly leads the group as the abbot receives them;

the head of the assembly steps forward and says, "Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged. He turns his body, inserts incense with his left hand, and steps back. Together with the assembly, he performs the ritual prostrations.

For the first unfolding of the mat, he says: "We have long heard of your reputation for the Way; today we are fortunate to behold your honored countenance. Our humble hearts are filled with boundless gratitude. For the second unfolding...
Regarding cold and warmth: perform three prostrations with touching the ground. If they are inner disciples or dharma-relatives, offer separate incense and perform the rites.

At the discretion of the presiding master, they may take their seats. The attendant burns incense, and tea is served. One must ask where the summer retreat was spent and inquire about one's hometown and style of calligraphy;

each must answer truthfully and not speak at length. Rising before the incense burner, express thanks for the tea, saying: "I humbly receive this refined preparation; I hereby offer my gratitude. The abbot then sees them off.

[The guest] exits. The head of the assembly says, "Venerable Master, please take care. [The guest] proceeds to the attendant’s office (shìsī) and offers thanks, saying, "I have troubled you with my presence;

I respectfully prostrate in gratitude. He returns to the *dàngguò* hall and stands in the outer row, waiting for the abbot to return his courtesy. Together they perform a greeting (*wènxùn*), and [the guest] leads him inside, saying:

"For some time now, I have respectfully wished that the Abbot, our Head of the Hall, may enjoy much well-being in your daily life. My previous prostration was not thorough, yet you have condescended to honor me in return; I am deeply moved by your kindness. The abbot replies, "My stay here has been inconvenient; I hope you will be patient and overlook it."

The assembly escorts him out. The head of the group (the *zantou*) turns to the upper seat, bows to the attendant, and enters with the assembly. They exchange greetings, saying: "It has been some time since we last had the honor of seeing you, Reverend Master Gao.

We trust that your health is flourishing. It was our duty to visit your quarters to pay our respects; instead, we have been honored by your gracious descent here. We are deeply moved. The other replies: "The mountain gate is fortunate to receive your distinguished visit from afar. Our thanks for your kindness were delayed, for which we feel much regret. At half-past noon, there is a light meal (*dianxin*).
That evening, a special soup (*tang*) is served, followed by the formal meal (*yaoshi*) at the designated seating. The attendant burns incense for the meal.

One incense stick. If the head official (shoushou) is invited to accompany [the guest], they shall personally rise to burn incense for the medicinal meal (yaoshi). When serving the accompanying guests with hot water, the attendant shall burn incense and offer the tea;

the abbot (zhuchi) shall personally serve the accompanying guests, which constitutes the fulfillment of the ritual. Upon finishing the meal, inform the abbot to escort the guest. On the following day, after the morning gruel is finished, invite them to offer tea.
The head of the assembly (canchou) leads the group to stand in formation before the dormitory hall, awaiting the abbot’s recitation of the sutra.

[The assembly] turns back and immediately steps forward to inquire after [the Master’s] well-being, saying: "We respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Venerable Monk, has spent the night in comfort and enjoys much prosperity in your daily life. Having once again received your gracious summons, we are overcome with gratitude. They take their seats. The attendant burns incense and serves tea.
Rising to go before the incense burner, they perform two prostrations with both hands extended (*liang-zhan*) and three full prostrations (*san-li*) to express thanks for the tea.

For the first extension, they say: "We have once again been honored by your preparation of this tea; we specifically offer our thanks. We are deeply ashamed at our own inadequacy. For the second extension, they say: "On this day, [Month and Day], we respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Venerable Monk, enjoys much prosperity in your daily life. [The assembly] remains seated.

He escorts him out two or three paces. The head of the assembly (sanchō) turns back and enters to see the Abbot, reporting: "We, [Name] and others, considering the great importance of the matter of birth and death and the swiftness of impermanence, have come specifically to seek refuge under the Venerable Master.
We humbly pray that you will accept us. He then performs a full prostration with his hands touching the ground, saying: "Thank you, Venerable Master, for granting us residence.

If the request is not yet granted to the entire group, he first secures residence for the head of the assembly, then seeks permission for the others in succession, until they are all registered at the Attendants' Office (shisō). [The attendant then reports: "I have just received the compassionate decree from the Abbot’s quarters..."
[Instructing him] to go to the superior quarters (*shàngliáo*) to register his name. The abbot must have an attendant (*xingzhě*) lead him to the office of the attendant (*shìsī*).

If he arrives in person, the attendant shall record his name; only then may the notice board be issued and sent to the Hall Office (*táng-sī*). The *rènwéina* (rector) shall then instruct an attendant to serve tea for the newly arrived guests.

[The guest] returns to the hall and ascends to his bed on the register. Lately, monastic communities have declined and ritual protocols have become inconsistent; these matters are therefore detailed below.
Regarding the custom for the formal mutual inspection (*kō daikan*): on the first day of the ninth month, one should pre-arrange to submit one's name at the *shisō* (the office of attendants).

Each person should prepare a large stick of incense and write two characters of their name upon it, then deposit it with the attendants. Recently, it has been observed in many places that when the time for the mutual inspection arrives, the head of the assembly (*sanzu*) leads [the group].
One should purchase a large piece of incense. Once one has been granted formal entry into the monastery (*guàdǎ*), one must then return each piece of incense or contribute money;

either practice is contrary to the Dharma. The assembly shall elect an administrator, or someone experienced in monastic affairs, to serve as the *cāntóu* (leader). On the appointed day, the attendant (*shìzhě*) shall provide a piece of incense to the *cāntóu*.
In the dormitory hall (*qǐntáng*), a candle shall be lit and incense prepared. The assembly shall stand in rows outside the burner while the attendant invites the Abbot.

[The Abbot] exits. The head of the assembly steps forward and says, "Please, Venerable Master, take your seat. The Abbot delivers a formal discourse (*chuiyu*). Once the head of the assembly has offered his response, he steps back and performs a greeting with the assembly.
He then searches for incense and performs two prostrations with opened sitting cloth and three full prostrations; the wording is identical to that previously mentioned.

If the discourse does not accord with the occasion, the head of the assembly shall not be granted immediate registration (*guadaba*). He must then go to the Office of Attendants to offer thanks. The Abbot’s guest master will invite him to come the following day.
After the morning gruel, tea is offered in the dormitory hall. The abbot returns this courtesy simultaneously with the formal thanks for being accepted into the community (*guàdā*).

After the tea, he escorts them out for two or three paces. The head of the assembly turns back and, together with the group, requests acceptance into the community, saying: "We, [Name] and others, considering the gravity of the matter of birth and death and the swiftness of impermanence, have come specifically to rely upon the Venerable Master.

We humbly pray that you will grant us your acceptance. Once the acceptance is complete, they return to the hall. In a major monastery, those who serve administrative duties shall record their names according to their respective offices. Next—
First, the announcement of the roster.
To the Office of the Hall: Format of the Roster: (At the Compassionate Command of the Abbot: One monk, [Name], as Attendant; [Name], as Head Seat.
On this day of this month, reported by the Attendant, [Name].

The Head of the Hall (Pingdaguada) shall report to the Hall Office (Tangsi) and the Attendants' Office (Chengshisi) regarding the new arrivals. He shall immediately order the hall attendants to invite the newly arrived monks for tea. Each monk shall carry his ordination certificate (duce).

The head of the group shall prepare an incense case and lead the assembly to the Hall Office, where they will be received. They shall perform a prostration with touching heads (duchuli) and exchange greetings regarding the weather.

The Master [Wēn] enters his seat, burns incense, and partakes of tea. Having finished, he rises and addresses the assembly, saying: "We, [Name et al.], have just received the Compassionate Command of the Honored One, ordering us to attend upon your person.

We humbly pray that you will deign to include us among your disciples. The Master replies: "The mountain gate is fortunate to share in this stillness and solitude with you all. The Head of the Assembly (Cāntóu) takes the ordination certificates (dùdí) and hands them to the Rector (wéinà). He performs a single prostration facing the Master.

Once everyone has ascended the platform and completed the roll-call, each returns their certificate except for the Head of the Assembly, whose certificate remains. The attendant (xíngzhě) then calls out.

[The Abbot] says: (Please invite the assembly’s Head Seat to enter the hall and take up residence. The head of the retreat group leads the assembly into the hall, stepping forward with the left foot first. They stand in a row in front of the Holy Monk (Śākyamuni).
The head of the retreat group burns incense and, together with the assembly, performs three full prostrations with opened sitting cloths (*kṣauma*).

They circumambulate the hall once, from the upper hall to the lower hall, and then stand again as before in front [of the Holy Monk]. After performing a formal greeting (*praṇāma*), they step back from the rear of the row first and stand at the position of the Holy Monk.

The Head of the Assembly (Cantou). The Rector (Weina) enters the hall and burns one incense stick; he stands in the upper section. An attendant from the Hall Office uses a tray and cloth to carry the ordination certificate (du-die), which the Rector returns to him.
The Head of the Assembly, together with the assembly, performs a prostration with touching (du-chu li yi bai).

The Head of the Assembly leads the assembly, turns before the incense burner, and moves toward the head of the row, performing another prostration with touching. The Head of the Assembly escorts the Rector out. [This occurs] after the meal and before the midday meal.

The Gate: Having finished the midday meal, they exit through the front gate. The head of the assembly (sanchō) does not cross the threshold. The rector (vinaya-dhara) has already issued a notice to all the quarters.
An attendant leads them to the various quarters; the wooden board is struck three times. The master of the quarter (ryōshu) receives them at the entrance and invites them inside.

They perform a single prostration with touching heads (tai-sokurei). After the greetings are concluded, they exchange formal courtesies. The head of the quarter (ryōgen) performs a single prostration with touching heads in return, exchanges words of greeting, burns incense, and offers tea.

[The guest] departs. The tea attendant invites [the guest], saying: "The Abbot invites the assembly and the Head Seat to come to the quarters this evening for the offering of hot water. [The guest] replies: "I shall decline this invitation.
Next, he visits the Head Seat’s quarters, the Treasury Office, and the quarters of the various head officials to pay his respects. The hall attendant announces his arrival.

Upon meeting him before the incense burner, [the host] performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*butsuri*) and exchanges greetings regarding the weather. [The guest] then departs. Nowadays, it is common not to receive one another; however, to merely exchange words [without formal greeting] is contrary to the Dharma.

When formally requesting admission to the monastery (*guàtā*), both classes of officials return the courtesy; the *tōng* (the announcer) performs a prostration. The *shìsī* (attendant office) does not prostrate, nor do they return the courtesy with a prostration. The Form for the Announcement:

[Admission of One Monk] [Name], Elder [X], On this day of this month, Reported by [Name] of the Hall Office. [Admission of a Monk from a Specific Location] Elder [Name], [Precept Name], of [City/County], Submitted by the Attendant Office. Respectfully addressed to the Abbot. Submitted by the Attendants of the Front Hall and the Various Quarters, including [Name] of [City/County] and [Precept Name].
Chapter: Small Temporary Residents Return to the Hall.

This occurs after winter and before the New Year; the timing is not fixed. Once the temporary residents have been assigned quarters by the Abbot, the Attendant Office issues a notice to the Hall Administration.

Immediately, tea was served. The Rector (Vina) received them in. They performed a prostration with unopened sitting cloths (chuli). After burning incense and drinking tea, they submitted this request:

"We, [Name et al.], have received the Master’s command to attend upon you; we humbly pray that you will grant us your acceptance. He replied: "The mountain gate is fortunate to share in this quiet seclusion together. He took the ordination certificates (duoche) and handed them to the Rector. The participants performed a prostration with unopened sitting cloths in his presence.

Once the register for the platform had been completed, the Rector returned the certificates to the participants, who performed a prostration with unopened sitting cloths in his presence. The leader of the group (canchou) then performed a prostration with unopened sitting cloths.

Prostrate. Each person collects their ordination certificate (*duòjié*). Together they go to the upper section of the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*) and enter. They perform one prostration with touching of the head to the ground (*chùlǐ*) facing [the *wéinà*].

They turn around and perform another prostration with touching of the head to the ground facing [him]. The words of the petition are: "Now, by great fortune, we have once again been graced by your warm care; our humble hearts are overcome with the utmost gratitude. He replies: "The quarters are not convenient."

"Fortunately, we beg for your leniency. The head of the assembly escorts the *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) out. The assembly exits the quarters and stands to the right. The attendant of the Hall Office and the storehouse keeper strike the small board inside the quarters three times.
The master of the quarters receives them in; they perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloths (*taichu li*) before him, burn incense, and drink tea.

After the tea ceremony is concluded, he addresses him, saying: "I have just been permitted by the *vinaya-dhara* to return to the upper quarters. I humbly hope you will grant me your favor and allow me to rely upon your presence. He replies: "This is a great fortune; let us together maintain this tranquil seclusion. They then perform a prostration with unopened sitting cloths.
One prostration. The head of the assembly turns to the left and performs one prostration with touching (sōriri). The assembly stands in a single file before the incense burner and bows.
The chief of the quarters leads them on a circuit around the tables, after which they again stand in a single file, bow, and disperse.

Next, the heads of the various quarters receive one another (performing one prostration with touching), exchange greetings regarding their health, burn incense, and offer tea. Subsequently, they visit the quarters for formal introductions, as well as the administrative office (kusoshi); these proceedings apply to all.
Perform a single prostration with full contact.
Regarding the installation of the West Hall Head Seat (Xitáng Shǒuzuò):

this refers to a person of great virtue who has been installed as a West Hall Resident (Dàfāng Xitáng). When the intention to serve as the Abbot arises, one should reveal this meaning during conversation; the Abbot should then endeavor to retain him. On the following day, after the tea ceremony has concluded, he should report, saying: "I, [Name]..."

The guest says, "I have come specifically because the matter of birth and death is great, seeking to rely upon you for shelter. He then performs a prostration with full prostration (chùlì). The abbot (zhùzhí) shall respond with a prostration; this maintains the ritual of host and guest. On another day, or immediately, a tea service is held for the two classes of officials (the administrative and monastic staff).

The abbot personally rises to burn a single incense stick, then returns to his original position and stands. He announces: "The West Hall Chief Seat from [Place Name] has not abandoned us and has come here to maintain our secluded retreat together. We trouble the two classes of officials to escort him back to his quarters. The person being escorted steps forward and says, "I have come specifically to seek refuge; I am deeply grateful for your kind reception. The abbot and the two classes of officials then escort him to his private quarters.

If he takes his leave, the Abbot’s Hall (méngtáng) is also escorted by the two classes of officials. The abbot occupies the seat of the host, and the guest performs a prostration with full prostration facing him. The guest’s words are: "On this day, I respectfully wish that the Abbot of the Hall may enjoy good health and well-being."

[The new abbot says: "I am of great merit. It is a blessing from my past lives that I have been graced by your inclusion. The Abbot’s Response: "The mountain gate is fortunate to share in this period of stillness and solitude. [The new abbot] escorts the outgoing abbot out. The person receiving him bows to the master of the quarters, who then bows to the attendant and offers congratulations. [The new abbot] escorts him out and bows to the two classes of officials (the *douban*).

The candidate advances to offer congratulations, turns to the right position, and exchanges formal greetings with the Head of the Monastery (Liaozhu). The candidate says: "I have been fortunate in past lives; I rejoice that we may together maintain this secluded retreat. The Head replies: "It is my great good fortune to have gained the privilege of attending upon you. Thereupon, the candidate carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) to express gratitude for the assigned bedding.

The Hall Attendant and the Treasury Assistant lead [the new appointee] to the Treasury Office. He performs his formal greetings (*renshi*) with the various Head Officers (*doutou*), the Monastery Officials (*liaozhi*), and the Elders (*jiujiu*). On the first and fifteenth days of the month, he partakes in the tea service along with the Elders (as arranged in their respective order).
The Abbot receives renowned and eminent guests from all quarters who come to pay their respects and attend to social affairs.

When those seeking to be formally enrolled (to "hang up their staff") arrive, they attend the tea ceremony; having finished, they address the Abbot, saying: "We have come specifically because the matter of birth and death is so great, to rely upon you, Venerable Master.

We humbly pray that you will accept us. They perform a full prostration. The Abbot replies: "I am deeply honored that you do not reject me; let us together maintain this quiet solitude. He then immediately invites the Head Seat and the Chief Administrator.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable Leader) serves tea. The Abbot rises in person, burns a single stick of incense, and makes the formal announcement regarding the escort as before.

The person receiving the escort steps forward and says: "We, [Name] and others, have once again been graced by the Master’s inclusion; we shall simply return to the Sangha Hall to join the assembly. The Abbot replies: "It is the duty of this mountain gate to extend such an escort. He then escorts them back to the Sangha Hall.

The Abbot, acting as the presiding host, performs a prostration with unopened sitting cloth (*buddha-luohan li*) facing them and sees them out the door. Immediately, the attendant offers congratulations and escorts him out, presenting him with [gifts].
The *liaozhu* (cell master) has completed his greetings. He then moves to the position of the presiding master (*zhuzi*) and completes the greetings with the two classes of officials.

The person receiving and escorting him then carries incense and proceeds to the Abbot’s quarters (*fangzhang*) to express thanks for the seating arrangement. A hall attendant (*xingzhe*) leads him to the administrative office (*kusī*), where he greets all the head officers (*toushou*). This concludes the formal greetings.
When a Dharma relative (*dharmabandhu*) arrives to attend to monastic affairs, they may do so at any time.

First, they shall visit the attendant (*śayanāsana-pāla*), explain their background in detail, and request that he inform the abbot (*sthavira*). Upon being granted an audience, they shall offer incense and perform the proper salutations.
If the Dharma relative is of the younger generation—such as a nephew or junior member—and has previously served as an attendant, they shall all receive the formal bow (*yī*) from the resident monks.
Offer incense and tea. Escort the guest to their seat and return the prostration. Whether they are to be enrolled in the hall (*guàdā*) or sent to their quarters, the ritual is the same as before.
[The Master] first casts incense to receive the guest for enrollment.

Due to actual urgent circumstances, one may arrive after the designated time. Whether it be because one has merely come to register as a guest (*guatada*) or because the attendant (*shizhe*) has created obstacles, one should immediately offer incense and present oneself for inspection.

Regardless of the location, place the incense lightly before the Abbot and say: "I have arrived temporarily to pay my respects to the Master. Then, perform a prostration by touching the ground (*chuli*).
If the Abbot does not acknowledge you and departs, collect the incense yourself and seek registration elsewhere; this is not restricted.
It was the proper time. Someone asked about his origins, and he answered truthfully. Once he had been granted registration, his name was added to the roster and he entered the hall.

After the formal greetings throughout the various quarters were completed, the head of the assembly led the group to the Hall Office to offer thanks. There, they submitted this request: "Where shall we settle our seating positions and the placement of our alms bowls?"

Immediately looking toward the assembly with joy, he replied without withholding his compassion: "I respectfully comply with your command. He then entered the Sangha Hall together with them to assign their seats.
If the retreat (jie-zhi) was about to begin, he would add the names to the official register. If one requested leave, it must be for a full half-month according to the hall’s regulations.

However, if a death notice arrives regarding parents or teachers, or if there is an urgent necessity to attend to affairs, one must sincerely inform the public officials. Yet, the primary aim of traveling to study and seek instruction remains focused on the Dharma.
To thoroughly investigate birth and death: for example, Ciming changed his robes and followed the military ranks for three years before going to see Fenyang;
he attended to menial duties until later he was able to clarify the Great Matter. During the assembly of Chijue Songyuan, it took nine months before one could even be granted formal registration.
How can the "brothers" of the present day—who drift from east to west morning and evening—be compared to such examples?

The Subject’s Petition for Permission to Register as a Resident Monk During the flourishing period of the monastic community, the formal ceremony of *xiè guàtā* (thanking for admission) was performed immediately upon a monk’s entry into the hall.

When Master Fozhao went from Yuyuan to Mount Jing, Qu Guyun served as his attendant during the entry ceremony; the Master held him in high esteem and treated him with special affection, employing the ritual of *xiè guàtā*.

[The details of] these matters shall all be included in the report of thanks to be made before the summer retreat. On the day following, for the ceremony of thanking for the hanging of the registration plaque (*guàdā*), once the attendant has finished serving the morning gruel, he shall post the notice at the upper section in front of the communal quarters.
The novice attendants (*xíngzhě*) of the Hall Office shall write the notice and solicit contributions, then hand them to the attendant to offer incense in return.
The attendants (shishi) hold a preliminary tea ceremony. From among the assembly, one person is selected by consensus to serve as the *santō* (head of the group).

On the day of the event, the attendants present a large piece of incense to the *santō*. In the *shindō* (sleeping hall), an incense table is solemnly prepared with a burner, candles, and other offerings.

The *santō* leads the assembly, who take their positions according to the prescribed diagram, arranged in groups of three. Each group is led by a minor *santō*, who carefully records the words spoken and the rules of etiquette for advancing and retreating.

One must first practice the ritual procedures in one place so that they may be manifested when the time arrives. When the time comes, the attendant and the head of the assembly enter together to request the Abbot to come forth.
Once he has taken his seat, the head of the assembly returns to the group and bows together with them. They then step forward and say, "Please, Venerable Master, sit cross-legged.

He turns from the incense burner back to his position and bows together with the assembly. They then advance before the burner and take incense from within their robes; the left hand searches for the incense.
Return to your positions and exchange greetings with the assembly. The head of the group (canshou), together with the original host, leads three people to unfold their sitting cloths.

The head of the group steps forward and says: "We, [Name] and others, have been fortunate in past lives to receive your compassionate protection; our humble hearts are filled with the utmost honor and joy. They again exchange pleasantries, perform three prostrations with touching the ground, and then all together exchange formal greetings.

Passing to the right, go directly to the end of the row. Ascend three by three; the words of salutation are the same as before. Wait until everyone has finished their individual prostrations, then perform a general inquiry (*praṇāma*) and withdraw.
Return to the communal quarters and wait for the return salutation. In every tradition, when thanking someone for granting one’s enrollment (*guādá*), everyone performs the salutation together.
This is intended to simplify matters, yet later students have not heard of this, and the profound principle is gradually fading away—how truly regrettable!

Notice for the New Ordination (For brothers newly returned to the hall: tomorrow, after the morning gruel, proceed to the Abbot’s Quarters to express gratitude for being enrolled in the register. This day of this month; reported by [Name] of the Attendant’s Office).

A Brief Notice on Offering Incense (The Head Seat, upon being granted formal residence, shall contribute one hundred cash each; [the funds] to purchase incense are to be collected by the attendant of the Hall Office, [Name], for reporting). (The paper is five or six inches long.)

Prostrations; returning the courtesy on the day of the formal thanks for being granted monastic status (*guàdā*). The Chief Administrator (*fāngzhàng*), the Guest Master (*kètóu*), and the Hall Steward (*tángsī kùzǐ*) each write a notice for the return of courtesy and post it before the various quarters.

The Chief Administrator’s notice is posted in the upper section, while those of the two classes of officials are posted in the lower section. Once the formal thanks for being granted monastic status have been completed in the dormitory hall, the Head of the Assembly (*cāntóu*)...

The leader leads the assembly to stand in a row at the lower section in front of the communal quarters (*zhòngliáo*). They wait for the Abbot to enter the quarters; upon his arrival, they perform a greeting, saying:

"Having waited for some time, we respectfully wish that the Reverend Abbot’s health remains flourishing and that you enjoy many blessings. It is our duty to offer our thanks; yet, you have condescended to honor us by visiting us. We, your humble servants, are moved beyond words. The assembly escorts the Abbot out and follows him into the quarters. They move to the upper section and stand there.

The Head of the Assembly (*cāntóu*) receives the Attendant (*shìzhě*) as he enters, saying: "We, [Name] and others, have had the fortune to rely upon your presence. Now that you have graced us with your visit, we, your humble servants, are moved beyond words."

[Expressing the utmost gratitude. He replies: "I offer my thanks with all sincerity; my humble feelings are overcome by the utmost gratitude. The head attendant escorts him out and receives the two classes of monks as they enter.

They perform one bow of *chuk-ri* facing each other (this is the single bow performed when returning to the hall). The words are the same as before. As the assembly turns toward the lower section, the assistant head attendant bows once of *chuk-ri* in thanks to the head attendant.

Format for the Abbot’s Proclamation (The Head Monk, after the morning gruel, returns his courtesy to the newly returned Head Seat of the Hall. This day of this month, the attendant *kètóu* [guest-head] *xiǎngzhě* [novice], so-and-so, respectfully transmits).

Notification for the Two-Rank Officials (Head Official and Administrative Officers): After the morning gruel, return greetings. This month’s [day], the newly returned hall head seat, the hall office acolyte [Name], respectfully submits this notice.

When a monk from another monastery requests lodging (*guàtā*), the attendant serving tea shall write a tea invitation form according to the guest’s seniority (*jièlà*). The name must be written in full, including both characters.

On the following day, at the time of washing the face, prepare a table with brush and inkstone and set them out in the Zhàotáng Hall. Invite each person by their respective name, and have them write: "I, [Name], respectfully accept your honorable command. If the request for lodging comes from the West [Hall], proceed as follows.

The Hall Head Seat (Dangshouzuo) shall also be inscribed on the tea invitation list according to the order of seniority in the precepts. Prior to the evening ceremony, the guest master (ketou) shall first take the list to the quarters and command the scribe to sign it.
The incense attendant shall have the guest master arrange the seating; the Head Seat is invited to act as the guest of honor.

If the Head Seat is a person of great virtue or a West Hall (Xitang) official, he takes a seat facing the Abbot. The head of the retreatants (cantou) takes the next seat. In many places, this is considered disrespectful. It is extremely [important].
This becomes excessively noisy and is a complete loss of ritual propriety. The abbot should mention this beforehand at the time of ascending the hall.

This is because the recipient of the honor has already expressed thanks for their formal entry (*guàtā*). It is similar to the tea ceremony. On the day of the event, after the midday meal, the drum is struck to assemble the assembly.

The incense-bearer bows to invite the abbot to enter; the abbot receives him and exchanges greetings. Next, he receives the accompanying guests, who inquire after his well-being. The phrasing of these words is the same as that used during ordinary tea ceremonies.
Each person shall enter their assigned seat according to the seating chart. The seating chart must have been previously submitted to the Abbot for approval.

The Incense-Burning Attendant (xiāngshì zhǐzhě) and the Guest-Receiving Attendant (qǐngkè zhǐzhě) shall together perform the rites. This is the same as the minor seating arrangement for the commencement of the retreat (the ritual for the medicinal soup is identical).

On the following day, the administrative office (kūsī) and the guest-head attendant (kètóu xíngzhě) shall prepare tea invitations according to the monastic precepts and post them before the various quarters. They shall request signatures, with the written invitation stating: "(Name) respectfully complies with your command. The document is presented to the Abbot.

The procedure for the *zhàngtóng* (Director of the Hall) is the same; one simply writes the name of the person below. In the *kūtáng* (Storehouse Hall), seats are arranged, with the *shouzuo* (Head Seat) acting as the host.
After the meal, the board in front of the *kūtáng* is struck. The senior administrative official (*shàngshǒu zhīshì*) and the *weina* (Rector) perform the ritual (as described previously).

On the following day, the attendants of the *tángsī* (Hall Administration Office) prepare a tea invitation form and request signatures, which is the same as before. Following the seating order of the *zhàotáng* (Observation Hall), the senior administrative official acts as the host. The *zhàotáng* board is then struck.
At the board, the first group of head officials performs the rites. Alternatively, four or six people take their positions and perform a mutual inquiry.
If there are five people, the Head Seat of the front hall stands alone while burning incense. The western group performs the rites, concluding with the Guest Prefect (zhīkè) bowing for incense.
They burn the *kōban* incense and take their seats for tea together; this is the ancient custom for a three-day discourse. Nowadays, however, various regions observe it for only one day.
The administrative officers (*chiji*) and head monks (*shusho*) all sign the formal document early in the morning and borrow seats from the Abbot’s quarters (*hōjō*).

The administrative officers and head monks sit below the Abbot by one rank. For the Abbot’s tea, the drum is struck; for the tea of the administrative officers and head monks, the wooden board is struck; they serve as hosts to one another.

When the attendants and the assembly rise to thank the Abbot for tea, the administrative officers and heads of departments also receive tea; however, only the head of the retreat group (zan-tou) leaves his seat to offer thanks.
This is merely a matter of seeking convenience and is not the proper tradition of the monastic community (sōrin).

Format for the Abbot’s Letter (For a newly enrolled monk: *So-and-so*, *So-and-so* Upādhyāya; on this day, after the midday meal, tea will be served in the Sleeping Hall. We specially request your gracious presence).
(On this day of this month, respectfully invited by [Name] of the Attendant Office).

Form for Inviting the Two Classes of Monastics (Newly Ordained): [Name], [Name] Upādhyāya, On this day, following the midday meal, we shall serve one round of tea at [Location]. We specifically request that you deign to attend out of compassion for us.
We humbly beseech the assembly’s grace to descend upon us with honor.
[Date], respectfully invited by the Head Seat Bhikṣu [Name] and the Administrative Bhikṣu [Name].
Supplementary Materials for Zen Forests, Volume Eight;
Supplementary Materials for Zen Forests, Volume Nine:
The Nirvana of the Incumbent Abbot of the Present Age.
Now, regarding the funeral rites for the entry into parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, there are established scriptures that leave no room for error.

At the Twin Trees, the ten great disciples wept with grief and remorse; at Vārāṇasī, the Śakras, Brahmās, devas, and nāgas wailed and leaped in lamentation, their tears flowing like grease from an axle.
When Mahākāśyapa returned from foreign lands, he raised an army to divide the śarīra and erect stūpas—was this not the proper ritual? According to the *Dahui Zhuan’an*...
The *Yiji* (Record of the Assembly) states: From the funeral rites of Baizhang down to Chan Master Zheng, the protocols may be said to have been fully established.

For Grand Master Ying, the *Wutu* (Five Diagrams) eliminates redundancies and serves as a practical manual for the Dharma-gate. Regarding the regulations of Baizhang, whenever a monk passes away, his belongings—

The funeral procession was completed and the funerary implements prepared; a memorial was submitted to the throne, and by imperial decree, the items were enshrined in the treasury as a fixed precedent.
During the time when the World-Honored One dwelt in the world, there was an ancient Buddha named Upānanda who manifested his entry into parinirvāṇa.

The World-Honored One commanded the assembly to gather, and he took his robes and bowl before the multitude to appraise and proclaim them, so that the fourfold assembly might observe and discern this body’s impermanence and realize the second fruit of the path.

They are beyond counting. Generally, one should cultivate one's own practice as an antidote to external conditions. When former masters passed away, they would leave behind a single robe sealed in a paper bag to serve as a request for the next abbot;

this was not a transmission of the Dharma. This was done to emulate the World-Honored One’s entrustment of his robe to await Maitreya’s appearance in the world to preach the Dharma. Those who come later should examine the source of this tradition.

The Venerable Master Xía, having been ill for some time, was expected to pass away soon. He requested the senior members of both monastic assemblies in advance to prepare his belongings and arrange for the ritual bathing and enshrouding.
Regarding his personal clothing and any minor surplus items, he instructed his junior disciples that they were not permitted to wear hempen mourning garments or wail in grief. He further requested—
When the Head Seat (Śrīpāda) presides over the funeral, all Buddhist rites are waived. The Head Seat, together with the assembly, recites the Verse on Impermanence:

"The Venerable Abbot [Name], who has entered perfect stillness (parinirvāṇa), is now about to proceed to the cremation pyre... The assembly recites the Verse on Impermanence three times: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, the extinction of suffering is bliss. Thereupon, the coffin is raised and the cremation is performed. All is clear and manifest.

To verify his life’s conduct: if there is an abundance of robes and alms-bowls, or if members of the royal court or ministers have provided for his funeral, these must be handled with full ritual propriety.

The robes and bowls should be kept solely in the Abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) or the administrative office (kusī), entrusted to a person of public integrity and diligence to guard them. Once they have been appraised and auctioned, that is the end of the matter; take care not to treat what does not exist as if it does, thereby wasting the monastery’s permanent assets.
As for the instructions and letters of legacy left by lay patrons (dānapati) who provide external protection, or by former masters from various mountains: [these should be treated accordingly].
In all cases, once these preliminary matters are completed,
they approach the shrine to recite mantras.
Whether he manifests illness, writes a verse, or enters into extinction, regardless of the time— morning or evening— the attendant immediately orders the guest-master acolyte to...

The Sangha Hall attendant informs the assembly. Striking the mallet once, he says: "The Abbot of this hall transmits these words to the great assembly: 'Wind and fire press upon us; we cannot meet you face-to-face. He strikes the mallet once more. Next, the various quarters are notified.

The hall office acolyte strikes the bell in front of the Sangha Hall to assemble the community, who then proceed to the Abbot’s quarters for condolences (though one must not yet raise the cry of mourning).
The Head Seat, together with the two classes of officials and the elders, consults on how to dispatch letters to invite someone to preside over the funeral rites. This must be done.

Select a senior elder from a neighboring monastery, or a venerable member of the Dharma family, or simply invite the head seat (shouzuo). If there is a final testament, it must be carried out accordingly.
The filial son, the attendants, and the close followers shall arrange for the ritual bathing, dressing in robes, shaving the hair, and placing the body into the coffin.

The final verse is affixed to the left of the shrine. The *vinaya-dhara* (Venerable) and the filial sons proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to light incense and request the Head Seat to perform the ritual for entering the shrine.

The dormitory hall is prepared, and the shrine, incense burner, candles, and offerings are arranged upon the altar. When the time arrives, the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community.

Once the ritual for entering the shrine has been performed, the *vinaya-dhara* recites: "Alas! The sublime authority is universally revealed; the traces of transformational teaching extend through the realms of humans and devas."

The wondrous body alone remains, giving rise to profound mechanisms from among the Buddhas and Patriarchs. We reverently contemplate the Abbot, whose solitary and perfect moon of wisdom suddenly gathers the waves of the ten thousand waters, and whose vast and great heart of compassion responds to the calls of the ten directions.

Having no place to behold his countenance, we open our hearts to find refuge in him. This assembly of true disciples chants the holy names and, for the aforementioned causes and conditions, recites the name of the Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Buddha. (Recite the Ten Holy Names. Then, chant the Great Compassion Mantra. The dedication says:

"The merit of the above chanting and recitation of scriptures is offered for the Abbot’s ground of non-arising retribution, which is wondrously and supremely adorned. To all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time... (Recite the *Lengyan Sūtra* again.)

Recite the *Yan-zhou* (Auspicious Mantra). For the dedication, recite: "The merit of chanting this scripture is respectfully offered for the sake of the Abbot, that his rank and station may increase and flourish.

That night, assemble the assembly for recitation and say: "Inform the assembly: The Abbot has already returned to true stillness; the community has lost its reliance. I. The Master of the Funeral.
As for the person presiding over the funeral, unless they are a mature and long-established master of virtue, how could they be fit for such an invitation?

For instance, when Master Yuanwu and Master Ning of Kaifufeng received Master Guo of Yuean to take charge of the final affairs, it was truly a model of dignified character. When the person presiding over the funeral arrives, the bell is struck.
The great bell is struck, and the assembly welcomes [the guest] at the gate. Upon reaching the front of the shrine, incense is lit, and the two classes of the assembly perform their formal greetings.

When the assembly disperses, the two classes of elders escort the guests to their seats. The two classes then offer incense and perform their greetings; at this point, they should offer a formal apology for their departure. The presiding mourner then takes his place at the head seat.

The Head Seat departs. The Head Seat rises to burn one stick of incense, returns to his position to offer tea, and the filial son immediately steps forward to inquire after his well-being, inserts incense, and performs three prostrations with fully spread sitting cloths (*dazhan sanbai*). The presiding mourner returns the bows. Next, the attendants of the Abbot perform their prostrations.

Next, the head of the assembly leads the group in offering incense and performing three prostrations. Following this, the Abbot (fangzhang) joins in the prostrations. Tea is served, and the two ranks of officials are escorted out.

The Director of Rituals, having completed the inspection of the quarters for the funeral rites, shall escort the two classes of senior monks and the filial sons to the guest quarters. First, discuss the mourning garments. There shall be no distribution of cloth by measured portions. If the presiding mourner is far away and has not arrived within three days, request that the next head official perform the ritual for moving the shrine (the *kankan* ceremony).
When the presiding mourner arrives, he must privately calculate with the Chief Seat (*shuso*) the quantity of robes and bowls [to be provided].

Divide [the funds] into three portions. From one portion, distribute money for the scriptures and money for the vegetarian feast (*zhāi*) among the assembly; this shall be used to express gratitude to the funeral officials (*sāng-sī*) and their staff.

One portion is for the Buddhist services and the mourning attire; the funeral officials shall manage its daily expenditures. One portion is for performing the feast, the procession, and the chanting of scriptures;

the funeral rites are as previously described. Only the *xueliu* (snow willow) is divided and enshrined. The format for the recitation is found below. The format for the consecration of the stupa, the chanting of sutras, and the dedication of merit is detailed further on.

"The True Dharma Eye of the Tathāgata, the golden-brocade *saṃghāṭī* robe—when unfolded, it pervades and transforms the great trichiliocosm; when gathered, there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation. It covers the thousand-fathom body without being long; it envelops the sixteen-foot body without being short.

Although it was transmitted from Mount Yuling, alas, it remains with us today. Master [Name], having completed his work of transforming conditions, has cast off his hands and departed. Picking it up at random as it comes to hand—"
