*Piao*. Once the distribution of robes (*cai*) has concluded, the tally of the cash is finalized. The presiding mourner (*zhumaang*) signs the list; the cash is handed over and the robes taken. One must not arbitrarily reduce the amount out of personal preference.

the protocol for their reception is the same. For the meal: The mourning attendants and junior disciples wear *mabu* (hemp) robes. The two classes of head officials wear *jebu* (ramie) robes. The presiding mourner wears a robe of raw silk. The Dharma... [text ends]

How distant are the instructions received within the courtyard; how much more remote is the solemnity of the grave-mound where the tree shall grow. Looking up toward the Garden of Enlightenment, I am overcome with grief beyond measure.
I humbly pray that you may ascend to the Great Earth of Dhyāna, flow with the waters of wisdom to moisten the withered grove, and open the Way so that hearts may turn back to the truth.
Sealing the moonlight, the light intensifies my deep remorse. Once again, I beseech the great assembly to recite: "The ten directions and the three periods of time... (and so forth).

its great achievements shall endure even as kalpa-stones crumble away. Its majestic power increases and resounds, while auspicious radiance shines everywhere, suddenly illuminating all hidden darkness and causing all that was submerged to emerge.

Form for a Death Announcement The monk [Name], Director of Funerals at [Name] Temple. To the right:
This [Name] reports with deep sorrow that the Abbot of our mountain gate has suddenly returned to the truth on the [number] day of this month. We respectfully prepare this announcement to inform you.
Respectfully submitted on the [day] of the [month] year. This memorial is signed by the monk [Name], Director of Funerals.
Envelope: Funeral Announcement. To the Abbot Dharma Master [Name] of [Place]. Respectfully sealed by the monk [Name], Director of Funerals at [Monastery Name].
And: Posthumous Letter.

When the funeral rites are completed, the presiding mourner requests the attendants and administrative staff to serve as special envoys (*zhuan-shi*) to travel by various routes and deliver the funeral notices to the monasteries, fellow practitioners, patrons, and officials.

Regarding the delivery of letters from deceased elders (*zun-su*), one must select capable individuals to serve as special envoys; these envoys must engage in face-to-face dialogue and exchange words with their recipients.

In this way, even when the great masters like Dahui visited Wujin, the monastic communities did not fall into desolation, and the practice of special envoys was maintained throughout the various regions.

First, go to the Guest Office (Kek-si) for introductions. The Guest Master (Chik-kak) will lead you up to the Attendants' Office (Si-si) for introductions. Prepare a tray and cloth to hold the letter and other items.
An attendant shall go to the Abbot’s quarters (Bung-wang) to inform the Abbot (Juji), who will immediately receive you. He shall then order the two classes of officials to be invited.

The special envoy steps forward, bows in greeting, and says: "Please, Venerable Abbot, sit cross-legged. If the Abbot utters a phrase of inquiry, the envoy must offer a response. Then, having inserted incense, he shall proceed with his formal communication.

Guest Protocol: The formal presentation of ritual implements is waived by the Abbot. For the personal greeting (*renshi*), one takes a seat and drinks tea. Upon rising before the incense burner and finishing the thanksgiving for the tea, one inserts a large piece of incense.

The first presentation of the implements says: "At this moment, I have had the honor of beholding your venerable countenance; my humble feelings are filled with the utmost joy and privilege. A second presentation follows, accompanied by inquiries regarding health and well-being.

Perform three prostrations with full prostration (*prahāṇa*). Rising, report: "The Venerable Master of [Place] passed away on the [day] of the [month]. His final letter and personal effects have been entrusted to me to deliver. Immediately present the letter and the items.
The Abbot says: "The Dharma-gate has declined; I cannot bear this profound grief. The attendant of the Venerable’s quarters receives [the letter].

The two classes of officials assemble and perform a greeting. The Head Seat takes his seat separately. The special envoy sits opposite the Abbot, one position back. They drink tea. Rising, the Abbot says:

"It is an unfortunate event for the Dharma-gate that the Monk of such-and-such place has passed away; I cannot bear this profound grief. The attendant prepares the brush and paper, and presents the writing materials to the Abbot.
The Abbot receives the letter. The attendant takes the letter; the Abbot accepts it, warms it over the incense burner, and hands it to the attendant to deliver to the Rector (Karmadāna).
The attendant opens the seal and reads the contents aloud. Once the reading is finished, the attendant bows to the special messenger and escorts him to a seat facing the Abbot.

Soup is served according to the usual protocol, and the special messenger is sent back to his lodgings. First, the Abbot’s personal greetings are performed; next, the attendants and the two classes of officials [pay their respects].

The affairs being concluded, the Guest Prefect leads the inspection of the quarters. First, they proceed to the Treasury Office; next, to the quarters of the Head Monks, the Single Quarters, the Monastic Hall, and the Four Quarters.
This is because offerings are made to each. That evening, the Attendant requests a special serving of hot tonic. Once the tonic is finished, the medicinal meal follows.

Upon arriving for the evening soup and fruit offering, a letter arrives from the Abbot (Dafang). The two *ban* (monks of rank) serve as attendants; next, the head of the *ban* and the *vinaya-master* (*weina*) serve as attendants.

The attendant requests the secretary to consult in person regarding the circumstances [of the deceased] and to compose the memorial text. Regarding the Abbot’s memorial text, it is mostly composed by the incumbent himself.

Those who have been dharma-relatives in the monastic circles (*jianghu*) and those who have handled affairs [for the deceased] should all prepare the memorial offerings and incense. The attendant shall oversee each of these matters one by one.

At the appointed time, the following morning, the Abbot invites [the assembly] for soup. After the gruel is consumed, he invites them for tea. In the lower section of the Dharma Hall, the ritual implements are hung and arranged for the memorial service.
The Attendant announces the ascent to the hall; the Ritual Assistant reports to the quarters. The "Ascent to the Hall" plaque is hung.

A table and cloth are prepared beneath the seat to hold the written materials. To the left of the seat, the position of the Abbot is set out. The Ritual Assistant notifies the Abbot’s quarters, the drum is struck, and the assembly gathers. The Abbot emerges.

Standing before the lower position at the foot of the Dharma seat, the drumming ceases. The incense table is advanced. The Guest Master leads the special envoy, and the Abbot steps forward to perform a prostration.

Incense is inserted. For the first unfolding of the mat, he says: "I, [Name], venture to hold these bequeathed writings; the intention behind this wooden memorial is exceedingly earnest, and my humble heart cannot help but feel the utmost gratitude. For the second unfolding, the formal greetings are exchanged.

He prostrates three times in greeting and presents the letter of remembrance. The abbot receives the letter, incenses it over the burner, and hands it to an attendant to deliver to the rector (karmadāna).
Once the reading is finished, the special envoy pays his respects to the abbot and stands behind the guest-master’s (karmadāna) row.

When the abbot has ascended and descended from the seat, he proceeds to the altar for the memorial service, where he lights incense, offers hot water, presents the offerings, and serves tea, performing prostrations. The special envoy then returns to pay his respects at the right side of the seat.

The *vinaya* master steps forward from the ranks and bows to the abbot. The incense-bearer attendant presents the incense box, and both classes of attendants offer incense. There is a formal inquiry regarding the borrowed incense.

Once the procession has concluded, the abbot and the two classes of attendants perform prostrations with open hands. The *vinaya* master recites the memorial text, and the abbot again performs prostrations with open hands.
The special envoy returns the bow. The *Śūraṅgama Mantra* is recited; the dedication of merit is the same as for the anniversaries of the various patriarchs. Both classes [of attendants]—four.

After the officials of the various quarters, those from the rivers and lakes, the administrative staff, and the local residents have all completed their offerings, they chant the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and perform the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*).

The dharma-relatives and junior disciples, as well as the administrative staff who have finished their duties, do not return the bows to the special envoy. The special envoy steps out before the altar, performs two prostrations with the palms opened and three full prostrations to thank the abbot;

if the abbot declines the formal bows, the envoy performs a touching-bow (*chuli*). Next, the envoy visits the various quarters to express thanks. The monastery gate then provides hospitality for the special envoy and the two classes of officers.

The attendants of the Radiance, the monastic community of the mountain gate, both great and small, and all members of the Dharma family, high and low, must observe the proper ritual etiquette. Following this, there shall be no memorial rites for the various mountains, the four quarters, or the rivers and lakes.
The posthumous letter from Master Wansu has arrived.

The Abbot opens the letter. The two classes of officials first offer condolences to the incumbent. An altar is set up in the center of the Dharma Hall. Before the offering, there is a formal address while incense is offered.
Three wails of mourning are sounded. The sutra is chanted. The Head Seat leads the assembly in circumambulation. Once the dedication of merit is complete, the offerings are presented.

Three prostrations. Three prostrations for the serving of hot water. When the food has been served, the drum is struck; for the special tea service, there are three prostrations. The sitting cloths are withdrawn.

For those who perform three prostrations for the prepared dishes—whether they be members of the two ranks of officials, those from the four monastic quarters, fellow practitioners from various regions, or dharma relatives and junior disciples—all must complete the offerings.
Then the Head Seat leads the assembly to offer condolences before the Abbot; the ritual protocol is identical to that described previously.

In the style of a farewell letter. (Chijue) Having resided in mountain retreats for some time, I have failed to benefit the teachings and the monastic community. Now that this slight illness has not improved, I feel I have let down the monasteries. As wind and fire now burn me from within, my longing for the clouds and mountains grows ever deeper. Since I cannot meet you face-to-face, I pray only that you hold yourself in high esteem. (Chijue) *Ji chu zhushan, wu bu jiaotong. Wei ji bu qi, you fu conglin. Ou feng huo yi jiao jian, wang yun shan er zeng lian.

Mian wei bu ji, zhen zhong shi qi.* (Chijue) Residing in mountain retreats for some time, I have failed to benefit the teachings and the monastic community. Now that this slight illness has not improved, I feel I have let down the monasteries. As wind and fire now burn me from within, my longing for the clouds and mountains grows ever deeper. Since I cannot meet you face-to-face, I pray only that you hold yourself in high esteem.

(Dharma-kinsman), having been unworthily appointed to reside on this mountain, I feel ashamed before my fellow disciples. As I have long been subject to old age and illness, I shall likely remain here for the rest of my life. I respectfully offer this letter by hand to briefly express my parting in person.

I hope that you, the direct successor who has heard the teachings from me in person, will strive to uphold the legacy of our former teacher. I am departing in haste; I pray you take care of yourself. (Note: "法眷" translates to *dharmabāndhava*, meaning "Dharma-kinsman. "同門之友" refers to fellow disciples or dharma-brothers. "因循老病" means "having been subject to old age and illness. "畢世" means "for the remainder of one's life. "手書" refers to a handwritten letter. "面別" means "parting in person. "嫡嗣" refers to a direct successor or heir. "力荷" means "to diligently bear or uphold. "匇匇" indicates a hurried or urgent departure. "伏惟珍重" is a formal expression of respectful farewell, meaning "I humbly pray that you take care of yourself.")

Though I dwell among the mountains as a neighbor, it is of no avail; I rely merely on the light from your neighboring wall. My dream-like state is fundamentally empty, and fortunately my worldly ties have already been severed.

I shall not be able to bid you farewell in person, yet my heart yearns for you with utmost intensity. I pray that your Buddha-nature may ever increase in brilliance and that the spirit of our school may flourish even further. In haste, I offer these unpolished words. I humbly beseech you to take care of yourself. *Note:
"鄰封" (línfēng) refers to a neighboring territory or residence; "宗風" (zōngfēng) refers to the tradition or spirit of a Buddhist school.*
(Venerable Elder), I have long been honored by your guidance. Yet, as destiny dictates our parting, I was subsequently summoned and compelled to accept this humble post.

Now, like dew upon a leaf or a flash of lightning, it has vanished in an instant; the clouds and mountains grow ever more distant. I venture to pray for your protection so that these teachings may endure. My prostrations and prayers are incomplete.
Envelope. (Seal of the letter;
respectful salutation; addressed to the Great Abbot of [Name] Temple; from the Bhikṣu Abbot of [Name] Temple; [Name]). Respectfully sealed.
Regarding the succession of the abbot’s affairs after his passing:

the two classes of officials shall convene the assembly for a formal discussion. They must select one whose insight into the essence of the school is clear, whose virtue is eminent and years advanced, whose conduct is pure and stainless, and who is worthy of the assembly’s trust.
This person shall be recommended by a formal petition from the assembly, ensuring that the selection accords with the consensus of all monastic communities throughout the land.
The public selection of officials is currently the standard for public opinion; let the affairs be known to the elders and seniors, and do not allow private interests to prevail.

When the monastic community gains capable individuals, the Dharma will endure for a long time. If one relies on wealth and power to cultivate favors or advances through fraudulent means, this Way will perish.
How can such a name and position be entrusted lightly?

Thus, as the sick monk’s illness grew grave and he was nearing his passing, the direct caregiver led the elders of the local community to stand before the patient; they arranged incense and candles in their presence.

Buddha-image recitation (the ritual form is shown below). If the illness becomes critical, one shall immediately inform the Hall Master of Longevity (*yanshou tangzhu*) and jointly report to the Rector (*weina*).

Request that the traveler’s belongings be sealed. The Hall Administrator (*tangsi*), the Treasury Attendant (*kuzi*), the Head Seat (*shouzuo*), the Administrative Officers (*zhishi*), and the Attendants (*shizhe*) shall together go before the patient.
They will transcribe the oral instructions. The patient’s attendant and public officials shall then collect the sutra chests, document chests, and clothing from their locations.

Seal and lock [the room]. Leave behind the deceased’s clothing and belongings; if there is not enough time to do so, the *vina* (chant leader) and the *shouzuo* (head seat) must also take charge of the proceedings.

The outer robe, prayer beads, incense box, foot-thong, sitting mat, shoes and socks, hair-cleansing towel, bone-receiving cloth, cotton wadding, and all other necessary items shall be gathered together into one bundle.
The hall master (*tangzhu*) and the attendant for the dying shall take custody of them. This applies even to those who have no personal luggage.

The entire monastic community must perform the formal rites of seeing off [the departing abbot]. This is presided over by the Abbot and the Head Seat (Shouzuo). Once the luggage has been packed, the keys are sealed and signed, then deposited with the Head Seat.
The robes and alms bowl are carried back to the Hall Office by the laborers from the four quarters; if he resided in a private cell, they are handled accordingly.

Only the deceased monk’s own quarters shall be left behind; one must appoint someone to guard them. If a deceased monk has no written instructions from relatives, his belongings must not be disposed of or bequeathed at will.

When Master Dàchuān resided at Jìngcí Monastery, the Head Seat and the Rector (Vina) personally drafted a bequest for a deceased monk’s belongings and were consequently dismissed from their positions and expelled from the monastery.
This serves as a stern warning for future generations to take as a lesson.

When a deceased monk who was ill passes away, the Hall Master (Tangzhu) informs the Rector (Weina). The Hall Office acolyte (Xingzhe) is then ordered to announce that the hot water for the bath has been prepared.

This is further notified to the Head Seat (Shouzuo), the Guest Prefect (Zhike), and the Attendant (Shizhe). The administrative office (Kusi) dispatches personnel to carry the bier and the bathing boat, arranging for the ritual bath of the deceased. The Rector then tests the temperature of the water.
Regarding the cold and heat [of the bath]: after the bathing is finished, wipe the deceased with a bathing robe and drape it over them. Hand over the clean hair-towel to the attendant (dai-chō).

The *Venerable Leader* (*vinaya-dhara*) supervises the dressing of the deceased and their placement in the coffin. Place the coffin within the *Enju-dō* (Hall of Longevity), arrange chairs, tables, and the memorial tablet, and provide offerings of incense and lamps.
The current assembly of monks shall chant sutras and perform the dedication of merit. At night, a perpetual lamp (*chōmyō-tō*) is lit; this is prepared by the hall attendants (*dōshi-gyōja*).
Snow Willow: Memorial Tablet (for the newly deceased, Venerable Upādhyāya [Name], Awakening Spirit).
Or, for a West Hall Abbot, it says: (Former Abbot of [Temple Name], Great Monk [Name] of the West Hall). The administrator.
Titles are assigned according to one's office.
The *shen* (Body) recites the sutras daily;

the *zhili* (Direct Ritual Practitioner) serves rice gruel; the *xingzhe* (Ritual Attendant) serves tea and soup during the three periods of the day and performs the incense offering. [The schedule begins with] morning gruel.

When the chanting of scriptures in the Great Hall concludes, the hall-attendant (tángsī xíngzhě) strikes the leading chime (yǐnqìng). Led by the Head Seat (shǒuzuò), the assembly proceeds to the front of the shrine (kàn).

The Administrative Officer (zhīshì) first offers tea and presents incense; the Abbot (zhùchí) then presents incense. The Rector (wéiná) recites the Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī and performs the dedication of merit (huíxiàng).

Next, the local laypeople recite the dhāraṇī. The village headman (xiāngzhǎng) steps forward and burns one stick of incense. This is performed identically at each of the three daily periods. Three days after the funeral procession has departed, [the rites are concluded].
[Recite the sutra] and then conclude. For the dedication, say:

"By the merit of the above recitation of the sutra, I dedicate it for the newly deceased Elder [Name], to adorn his place of retribution. [Recite] "The ten directions and three periods of time... and so forth. (In the case of public figures, do not use their full names; refer to them by a single character.)

The hair is divided into sections and placed in the shrine. The *vinaya-dhara*, the guest master (*kaji*), and the attendant (*shisho*), together with the hall administrators and attendants, proceed to the Head Seat’s quarters (*shuso ryo*) to produce the seal for the sections and affix it to the numbered envelopes.
These are kept at the Head Seat’s location. Either in the morning or at noon, the guest master and attendant go to their respective bowl-positions (*hatsu-i*).

The distribution of the items was conducted in the same manner as the previous distribution. When the monastic community arrived for a short time, there were [a certain number] of people; the *karmadāna* and the *śayanāsana* (head seat) verified the count.
The remaining items were distributed. The robes and bowls were abundant. During the distribution of the items, the chanting of the sutras was suspended.
IV. Requesting for Buddhist Rituals (Foshi):
The Hall Superintendent (Tangsi) shall check the previous list and request the rituals in their proper sequence. Prepare a tray, a cloth cover, an incense burner, candles, and an incense box.

The Rector (Weina), accompanied by an attendant, shall go to the Abbot’s quarters (Fangzhang) to request the Master to hold the torch. He shall insert incense and announce: “The Venerable Elder [Name] has passed away; it is [number] days since the tea memorial service. We respectfully request the Master to preside.”

The procedure for holding the torch is the same as that for the various quarters’ invitations. The two classes of officials are notified to prepare a list at the Hall Office (*dangsi*). For a senior deceased monk, one must invite the elders.

Once the assembly has gathered, the sealed casket containing the deceased’s belongings is presented; these items are laid out upon mats, and the attendants of the Hall Office present each article one by one.

The public treasury shall collectively appraise the value of all items. The guest prefect shall assign single beds and arrange the character-numbered labels for "Heaven," "Earth," "Mystery," and "Yellow.

The attendant shall affix these numbers to the robes; those that are half-new are designated as "old," and those that are half-old are designated as "tattered. The appraisal of their value must be conducted in secret so as not to be heard by the multitude.
As for books, Buddha images, sutra scrolls, and playthings, they shall be distributed by drawing lots for the sake of forming karmic connections. All movable utensils belong to the public treasury.
If there is a deficiency in the supplies for the quarters, they shall be struck from the accounts and handed over.
The attendant of the patient, or his junior disciples, or those with physical strength and capability, should labor on this; there shall be a distribution of snacks.
The Great Locking-in of the Shrine:

After the recitation and offerings are completed, the funeral procession shall depart early tomorrow morning. This evening, the attendant of the Hall Office shall report to the Abbot, and the Head Seat shall post the notice board to inform all the quarters.

The preparatory office prepares the sacrificial offerings. The storehouse assigns personnel to set up and hang the sacrificial mats. Local residents and Dharma relatives arrive at the preparatory office to pay their tribute and receive the offerings in return.

A sacrificial text is composed, and two small pieces of incense are prepared. If the offering is for the West Hall, the Great Senior Monks, or the two classes of officials of the Abbot’s quarters, the *Venerable Karmadāna* shall proclaim the sacrificial text.
Once the evening meditation session has concluded, the signal bell is struck in front of the Sangha Hall.
The bell is struck to assemble the community. Before the shrine, the recitation is performed. The ritual master (zhishi) first serves food and tea.

Once the abbot has finished burning incense, the rector (weina) steps forward from the ranks to burn one stick of incense. Having completed this, he requests the person appointed to perform the Buddhist service. [The rector] returns to his position.

The person who accepted the request steps forward from the ranks to burn one stick of incense, bows with hands at the side to the right, and proceeds to bow before the abbot. Next, [he bows] before the ritual master.
Inquire after their well-being. Proceeding to the end of the row, do the same for the western section; then, together with the assembly, perform a general inquiry after their well-being.

From the end of the western section’s row, enter and stand to the right of the shrine. Once the Hall Attendant and the Treasury Assistant have finished the ritual service by placing the tray and taking the lock, the practitioner locks the shrine and immediately returns to his original position.
If one sees an officer, he enters from his own rank and performs the ritual service. The Rector then bows.

The assembly rises from their seats to offer incense. The Abbot steps forward from the ranks to present incense; the attendant holds the censer. Both classes of officers perform the ritual of "borrowing incense" (asking for permission to offer incense) by bowing.

Once the rising from the seats is complete, the Rector faces the shrine and leads the recitation, chanting the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* and performing the dedication of merit. The Guest Master chants the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* in a steady, even tone.

After the dedication of merit, the Abbot stands with the head administrative officer and the person offering the sacrifice, who exits to the right to offer a pinch of incense and inquire after the well-being [of the deceased].

Inquire. Enter from the west side of the hall. Offer hot water and tea at the upper right of the shrine; the attendants descend. Exit to the front of the incense burner, insert incense, withdraw, inquire with a bow, and perform prostrations.
At the upper right of the shrine, the memorial text is recited. Upon completion, chant the *Mahākaruṇā-dhāraṇī* for the dedication of merit.
Next, the head of the assembly leads the group in chanting the sutras: the monks of the quarters chant the sutras, and the lay associates accompanying the spirit chant the sutras.

5. Prior to the funeral procession, the supervisor is instructed to prepare firewood for cremation and the ritual branches for the funeral. Personnel are assigned to carry the coffin and to hold banners, canopies, incense tables, drums, and musical instruments;
thus, all funeral rites are fully prepared. During the preceding night, the abbot’s quarters are covered, and the two classes of officials post notices to inform the community.

The Dormitory. Sending Off the Deceased. After the early congee has been served and the mallet has struck for the meal, strike the mallet once more and say: (After the congee is finished, upon hearing the bell, all shall assemble to send off the deceased.

With the exception of those on duty in the hall or guarding the dormitory, everyone must attend together. This is respectfully announced. On the occasion of a National Festival, there is no circuit of the hall. Strike the mallet once more;
then, bow before the Senior Monk, turn back to bow before the Abbot, and perform one circuit of the hall. In the outer hall, proceed from the lower end of the hall to—
Ascending the hall, he enters the hall to inquire after the assembly and then withdraws. After the morning gruel is finished, the funeral rites are prepared in their proper sequence.

The Hall Attendant and the Treasury Officer inform the Abbot and the two classes of attendants; the bell before the Sangha Hall is struck to assemble the community. Upon arriving before the coffin, the Rector recites the liturgy (the form of which is shown below).
Once the ritual for requesting the raising of the coffin is completed, the gong is struck and the coffin is carried out to the head of the mountain gate. (If offerings are to be made...)

[The ritual for] turning the shrine for tea and incense: [The coffin] rests with its face toward the interior. The head seat (*śrāmaṇera*) leads the assembly, standing in two rows facing inward. The *karmadāna* stands beneath the canopy facing inward.
With palms joined, he recites the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-mantra* or the four sacred names of the Western Paradise. The head seat leads the assembly in chanting the mantra as they follow the shrine.
The attendants stand in formation with palms joined and heads bowed, waiting until the monastic assembly has passed; they then escort the deceased behind them. All.
The temple attendant leads the funeral procession; the *vinaya-dhara* follows the coffin.

When the body reaches the *nirvāṇa-maṇḍala* for cremation, the abbot offers incense, the administrative officers (*karmadāna*) offer hot water and tea, and the *vinaya-dhara* offers incense and requests the abbot to preside over the rite.

The Ritual Master holds the ritual implement; the Abbot stands to offer incense and bows to the assembly. He steps forward and stands. An attendant holds an umbrella. The Prior bows in greeting and passes the torch.
Once the torch has been lit, the Rector performs the "Mountain Peak" service. The Head Administrative Officer offers tea and incense.
The Guest Prefect recites the *Śūraṅgama Mantra* with even intonation and performs the dedication of merit. Laypeople recite the sutra (the so-called "River and Lake Sutra"). The Master speaks.
When a fellow native dies while on pilgrimage, the *vīnā* (chant leader) goes back and forth to oversee the matter.
The attendants of the Hall Office provide a meal for the deceased, collect the remains, and escort them back to the *Yanshou Hall* for veneration. There, they recite sutras for three days.

The ancient method of the forest monasteries for chanting the distribution of robes (*cai yi*) is to return the bones to the temple first, and only chant the robes on the following day. Lately, people chant the robes on the very same day they collect the ashes and gather the bones;

who is there to witness this? You should examine this carefully. If the chanting of the robes occurs after the midday meal, the attendant of the Hall Office (*tangsi xingzhe*) shall do so after the morning gruel has been finished.
The abbot’s quarters are covered. The two classes of attendants hang up the robe-signboard and notify all the monastic halls. They arrange tables, stools, and rope-cots in front of the Sangha Hall.

The Abbot and the Head Seat take their respective positions; the two classes of attendants sit in a vertical row. Inside the gate, a long mat is laid crosswise, with brushes, inkstones, and counting sticks set out, and a net is hung.
Mats are spread upon the floor, and four attendants from the various quarters are assigned to carry the robe-caskets and arrange the mats.

[The attendant] ascends [to the hall]. The Hall Attendant (Tangsi) and the Practice Assistant (Xingzhe) report to the Abbot and the two sets of officials—the *vinaya-dhara* (Weina) and the *śaikṣa* (Shizhe).

They strike the bell in front of the Sangha Hall to assemble the community. The *vinaya-dhara*, the Guest Master (Zhike), and the *śaikṣa* enter the hall together with the assembly to perform a formal greeting (*wensun*).

They take their seats in their respective positions. The practice assistant lines up in a single file to perform a greeting. Carrying the food baskets (*long*) before the two sets of officials, he circulates to present them for inspection while they remain sealed. He then passes out the keys, opens the baskets, and enters the hall.

The attendant takes the robes and belongings out and arranges them on the mats according to their labels. The empty baskets are opened and placed on the ground. The *vinaya-dhara* strikes the *qing* and recites (the ritual form is shown below).

When finished, he makes this formal announcement: "The method for distributing robes is based upon established regulations. Whether new or old, long or short, you should take care of your own portion; there is no need to demand full value, nor may you combine it with other new gifts.

Once the sound of the *qing* has ceased, no regrets or reversals are permitted. This is respectfully announced. He withdraws the *kāṣāya*, places it within the *qing*, puts on the shoulder-cord (*luo*), and holds up the ordination certificate (*duodie*), saying:

(One ordination certificate for a deceased monk. To be torn in the presence of the assembly and submitted to the authorities. At the place where the name is written, make three horizontal cuts and pass one's finger through the perforations.
Present it to the assembly once. Ring the chime once and say: (Having finished cutting it. Then, present the robes according to their numbers in order and chant the distribution of the robes.
The *weina* lifts up the robe and says: (Item No. 1, "Heaven" character; one set of alms bowl; first bid, five hundred coins. The attendant of the Hall Office receives it as he chants.

From five hundred [units] down to one *bai*, and from one *guan* down to ten *guan*, these serve as the standard increments for calling out prices. The chanting proceeds in this sequence until the *qing* gong is struck.
At that point, the practitioner calls out the fixed name of the deceased, and the *zhike* (Guest Reception Officer) reports it to the *shangdan* (Bedding Officer).

The *shizhe* (Attendant) then issues the clothing and belongings according to the list, records the number of cash notes, and affixes the seal of the Hall Treasury Officer. He delivers the items to the person chanting for the distribution; once the clothing has been placed in the basket, the cash is handed over in exchange for the garments.

No reduction or withdrawal is permitted. Upon concluding the chant, the merit is dedicated and the assembly disperses. The robe inventory is then finalized and chanted; the head seat (shouzuo) signs off (the *weina* collects the draft), and the robes are distributed.
The attendant of the Sacred Monk (Shengseng) collects the robes, with a strict three-day limit for their collection. Those who do not arrive are reported and urged until the full amount is secured.
An inventory is prepared, and funds for the distribution of sutras are allocated according to the fixed format of the three-tiered board-inventory (*banzhang*) as follows. If there are elders...

All fields, lands, gold, and grain shall be returned to the permanent endowment (*sangha*). Outstanding debts from many years ago shall be cleared according to the circumstances; for new debts, only the principal shall be collected, with the permanent endowment taking a commission:

ten *kuan* for every hundred *kuan*, but none shall be taken if the amount is less than one hundred *kuan*. The two classes of officials and all the monastic quarters shall prepare a list and distribute the funds for sutra-copying;
those who have arrived temporarily shall receive half a share. Those who do not send [funds] for the deceased shall not be included. A formal ledger shall be prepared for the assembly.
The cost for the sutra is two hundred cash; the cost for the Buddhist ritual (buddha-shi) is one *guan*. The abbot’s office shall provide an equal amount for its own ritual expenses.
The distribution of funds for the hall administrators and attendants shall be based on a three-part division of the total number of *guan* from the monastic community’s sutra fund.

It is forbidden to arbitrarily establish categories such as "construction" or similar items, which would lead to the minting of coins and provoke disputes. The Head Seat and the Abbot shall take personal responsibility for ensuring these matters are carried out.

Once the entry into the stupa and the construction of the wooden screens are completed, the attendant of the Hall Office (Tangsi Xingzhe) presents the document to the Abbot and the two classes of officers for their signatures. Then, either after the morning gruel or the midday meal,
he spreads out the mats and screens before the Sangha Hall, prepares brushes, inkstones, and counting-slips, and orders the assembly to review them, correcting any errors.
Single determination. The Hall Attendant and the Ritual Assistant inform the two classes of officials at the Abbot’s quarters. A notice board is posted to notify the assembly. Ashes are escorted out;

incense and lamps are prepared according to the ritual protocol. The bell before the Sangha Hall is struck, and the assembly gathers. The administrative official of the Yanshou Hall burns incense, followed by the Abbot lighting incense.

The Rector performs the ritual for "Raising the Bones" (qigu), which is identical to the funeral procession. Prior notice is given to prepare the three stupas with incense and to sweep and sprinkle them.

The bones are brought to the stupa. The administrative official (zhishi) offers incense and tea; the abbot (zhuchi) burns incense; the rector (weina) requests the ritual for entering the stupa; the Great Compassion Mantra is recited;
the guest prefect (zhike) recites the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in a standard manner; and the local laypeople recite a scripture for the dedication of merit.

On Managing the Affairs of a Deceased Monk: Now, within the two realms of existence, who is free from birth and death? Regarding the abundance or scarcity of robes and alms bowls, the funeral rites must accord with established regulations; all Buddhist services should be performed accordingly.

In cases of scarcity, it is a source of merit to establish connections through these rites. The three grades of memorial tablets and accounts shall serve as a permanent standard for all deceased monks. Regarding all deceased monks...

The oral instructions: The robes and bedding shall be handed over to the Hall Office. At the conclusion of the seventh day, or the fifth seventh-day period, the *jingdan* (bedding list) for all quarters is prepared and a ritual text (*shu*) is composed.

Either a seat is established or the confession is proclaimed at the head of the wooden mallet to solemnize the deceased; through this, the karmic retribution of the departed may be moved and verified.

It is not a matter of being slighted. The public realm does not tolerate such humiliation and fragmentation. When Master Zang-sou was residing at Jingshan, the rector informed him that there were no deceased monks for whom the quarters could be dismantled;
he immediately resigned from his post and left the monastery. This was known to all within the monastic community.

Baizhang established the monastic groves (conglin) for the sake of those who were aged or infirm and had nowhere else to turn. Now, however, it is otherwise; they violate the original intent and focus solely on material abundance.
With robes and alms bowls, one should look upon the poor and the sick with compassion; how else could one do so? The Ritual for Recitation (for Protecting the Sick):

There is a certain sick bhikṣu (so-and-so) who, on behalf of the karmic enemies accumulated over many lifetimes, seeks to repent for the transgressions committed throughout kalpas.
With special devotion, he respectfully assembles this pure assembly to recite the sacred names and wash away deep-seated calamities. We now rely upon the Great Assembly to recite:
*The Pure Dharma-body Vairocana Buddha* (recite the ten sacred names). We pray that [the name of the person] may, with single-mindedness...
Purity. The four great elements are light and tranquil; life-span and wisdom-life are extended; the physical body and the Dharma-body are firm and stable.
Once again, I beseech the venerable assembly to take thought for all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time (and so forth).
(About to be gravely ill: The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color. (End of the eight-line verse. On this day, there is a sick bhikṣu named [Name].

The night has passed; life and death alternate in succession, and cold and heat shift one after another. Its coming is like lightning flashing across the vast sky;
its departure is like waves settling upon the great ocean. On this day, there is the Venerable Elder [Name], who has newly entered parinirvāṇa, as his conditions for birth have come to an end.
The great life has suddenly departed; one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and thus finds true bliss in nirvana.

With reverence, we assemble the great multitude and solemnly approach the funerary shrine to recite the sublime names of the various sages, offering the pure spirit to the Pure Land. We rely upon the assembly to recite:
Vairocana Buddha of the Pure Dharma Body. (Recite the ten sacred names. [Then] chant the Great Compassion Mantra. The above constitutes the recitation.

(Tea-p’i / Cremation): On this day, there is the newly passed away Elder [Name]. Having followed conditions to enter peaceful extinction, we now perform the cremation according to the Dharma.

We rely upon the venerable assembly to assist the awakened spirit. *Namo* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful.
Homage to the Buddha. (Recite ten times. Having above praised the holy name to assist in rebirth, I pray that the mirror of wisdom may radiate its brilliance and the true wind disperse its splendor.
Within the Garden of Bodhi, may the flowers of awakening bloom; within the Ocean of Dharmatā, may the defilements of the deluded mind be washed away.
With three libations of tea poured and one incense burner lit, I bid you farewell upon your journey through the clouds. I pay homage to the assembly of sages.

Regarding the three grades of registers for the *sang* (funeral expenses) and the large-scale registers: one thousand *kan* and two thousand *kan* shall serve as the standard. Compiled during the Jiading era while serving as a deputy seat-holder at Guifeng in Xingzhou. This record was written to prepare for daily practice.

The preface states: "Having shed the secular world and left one's kin, with shaven heads and square robes, one generally undergoes training within the monastic communities (*conglin*). It is essential...

One must thoroughly understand the rules and regulations. Yet, when one’s conduct is unfamiliar with the Dharma-measures and one’s movements do not accord with the Vinaya, even if one has virtuous friends and good companions, how could they be willing to apply the deep probe and the painful prick?
Habituation leads to corruption, and reform is consequently difficult. This causes the monastic assembly to fall into desolation and further induces people’s minds to become lax.
Having repeatedly observed these common faults before our very eyes, we have thus come to practice [this negligence] for a hundred...
This manual serves as a model for practice. From beginning to end, from morning until evening, one must strive to avoid failure at every turn; one must strictly observe each and every instruction.
Only then may one dare to say that one has investigated the self and clarified the mind, understood life and mastered death, and realized that worldly dharmas are themselves supramundane dharmas.
This may be transmitted by those who have traveled the path to those who have not yet traveled it, so that they may not fail in their purpose.
To care for one’s own body and mind is also a way to repay the profound kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs (listed below). Regarding the rules for entering the assembly:
when sleeping, do not be ahead of others; when rising, do not lag behind others. Before the five-watch bell has sounded, raise your body gently and rise first.
Place your pillow at the foot of the bed without folding it up, lest the noise startle your neighbors. Shake off all lethargy and wrap yourself in your bedding.

Sit upright with the body straight. Do not fan the air to cause others to become distracted. When you feel drowsiness coming, place your bedding at the foot of the bed, take a hand towel, turn around, and descend to the floor.
Drape the towel over your left hand and recite this verse: "From dawn at the hour of Tiyin until evening, all sentient beings have naturally interacted.

If by my feet I have inadvertently harmed your form, I pray that you may immediately be reborn in the Pure Land. Oṃ yid-te lü-yi svāhā. With light hands, lift the curtain and exit to the rear hall. Do not...

Obtain slippers. When coughing, make a sound. An ancient saying goes: "When lifting the curtain, one must let the hand hang behind; when leaving the hall, one must strictly avoid wearing slippers. Wash the face with a basin using light hands. Do not use too much water.
Dip the right hand into the tooth-cleansing powder and rub the left side of the mouth; dip the left hand and rub the right side.

One must not dip again, for fear that dental disease or bad breath might exceed those of others. When rinsing the mouth, one must lower the head. Spit out the water by guiding it downward with the hand. Straighten [the body].

When water spills from the waist [of the basin], one must fear splashing it into the neighboring buckets; thus, one must not wash one’s head. There are four matters that are disadvantageous to both oneself and others:

(1) soiling the bucket, (2) greasy towels, (3) matted hair, and (4) damaging the eyes. One must not make sounds within the nose. One must not spray water onto the face. One must not vomit at a loud voice.

One must not soil the face or the bucket with nasal mucus or saliva. As the ancients said: "Washing the face at the fifth watch was originally for the purpose of spiritual cultivation; to vomit and drag the basin about, creating noise and disturbing the assembly, is contrary to this intent."
When wiping the face, do not compete for the hand-towel. Do not use the towel to wipe the head. Once finished, it must be spread out and hung, or dried over a fire.
When entering the upper hall, the left foot enters first; when entering the lower hall, the right foot enters first.
Upon reaching the sleeping mat at one's assigned seat, fold it in half and sit down. If changing into a *zhidu* (straight robe), one must cover the old one with the new one before removing the old.

[The robe] must be mended; it must not be worn so as to expose the white undergarment, nor should one fan the air. When burning incense and prostrating, it is appropriate to don the *kāṣāya* before the bell has sounded.

First, join the palms at the crown of the head and recite this verse: "Excellent is this garment of liberation, This signless field of merit. I now receive it upon my head; May I wear it in every life."
Oṃ siddhaye svāhā. Regarding the method of folding the *kāṣāya*: first fold it with the hands together, then untie the loops.
One must not hold the *kāṣāya* in the mouth, nor hook it with the chin. Once folded, set it down and depart after performing a formal greeting (*praṇāma*).
When prostrating in the hall, one must not occupy the center (reserved for the Honored Abbot). One must not chant the Buddha’s name aloud, nor walk while prostrating.
When passing by the side of another’s head, one must be mindful. At the fifth watch, the Abbot and the Head Seat occupy the Hall; the front gate is not permitted to be opened for entry or exit.

Only after the small silence has been established may one fold the bedding. As for the method of folding the bedding and adjusting the pillow: first, find the two corners and straighten them with the hands.
One must not shake them to make a noise, nor create drafts, nor occupy the space of the neighboring position. First, fold the portion in front.

Fold one half toward the body and place it over the *kaṣāya* (outer robe). Whether performing prostrations in the hall or returning to the communal quarters, when the board for the meal (*guàntáng bǎn*) sounds and one returns to the bowl position, one must adjust the shoulder and turn clockwise (placing the robe over the left shoulder). When ascending the platform, one must not have one's back to others.
If entering through the front gate, one should enter from the southern side; one must not enter from the center or the northern side (to show respect for the abbot). Return [to the quarters].

Regarding the position at the *pātra*: one should bow low to pay respects to the senior, middle, and junior seats. If the senior, middle, and junior seats have already been occupied when one arrives, one must join the palms. As the ancients said:

"If one does not show respect to the senior, middle, and junior seats, there is no difference from a gathering of Brahmins. The verse for ascending the platform says: "Ascending this bed of unimpeded liberation, May the light of human wisdom be pure.
Upon hearing the long plank signal, one lowers the *pātra*, raises the body, and stands upright and steady; thereafter, one turns the body (also in accordance with...).

With palms joined at the upper shoulders, recite the verse: "Holding the alms bowl, may all sentient beings become accomplished vessels of the Dharma and receive the offerings of devas and humans. Then take up the bowl, supporting it with the left hand.

With the right hand, he loosens his ring; with the left hand, he holds his bowl. He turns his body to stand upright, then squats down and sets the bowl on the ground to avoid striking others with his waist or back.

When the bell sounds in front of the hall, he descends from the platform to perform a greeting (to welcome the abbot). He must step forward one pace so that his *kāṣāya* does not drape over the edge of the platform.
He must not lean forward to sit upon the three pure grounds, nor should he swing his arms to the left or right. Furthermore—

Lower the bedding slightly and sit down without dropping the body abruptly. Take the bowl and place it before you. Upon hearing the sound of the wooden mallet, join your palms and recite the verse of mindfulness:

"The Buddha was born in Kapilavastu; he attained enlightenment in Magadha; he preached the Dharma in Vārāṇasī; he entered parinirvāṇa in Kuśinagara. Regarding the method for unfolding the bowl: first, join your palms.

The verse for reflection says: "The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; I now have the opportunity to unfold it. May I, together with all sentient beings, equally realize the emptiness and stillness of the three spheres.

Then, untie the cloth wrapper (*vastra*) and spread out a clean towel (*mārjanī-paṭṭa*) to cover your knees. Fold the corners of the wrapper so that they do not hang down. Next, spread out the bowl-cloth (*pātra-vastra*).

With palms facing upward, take the bowl and place it upon the cloth. Using the index fingers of both hands to hold it steady, take the steamed rice grains and unfold them one by one from the smallest portion.

One must not make any clattering sounds. Protect the fourth and fifth [fingers]. Use the index finger for touching. Fold the bowl-cloth and wipe it. Place it horizontally across the upper part of the body.
As for the bag for the spoon and chopsticks, place it below the bowl-cloth. When taking them out, the spoon comes first; when putting them away, the chopsticks come first.
The handle is the clean end; point it upward toward the shoulder. Place the bowl-brush within the third seam of the bowl-rim, protruding about half an inch, and store raw food therein.
When eating rice, one must not let rice fall from the tips of the spoon or chopsticks; no more than seven grains should be taken. To take too much or too little is considered stingy eating.

When the *vinaya-dhara* recites the Buddha’s name, the fingers must not be uneven; they must be held level at chest height. One must not rest the hands against the side of the mouth. As the ancients said:

"To join the palms unevenly and not hold them at the chest; To interlace the ten fingers and thrust them into the nose; To drag one's sandals and lift the curtain—these are not refined manners; To belch and release gas while boasting of one's heroism. [Regarding] both hands...

Holding the alms bowl to receive food, one should contemplate with these verses: "When receiving food, may all sentient beings take the joy of meditation as their sustenance and be filled with the delight of the Dharma. If one sees the bowl become full...

The verse for recitation says: "If one sees the bowl full, one should wish that all sentient beings be fully satiated with all roots of goodness. Whether the food is much or little, one should raise the hand to signal a stop.

Upon hearing the gong for universal distribution of food, look at the upper and lower shoulders and face the other person directly to bow for the food. One must not shake both sides of the bowl with the hands while facing them directly. Having finished the bow, recite the verse of reflection:

"This food, with its color, fragrance, and flavor, is offered above to the Buddhas of the ten directions; in the middle, it honors the various worthies and sages; below, it reaches the classes of the six realms of existence. It is bestowed equally without distinction."

Separately following [the food], they all receive it until fully satiated; now, through this giving and receiving, one attains immeasurable *pāramitās*. One should perform five reflections: (1) calculate the labor involved and the distance from which the food has come; (2) weigh one’s own virtue and conduct to determine whether one is worthy of such offerings.

Third, to guard the mind and remain free from the faults of greed and so forth; fourth, to properly employ wholesome medicine to treat the withered body; fifth, because one must receive this food in order to accomplish the work of the Path.

The birth-verse says: "You hosts of ghosts and spirits, I now bestow upon you this offering. This food pervades the ten directions; may all ghosts and spirits partake together. Regarding the method of eating: one must not bring the mouth to the food, nor bring the food to the mouth.
When taking up or setting down the bowl, or picking up or putting down the spoon and chopsticks, there must be no noise, and one must not cough.

One must not store nasal mucus. If one sneezes, one should cover it with the sleeve of one's robe. One must not scratch one's head, for fear that wind-blown dandruff might fall into the bowls of neighboring seats.
One must not pick at the teeth. One must not make noise while chewing rice or sipping soup.
One must not pick food from the center of the bowl. One must not take large mouthfuls of rice. One must not wait with the mouth open for the food. One must not...
One may receive leftover rice and food, but one must not eat by holding scattered grains in the hand. If there are vegetable scraps, they should be placed in a secluded spot.
When fanning oneself, one must not fan so as to disturb the shoulders of those sitting nearby; if one is personally afraid of the wind, one should inform the *karmadāna* and sit outside the hall.
One must not rest the elbows upon the knees. One should accept food according to one's need and must not ask for more than required. The bowl must not be used to hold wet food. Do not...
One may take the soup broth into the head-bowl to wash down the rice, but one must not pick vegetables into the head-bowl to mix with the rice while eating.
When eating, one must observe those above and below; one must not be too slow. Before being invited to eat more, one must not rinse the bowl.

One must not make a slurping sound while rinsing the bowl-brush. If food has not yet arrived, one must not give rise to anger or demand it. As the ancients said: "The fool looks around in all directions and gives rise to sorrow."

[The text describes improper conduct: "Angry, swallowing saliva at every thought, coughing frequently; slurping porridge and sipping soup until the mouth is full; opening the mats and spreading out the bowls, making noise that reaches the neighbors.

Regarding the method for washing the bowls: Fill the head bowl with water. It is not permitted to wash spoons or chopsticks inside it. Wash the steamed rice in sequence. One must not gargle or rinse [with the water].

One must not spit water back into the bowl. One must not first fill the bowl with hot water to wash it. Until the water has been discarded, one must not first fold away the knee-cloth (*jīwēn*). Do not...

One may use a knee-cloth to wipe away sweat, but must not drip water onto the ground. The verse for folding the water [cloth] says: "This water from my washing of the bowl has a flavor like celestial nectar.

I bestow it upon you, all you ghosts and spirits, so that you may all be fully satiated. Oṃ ma-hū-ra-se svāhā. Having finished with the bowl, press it down firmly with your fingers and enter in due order.

Fold the *fù* (cloth). Join the palms. Recite the verse for the conclusion of the meal: "Meal finished, physical strength is restored; Majestic power shakes the ten directions and the three periods of time. Causes are turned back and fruits are realized beyond thought; All sentient beings attain supernatural powers.
Strike the mallet once. The abbot descends from his seat. The bowls are hung up in order. Exit the hall.

After the scripture recitation in the Dharma Hall is completed, return to the assembly quarters. Strike the large board three times. Bow in greeting. Do not fail to return [to the quarters], lest you show contempt for the assembly. Upon entering the door...
Divide the hall into four sections and take your places according to rank. The *Liaozhu* (Head of the Quarters) steps forward to burn one incense stick, then returns to his position.
The *Chadou* (Tea Master) stands in the center and cries out: "Not well? The assembly responds with a collective *vandana*.

When attending a tea ceremony, one must not sit with robes trailing on the floor, nor talk and laugh in groups, nor bow to others with only one hand, nor conceal tea leaves within the sleeves. As the ancients said: "When sitting in formal meditation upon the platform, one must not let the robes trail."

To ferry people across with one hand—what kind of standard is that? To hoard leftover tea leaves for oneself—this invites derision from onlookers. At all times, fellow practitioners at the neighboring table must strictly avoid whispering into each other's ears.

When reading the scriptures, one must not unfold them wide (meaning both sides at once). One must not carry the scriptures while walking through the quarters. One must not let the scripture-strap hang down. One must not make noise.
One must not lean one's back against the headboard. As the ancients said: "To chant aloud and disturb the crowd, or to lean one's back against the headboard..."

Do not treat the assembly with contempt while sitting in meditation. Enter the hall early, without waiting for the striking of the board. Discard the ancient custom [of wearing the robe] and don the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*).
Place the handkerchief over the left shoulder; if you have no handkerchief, untie the sash and fasten it to the rack. Fold and hang the *luozhiduō* (outer robe) so that it is neat and orderly.

Secure it firmly, and additionally suspend it about one chi below [the other items] as a marker for identification. Do not urge others from outside the hall, nor engage in conversation or laughter with anyone.
Carry water in your right hand when entering the latrine. When changing shoes, they must not be mismatched. Place the clean bucket before you.
Snap your fingers three times to startle away the dung-eating spirits (*śakuni*). Sit upright; do not strain yourself or make noise. Do not converse with others across the wall. As the ancients said:

"In the latrine, one should only snap the fingers lightly; When crowded by people, how can one bear to make chaotic noise? Upon entry, use a tally to distinguish the 'touched' from the 'clean'; Upon exit, water is required; avoid crossing lines vertically or horizontally. [One must] not... (The text here indicates a prohibition).
Pour water on both sides to wash and cleanse the thumb and the two fingers. Do not use too many wooden sticks (*śalākā*). As the ancients said:
"When the bath-water is little, do not pick up the sticks. When you have finished using them, wash them and place them in an empty spot by the latrine;

it is improper for many people to guard over the communal property. Return the clean bucket to its original place. With dry hands, insert your undergarment into the leg of your trousers and exit. Hold [the handle] with your right hand.
Bucket. Changing shoes. One must not grasp the door leaf or the door frame with wet hands. With the right hand, one first picks up ash and then earth;
one must not handle ash or earth with wet hands. One must not spit while mixing mud. When washing the hands, one must use soap-nuts (*sāpāraja*). Wash until the elbows are clean.
When exiting or entering the latrine, one must recite the mantra for each instance. Upon entering the latrine: *Oṃ hulu dāye svāhā*. Wash.
Purify. (Oṃ hana vidhvamsaya svāhā). Wash the hands. Oṃ (cukrāya svāhā). Purify the body. (Oṃ śrī hevahe svāhā). Remove impurities. Oṃ (vajra nṛtya svāhā).
Even when attending to minor bodily functions according to the rules, one must wash and purify oneself. Use water for rinsing and washing, and continue to chew *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks).
Return to the hall to sit in meditation. One must not return to the hall before the signal board has sounded. It is not permitted to wash clothes before the midday meal. Before the meal...
After the formal entry [into the hall], one must not open the chests or cabinets. If there is an urgent matter, one must inform the administrative officer (zhushi).

When the assembly ascends to the robe-storage pavilion (yige), they must inform the head of the quarters (liaozhu). Once the name has been called, the board is struck three times; upon ascending the pavilion, the storage baskets are opened.

Within the Sangha Hall, it is forbidden to converse or laugh with others, much less look at books or registers. One must not walk back and forth between the upper and lower sections, nor pass straight through the hall, nor sit upon the mats.

When threading a needle or handling money, one must not sit with legs dangling over the edge of the platform. The space of one *chi* (approx. 30 cm) in front of the platform constitutes three areas of purity:

(1) where the alms bowl is laid out, (2) where the *kāṣāya* is placed, and (3) the direction toward which the head is turned. One must not walk upon the platform. One must not kneel on the knees to open a chest or cabinet. One must not step onto the ground from the platform by treading upon the cords of the platform.

While wearing straw sandals while traveling in the mountains, one is not permitted to perform *caṅkrama* (walking meditation) in the Buddha hall. An ancient saying states: "It is not permitted to be half-naked."
Ascending the hall: do not step on the Dharma Hall with straw sandals. Yielding to the senior monks: one must go barefoot; wearing monk’s shoes is not permitted.

One must not walk hand-in-hand discussing the right and wrong of worldly matters. As the ancients said: "Having bid farewell to both parents and abandoned one's own teacher, seeking out a spiritual friend—what does one intend to achieve? Never having spoken of the matters of the Zen school, who is at fault for this failure in white-haired old age?
One must not lean against the railings before the hall. One must not run about recklessly or hurriedly. As the ancients said: "One's gait must be slow; one practices like a horse..."

One’s deportment must be dignified; one’s speech should be kept low-voiced; and one should emulate the rules of Upāli. It is forbidden to wander idly within the halls or pagodas. As the ancients said: "Do not ascend the Buddha hall without purpose; do not stroll through the pagoda at will.

Unless it is for changing the water or replenishing the incense and lamps, even a merit as vast as the sands of the Ganges would be exhausted. After the meal, when washing clothes, one must not expose the torso. One must not pour from the hot-water pitcher.
Bamboo poles and irons, once used, must be returned to their original places. When washing the feet, one must not quarrel over the basins.

If you have sores or scabs, you must wait until after [the meal] to wash them in a secluded place (each should employ such expedients as to avoid disturbing the minds of the assembly). Do not wait for the board to be struck.

In succession, they return to the hall. After the formal sitting (zōsan) is concluded, each person leaves their half-mat and descends to the floor. If it is a "Great Release of the Sitting" (dai-hōzan), the board sounds in front of the Head Seat’s quarters;

immediately, one turns around to face outward and proceeds to join the assembly, which must be done at the proper time. When the small board sounds, entry into the hall is not permitted, nor may one stand outside the hall.
When the Abbot and the Head Seat exit the hall, they descend from their seats and perform a bow (monshin). Each then takes their seat at the designated table for the medicinal meal (yaku-seki).

One must not rise before others to serve food, nor call out for anything. Upon finishing the meal, one should leave the quarters; it is not permitted to exit through the three gates, nor enter small auxiliary quarters.
One must not leave the Sangha hall or walk along the corridors with the upper robe exposed. Do not wait until the board signaling departure from the quarters is struck;
instead, don your robes in advance and return to your seat on the mat to practice meditation, vowing to accomplish the work of the Way. When the evening bell tolls, join your palms and recite:

The verse says: "Hearing the sound of the bell, afflictions grow light; Bodhi increases and wisdom arises. Leaving behind hell, one escapes the fiery pit; may we attain Buddhahood to deliver all sentient beings. One must not fiddle with the prayer beads (*mālā*). One must not converse or laugh with those in neighboring quarters.
If relations with those in neighboring quarters become strained, one should encourage them with kind words and never harbor feelings of resentment. One must not enter or exit through the front gate.

After the *huo* (the signal for the end of meditation) has been given, one descends from the meditation seat (*zazen*), removes the sitting cloth, and washes the hands in the purification basin (*jingshou*). One does not sit again until the next invitation to meditate.

One should wait until the Head Seat has removed his pillow before sleeping; those who are very weary may then lie down. As for the *kāṣāya*, it should be wrapped in a cloth and placed beside the pillow;
placing it at the foot of the bed is inconvenient according to principle. Fellow practitioners seeking the Way should devote themselves to diligent practice during the three periods of day and night.

When performing prostrations and burning incense, one must wait until the night is deep. When repenting and making vows, one must not disturb the neighboring monks when rising or sitting, lest they be awakened from sleep.
One must lie on the right side. Lying face up is the sleep of a corpse; lying face down is the sleep of a lecher, which results in many bad dreams. It is like opening a bath:

one takes the bathing implements in the right hand and enters the bathhouse through the lower gap. Inside the door, one bows in greeting and gazes toward an empty space. Upon returning to one's place, one must bow to those above and below.
Once finished, first drape the towel, then hang the five-strip robe (*pañcakaṣāya*) on the rack, unfold the bath-cloth (*snāna-vastra*), take the bathing implements, and set them down.

On one side, he unties his upper garment, removes his lower robe, wraps his body with a foot-cloth (*pāda-vastra*), and fastens his bathing skirt (*snāna-śāṭī*). He then folds his undergarments and trousers inside a cloth bundle.

Next, he hangs his *cīvara* (outer robe) and five-strip robe together and secures them in one place. Having placed the upper garment into the bundle, he puts on his slippers and enters the bathhouse. As the ancients said:

"When the bath drum sounds for the third time and one enters the hall, one must distinguish between the clean and the defiled by separating the upper and lower garments. Loud speech or laughter are both impermissible; do not allow coarse conduct to violate the dignified demeanor. This must not be transgressed.

Enter the bathhouse barefoot. When bathing, you must go to a vacant space in the lower section and bathe according to your turn; those in the upper section must yield [to you] (as they are head monks or senior elders).
Do not allow hot water or splashes to hit the bodies of others. You must not soak your feet in the bucket. You must not relieve yourself in the room.
Wash in a secluded spot. Do not prop your feet upon the bucket. Do not scrub your feet on the edge of the basin. Do not speak.
Laugh not. Do not scoop up water. Do not take up a bucket to pour over yourself; you must protect your entire body. Do not allow water to splash onto other bathers.
Do not use excessive amounts of hot water. Your foot-cloth must not leave your body.
Those whose feet do not enter the tub, or those washing festering sores or applying ointment for scabies, should enter the bath last. Do not bring public or official items into the bath.
Wipe the head and face with a towel. Upon emerging from the bath, one must bow to those above and below and sit with the shoulders exposed.

Put on the upper garment in sequence, first using the *zhiduō* (straight robe) to cover the body, then putting on the lower garment. When removing the hem of the skirt or the sleeves of the shirt, they must be tucked inside the skirt or shirt.
Avoid damp corners for the *fu* (wrapping cloth). Do not drape a damp foot-cloth over your hands. Instead, bow to those on your left and right and exit the hall.
If there are donors who have provided a bath, recite the sutras as you wish and perform the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). Sit first on the round bench by the brazier, facing the fire.

Turn around to face the fire. Upon greeting, take your seat. One must not remove one's shoes outside the bench. One must not fiddle with the fire tongs, incense spoons, or ladles. One must not poke at the fire.
One must not lean shoulder-to-shoulder or exchange words and laughter head-to-head. One must not warm snacks over the fire. One must not dry shoes or socks.
One must not toss grease or filth into the fire. One must not dry clothes or bedding. One must not stir up the rising flames.

[The robe] is tattered; the hem of the trousers is exposed; one's ritual etiquette is lax and negligent, which stirs the thoughts of the assembly. I have briefly recorded the essential rules for daily conduct.

When attending the assembly, there are specific regulations and statutes for each matter. In all your actions, look to the examples of those of superior character; be careful not to follow the vulgar and base.

In the monastic forests, integrity and solemnity are paramount. One should examine oneself three times each day. Since time immemorial, have any Buddhas or patriarchs ever committed even a hair’s breadth of transgression?

I do not presume to address this to those of long-standing virtue; I merely record these words as an exhortation for beginners. I shall not weary you with further detail, but pray that you will understand and take this to heart.

In admiration of the Ten Codes of Conduct, Master Xiaoweng practiced the ancient Way. Fearing, however, that students might transgress beyond the prescribed rules, he composed ten verses for their guidance;
they are concise and easy to understand, yet their profound meaning is significant.

It is the same by day as it is by night. When sleeping, one should rise later; when waking, one should rise first. Fold the single mat and roll up the blanket while waiting for the opening of the quiet period.
In all movements and turns, keep the left shoulder forward.
When washing your face at dawn, do not be reckless. When rinsing your mouth, keep your head bowed and use only a small amount of water. If your head itches, you must wait until after bathing.
Once your hand-towel is dry and clean, it will not cause any hindrance.

Prostrating and reading sutras dispel the demon of sleep; do not mistake this for the work of a common laborer. When one day the mother-born eyes suddenly burst forth, only then will you realize that by holding onto medicine, your illnesses have only multiplied.

When the body and mind are tranquil and the bowl is being unfolded, the chopsticks should be taken out first and the spoon inserted first. When folding the eating cloth, it must be done at the very end;
do not fail to offer salutations with palms joined to those on both sides.

After the congee and the formal greeting, tea is served in the hall. When the evening meditation and the medicinal meal conclude, do not be noisy. As you exit the hall and enter the quarters, act in accordance with the pure regulations;
only then will you see that there are true masters within the monastic community.
When entering the room or ascending the hall for recitation, one must naturally conform to the regulations and maintain dignified deportment.
Lately, a certain class of people has become shameless, wearing small-sleeved garments beneath their monastic robes.
The seat-head strikes the board at the entrance with a sharp clatter; what Zen practitioner would dare enter the hall?
A fine of a hundred coins is still bearable, but a notice hung high on a plaque is difficult to withstand.

When putting on or removing garments, ensure they are neat and orderly; when closing the door, do so slowly, and when placing the tally, keep it low. Recite mantras silently and snap the fingers lightly;
always carry the cleansing bucket with the right hand.

When entering the bath and donning the robe, one should maintain dignity and composure. When requiring hot water, strike the wooden board with measured grace. One should not place foot-cloths upon the bathing trough;
how could both feet possibly be placed inside the bucket?

Wearing a straw hat and carrying a bundle, you call yourself a "water-and-cloud" wanderer; in seeking the Master, do not lament your toil. The Dharma-gate is cold and desolate, so you must guard it well;
do not act like the common fire-brigade that merely rushes to extinguish flames.
The Daily Recitation Verses for the Upright:

Now, as for the sons of the Śākya, the śramaṇas, their minds and forms differ from the mundane; they practice in secret and apply themselves in obscurity, such that neither ordinary people nor sages can know it.

Even those of long-standing virtue and advanced age regard these as redundant words. Yet how could those who are beginners or later students abandon them? I have transcribed them here from within the Tripitaka.
The oral instructions and the daily regulations (qinggui) in verse form are not repeated here; I hope you will rely upon them and put them into practice. They are respectfully set forth below.
When sleeping: (If at the time of going to sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings may be entirely secure and attain great sovereignty.)
When rising from sleep (at the beginning of awakening), one should wish that all sentient beings attain the awakening of omniscience and survey the ten directions.
When using the toilet (for the great or small excretions), one should wish that all sentient beings cast off greed, hatred, and delusion, and eliminate the defilements of sin.
Washing the hands (Having finished the task, approach the water. One should wish that all beings may swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma).
Washing the face (Rinse the face with water. One should wish that all beings may attain the gateway to purity and be forever free from defilement).
Ascending the Hall (If one sees the Buddha at this time, one will obtain an obstruction of the eyes; yet one shall see the Buddhas of the ten directions).
Ascending the Pavilion (Ascending the multi-storied pavilion, one obtains an obstruction of the eyes; ascending the tower of the True Dharma, one perceives all things clearly).
Beholding the Stūpa (When seeing a Buddha stūpa: Behold it with reverence; as venerable as a stūpa, receiving offerings from devas and humans).
Prostrating to the Stūpa (Bowing one’s head to the stūpa: Behold it with reverence; among all devas and humans, none can see its crown).
Washing the feet (When washing the feet: [the feet] are washed; endowed with supernormal powers, his movements are unimpeded).
Bathing (Bathing the body: [the body] is bathed; body and mind are free from defilement, radiant and pure within and without).
Receiving Food (When receiving food, [it is] fully perfected and complete; it is all-encompassing enlightenment).
Offering Conjee (Conjee has ten benefits that greatly assist the practitioner; its retribution is boundless, culminating in eternal bliss).
Offering the Meal (To bestow the three virtues and six flavors upon the Buddha and the Sangha, universally making offerings to all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm).
Eating: (When eating the meal or even a small portion of food, one should wish that all sentient beings take the joy of meditation as their food and be filled with the bliss of the Dharma).
Having finished eating (the meal completed; all that was to be done has been accomplished;
possessing all Buddha-dharmas), when receiving [food] (whether receiving flavors, one attains the supreme flavor of a Buddha, fully satisfied with ambrosia).
Plucking the grass (Purify by plucking the grass and moving it within the hand; it is like waves upon water. There is no pure water here in the hand. *Svāhā* at the place of purification).

Prostrating to the Buddhas: (The nature of the worshiper and the worshipped is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable. My place of practice is like a celestial jewel, within which the reflections of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear. My own body and shadow appear before all Buddhas;
with head touching their feet, I take refuge and pay homage.)
Praise of the Buddha: (Your countenance is most wondrous; your radiance illumines the ten directions. I have made offerings to you in the past, and now I come again to behold you in person.
The Return Scripture: (The precious caskets return to the treasure-realm; the definitive meaning is truly inconceivable. May I, together with all sentient beings, enter the ocean of Sarvajña.)

I pray that the sutras may cause the long-lasting sufferings of the three miserable realms to cease forever, that the six destinies may rest and no longer follow the causes of drowning, that boundless sentient beings may awaken to True Suchness, and that all living beings may ascend to the other shore.
