Opening the Sutra: "The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma is encountered with difficulty by hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis. Now that I have seen, heard, and attained its upholding, I pray that you will explain the Tathāgata’s true meaning."
Next, the mantra for offering to the Buddhas and devas: Oṃ mahe-tara-si svāhā.
The Five Contemplations:
1. Calculating the labor expended and measuring the distance from where it was brought [considering the plowing, sowing, harvesting, threshing, winnowing, and cooking].

2. Reflecting upon one’s own virtues and deficiencies regarding whether one is worthy of offerings (*pātra*). (Whether one is complete in sitting meditation, studying the scriptures, and managing the affairs of the Triple Gem—or, as another says, whether one has attained the fruit of being free from thieves—one is complete in being worthy of offerings;
however, due to the circumstances of coming and going, one is deficient.)

III. Guarding the Mind to Avoid Transgressions; Taking Greed and the Like as the Primary Concerns. (For those who have left the household life, there are three transgressions of the mind: craving arises from superior flavors, delusion arises from middling flavors, and anger arises from inferior flavors.
Failing to recognize shame and remorse, one falls into the three evil realms—namely, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals. Craving superior flavors is taken as the primary concern.)

IV. Properly Administering Good Medicine. To treat the withered body (the human person is a provisional combination of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind; if even one element is out of harmony, then one hundred and one kinds of diseases arise).
The four hundred and four diseases are incidental illnesses, while hunger and thirst are the primary ailments; one must rely on food and drink to treat them.

Fifth, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path, one should accept this food. (If one does not rely on food and drink, there will be no power to advance upon the Path; therefore, one should accept this food to sustain the affairs of the Triple Gem.)

Ten benefits: (1) physical beauty, (2) strength, (3) longevity, (4) happiness, (5) clarity of speech, (6) accomplishment of the path, (7) digestion of food stored overnight, (8) elimination of wind-disorders, (9) alleviation of hunger, and (10) alleviation of thirst).
Three Qualities: (1) light and soft; (2) pure and clean; (3) appropriate to the Dharma. Six Tastes: (1) sweet; (2) pungent; (3) salty; (4) bitter; (5) sour; (6) bland.
Cleanse [the temple]. The monthly headings shall begin with the first month.
Offerings of incense, candles, tea, and fruit to the halls and shrines; formal greetings from officials and patrons; the advancement or retirement of the two orders of monks;
and all other ritual protocols of the mountain gate must be conducted with appropriate gravity and propriety, never deviating from established precedent. In this way, may [the community] flourish.
To avoid the reproach of negligence or deficiency, one should adapt the *vinaya* according to local circumstances—neither too lax nor too restrictive.

On the full moon of the second month, the anniversary of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, the attendants of the Hall Office shall lead the assembly in offering *dakṣiṇā* (monetary offerings) to the treasury keeper to provide for ritual offerings.
In the morning, they shall first offer incense and rotate the *Tripitaka* in the Scripture Hall, performing circumambulation and chanting sutras to offer prayers.
Regarding the longevity [of the community]: it is the custom in various regions to close the ritual hearths. However, this restriction does not apply to mountain temples where the cold is severe.

During the third month, on the occasion of Cold Food Festival (Han-shi), the ancestral hall and shrine altars shall be prepared with offerings. The sutras shall be recited according to established precedent, and the ancestral pagodas shall be swept and sprinkled.
The gathering of tea leaves and bamboo shoots is prohibited, and the mountain forests shall be shaded and nurtured. The Rector (Vina) shall issue a draft notice for these matters.

On the first day of the fourth month, lock the *danguo* (guest quarters) gate. If there is an incense offering (*gaoxiang*), arrange the seating chart (*tu*) in advance; if there is no incense offering, a general discourse (*pushe*) must still be given.

On the Buddha’s Birthday, the administrative office (*kusī*) shall solemnly prepare the Lumbinī Garden; chant scriptures for the Buddha-bath ceremony, display the portrait and canopy, and arrange the seats for the robes and alms bowls.
The Abbot shall summon the monastics of the various schools for a snack; the *vinaya-dhara* shall prepare incense and candles. On the twelfth day, the various quarters [shall observe the same].
Decoction for boiling. On the thirteenth day, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is commenced in the Great Hall; the assembly all perform prostrations, as the Venerable Fifth Patriarch personally practiced this.
Nowadays, because of the obstruction of incense and candles, they do not prostrate—this is contrary to the Dharma. On the fourteenth day, there is the small seating decoction.
After the recitation in the Earth Deity Hall, the decoction and medicine are boiled in the Sangha Hall, followed by a brief sermon (*xiǎocān*). On the fifteenth...

On the evening of the sixteenth day of the first month of the summer retreat, the master ascends the hall to preside over the *bǐfú* (dharma-staff) ceremony. During the fifth lunar month, the warm curtains are lowered at the base of the Sangha Hall and the cool curtains are raised at the top.

The *Qīngmiáo Huì* (Green Sprout Assembly) is established; the sutra scrolls for the various quarters are prepared in advance. As the plum rains have been delayed, the drainage ditches are cleared and leaks are repaired.

The curtains for the Sangha Hall are hung, and the Abbot serves the summer tea. The two classes of officials (*liǎngbān*) and those in single quarters each take turns serving for one day. All [proceedings] are conducted accordingly.
Within the hermitage and the stupa, there are those who are mature and experienced; these too should be treated with care and respect.
During the month of June, when the heat is intense, the head monk shall withdraw the bedding. In midsummer, one should prepare the face [of the altar].

Brothers may sit or lie down as they please, yet the matter of life and death is of great importance; one must strive to realize the truth within a fixed period. The abbot must constantly urge and exhort the students; this is no small matter.
During the long summer retreat, Master Xiaoweng Dachuansong of Songyuan accompanied the assembly three times by day and three times by night, never ceasing for even a moment.
The rector supervised him as he pounded charcoal lumps and dried the mats for the Sangha Hall.
In the seventh month: on the twelfth day, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is distributed among the various quarters; on the thirteenth day, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is distributed in the Great Hall;
on the fifteenth day, the retreat is concluded and the Ullambana Festival is established. In preparation, the sutra racks for all the quarters are brought out to repay the kindness of one's parents.
On the first day of the eighth month, open the guest quarters. The guest master shall spread out mats and cushions, plaster the windows, and extend a welcome to those arriving from afar.

As brothers enter and exit to visit one another, inquire after their well-being, prepare for the cold season, or pay visits to their parents, take care not to neglect established standards or traditional regulations.

On the first day of the ninth month, monks from all quarters come for a great mutual inspection. They register their stay, strike the board for seated meditation, arrange their bedding and seats, paper the windows, and hang the warm curtains.
On the first day of the tenth month, the furnace is opened and charcoal is kept constantly ready. On the fifth day of the same month, the memorial service for Bodhidharma is observed.

In the eleventh month, on the Longzhi (Winter Solstice) festival, the winter vegetarian feast is prepared according to custom; the officials and lay patrons provide offerings in accordance with established precedent.

In the twelfth month, the Buddha attained enlightenment. In maintaining the monastery, one must manage accounts of money and grain, measure rice, wheat, and the five flavors, and attend to the advancement or retirement of the two orders;
in every matter, one follows established precedent. The principles of worldly affairs and the Buddha-dharma are one and the same.
Male: Venerable Baizhang. Regarding the text for the novice’s reception of the precepts:
when a temple attendant first receives a certificate of ordination (*duòdì*), he presents it upon a tray and cloth-covering to his own teacher and to each of the two classes of officials.

He offers incense and performs three prostrations. On an auspicious day, offerings are prepared for the tonsure ceremony. (According to the Vinaya: a seat is prepared at the chosen location; it is ordered that this be done in the open air, where scented water is sprinkled over a circumference of seven feet, with the four corners [marked].)

Regarding the hanging of banners: nowadays, these are mostly placed in the Great Hall and must face the Buddha, or seats may be arranged opposite one another. If within the Dharma Hall, images, banners, flowers, incense, and candles must be set out according to the ritual protocol. Today, the Rector (Weina) coordinates with the Preceptor (Śīlācārya) and the Chant Master (Brahmācārya) for the invitation ceremony.
The attendant (Upasthāyaka) shaves the head the night before, leaving only a tuft of hair at the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa).

On the following day, the seat for the Preceptor is prepared; it is positioned to the side of the Abbot’s seat, and upon the table are placed the hand-bell (hasta-ghaṇṭā), the pure water pitcher (śuci-kalaśa), and the text of the precepts (śīla-sūtra).
The ritual staff (jiechi). Opposite [the master], the seat for the Dharma teacher (fansi) is set up, with a large gong placed upon the table.

Before the incense burner of the Holy Monk (shengseng), the monastic robes (jiasha), the cassock (zhidu), and the ordination certificate (dudie) are laid out. The attendant from the Self-Service Hall (xingtang) sounds the bell (yue) to lead the person seeking tonsure.

Incense is offered at the Self-Service Hall, the Earth Deity Hall (tudi tang), the Patriarchal Hall (zutang), and the Buddha Hall (fodian); three prostrations are performed, and they stand in line. The bell is then sounded in front of the Sangha Hall (sengtang).
The assembly gathers. The Precept Master and the Dharma Master enter the hall and perform three full prostrations with their sitting cloths fully spread. They take their seats.

The attendant who leads the invitation enters the hall, bows before the Sacred Monk, and proceeds to the Precept Master. He performs three full prostrations with his sitting cloth spread, kneels with palms joined, and asks:
"Is the Sangha assembled? He replies, "It is assembled. "Is it harmonious? "It is harmonious. "The Sangha is now in harmony; what shall we do?
We shall perform the tonsure and confer the precepts for the temple attendant. So be it. [The ritual master] leads the petitioner to remove his sitting mat, rises, and strikes the chime.

He leads the person to be tonsured into the hall. They perform three prostrations before the Sacred Monk (the image of the Buddha). Next, the Precept Master performs three prostrations. Having finished, he kneels down. The Chant Master...

The *Jianfan* (Sanskrit: *Brahma*) says: "The practitioners of the five supernatural powers among the immortals—those who compose incantations for the sake of those who possess shame and modesty, and who gather in those who lack them—the Tathāgata established the prohibitions and precepts. He proclaims them every half-month. Through the benefit of proclaiming the precepts, I bow my head in homage to all Buddhas.

"What is *Brahma*? How does one reach the ultimate further shore in this sutra? I pray that the Buddha will open the subtle honey and extensively preach it for the sake of sentient beings. "Those who perform the *Jianfan* cease all clamor and disorder.
When the *Jianfan* is concluded, the precepts are proclaimed for those who have shaved their heads and received the ordination. The Preceptor rises, and the great assembly...

At the lower level, the Preceptor for the Precepts holds the incense burner and says: "The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of meditative concentration, the fragrance of liberation, and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation—these clouds of radiant light pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
They are offered to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions, the infinite Dharmas of the ten directions, and the infinite Sanghas of the ten directions.
May all who see or hear this be universally perfumed and realize nirvana. This is spoken for the sake of those who have had their heads shaved and received the precepts. Thereupon...
On this auspicious day, having shaved my head and received the precepts, I open this gateway of merit.

First, I pray that the Emperor may live ten thousand years, his ministers may govern for a thousand autumns, the world may enjoy peace, and the Wheel of Dharma may turn eternally. To the deities of the monastery and the local spirits:
May their majestic radiance increase; may they protect the Dharma and protect all people, free from all calamities. May donors from the ten directions be adorned with merit and wisdom.

May those who have assembled at this site of enlightenment experience peace and happiness in body and mind. May teachers, elders, and parents excel and flourish in their spiritual endeavors. May novice monks who have shaved their heads practice without hindrance.

May all beings in the three miserable realms and eight difficulties be liberated from the wheel of suffering. May all those within the nine states of existence and four modes of birth together ascend to the shore of awakening.
I rely upon the assembly’s recitation: *Vairocana Buddha of the Pure Dharma-body* (the ten sacred names concluded).

The assembly takes their seats. The attendant leading the invitation holds the incense burner and says: (For the words of the request, you should state them yourself. If you are unable, follow my voice. Wherever it says "so-and-so," substitute your own name.
"Virtuous One, please attend with one mind. I, [Name], now request the Virtuous One to serve as the Preceptor for shaving my head and receiving the precepts."
"Venerable One, I pray that you act as my preceptor for the tonsure and the reception of the precepts. Relying upon the Venerable One, I shall receive the tonsure and the precepts.
Out of compassion," [the candidate says]. The hair-cutter performs one prostration; for the second time, out of compassion, he performs two prostrations;
for the third time, out of compassion, he rises and performs three prostrations, then kneels with his right knee on the ground and joins his palms. The Preceptor says:
"Good son," he replied, "I shall comply. The source of the mind is profoundly still; the ocean of Dharma is deep and vast.

Those who are deluded by it will sink and drift for eternal kalpas, while those who awaken to it are liberated in this very place. If you wish to devote yourself to the wondrous Way, there is no way to transcend leaving the household life.
It is as expansive and unconfined as space, and as pure and bright as the full moon. When the conditions for practice are complete, the fruit of the Way is not far off. Beginning from this moment...
Through the power of mindfulness, one ultimately realizes the stage of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, the Great Awakened World-Honored One renounced his precious throne as a Wheel-Turning King;
at the dead of night, he leaped over the city walls. He cast off his exquisite and regal dragon-robe and severed his hair upon the green mountains.

He allowed a magpie’s nest to rest upon his crown and let a spider’s web hang between his brows. By cultivating quiescence, he realized the true and eternal; by severing worldly toil, he attained perfect enlightenment.

Awakened Ones! None of the Buddhas of the three periods of time have ever taught that one attains the Way while remaining a householder. Among the six patriarchs of our lineage, who was it that practiced defilement to save others?

Therefore, from Buddha to Buddha there has been the passing of the hand, and from patriarch to patriarch the transmission has continued; only by remaining unstained by worldly conditions does one become a vessel for the Dharma.

Thus, the celestial Māras fold their hands in submission and the non-Buddhists turn their hearts toward the truth. Above, this repays the fourfold debt of gratitude; below, it delivers the myriad living beings.

It is suffering. Thus it is said: "Wandering through the three realms, one cannot escape the bonds of affection; casting aside affection to enter the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) is the true way to repay kindness. After leaving the household life, one’s conduct transcends ordinary sentiment:

one does not bow to kings, nor does one bow to parents. You may now leave this seat, and with single-minded sincerity, pay your respects to the King for the bounty of his land and water, and to your parents for the virtue of their procreation; thereafter, you shall no longer bow.
He performs one prostration. The attendant who leads the invitation strikes the chime and leads him out of the hall. Facing north, he bows in farewell to the King;

next, he bows to his parents, performing three prostrations for each while contemplating them with affection. He then changes his skirt and upper garment and is led before the Sacred Monk, where he performs three prostrations.
Turning, he bows once before the Preceptor, then kneels on his right knee (*hukuei*) with palms joined. The Preceptor takes up the ritual flask.

The Consecration: Taking a few drops of water on his finger, he sprinkles them upon the crown of the head. He takes up the razor and shaves the hair. The assembly recites the verse together three times:

"Excellent, O Great Man! You have realized the impermanence of the world; you have abandoned the mundane to seek Nirvana—rare indeed, and inconceivable! Having spoken thus three times, the śrāmaṇera withdraws and performs one prostration.

The Preceptor leads the śrāmaṇera before the Master. He kneels with his right knee on the ground (hukuei) and joins his palms. The Master holds the razor and says: "This final knot is called the *cūḍā*."

"Only the Master alone can sever it. I shall now remove it for you; do you now grant permission? [The candidate] replies, "So be it. Having completed the rite of becoming a Buddha, the assembly recites the verse for shaving the hair three times:

"To destroy the form and guard the will, To sever love and have no kin, To leave home and propagate the holy Way, Vowing to deliver all beings. Having recited this three times, they perform three prostrations.

Kneeling with palms joined, the Preceptor (Honshishu) holds the *kāṣāya* and performs the ritual. The assembly recites the verse together three times: "O how great is this robe of liberation! The field of merit, the formless robe.
Donning it to uphold the Tathāgata’s precepts, May we widely deliver all sentient beings. Having spoken thus, the robe is bestowed and the *kāṣāya* is donned.

One prostrates three times to the Preceptor, three times to the Holy Sangha, and three times to the Ordination Master (*Kaishi*). Kneeling with palms joined, the Ordination Master says: "Virtuous son, the Dharma..."
It is like the great ocean, which becomes deeper as one enters it step by step. Now that you have left the household life, you must first receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts;

only then may you draw near to the Great Sangha. Next, you shall receive the Ten Precepts of a Śrāmaṇera, whereupon you may share in the benefits and offerings of the Sangha. Success in these matters depends upon single-minded sincerity.
Do not be negligent or disrespectful. I now invoke the Triple Gem on your behalf to bear witness to this Buddhist rite. Holding the incense burner, I pray thus:

With single-minded devotion, I reverently invoke the boundless Buddha-treasure; the golden scriptures of the ocean-store; those of the ten stages and three levels of worthiness; and those of the five fruits and four stages of progress.

May we together receive this descent of grace and jointly serve as witnesses. (Third Invocation) It is said: "O son of noble family, if you wish to seek the refuge and precepts, you must first purify your transgressions and flaws.
Just as one washes a garment before applying dye, you must now, with utmost sincerity, follow me in repentance:

'All the evil karma I have created in the past arises from beginningless greed, anger, and ignorance; born of body, speech, and mind, I now repent for it all. The śrāmaṇera performs three prostrations and then kneels with palms joined.
[The Buddha] said, "Good son, since you have purified the karma of body, speech, and mind, you have taken refuge in the Triple Gem:
the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. You have taken refuge in the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Honored One; you have taken refuge in the Dharma, the Honored One who is free from desire;

you have taken refuge in the Saṅgha, the Honored One among the assembly. Having completed your refuge in the Buddha, having completed your refuge in the Dharma, and having completed your refuge in the Saṅgha, [you have approached] the Tathāgata..."

The Truly Perfectly Awakened One is my Great Teacher; I now take refuge in him. From this day forward, I shall call the Buddha my teacher and will no longer take refuge in demons, heretics, or outsiders.
Out of your compassion, [I take refuge in the Buddha]. (Recite this three times in total. With each recitation, the śrāmaṇera performs one prostration;
upon the third recitation, he performs three full prostrations with wide-spread kneeling, then kneels with palms joined. The Preceptor says:
"Good son, since you have already abandoned the heterodox and returned to the orthodox, and your precepts are now complete, if you wish to recognize their characteristics and maintain them,
you should receive the five precepts for as long as life lasts."
Not killing, not stealing,
and not engaging in sexual misconduct.
"Not speaking falsely and not drinking alcohol are the characteristics of the five precepts. Are you able to uphold them? He replied, "I am able to uphold them."
Regarding the five branches of pure precepts mentioned above, not one may be transgressed. "Are you able to uphold them? He replies, "I am able to uphold them.
"In this manner, I shall uphold them. The śrāmaṇera performs three prostrations, then kneels with palms joined. The Preceptor says:

"Good son, the five precepts are the primary cause for entering the Path and the foremost means of escaping the three miserable realms. Next, you shall receive the ten śrāmaṇera precepts; this is the formal..."

Providing for the ritual requirements, exerting diligent effort, dwelling in reliance upon a teacher, and receiving benefits in common with the Saṃgha—this is what constitutes a *śrāmaṇera* who accords with the Dharma;
you should receive this upon the crown of your head.
For as long as life lasts,
one shall refrain from killing living beings and refrain from stealing.
Abstain from sexual misconduct,
abstain from false speech,
and abstain from intoxicants.
One does not wear flower garlands or necklaces;

one does not anoint the body with fragrant oils, nor engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances; one does not go specifically to watch or listen to such things, nor sit or lie upon high, wide, or large beds.

"Not eating at improper times and not handling gold, silver, coins, or treasures are the characteristics of the śrāmaṇera precepts. Are you able to uphold them? He replies, "I am able to uphold them."

Regarding the ten branches of pure precepts mentioned above, you must not transgress against any one of them. Can you uphold them? He replies: "I can uphold them. "In this manner shall they be upheld.
The śrāmaṇera performs three prostrations, then kneels with palms joined. "Good son, after you have now received these precepts, you must receive them upon the crown of your head and uphold them;
you must not violate them. The precepts you uphold are for the purpose of making offerings to the Triple Gem and practicing diligently."

Cultivate the field of merit. Toward your *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*, act exactly according to the teachings. Toward those of superior, middling, and inferior standing, maintain a mind of constant reverence.
Practice the Path with diligent application. Repay the kindness of your parents. As for clothing, take only what covers the body, not for its decorative patterns.

As for food, take only what sustains life; do not indulge in flavors. Fragrances, flowers, and cosmetics must not come near the body. Regarding beautiful forms and perverse sounds, let there be none at all.

In seeing and hearing, and in the slow movements of speech and action, do not proclaim the shortcomings of others. If there are those who dispute, reconcile their two sides. Maintain the distinction between men and women;
do no harm to plants or trees. Do not befriend those who are not virtuous; do not take as a master anyone who is not a sage. As for the dharma-robes and the alms-bowl, always keep them with you.

Do not eat at improper times; do not speak what is not in accordance with the Dharma. Diligently apply yourself to contemplating the meaning; by warming to the old, you shall know the new. When sitting, [remain composed].
Meditate in dhyāna. Upon rising, recite the scriptures. Close the gates to the three evil realms and open the door to Nirvāṇa. Within the dharma of the bhikṣu, increase right action;
let the bodhicitta never regress and let the wisdom of prajñā shine ever-brightly. Widely transform sentient beings and pray for the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
With such an application of mind, one is a true disciple of the Buddha. The Preceptor of Precepts holds the incense burner and dedicates the merit, saying: "The above..."

The Merit of Shaving the Head and Receiving the Precepts: We respectfully pray that the Dharma-protecting devas, nāgas, and the true sovereigns of the *ārāma* each extend their majestic influence to settle the spirits and protect the Dharma.
May the Abbot, the Head Monk, always serve as a bridge and raft across the sea of suffering; may the high-ranking administrators forever act as the pillars and beams of the Dharma-gate.
May the pure assembly of the entire hall together board the vessel of Prajñā; may the novice monks who have shaved their heads swiftly attain [enlightenment].

To the shore of Bodhi; to fully repay the four debts of gratitude; to provide equal sustenance for all beings within the three realms of existence; and so that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm may together realize the Wisdom of All Modes.
To all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, and to all Honored Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas (and so forth).

The Preceptor strikes the large chime and says: Abiding in the world like empty space, Like a lotus flower unsullied by water, With a mind pure and transcending that— I prostrate and pay homage to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
I take refuge.
Having attained Bodhi, the Buddha’s resolve for the Way never regresses.
The Dharma is sarvajñā (all-knowledge); he has attained the gate of the great dhāraṇī.
The Sangha ceases its disputes and together enters the ocean of harmony.
The aforementioned merit of shaving the head and receiving the precepts constitutes an infinite and most excellent cause, which radiates throughout the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

I pay homage to the assembly of noble ones. [The master] leads the attendant to ring the hand-chime. When they arrive at the place where the *brahman* master performs his work, the world is like empty space; the sands...
The candidate immediately performs three prostrations to the Precept Master. Turning around, he performs three prostrations to the Holy Sangha.

Having finished, he bows in greeting and exits the hall, standing at the lower end. The Inviter and the others exit the hall together. Before the Precept Master, the Dharma Master, and the Holy Sangha, he performs three full prostrations with the robes spread out, then exits the hall.
The Hall Attendant strikes the bell in front of the Sangha Hall three times; the assembly descends from the hall to offer congratulations to the Abbot.

The Preceptor and the Upādhyāya proceed to the Abbot’s quarters to offer thanks. For the first prostration, the words are: "Having been appointed to confer the precepts, I did not dare decline; yet my human affairs have been neglected, causing me to delay in paying my respects to the Honored One.

For the second prostration, the words are: "On this day, [Name] respectfully addresses the time. We humbly wish that the Abbot, the Venerable Monk, may enjoy many blessings in his daily life. They perform three prostrations with the head touching the ground (*chuli*). The response is: "..."

(When a śrāmaṇera has his head shaved, it involves a laborious task for the master. The attendant or junior disciple proffers congratulations. He performs three full prostrations without folding the sitting mat (*kaṭhina*). He then steps forward and says:

(The śrāmaṇera receives ordination. The entire assembly rejoices together. Gazing up at his venerable dignity, the humble feelings of those below cannot overcome their utmost sense of gratitude. He performs three prostrations again. Having completed the three prostrations for the exchange of greetings, he withdraws his implements.

Next, the śrāmaṇeras perform three full prostrations without folding their sitting cloths (niṣīdana). Advancing forward, they say: "We, [Name] and others, having received the mark of the shaven crown and the fortune to don the four robes..."

Not dwelling in the dust of worldly toil, forever freed from the net of craving. (With the utmost depth of emotion and profound gratitude), three prostrations. Three prostrations for inquiries of health. The sitting mat is folded away.

Next, the Abbot makes a circuit of the quarters to offer greetings. Next, the Śrāmaṇeras make a circuit of the quarters to offer thanks. They settle in their quarters within the Śrāmaṇera hall and await the appointed time to ascend the platform for ordination.

The words of thanksgiving for the precepts are as follows: "We, [Name] and others, having attained the rank of the precepts, have unworthily joined the ranks of the Sangha. We look up to and deeply appreciate your protection and grace; we hereby offer this prostration of thanks. The response is: "I have long been sustained by..."

The Buddha’s prediction was fulfilled; the Sangha’s precepts were perfected. Firmly enduring and upholding them, they supported the power of the religious tradition. They proceeded to enter the hall in succession.

Following the example of a newly ordained *śrāmaṇera* entering the hall after receiving the precepts, they then entered the hall to attend upon the Abbot (*sthavira*). Next, they reported to the Head Seat (*śayanāsana*) and the Rector (*karmadāna*). This was for the morning gruel and the universal meal.
After the striking of the mallet, the new ordinands, led by the head of the assembly, enter through the front gate and stand in a line before the incense burner.

They offer the formal inquiry and insert incense sticks, then together perform three prostrations with their sitting cloths unfolded. Stepping forward, they say: "We, [Name] and others, having entered the ranks of the monastic community and attached ourselves to the pure assembly, now attend the hall on this day;

our humble hearts are overcome with the utmost trepidation. They withdraw and together perform another three prostrations. The words of the inquiry are: "On this auspicious day, we respectfully wish that the Abbot, the Founding Master, Great Monk, the Head Seat, and the venerable assembly of Great Chan Masters, may enjoy much blessing in your daily life. Again, they together perform three [prostrations].
Prostrate. Fold the sitting mat. Exchange greetings. Turn around and stand in the front row facing the abbot. Exchange greetings while facing north.

Circumambulate the hall once. Proceed to the outer hall; first descend to the lower section, then turn to the upper section, and return to the interior of the hall. Exchange greetings before the incense burner.
The head of the assembly leads the group out through the front gate.
Instruction for the Junior Monks (Tongxing):

Following the conclusion of the five rounds of formal inquiry (wucan) and the ascent to the hall (shangtang), one should instruct the junior monks. The head of the inquiry (canchou) and the attendant (xingzhe) shall direct the food-caller (heshi xingzhe) to notify the attendants of their respective duties.
The attendant in front of the hall shall hang the notice board to inform the assembly. When the evening bell tolls, the wooden clapper (ban) shall be struck three times in front of the hall.

[The bell] tolls for the assembly. The practitioners line up in the upper hall. The head of the assembly (candou) enters the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang) and requests the abbot to come forth and take his seat.

The head of the assembly steps forward, offers incense, and strikes the board for the formal session (mingsan). Together with the assembly, they perform a bow (wensun) and nine prostrations (jiubai). Stepping forward, they hold their breath and listen attentively to the instructions.

Once this is concluded, they again perform three prostrations together with the assembly, bid farewell with the words "Be careful" (zhenzhong), and withdraw. Prior to this, the incense has been prepared and lit in the hall.
Regarding the "Candle" (zhù): it is the duty of the attendant (shìzhě) to oversee this.

The head of the assembly (cāntóu) for the general discourse in the Hall of Good Conduct (liáng xíng táng pǔshuō) shall first go to the Attendant’s Office (shìsī), where they shall offer incense and prostrate. They shall then report to the attendant, who will submit the request to the Abbot (zhùchí). If the Abbot grants permission...

[The Abbot] requests [the assembly]. The head of the assembly (sanchō) strikes the wooden board to gather the congregation, who line up in the dormitory hall. The head of the assembly follows the attendant into the room to invite the Abbot to come forth.
Once the Abbot has taken his seat, the head of the assembly bows with the assembly, steps forward to offer incense, and the food-caller (gejaku gyōja) calls out: "Attention! (Katsu!)

(If uncertain: Perform nine prostrations with the assembly. Exchange greetings. The head of the assembly steps forward and says: "We have long contemplated the Master’s instructions; we humbly pray that you will compassionately reveal the causal conditions. He then withdraws, exchanges greetings, and retires.
On the following day, the hall attendant hangs the sign for a general discourse (*pūsē*) and notifies the assembly. A seat is prepared facing inward.

The incense table and candle stands are prepared. The head of the *sanchou* (senior attendant) reports and requests that the two ranks of officials stand in formation. The deputy head of the *sanchou* leads the assembly, while the two orders of officials welcome them at the gate. They enter the hall.

The head of the *sanchou* and the hall master proceed to the attendants' office (*shisō*) and together invite the abbot to descend to the hall. The assembly receives and welcomes him as he enters the hall and takes his seat.

One group of attendants performs a formal greeting (*monjun*) and stands to one side. The two ranks of officials remain as usual. After they have stepped forward from their positions and completed the formal greeting, [the ceremony proceeds].

The attendant burns incense and offers it in a single coil, inquires after the well-being of the abbot, and requests the Dharma as is customary. The head of the assembly leads the group in a single file to offer incense;

they shout "Attention! (hē-cān) and perform three prostrations. After withdrawing to the rear of the east and west sections, they stand in a single file and listen attentively to the instructions of the Dharma.

Once the teaching has been concluded, the head of the assembly leads the group to stand in their previous formation and perform three prostrations. They then exit through the door and stand to the right, bowing to see the abbot off.
The abbot and the two classes of officials follow him to the dormitory hall, where they insert a large piece of incense and perform nine prostrations before withdrawing.

Next, they proceed to the Office of Attendants (Sisi), insert incense, and perform three prostrations. The head of the assembly and the deputy head then go before the two classes of officials and bow individually to express their thanks; at this point, the offering of incense is waived.
Understanding the Ritual Implements for Alerting the Assembly:

As for the bells, fish-shaped gongs, drums, and wooden clappers, they serve to alert the assembly. Morning and evening, they never deviate from their established standards. Like a command issued through the ages, the monks gather like clouds rising and water flowing; their vast numbers are a sight to behold.

When the gates of meditative stillness are deeply closed, they understand the meaning upon hearing the sound; they attend the communal services to burn incense and cultivate their practice, maintaining an air of solemnity and harmony.

The timing must accord with the seasons; in all matters, one must never fail or err. Whether the Emperor ascends or descends from the throne, when officials, venerable elders of various mountains, and lay donors arrive or depart, during the recitation of mantras at dawn and dusk, or for the morning and midday meals, the tower bells shall be struck respectively.

As for the dawn bell: it shatters the long night and awakens those who sleep. As for the dusk bell: it illuminates the dark alleys and revives the deluded. The striking of the mallet must be slow, and the sound raised gradually.
For the long bell, strike thirty-five times for each round; three strikes at the beginning and three at the end. Three rounds total one hundred and eight strikes.
May the bitterness of the six realms and three paths be stilled and their suffering ceased. When wishing to ring the bell, first recite this verse before striking it:

*May the sound of this bell transcend the Dharma-realm, Reaching even the dark depths of the Iron Ring Mountains. Hearing its resonance, may all defilements be purified, And all beings realize perfect enlightenment.* *Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.* (High [pitch])

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*) states: "If one recites the sacred name of the Bodhisattva according to the Dharma, the sound of the bell ringing will shake the underworld, and those suffering there shall all attain liberation.

Furthermore, the *Transmission of the Dharma* (*Fufa zhuan*) states: "King Zabian died and was reborn as a thousand-headed fish; he was constantly being decapitated by a wheel of swords, and his pain was unbearable. Only upon hearing the sound of the bell did the wheel of swords cease to fall. If one strikes it morning and evening, its merit is vast indeed.
Regarding the bell before the Sangha Hall, there is no fixed time limit; the *Weina* (Rector) is in charge of it. The attendant of the Hall Office must inform the *Weina* before striking it.

For the Dharma Drum, strike three times when preaching the Dharma; for the morning informal discourse (*chángcān*), strike one long toll; for entering the room (*rùshì*), three strikes; for the general discourse (*pǔshuō*), five strikes—all of which must be struck slowly.

For the small seat (*xiǎozuò*) and the medicinal soup (*tāng*), as well as for tea served specifically for a guest, strike one toll each. When retreating from the seat, strike three times; for holding the whisk (*bǐfú*), strike one toll.
If borrowing a seat or a drum, strike the drum located below the Dharma Hall during the two meal periods of rice gruel and porridge; strike the drum three times.
The mallet. For the nine strikes upon the foundation pillar, one must employ three beats and nine strikes. The signals given by the drums each have their specific purpose:

for ascending the seat, the small *sǎn* (private instruction), and the general discourse, there is the Dharma drum; for the turning of the Tripitaka, there is the Tripitaka drum; for opening the bath, there is the bath drum; and for the midday and morning meals, there is the meal drum.
For tea services and the striking of the *ge-ge* drum, one must ensure that the time is known. For the great communal work (*fǔqǐng*) and for meals, the large wooden fish is struck;
for the kitchen staff’s communal work, the small wooden fish is struck. At the end of the period of seclusion (*kāijìng*), the board in front of each quarters is struck three times.
For meals, the large board is struck three times. Striking the large board after the wooden fish is called the "long board. If there is a tea service, it must...

Strike slowly. Respond by performing the ritual prostrations. Ring the bell three times for the invitation to tea and recitation. For the abbot’s invitation to tea, strike the board in the *shentang* (sleeping hall).

For the tea service of the *kusō* (kitchen office) and the *tudang* (storehouse hall), strike the board in front of the storehouse hall. For sitting meditation and formal Zen sessions, strike the board in the *zhao tang* (recitation hall).

For tea served upon leaving or entering the quarters, and for tea on the first and fifteenth days of the month, ring the bell in the various quarters. In the early morning, for the *wennan* (greeting/prostration), strike the board in front of the various quarters to notify the assembly. To report to the assembly, strike the various quarters’ bells.
Front Plaque. Incense is offered during the circumambulation of the hall; bells are installed in various locations. One must not engage in licentious conduct or violate the laws and regulations.

Herein I have briefly recorded these matters to be handed down for all eternity. As it is said, "The bells ring and the tripods are served"—the ritual music of the Three Dynasties is fully embodied herein.
*Chanyuan Qinggui*, Volume Ten (End): *Chanlin Beiyong Qinggui*.
The *Chanyuan Qinggui* originated with Baizhang’s establishment of ritual and music to prevent human failings. Ritual was used to establish the Middle Way;
music was used to guide one's nature and emotions. Incense, candles, tea, and soup constituted its rituals; bells, fish-shaped gongs, drums, and wooden clappers constituted its music.
If rites and music are not lost, it is like a net having its main cord or a garment having its collar. By grasping the main cord and lifting the collar, one ensures there is no disorder.
Their practice depends upon a master; without such a person, the main cord of the net and the collar of the garment will fall into chaos.

Master Donglin Zeshan compiled the monastic regulations and ritual laws of former and later venerable masters, categorizing them into ten volumes, titled: [Title of the work] (Note: The specific title is implied by the context of the preceding text).

It is said that this *Chanlin Beiyong* (The Comprehensive Manual for Chan Monasteries), with its detailed explanations of dignified deportment and minute conduct, is a work of consummate beauty. It was intended to be carved onto printing blocks for wide circulation;

however, it is regrettable that the author passed away into stillness. At the time of his death, he entrusted the work to his disciples and charged the Librarian (Cangzhu) with the task. They exerted their utmost efforts to complete the undertaking, intending to rescue the declining tradition and provide a model for all ages.
On the day of the conclusion of the retreat in the Ding-si year of the Yan-you era, the Bhikṣu Yunxiu of Tiantong respectfully inscribed this for Master Zeshan.
Having observed that the Baizhang Qinggui had long been subject to errors in transmission, making it difficult for those newly entering the assembly to recognize its true meaning,
he has, following the use of the mallet and whisk, selected from the teachings of ancient and modern masters of virtue to establish a present-day standard for practice to be circulated in the world.

It is said that these are fully utilized in the Chan monasteries and are recorded in detail in this published edition. Thus, the transmission of its fragrant influence to future generations and its grand, brilliant legacy begins from this point onward.
Written on the first day of the fourth month in the first year of the Zhizhi era (the Xinyou year). By De-ming of Yuyang Monastery.
